items.title: Datalab Releases OmniParseBench: An Open OCR Benchmark With 16,288 Pass/Fail Tests to Audit OCR Parsers
items.summary: Datalab has released OmniParseBench , an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash. Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys. TL;DR Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages. Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key. Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points. Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.* Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag. * used in building some tests What is OmniParseBench? OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable. Why build another OCR benchmark? Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in. ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code . What do tags and derivations add? A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score. The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents. Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations . items.summary_html:
Datalab has released OmniParseBench, an open OCR benchmark for document parsers. It scores parsers with 16,288 yes/no tests on 2,937 pages from 2,343 documents. The pages span 92 languages. The dataset and code are public. It helps engineers answer a sharper question than a leaderboard does: which parser handles documents like mine? Datalab sells a parser, and its own top setting, Datalab accurate, ranks second on the launch leaderboard, behind Gemini 3.8 Flash.

Is it deployable? Yes. OmniParseBench is an evaluation harness, not a model. It installs with uv pip install omni-parse-bench, needs Python 3.11+, and scores outputs offline with no API keys.

TL;DR
  • Size: 16,288 tests, 2,937 pages, 2,343 documents, 22 suites, 92 languages.
  • Runs on: any machine with Python 3.11+. Scoring needs no network. Vendor runs need each vendor’s API key.
  • Performance: the top 3 reported systems sit within 1.3 headline points.
  • Best: Gemini 3.8 Flash leads at 92.9; Datalab accurate follows at 92.7.*
  • Bottom line: every score is a share of pass/fail tests, sliceable by tag.

* used in building some tests

What is OmniParseBench?

OmniParseBench is a document-parsing benchmark from Datalab where every test is a yes/no question about 1 page. A parser’s score is the share of tests it passes. Datalab built it to be clear, auditable and explorable.

Why build another OCR benchmark?

Datalab names two problems with existing benchmarks. olmOCR-bench showed that pass/fail unit tests work. Datalab now calls it saturated. In its view, top systems are separated by output conventions and overfitting, not reading. Each olmOCR-bench test also sits in 1 bucket, set by its page’s source. A handwritten table gets averaged into whichever bucket its page landed in.

ParseBench from LlamaIndex splits parsing into 5 capabilities, each with its own metric. Datalab argues those scores share no unit, so they cannot be compared or combined cleanly.

How does OmniParseBench scoring work?

The final score is the mean of 3 family scores: text, tables and layout. Five test types feed those families:

  • present: a text, number or equation appears (text)
  • order: text A comes before text B (text)
  • repeat: a line appears exactly N times (text)
  • table_cell: a cell sits under given headings and beside given neighbors (tables)
  • layout_kind: the block holding a line is a heading, text or table (layout)

Numbers must match digit for digit, though 1,240 matches 1240. Equations are compared by what KaTeX renders, so \frac{a}{b} equals \dfrac{a}{b}. Each decision is pass, fail, unsupported or error. The last 2 are left out of every score. No model judges the outputs; the scorer is open code.

What do tags and derivations add?

A test checks one or more args, each of which is the content at one place on the page. Each arg carries tags on 5 axes: structure, rendering, role, script and language. Scripts use ISO 15924 codes; languages use ISO 639-3 codes. Tags never decide a verdict or the headline. They only select tests, so any slice gets its own score.

The table tag covers 6,767 tests on 1,000 pages from 875 documents. English covers 10,089 tests. Non-English languages cover 1,931 tests on 529 pages from 321 documents.

Every test also records its derivation, meaning how its answer was established. There are 10 derivations. They include publisher JATS XML, the PDF text layer, authored pages, olmOCR-bench tests, model panels and human review.

&&&

What are the OmniParseBench launch results? *Used in creating and verifying at least some tests, per Datalab.

Claude Sonnet 5.5 posts the top text (93.1) and tables (95.4) scores. Its layout score of 77.5 pulls its headline to 88.7. Reducto leads layout at 95.8. Datalab also plotted each headline against median latency and price per 1,000 pages. Latency was measured on 200 sampled pages, sent 8 at a time.

Datalab does not top its own benchmark. It flags the two models that helped build tests, and it tells readers to weigh the fact that it sells a parser. It commits to reporting OmniParseBench scores for future releases. Its advice: the best benchmark is your own documents.

How do you run OmniParseBench?

uv pip install omni-parse-bench                 # score(): no network, no API keys
uv pip install 'omni-parse-bench[harness]'      # + vendor adapters, to predict

opb benchmark --out runs/ --limit 5 --providers datalab openai/gpt-5.6-sol

Vendors need keys such as DATALAB_API_KEY or OPENROUTER_API_KEY. The CLI shows its plan and asks before calling any vendor. Runs are resumable. The query guide shows how to compare runs by tag, suite or test type.

items.title: A gifted engineer. A love for Saudi Arabia. A bugging device wrapped in toilet paper.
items.summary: Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national employed as an OpenAI engineer, looks behind a television where a recording device had been placed in a conference room. DOJ/Reuters Abdulrahman Alfozan loved Saudi Arabia. One day before arresting the former OpenAI engineer on charges of bugging the office , the Justice Department worried he would flee back to his home country. Alfozan, his wife, and another family member had already booked one-way tickets, the department said in a court filing. It wouldn't be unusual for Alfozan's thoughts to return to the Gulf. The idea of moving back had followed him through his years working in tech. It inspired him to found a nonprofit that connects Silicon Valley talent with Saudi companies, and to join a WhatsApp group with other Gulf professionals. But he stayed in the US for one big reason, he said in a translated interview released in September, in which he detailed his life and work. "The best place for me to build technical expertise was Silicon Valley," Alfozan said. "You learn from the source, then bring those skills and experiences back home." Now, about a year after Alfozan took a job at OpenAI, the company said that it found a recording device "concealed in toilet paper." The device was placed on the back of a television in an executive conference room, according to a complaint filed in the Northern District of California. OpenAI wrote on X that it fired the employee — unnamed at the time — and referred the case to the FBI. The Justice Department arrested Alfozan, who is 35, on October 9 and charged him with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan has not yet filed a plea. His lawyer, William Pernik, said in a statement that the allegations "appear wholly out of character for him." "Mr. Alfozan came to this country years ago as a young person with a dream," Pernik said. "He spent years studying, working and contributing to an American technological sector that leads the world, a sector built in large part by immigrants like him." From Saudi Arabia to Silicon Valley Alfozan grew up in the Eastern Province of Saudi Arabia , where he went to school through high school. His father taught at a technical college in Dammam, and he introduced Alfozan to computer science professors and students, Alfozan said on the September podcast. A turning point was when Alfozan got into Mawhiba, Saudi Arabia's program for gifted students, he said. He bonded with his computer science teachers who would "stay after school or during breaks answering questions that had nothing to do with the curriculum," he said. His first trip to the US was through Mawhiba, he said, when he went to Texas for an Olympiad training program in 2008. Alfozan continued traveling to the US before college, posting on X about his trips to NASA's John F. Kennedy Space Center and the National Center for Supercomputing Applications. He had an entrepreneurial spirit since high school. On the podcast, he described watching family members in real estate log everything manually in spreadsheets. He built a system to manage it, gave it to his relatives for free, and then began selling it to other real estate offices, he said. Alfozan got into the gifted student program at King Abdullah University of Science and Technology. He was accepted to MIT, where he studied computer science and engineering. Alfozan remained a proponent of the major throughout his time at OpenAI, calling it the "most appropriate entry point" in another translated interview posted on YouTube. While at MIT, Alfozan interned at Akamai Technologies, SAP, and Microsoft , according to his LinkedIn. On the September podcast, he said he spent one winter break working on a 30-megawatt power plant in Ghana. MIT told Business Insider that Alfozan was enrolled as an undergraduate from September 2011 to January 2014 and from February 2016 to May 2016, but that no degrees were conferred. Before taking a job, Alfozan asked himself a big question: "Should I return to Saudi Arabia immediately, or should I stay in the United States and continue building experience?" He said he fielded multiple offers and decided on Facebook because of its talent density . In many ways, he fit right into the Valley's tech culture. He said that his role model was Elon Musk and trumpeted X as the best platform for tech professionals. He maintained an active GitHub profile , contributing to a variety of projects. He sent congratulatory notes on social media about fundraising rounds and startup launches. He called one founder's post about how Alfozan had helped save his startup inspiring, saying they "took the idea of vibe coding and pushed it to the extreme." Missing home A few years into his Facebook job, Alfozan was homesick. "How can we contribute to the Kingdom while we're still living abroad?" he remembered asking himself on the September podcast. "We were physically in California, but surely there had to be ways to help from a distance." He and some friends created a nonprofit consulting group, Saudi Silicon Valley, which listed alums of Palantir and Apple in its deck . The group's email was disconnected, and leaders did not respond to requests for comment. Alfozan also had a WhatsApp group chat with about a dozen professionals from the Gulf called "Sunday @ 6," he said in an interview with the Arab Gulf States Institute . That group met on Sunday nights to discuss technology in Arabic, he said. Eventually, Alfozan said, he became a founding engineer at Nash, a Y Combinator-backed startup. He also entered the venture capital space, becoming a partner at RAED Ventures. Neither organization responded to requests for comment. In 2025, he took a job at OpenAI. After a year in the AI lab, he told the YouTube interviewer that there were so many developments that he couldn't count them. The product team that he worked on had just launched its first product that September, he said. Alfozan appeared in federal court on Tuesday, according to a statement from the Justice Department. While he did not deny the allegations, Alfozan's lawyer cautioned against jumping to conclusions, noting that he was charged with violating a federal recording statute, not with stealing trade secrets or acting as a foreign agent. "There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us," said Pernik, the lawyer. "Where someone was born is not evidence of anything." Alfozan's one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia would have been one of many trips. He said on the September podcast that he returned home three or four times a year. He also said he advised several Saudi startups. The podcast host jumped in, calling Alfozan a bridge between the East and the West. "Exactly," Alfozan responded. Editor's note: October 14, 2026 — This story was updated to include a comment from MIT confirming Alfozan's enrollment but clarifying that no degrees were conferred. items.title: How Much Autonomy Should an AI Agent Have? The Economics of Verification and Recovery
items.summary: Maximum autonomy is not an engineering objective. A marginal test for how far to delegate, and when adding agents makes things worse. This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program, working from a research brief I prepared. Cited figures were checked against the current public version of each source in October 2026. The models are a synthesis of published evidence and standard reasoning, not results from a study I ran. Agent platforms are often described with a maturity ladder: autocomplete, then chat, then tool use, then autonomous agents, then teams of agents. The ladder implies that higher is better and that the job of a platform team is to climb it. That framing hides the actual design decision. Autonomy is not a level you reach. It is a scope you delegate : which steps run without a human decision, which actions the system may take on its own, and how far an error can travel before something checks it. Every increment of scope saves some human orchestration and adds some verification, recovery, coordination and risk. The right amount is wherever the next increment stops paying. For some workflows that is full autonomy. For others it is none. This article sets out a way to find that point, with the evidence on where it tends to sit and the counterexamples that keep it honest. Delegating is not the same as supervising less Start with what changes when scope grows. In an interactive setup, a person decomposes the task, issues a request per step, reads each result and decides the next move. In a delegated setup, the system does the decomposition and sequencing, and the person sees the outcome. Delegation removes orchestration labour: the prompts, the waiting, the context switching. It does not remove the need to know whether the result is right. That work moves to the end, where it is often harder, because the reviewer now has to reconstruct decisions they did not watch being made. Delegation also changes what happens on failure: an error made at step 3 can shape steps 4 to 30 before anyone sees it. So each expansion of scope trades a known, visible cost (human orchestration) for less visible ones (end-to-end verification, recovery, and the expected cost of errors that propagate or escape). The marginal rule For a candidate increase in delegated scope, the decision is a comparison of increments, measured per accepted result: Expand scope when: orchestration labour saved > extra verification + extra recovery + extra coordination + extra compute + cost of extra delay + extra expected failure loss all evaluated at the acceptance standard the workflow already requires. This is a conceptual rule, not a fitted model. Its practical value is that it forces each term to be named, and it makes clear that the answer is local. Nothing in it says the optimum is in the middle. If verification is objective and cheap, actions are reversible and errors are rare, the inequality may hold all the way to full autonomy. If verification is expensive or failure is irreversible, it may fail at the first step. Intermediate optima are common in practice, but they are not guaranteed. One quantity does a lot of work in that comparison: R_v = cost of confidently verifying the agent's result ÷ cost of producing an acceptable result by hand When R_v approaches 1, checking costs as much as doing, and delegation cannot save labour. When R_v is small, there is room. But a small R_v is not sufficient. It says nothing about how often the agent fails, what a missed failure costs, whether the action can be undone, or how much it costs to build and maintain the system. Treat R_v as a screen in architecture reviews, not a threshold. Nobody has measured a universal cut-off. How errors travel A deliberately unrealistic model shows why scope and checkpoints matter. Suppose a run has n strictly dependent steps, each correct with independent probability q , no step repairs earlier errors, and any error spoils the whole result. items.summary_html:
Maximum autonomy is not an engineering objective. A marginal test for how far to delegate, and when adding agents makes things worse.

This story was written with the assistance of an AI writing program, working from a research brief I prepared. Cited figures were checked against the current public version of each source in October 2026. The models are a synthesis of published evidence and standard reasoning, not results from a study I ran.

Agent platforms are often described with a maturity ladder: autocomplete, then chat, then tool use, then autonomous agents, then teams of agents. The ladder implies that higher is better and that the job of a platform team is to climb it.

That framing hides the actual design decision. Autonomy is not a level you reach. It is a scope you delegate: which steps run without a human decision, which actions the system may take on its own, and how far an error can travel before something checks it. Every increment of scope saves some human orchestration and adds some verification, recovery, coordination and risk. The right amount is wherever the next increment stops paying. For some workflows that is full autonomy. For others it is none.

This article sets out a way to find that point, with the evidence on where it tends to sit and the counterexamples that keep it honest.

Delegating is not the same as supervising less

Start with what changes when scope grows. In an interactive setup, a person decomposes the task, issues a request per step, reads each result and decides the next move. In a delegated setup, the system does the decomposition and sequencing, and the person sees the outcome.

Delegation removes orchestration labour: the prompts, the waiting, the context switching. It does not remove the need to know whether the result is right. That work moves to the end, where it is often harder, because the reviewer now has to reconstruct decisions they did not watch being made. Delegation also changes what happens on failure: an error made at step 3 can shape steps 4 to 30 before anyone sees it.

So each expansion of scope trades a known, visible cost (human orchestration) for less visible ones (end-to-end verification, recovery, and the expected cost of errors that propagate or escape).

The marginal rule

For a candidate increase in delegated scope, the decision is a comparison of increments, measured per accepted result:

Expand scope when:
  orchestration labour saved
    >  extra verification + extra recovery + extra coordination
       + extra compute + cost of extra delay + extra expected failure loss
all evaluated at the acceptance standard the workflow already requires.

This is a conceptual rule, not a fitted model. Its practical value is that it forces each term to be named, and it makes clear that the answer is local. Nothing in it says the optimum is in the middle. If verification is objective and cheap, actions are reversible and errors are rare, the inequality may hold all the way to full autonomy. If verification is expensive or failure is irreversible, it may fail at the first step. Intermediate optima are common in practice, but they are not guaranteed.

One quantity does a lot of work in that comparison:

R_v = cost of confidently verifying the agent's result
      ÷ cost of producing an acceptable result by hand

When R_v approaches 1, checking costs as much as doing, and delegation cannot save labour. When R_v is small, there is room. But a small R_v is not sufficient. It says nothing about how often the agent fails, what a missed failure costs, whether the action can be undone, or how much it costs to build and maintain the system. Treat R_v as a screen in architecture reviews, not a threshold. Nobody has measured a universal cut-off.

How errors travel

A deliberately unrealistic model shows why scope and checkpoints matter. Suppose a run has n strictly dependent steps, each correct with independent probability q, no step repairs earlier errors, and any error spoils the whole result. Then:

P(clean run) = q^n
For 30 dependent steps (hypothetical):
  q = 0.980  →  0.98^30  ≈ 54.5%
  q = 0.990  →  0.99^30  ≈ 74.0%
  q = 0.995  →  0.995^30 ≈ 86.0%

These are not measurements of any agent. Real errors are correlated, many are harmless, and agents retry. The point is the mechanism: the longer an unchecked chain, the more per-step reliability you need for the same end-to-end success rate, and the further an error can travel before it is caught.

The engineering response is not to forbid long chains. It is to break them with checks whose outcome does not depend on the agent’s own judgement: schema validation, tests, reconciliation totals, read-back of the state an action actually changed. A rough way to think about the cost of what slips through is:

expected downstream cost of missed errors  ≈  Σ_i  p_i × (1 − d_i) × R_i
p_i  probability of an error at step i
d_i  probability a check catches it before it propagates
R_i  cost to recover from it if it is not caught

That expression assumes the costs add up and are not counted twice. Even as a rough guide, it points at the levers: lower p with better models and tools, raise d with independent checks, and lower R by making actions reversible.

Reversibility deserves its own emphasis. A drafted email, a proposed diff or a staged data change can be undone cheaply. A payment, a deletion or a message sent to a customer cannot. For high-consequence write actions, the authorization boundary must be enforced outside the model: scoped credentials, policy checks on the tool call, and verification of the effect after it happens. Instructions in a prompt are not a permission system.

When more agents help, and when they hurt

Multi-agent designs add a second axis: not just how much is delegated, but how many delegates there are. For the timing dimension, a simple Amdahl-style model is enough to show the trade-off. With a parallelisable share f of the work, m agents, and a coordination and synthesis overhead o(m) expressed as a share of single-agent time:

Speedup S(m) = 1 / [ (1 − f) + f/m + o(m) ]
Multi-agent is faster than one agent only if:  o(m) < f × (1 − 1/m)

An illustrative sensitivity, with four agents and an overhead of 10%:

m = 4, o = 0.10 (hypothetical)
  f = 0.25  →  1.10×
  f = 0.50  →  1.38×
  f = 0.75  →  1.86×
  f = 0.90  →  2.35×

When little of the work can run in parallel, coordination eats most of the gain. This is an idealised timing model, not an empirical scaling law, and it says nothing about correctness. Several agents can improve quality through independent search or specialisation; badly designed coordination can degrade it.

The best controlled evidence I know of matches the structural point. In a study of 260 configurations spanning six agent benchmarks, five architectures and three model families, with tools, prompts and compute standardised to isolate the architecture, performance relative to a single agent ranged from +80.8% on decomposable financial reasoning to −70.0% on sequential planning (Kim et al., arXiv v3, April 2026). The authors also report that coordination yields diminishing returns once the single-agent baseline is already strong, that tool-heavy tasks tend to incur multi-agent overhead, and that architectures without centralised verification tend to propagate errors more than those with centralised coordination.

These are benchmark task-performance results under controlled budgets. They are not field productivity, wall-clock time or cost. What they establish is that the sign of the multi-agent effect depends on how the task is structured, which is enough to refute “more agents are better” as a general rule. It does not establish the opposite.

What high-autonomy field data can and cannot show

The most striking recent field evidence for autonomy comes from Perplexity. Using production data from its own products, authors affiliated with the company compared sessions where near-identical queries were given to an autonomous agent product (Computer) and to its search product. The agent did about 26 minutes of autonomous work per session against 33 seconds for search. On matched tasks, they estimate completion time fell from 269 to 36 minutes, with estimated time and cost reductions of 87% and 94% relative to people using search alone, and per-query dissatisfaction 55% lower (Yang et al., arXiv, June 2026).

That is real evidence that delegation can create large value for some tasks. It is also observational, from the vendor’s own telemetry. Users chose which product to use for which task, and the 269 and 36 minutes are estimated human-equivalent completion times, not stopwatch measurements. The comparison does not isolate the causal effect of autonomy from task selection and user selection. It should move your prior, not settle the question.

The developer-productivity evidence shows how easily attribution goes wrong when people and agents work together. In METR’s 2025 randomized trial, experienced open-source developers took about 19% longer with AI tools while believing they were faster (METR, 2025). By early 2026, METR’s follow-up pointed toward speedup but could not measure it reliably, partly because time is hard to attribute when developers run several agents concurrently (METR, February 2026). If a well-designed study struggles to time agent-assisted work, a dashboard of agent sessions will struggle too.

The arm most comparisons leave out

Agent architectures are usually compared with each other, or with a human doing the task by hand. A competently engineered deterministic workflow belongs in the comparison too: a script, a rules engine, a typed pipeline, a template with validation.

For the stable, high-volume part of a process, deterministic code has properties agents cannot match: zero marginal reasoning cost, identical behaviour on identical input, failures that are loud and local, and a verification cost that is paid once, in tests, rather than per run. Where it falls short is on the long tail: inputs nobody anticipated, unstructured context, decisions that need judgement.

That suggests a design worth testing rather than assuming: a deterministic core with bounded agent exceptions. The common path runs as code. When an input falls outside what the code can handle, a scoped agent takes it, with narrow tool permissions, a defined output contract and an independent check before the result re-enters the main flow. The agent’s scope is set by the exception rate and the cost of its errors, not by an autonomy ladder.

This is not proven superior in general. It is one arm of an honest comparison.

Choosing scope in practice

A compact way to read a workflow before deciding how much to delegate:

Property of the work              Pushes toward more scope   Pushes toward less scope
--------------------------------  -------------------------  --------------------------
Verification                      objective, cheap, automated  subjective, expensive
Reversibility of actions          drafts, staged changes       payments, deletes, sends
Task structure                    decomposable, parallel       sequential, tightly coupled
Input variability                 high, needs judgement        low, rules suffice
Cost of an escaped error          low, bounded                 high, unbounded
Frequency and volume              high (amortises build)       low (build never pays)

No single row decides. A workflow with cheap verification but irreversible actions might justify full autonomy up to the final write, and a human or a hard policy gate at that point.

A five-arm pilot

If the decision matters, test it. The design below is a proposal, not a study I have run, and not every arm will be feasible every time:

  1. Arms: human only; human with an interactive assistant; a competent deterministic workflow; a single agent; a multi-agent design. Match the agent arms on total model, token and tool budget wherever possible.
  2. Common acceptance: define an accepted result in advance and judge it the same way in every arm, ideally with blinded review.
  3. Stratify: legacy versus new systems, objectively verifiable versus judgement-heavy outputs, reversible versus irreversible actions, sequential versus parallelisable tasks, and staff experience.
  4. Measure: active human minutes by stage, reviewer time, compute and tool cost, abandoned runs, escaped defects within a fixed window, lead time, and a downstream outcome where one exists.
  5. Assign comparable tasks at random where you can, counterbalance for learning effects, and report results both for everything assigned and for what was actually used.

The output is not a winner. It is a map: which arm is best for which kind of work, at what cost, with what residual risk.

Where this argument is weak

Verification can be automated. As evals, tests and automated review improve, verification cost falls and the optimum shifts toward more autonomy. A pilot is a snapshot.

Quality gains may dominate. Independent agents exploring different approaches can find better answers. The timing model ignores this entirely.

Errors are not independent. The q^n model overstates compounding when steps repair each other and understates it when one bad assumption corrupts everything after it.

Benchmarks are not workplaces. The controlled multi-agent evidence measures task performance, not labour or value in an organisation.

Full autonomy is sometimes right. For high-volume, reversible, well-specified work with objective checks, the marginal rule can point all the way to the top. That is a valid outcome of the analysis, not a failure of it.

The decision

Platform teams do not need an autonomy ambition. They need a rule for each workflow: delegate the next increment of scope only when the orchestration it saves outweighs what it adds in verification, recovery, coordination, delay and risk, against the best non-agent alternative. Sometimes that rule says “one bounded agent behind a deterministic core.” Sometimes it says “a team of agents.” It rarely says “as much as possible.”

Sources

  • Yang, Zyskowski, Yonack & Ma (June 2026), How AI Agents Reshape Knowledge Work: Autonomy, Efficiency, and Scope, arXiv:2606.07489. arxiv.org/abs/2606.07489
  • Becker et al. / METR (2025), Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity. arxiv.org/abs/2507.09089

items.title: Linus Torvalds let Claude Code fix the Linux page cache. Then reviewers found a race.
items.summary: Linux creator and longtime lead maintainer Linus Torvalds turned to Anthropic’s Claude Code to tackle a kernel performance problem that developers have struggled with for more than two years. On Tuesday, he submitted a 10-patch series that delivered a 23-fold throughput improvement in a synthetic benchmark running on his Ryzen Threadripper. Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches. The new patches eliminate folio reference-count operations from a common buffered-read path, although Torvalds warned that the benchmark gains would be considerably smaller in real-world workloads. Reviewers have since identified a race condition and raised concerns about memory reclamation. Torvalds has handed further development to Kiryl Shutsemau , a Linux kernel developer who previously worked on the same bottleneck. Torvalds had spent 18 months running a broken version of his own fix for the page-cache reference-counting bottleneck, while other developers had encountered problems with their approaches. Page cache contention problem On Torvalds’ Core i7-8565U laptop, folio reference-count contention accounted for 99.92% of cross-core load HITMs in eight-thread tests, according to Hardware Busters . The bottleneck was flagged in 2024 by Matthew Wilcox, an Oracle engineer and longtime Linux kernel memory-management developer, after it surfaced in a customer workload. Claude Code writes the patches On Sunday, Phoronix’s Michael Larabel spotted an experimental branch named noref-filemap-read-with-llm in Torvalds’ tree, which rarely contains anything outside the main development branch. The eight-patch series, based on Linux 7.3-rc6, came with a clear account of what Claude Code did. Torvalds said the assistant wrote the implementation, tests, and initial documentation, and reviewed the code under his direction. He ran the benchmarks himself, despite having previously criticized developers for claiming AI writes 99% of their code . Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement. The subsequent 10-patch rcu-free-v3 series instead uses a new PG_rcu_free flag and RCU-delayed reclamation to protect the folio through the userspace copy, provided it doesn’t fault. Earlier approaches copied data without holding a folio reference and checked its validity afterward, leaving races involving reclamation and replacement. Threadripper benchmark results The original eight-patch branch nearly tripled throughput on Torvalds’ laptop, pushing eight-thread performance from 10 million to as many as 33 million reads per second while cutting kernel cycles per read from roughly 2,950 to 725. The revised series delivered a much larger gain under heavy contention on his 64-thread Threadripper, where throughput jumped from 13.3 million to 304 million reads per second and cycles per read fell from nearly 20,000 to 735. The original eight-patch branch nearly tripled throughput on Torvalds’ laptop, pushing eight-thread performance from 10 million to as many as 33 million reads per second while cutting kernel cycles per read from roughly 2,950 to 725. The performance gains came with trade-offs. In the first implementation, delayed reclamation forced an expedited grace period whenever a CPU queued more than 1,024 pages, according to Hardware Busters . Reads into unmapped user pages also triggered an additional fault before falling back to the existing path, pushing a 16-byte single-thread read from about 4,150 to 6,550 cycles. Whether that regression persists in rcu-free-v3 remains unclear. Maintainers question the reclamation design Wilcox questioned the new PG_rcu_free flag and proposed using a page type instead, along with reclaiming inactive-list folios after an RCU grace period. Torvalds rejected both approaches, arguing that the flag must be set while a folio can still be mapped into userspace and that inactive-list reclamation wouldn’t cover truncate and hole-punch operations. Shutsemau subsequently suggested restricting the flag to 64-bit systems, an approach supported by Arm engineer and Linux memory-management maintainer David Hildenbrand . Shutsemau also identified a race in filemap_read_rcu_batch() , where folio replacement followed by an extension of i_size could expose data that had never been written. Torvalds recommended moving the file-size read earlier and consolidating the folio checks, which Shutsemau incorporated into a revised patch.

items.title: Fish Audio Releases Drama 3, a 35B Open-Weight MoE Text-to-Speech Model
items.summary: This week, Fish Audio released Fish Audio Drama 3 . Drama 3 is a text-to-speech model from Fish Audio that takes plain-language acting direction. It is a 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B parameters active per token. The weights are on Hugging Face , and the model is also live in the Fish Audio API . For developers, it is a self-hostable option for scripted dialogue, audiobooks and dubbing. TL;DR Size: 35B total parameters, about 3B active per token (8 of 256 experts plus 1 shared). Context length: Not disclosed. Runs on: 1 NVIDIA GPU with at least 48 GB in FP8. No CPU, Apple MPS or AMD ROCm. Official benchmarks use 1 H200. Performance: Fish Audio’s highest-scoring model on Artificial Analysis, but still behind several closed APIs on quality Elo. Best: 95.9% on brands, places and technical terms in Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness. Worst: 86.3% on exact sequences (codes, paths, emails), its weakest pronunciation category. Bottom line: Best: directable, multi-speaker speech with open weights. Worst: 48 GB GPU floor and a revenue-capped license. What is Fish Audio Drama 3? Drama 3 turns a script along with bracketed directions into acted speech. Writers place cues like [barely holding it together] before a line. Paired tags such as change only the enclosed words, per the Drama 3 docs . Directions can be written in any language, independent of the spoken line. The model supports 83 languages . Speaker tags <|speaker:0|> to <|speaker:15|> allow up to 16 characters in 1 request. The API takes 1 voice ID per speaker, so a full scene renders in a single call. How does the Drama 3 architecture work? According to the launch post , the backbone starts from the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B language model. It has 40 layers, grouped as 3 Gated DeltaNet layers per 1 gated full-attention layer. Only 1 layer in 4 keeps a KV cache. DeltaNet layers store history in a constant-size state instead. A new Codebook-MTP decoder replaces the per-frame Fast AR decoder used in S2 . It has 4 shared layers feeding 9 layers, 1 per acoustic codebook. Only codebooks 0 and 1 feed back into the backbone; S2 fed back all 10. The audio tokenizer is unchanged from S2. It is built on the Descript Audio Codec and outputs 44.1 kHz audio. It runs at about 21.5 frames per second. Training ran 3 pre-training stages, then instruction tuning, then reinforcement learning. RL used GRPO without a KL penalty and a single learned human-preference reward model. && How does Drama 3 perform on benchmarks? Fish Audio reports Drama 3 at 93.2% overall on Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness , ranked #1. Its predecessor S2.1 Pro scored 88.1%. Human listeners judge hard English words across 4 categories: Brands, places, technical terms: 95.9% (S2.1 Pro: 87.3%) Context-dependent readings: 95.3% (86.1%) Shorthand such as numbers, dates and units: 93.6% (92.7%) Exact sequences such as codes, paths and emails: 86.3% (79.4%) This benchmark tests pronunciation, not emotional delivery. Fish Audio describes emotive quality only qualitatively. On the Artificial Analysis quality leaderboard , ‘Drama 3 Preview’ holds an Elo of 1242. That beats S2.1 Pro at 1190 but trails Eleven v4 Turbo at 1328. What hardware does Drama 3 need? The Fish Speech install guide lists at least 48 GB of NVIDIA GPU memory in FP8. CPU, Apple MPS and AMD ROCm are not supported. MoE experts ship in FP8, with the remaining weights in bf16. The model card reports streaming results on 1 H200. At 1 stream, median time to first audio is 88.9 ms with a real-time factor of 0.131. At 16 streams, throughput reaches 927.6 frames per second. Serving runs through SGLang-Omni , whose fused kernels are validated only on Hopper GPUs. How do you access Drama 3, and what does it cost? In the hosted API, set the model header to drama-3 on POST /v1/tts . The docs warn that a missing or misspelled header silently falls back to s2.1-pro . List price is $50 per 1M characters. A $10 launch price runs until November 12, 2026, per the launch post . The weights use the Fish Audio Community License v1.0 . Research and non-commercial use are free. Commercial use is free under USD 500,000 in annual revenue. Hosting Drama 3 as a third-party API needs a separate license. Products must display ‘Built with Fish Audio.’ Cloning a real voice without consent is prohibited. Drama 3 vs closest competitors Feature Fish Audio Drama 3 Fish Audio S2 Pro ElevenLabs Eleven v4 Turbo Qwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-Plus Total size 35B (MoE) 5B (4B Slow AR + 400M Fast AR) Not disclosed Not disclosed Active parameters ~3B Not MoE Not disclosed Not disclosed Weights Open, Community License v1.0 Open, Research License API and apps API (Model Studio) Languages 83 80+ 90+ 8 listed, plus dialects Self-host hardware 48 GB+ NVIDIA, FP8 24 GB+ NVIDIA, or CPU Hosted only Hosted only Latency 88.9 ms TTFA p50, H200 ~100 ms TTFA, H200 ~150 ms median time to first speech Not disclosed AA quality Elo ( source ) 1242 (Preview) 1116 1328 1266 API price per 1M chars $50 list, $10 to Nov 12 $15 $40 $20, Singapore Key Takeaways Drama 3 is a 35B MoE TTS model with ~3B active parameters. Plain-language direction and 16 speakers per request target scripted audio. 93.2% on AA Pronunciation Robustness; exact sequences lag at 86.3%. Self-hosting needs 48 GB+ of NVIDIA memory in FP8. Free commercial use stops at USD 500,000 in annual revenue. Check out the weights on Hugging Face , the technical report , the GitHub repo and the launch post . items.summary_html:
This week, Fish Audio released Fish Audio Drama 3. Drama 3 is a text-to-speech model from Fish Audio that takes plain-language acting direction. It is a 35B mixture-of-experts model with about 3B parameters active per token. The weights are on Hugging Face, and the model is also live in the Fish Audio API. For developers, it is a self-hostable option for scripted dialogue, audiobooks and dubbing.

TL;DR
  • Size: 35B total parameters, about 3B active per token (8 of 256 experts plus 1 shared). Context length: Not disclosed.
  • Runs on: 1 NVIDIA GPU with at least 48 GB in FP8. No CPU, Apple MPS or AMD ROCm. Official benchmarks use 1 H200.
  • Performance: Fish Audio’s highest-scoring model on Artificial Analysis, but still behind several closed APIs on quality Elo.
  • Best: 95.9% on brands, places and technical terms in Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness.
  • Worst: 86.3% on exact sequences (codes, paths, emails), its weakest pronunciation category.
  • Bottom line:
    • Best: directable, multi-speaker speech with open weights.
    • Worst: 48 GB GPU floor and a revenue-capped license.
What is Fish Audio Drama 3?

Drama 3 turns a script along with bracketed directions into acted speech. Writers place cues like [barely holding it together] before a line. Paired tags such as change only the enclosed words, per the Drama 3 docs. Directions can be written in any language, independent of the spoken line.

The model supports 83 languages. Speaker tags <|speaker:0|> to <|speaker:15|> allow up to 16 characters in 1 request. The API takes 1 voice ID per speaker, so a full scene renders in a single call.

How does the Drama 3 architecture work?

According to the launch post, the backbone starts from the Qwen3.5-35B-A3B language model. It has 40 layers, grouped as 3 Gated DeltaNet layers per 1 gated full-attention layer. Only 1 layer in 4 keeps a KV cache. DeltaNet layers store history in a constant-size state instead.

A new Codebook-MTP decoder replaces the per-frame Fast AR decoder used in S2. It has 4 shared layers feeding 9 layers, 1 per acoustic codebook. Only codebooks 0 and 1 feed back into the backbone; S2 fed back all 10.

The audio tokenizer is unchanged from S2. It is built on the Descript Audio Codec and outputs 44.1 kHz audio. It runs at about 21.5 frames per second.

Training ran 3 pre-training stages, then instruction tuning, then reinforcement learning. RL used GRPO without a KL penalty and a single learned human-preference reward model.

&&

How does Drama 3 perform on benchmarks?

Fish Audio reports Drama 3 at 93.2% overall on Artificial Analysis Pronunciation Robustness, ranked #1. Its predecessor S2.1 Pro scored 88.1%. Human listeners judge hard English words across 4 categories:

  • Brands, places, technical terms: 95.9% (S2.1 Pro: 87.3%)
  • Context-dependent readings: 95.3% (86.1%)
  • Shorthand such as numbers, dates and units: 93.6% (92.7%)
  • Exact sequences such as codes, paths and emails: 86.3% (79.4%)

This benchmark tests pronunciation, not emotional delivery. Fish Audio describes emotive quality only qualitatively. On the Artificial Analysis quality leaderboard, ‘Drama 3 Preview’ holds an Elo of 1242. That beats S2.1 Pro at 1190 but trails Eleven v4 Turbo at 1328.

What hardware does Drama 3 need?

The Fish Speech install guide lists at least 48 GB of NVIDIA GPU memory in FP8. CPU, Apple MPS and AMD ROCm are not supported. MoE experts ship in FP8, with the remaining weights in bf16.

The model card reports streaming results on 1 H200. At 1 stream, median time to first audio is 88.9 ms with a real-time factor of 0.131. At 16 streams, throughput reaches 927.6 frames per second. Serving runs through SGLang-Omni, whose fused kernels are validated only on Hopper GPUs.

How do you access Drama 3, and what does it cost?

In the hosted API, set the model header to drama-3 on POST /v1/tts. The docs warn that a missing or misspelled header silently falls back to s2.1-pro. List price is $50 per 1M characters. A $10 launch price runs until November 12, 2026, per the launch post.

The weights use the Fish Audio Community License v1.0. Research and non-commercial use are free. Commercial use is free under USD 500,000 in annual revenue. Hosting Drama 3 as a third-party API needs a separate license. Products must display ‘Built with Fish Audio.’ Cloning a real voice without consent is prohibited.

Drama 3 vs closest competitors FeatureFish Audio Drama 3Fish Audio S2 ProElevenLabs Eleven v4 TurboQwen-Audio-3.0-TTS-PlusTotal size35B (MoE)5B (4B Slow AR + 400M Fast AR)Not disclosedNot disclosedActive parameters~3BNot MoENot disclosedNot disclosedWeightsOpen, Community License v1.0Open, Research LicenseAPI and appsAPI (Model Studio)Languages8380+90+8 listed, plus dialectsSelf-host hardware48 GB+ NVIDIA, FP8 24 GB+ NVIDIA, or CPU Hosted onlyHosted onlyLatency88.9 ms TTFA p50, H200~100 ms TTFA, H200~150 ms median time to first speechNot disclosedAA quality Elo (source)1242 (Preview)111613281266API price per 1M chars$50 list, $10 to Nov 12 $15 $40 $20, Singapore Key Takeaways
  • Drama 3 is a 35B MoE TTS model with ~3B active parameters.
  • Plain-language direction and 16 speakers per request target scripted audio.

  • Self-hosting needs 48 GB+ of NVIDIA memory in FP8.

items.title: Part XIV — Broadcast Variables: The Driver Bottleneck Nobody Profiles
items.summary: Broadcast joins are sold as free money: skip the shuffle, ship the small table everywhere. But “small” is measured against the driver’s heap, the collect has to survive a 300-second timeout, and every byte lands on the one node nobody profiles — until it dies at 2:47 AM. Part I | Part II | Part III | Part IV | Part V | Part VI | Part VII | Part VIII | Part IX | Part X | Part XI | Part XII | Part XIII | Part XIV The Night the Driver Died Collecting a “Small” Table Tuesday, 2:47 AM. The daily revenue reconciliation job — the one finance opens before their standup — failed for the third night in a row. Same signature every time: the driver container got killed by YARN, java.lang.OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space, buried inside a BroadcastExchangeExec. Forty r5.2xlarge executors sat at 3% CPU while the single driver node thrashed, retried, and died again. The join was textbook. A 1.9TB fact table of payment events joined against dim_merchants, the merchant dimension. When the pipeline was built eighteen months ago, that dimension was 3.2GB — comfortably "small." A well-meaning engineer had added /*+ BROADCAST(merchants) */ to the query and moved on. Nobody revisited it. Merchant onboarding had since grown the dimension to 14.6GB, and nobody noticed because the broadcast hint doesn't care how big the table is. It just collects. Three failed attempts, 6 hours 12 minutes of wall clock, roughly $412 in EMR spend to produce zero rows — 97% of it burned by executors waiting on a driver that was already dead. The “optimization” had become the single point of failure, and it was the one component in the whole cluster nobody had ever profiled. So: what does a broadcast actually cost the driver, where does the data physically go, and how do you size it so the free lunch stops killing the host? The Mechanic Underneath: Broadcast Is a Collect, Not a Shuffle Here is the mental model most engineers get wrong: a broadcast join does not avoid moving data. It avoids moving the big table. The price is that the entire build side is materialized inside the driver’s heap first — collect()-style, all of it, on one JVM — and only then fanned out to every executor. Every broadcast is three phases, and phase one runs on your least-observed node: Collect. The driver executes the build side of the plan and pulls every row into its own heap, then builds an in-memory hash table (HashedRelation / LongHashedRelation) for the join keys. Serialize and torrent. The hash table is serialized and split into 4MB blocks (spark.broadcast.blockSize, default 4m), then distributed via TorrentBroadcast — a BitTorrent-style peer-to-peer protocol where executors fetch blocks from the driver and from each other . Materialize everywhere. Each executor stores the full broadcast in its BlockManager and probes it locally. No shuffle of the big table happens at all. The trade is real and usually worth it — but it is a trade, not a freebie: You trade cluster-wide shuffle I/O for driver-side memory pressure. The shuffle you avoided was spread across 40 executors. The collect you replaced it with lands on one heap. You trade it again for N copies. A 900MB broadcast on 40 executors is 36GB of cluster memory holding the same bytes. Small tables make this irrelevant; “small” tables that grew quietly make it a leak. You inherit the driver’s two hard budgets: heap and time. The collect must fit in driver memory and finish within spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (default 300 seconds), or the job dies before a single task launches. Phase One Runs on the Driver, and the Driver Is Not a Data Node The driver is sized for orchestration: scheduling tasks, holding the DAG, serving the UI. It is typically the smallest node in the cluster — an m5.xlarge with spark.driver.memory=8g while executors get 64GB each. Broadcast is the one operation in all of Spark SQL that treats the driver like a data node, and it does so unconditionally once the decision is made. What actually lives in the driver’s heap during a broadcast is worse than the table’s on-disk size. The rows arrive deserialized as JVM objects (no Tungsten off-heap encoding here), then get reorganized into a hash table with per-row overhead. A 14.6GB Parquet dimension easily becomes 20GB+ of heap. The driver doesn’t spill broadcast builds gracefully — it just dies. This is why the failure signature is so distinctive: the job fails fast-ish (during planning/exchange, before real work), the stack trace names BroadcastExchangeExec, and the executors look idle in the UI because they never got anything to do. TorrentBroadcast: BitTorrent for DataFrames, in 4MB Chunks Once the driver survives the collect, distribution is genuinely clever. TorrentBroadcast chops the serialized relation into blocks (default 4MB via spark.broadcast.blockSize) and serves them peer-to-peer: the first executors pull from the driver, later ones pull from each other. The driver is not a bottleneck for distribution — only for the collect. Each block lands in the executor’s BlockManager, counted against regular storage/execution memory. Two consequences worth knowing: Broadcasts compete with caching and shuffle on executors. Five 2GB broadcasts on a busy executor is 10GB of BlockManager that isn’t available for anything else. Nobody sums these up because each broadcast is configured — and justified — in isolation. Broadcasts are per-job, not per-cluster. The same dimension broadcast in twelve concurrent jobs is twelve copies in flight. At 2 AM with one job running, fine. At 9 AM with the whole org’s dbt models firing, the math changes. The 10MB Threshold Is a Gate, Not a Guarantee spark.sql.adaptive.enabled aside, the static planner broadcasts a relation when its estimated size is under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold — default 10485760 bytes (10MB) . "Estimated" is doing heavy lifting: without table statistics, the estimate can be wildly wrong, and with stale statistics it's wrong in the dangerous direction. Worse, the SQL hint /*+ BROADCAST(t) */ bypasses the gate entirely. It is an instruction, not a suggestion. It broadcasts a 14.6GB table with the same confidence as a 14KB one, and it will keep doing so every night until someone reads the query. Hints are the number one source of broadcast incidents I've seen, because they encode a size assumption from the day they were written and never expire. Setting the threshold to -1 disables auto-broadcast completely — a legitimate choice for pipelines where every join is large and you'd rather pay for shuffles than debug 3 AM driver OOMs. The Three Failure Shapes of Broadcast In production, broadcast fails in exactly three ways, and each has a different smell: Driver OOM during collect. Stack trace in BroadcastExchangeExec, fast failure, idle executors. Cause: build side bigger than driver heap. Fix: shrink the build side or grow the driver. Broadcast timeout. Could not execute broadcast in 300 secs. The collect technically fits but is slow — usually a build side that itself requires a heavy scan or shuffle. Fix: spark.sql.broadcastTimeout, or better, make the build side cheap (pre-aggregate, filter early). Executor memory pressure. No single failure; everything is just slower, with excessive GC and spilled blocks. Cause: too many or too-large broadcasts sharing BlockManager with real work. Fix: audit what you’re broadcasting — the sum, not each one. Note what is not on this list: skew. Broadcast is actually the correct answer to a skewed join when the skewed side is the small side — the whole point is that every executor gets the full build side, so a hot key on the probe side just probes a local hash table. Part VII’s skew playbook covers the salt-and-split approach for when both sides are large; broadcast covers the asymmetric case. The failure mode is never “broadcast can’t handle skew” — it’s “the small side wasn’t small.” The Fix, and What It Cost The naive state of our reconciliation job: a BROADCAST hint written eighteen months ago, default driver memory, and a dimension table that had quietly 4.5x'd. # Naive: a hint that encodes a size assumption from 18 months ago, # broadcasting a 14.6 GB dimension into an 8g driver heap. revenue = ( payments .hint("broadcast", "merchants") # BROADCAST hint: bypasses the 10MB gate entirely .join(merchants, "merchant_id") ) # Result: driver OOM in BroadcastExchangeExec, 3 attempts, 6h12m, $412, zero rows. The engine-aware fix had three parts, in order of leverage: # Optimized: shrink the build side, let the planner decide, size the driver honestly. spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", 100 * 1024 * 1024) # 100MB: explicit, reviewed spark.conf.set("spark.sql.broadcastTimeout", 600) # 600s: the build side needs a scan first # spark.driver.memory=16g # set at submit: broadcast collect must fit with headroom merchants_small = ( merchants .filter(F.col("is_active")) # 14.6 GB -> 900 MB: only active merchants join .select("merchant_id", "fee_tier") # drop the 40 unused columns before the collect ) revenue = payments.join(F.broadcast(merchants_small), "merchant_id") # F.broadcast() still hints, but the build side is now 900MB against a 16g driver. The filter + select before the join is the highest-leverage line in the whole fix: the dimension was 14.6GB on disk mostly because of dead merchants and forty columns the join never touched. The broadcast decision was never the real problem — the unexamined build side was. Before/after: driver OOM loop, 6h12m wall clock, ~$412 EMR spend, zero rows → stable nightly run, 38 minutes , ~$31. Driver heap peak went from dead-at-8g to a comfortable 2.3GB on a 16g driver. And the hint is gone — the 100MB threshold is a reviewed config, not a fossilized guess. The Catch: Broadcast Still Copies, Still Centralizes, Still Lies by Omission Three honest counterweights before you go broadcast everything under 100MB. First, broadcast replicates to every executor , so its true cluster cost is size × executor count. A 900MB broadcast across 200 executors is 180GB of duplicated memory. On large clusters, the "small" table stops being small in aggregate, and a sort-merge join with a well-partitioned build side can be cheaper in total bytes moved. Do the multiplication; nobody does the multiplication. Second, the hint problem doesn’t go away, it just moves. F.broadcast() in PySpark is the same fossilized assumption as the SQL hint. Prefer the threshold config where the build side is genuinely stable, and re-measure quarterly. Dimension tables grow. That is their nature. Third, broadcast doesn’t fix a slow build side. If computing the small table requires its own two-hour shuffle, you’ve just moved the bottleneck into the driver’s critical path, serialized. Pre-aggregate it, persist it, or materialize it as a table — don’t make the driver compute it fresh every night under a 300-second gun. Takeaways A broadcast join is a driver-side collect first and a join second — size it against the driver’s heap, not the cluster’s. Hints are size assumptions with no expiry date — audit every BROADCAST hint against the table's current size, or delete it and use the threshold. Shrink the build side before tuning anything else — filters and column pruning beat every config knob, because the collect is the whole cost. spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (300s default) is the second budget — a build side that needs its own heavy scan will time out on a driver that could have held it. True broadcast cost is size × executor count — on big clusters, duplication can exceed the shuffle you avoided. Broadcast is the right answer to one-sided skew — a hot key on the large side is harmless when every executor holds the full small side locally. A shuffle spreads the pain across the cluster; a broadcast concentrates it on the one node you never look at. If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X . Part XIV — Broadcast Variables: The Driver Bottleneck Nobody Profiles was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

A 14.6GB Parquet dimension easily becomes 20GB+ of heap. The driver doesn’t spill broadcast builds gracefully — it just dies.

This is why the failure signature is so distinctive: the job fails fast-ish (during planning/exchange, before real work), the stack trace names BroadcastExchangeExec, and the executors look idle in the UI because they never got anything to do.

TorrentBroadcast: BitTorrent for DataFrames, in 4MB Chunks

Once the driver survives the collect, distribution is genuinely clever. TorrentBroadcast chops the serialized relation into blocks (default 4MB via spark.broadcast.blockSize) and serves them peer-to-peer: the first executors pull from the driver, later ones pull from each other. The driver is not a bottleneck for distribution — only for the collect.

Each block lands in the executor’s BlockManager, counted against regular storage/execution memory. Two consequences worth knowing:

  • Broadcasts compete with caching and shuffle on executors. Five 2GB broadcasts on a busy executor is 10GB of BlockManager that isn’t available for anything else. Nobody sums these up because each broadcast is configured — and justified — in isolation.
  • Broadcasts are per-job, not per-cluster. The same dimension broadcast in twelve concurrent jobs is twelve copies in flight. At 2 AM with one job running, fine. At 9 AM with the whole org’s dbt models firing, the math changes.
The 10MB Threshold Is a Gate, Not a Guarantee

spark.sql.adaptive.enabled aside, the static planner broadcasts a relation when its estimated size is under spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold — default 10485760 bytes (10MB). "Estimated" is doing heavy lifting: without table statistics, the estimate can be wildly wrong, and with stale statistics it's wrong in the dangerous direction.

Worse, the SQL hint /*+ BROADCAST(t) */ bypasses the gate entirely. It is an instruction, not a suggestion. It broadcasts a 14.6GB table with the same confidence as a 14KB one, and it will keep doing so every night until someone reads the query. Hints are the number one source of broadcast incidents I've seen, because they encode a size assumption from the day they were written and never expire.

Setting the threshold to -1 disables auto-broadcast completely — a legitimate choice for pipelines where every join is large and you'd rather pay for shuffles than debug 3 AM driver OOMs.

The Three Failure Shapes of Broadcast

In production, broadcast fails in exactly three ways, and each has a different smell:

  • Driver OOM during collect. Stack trace in BroadcastExchangeExec, fast failure, idle executors. Cause: build side bigger than driver heap. Fix: shrink the build side or grow the driver.
  • Broadcast timeout. Could not execute broadcast in 300 secs. The collect technically fits but is slow — usually a build side that itself requires a heavy scan or shuffle. Fix: spark.sql.broadcastTimeout, or better, make the build side cheap (pre-aggregate, filter early).
  • Executor memory pressure. No single failure; everything is just slower, with excessive GC and spilled blocks. Cause: too many or too-large broadcasts sharing BlockManager with real work. Fix: audit what you’re broadcasting — the sum, not each one.

Note what is not on this list: skew. Broadcast is actually the correct answer to a skewed join when the skewed side is the small side — the whole point is that every executor gets the full build side, so a hot key on the probe side just probes a local hash table. Part VII’s skew playbook covers the salt-and-split approach for when both sides are large; broadcast covers the asymmetric case. The failure mode is never “broadcast can’t handle skew” — it’s “the small side wasn’t small.”

The Fix, and What It Cost

The naive state of our reconciliation job: a BROADCAST hint written eighteen months ago, default driver memory, and a dimension table that had quietly 4.5x'd.

# Naive: a hint that encodes a size assumption from 18 months ago,
# broadcasting a 14.6 GB dimension into an 8g driver heap.
revenue = (
    payments
    .hint("broadcast", "merchants")  # BROADCAST hint: bypasses the 10MB gate entirely
    .join(merchants, "merchant_id")
)
# Result: driver OOM in BroadcastExchangeExec, 3 attempts, 6h12m, $412, zero rows.

The engine-aware fix had three parts, in order of leverage:

# Optimized: shrink the build side, let the planner decide, size the driver honestly.
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", 100 * 1024 * 1024)  # 100MB: explicit, reviewed
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.broadcastTimeout", 600)  # 600s: the build side needs a scan first
# spark.driver.memory=16g  # set at submit: broadcast collect must fit with headroom
merchants_small = (
    merchants
    .filter(F.col("is_active"))          # 14.6 GB -> 900 MB: only active merchants join
    .select("merchant_id", "fee_tier")   # drop the 40 unused columns before the collect
)
revenue = payments.join(F.broadcast(merchants_small), "merchant_id")
# F.broadcast() still hints, but the build side is now 900MB against a 16g driver.

The filter + select before the join is the highest-leverage line in the whole fix: the dimension was 14.6GB on disk mostly because of dead merchants and forty columns the join never touched. The broadcast decision was never the real problem — the unexamined build side was.

Before/after: driver OOM loop, 6h12m wall clock, ~$412 EMR spend, zero rows → stable nightly run, 38 minutes, ~$31. Driver heap peak went from dead-at-8g to a comfortable 2.3GB on a 16g driver. And the hint is gone — the 100MB threshold is a reviewed config, not a fossilized guess.

The Catch: Broadcast Still Copies, Still Centralizes, Still Lies by Omission

Three honest counterweights before you go broadcast everything under 100MB.

First, broadcast replicates to every executor, so its true cluster cost is size × executor count. A 900MB broadcast across 200 executors is 180GB of duplicated memory. On large clusters, the "small" table stops being small in aggregate, and a sort-merge join with a well-partitioned build side can be cheaper in total bytes moved. Do the multiplication; nobody does the multiplication.

Second, the hint problem doesn’t go away, it just moves. F.broadcast() in PySpark is the same fossilized assumption as the SQL hint. Prefer the threshold config where the build side is genuinely stable, and re-measure quarterly. Dimension tables grow. That is their nature.

Third, broadcast doesn’t fix a slow build side. If computing the small table requires its own two-hour shuffle, you’ve just moved the bottleneck into the driver’s critical path, serialized. Pre-aggregate it, persist it, or materialize it as a table — don’t make the driver compute it fresh every night under a 300-second gun.

Takeaways
  • A broadcast join is a driver-side collect first and a join second — size it against the driver’s heap, not the cluster’s.
  • Hints are size assumptions with no expiry date — audit every BROADCAST hint against the table's current size, or delete it and use the threshold.
  • Shrink the build side before tuning anything else — filters and column pruning beat every config knob, because the collect is the whole cost.
  • spark.sql.broadcastTimeout (300s default) is the second budget — a build side that needs its own heavy scan will time out on a driver that could have held it.
  • True broadcast cost is size × executor count — on big clusters, duplication can exceed the shuffle you avoided.
  • Broadcast is the right answer to one-sided skew — a hot key on the large side is harmless when every executor holds the full small side locally.

A shuffle spreads the pain across the cluster; a broadcast concentrates it on the one node you never look at.

If this saved you a 3 AM pager incident, follow me on Medium for Twice a week for the next 3 Months of Advanced Data Engineering & AI. Let’s connect on LinkedIn and X.
