items.title: A Trip from Covariance to Correlation and Back
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on Statforbiology, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

When we have a multi-trait table of data, we might be interested in investigating variability structure and the reciprocal relationships (whether causal or non-causal) among variables. For example, let’s consider the ‘mtcars’ dataset, shown below:

data(mtcars)
head(mtcars)
##                    mpg cyl disp  hp drat    wt  qsec vs am gear carb
## Mazda RX4         21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.620 16.46  0  1    4    4
## Mazda RX4 Wag     21.0   6  160 110 3.90 2.875 17.02  0  1    4    4
## Datsun 710        22.8   4  108  93 3.85 2.320 18.61  1  1    4    1
## Hornet 4 Drive    21.4   6  258 110 3.08 3.215 19.44  1  0    3    1
## Hornet Sportabout 18.7   8  360 175 3.15 3.440 17.02  0  0    3    2
## Valiant           18.1   6  225 105 2.76 3.460 20.22  1  0    3    1

Considering the different cars (along the rows), we might be interested in investigating the structure of variability for fuel consumption (mpg), number of cylinders (cyl), displacement (disp) and horsepower (hp). How much does each variable change across the different cars? How much does each variable change when another variable changes? Is there any kind of joint variation, either positive or negative?

One suitable statistic to answer these question is the covariance, that is:

where and are the means for each variable and is the number of individuals. In words, covariance is the sum of products of the ith deviations from the mean for both variables. In this setting, the variance is just the covariance of a variable with itself.

For a data table, variances and covariances can be calculated by using the cov() function, that returns a matrix (the variance-covariance matrix, indeed):

matr <- mtcars[,1:4]

# Covariances
Sigma <- cov(matr)
Sigma
##              mpg        cyl       disp        hp
## mpg    36.324103  -9.172379  -633.0972 -320.7321
## cyl    -9.172379   3.189516   199.6603  101.9315
## disp -633.097208 199.660282 15360.7998 6721.1587
## hp   -320.732056 101.931452  6721.1587 4700.8669

While covariances indicate direction (positive or negative association), their values depend on the scale of measurement, making it difficult to gauge the strength of the relationship at a glance. For this reason, covariances are usually ‘standardized’ by dividing by the product of the standard deviations to obtain Pearson’s correlation coefficient:

where and are the standard deviations for and . Unlike covariances, correlations go from -1 to 1 and the correlation matrix has 1s along its main diagonal (since the correlation of any variable with itself is 1). In R, the matrix of correlation is obtained by using the cor() function:

# Correlations
R <- cor(matr)
R
##             mpg        cyl       disp         hp
## mpg   1.0000000 -0.8521620 -0.8475514 -0.7761684
## cyl  -0.8521620  1.0000000  0.9020329  0.8324475
## disp -0.8475514  0.9020329  1.0000000  0.7909486
## hp   -0.7761684  0.8324475  0.7909486  1.0000000

This brings us to the main question of this post: Given a variance-covariance matrix, can we compute the correlation matrix? And can we do the reverse—moving from a correlation matrix back to a variance-covariance matrix? With reference to the matrices above, can we go from ‘Sigma’ to ‘R’ and from ‘R’ to ‘Sigma’? I often find myself needing to make these conversions, especially when working with mixed models or time series analysis.

From covariance to correlation

Considering the previous expression, it is easy to see that, if we take the covariance between ‘disp’ and ‘mpg’ above (-633.0972), the correlation can be obtained as:

-633.097208 / (sqrt(36.324103) * sqrt(15360.7998))
## [1] -0.8475514

and all the necessary information is contained in the variance-covariance matrix.

Of course, doing these calculations for all covariances one by one is tedious. The question is: is there any simple way to go from a covariance matrix to a correlation matrix with one single operation?

The answer is found in matrix algebra; let’s take a look at the variance-covariane matrix: what we have to do is to take each element in this matrix and divide it by the square roots of the diagonal elements in the same column and in the same row (see figure below). Consequently, our task is:

  1. take the diagonal elements
  2. take each ith row and divide all its elements by the ith diagonal element (row-scaling)
  3. take each ith column of the resulting matrix and divide all its elements by the ith diagonal element (column-scaling)

Row-scaling can be performed by using matrix-algebra; in particular, we can take a diagonal matrix of weights and multiply it by the square matrix we want to scale, as shown below.

We see that all elements of the first row were multiplied by the first weighting element, all elements of the second row were multiplied by the second weighting element and so forth.

Column scaling is done similarly, but in reverse order: we take the target matrix and post-multiply it by the diagonal matrix of weights, as shown below.

We see that all elements of the first column were multiplied by the first weighting element, all elements of the second row were multiplied by the second weighting element, and so forth.

Consequently, we can take our variance-covariance matrix and:

  1. Take the square roots of the diagonal elements (standard deviations) and load them into a diagonal matrix
  2. Invert this diagonal matrix
  3. Pre-multiply and post-multiply the variance-covariance matrix by this diagonal matrix of inverted standard deviations
# from covariance to correlation - 1
StDev <- sqrt(diag(Sigma))
StDevMat <- diag(StDev)
InvStDev <- solve(StDevMat)
InvStDev %*% Sigma %*% InvStDev
##            [,1]       [,2]       [,3]       [,4]
## [1,]  1.0000000 -0.8521620 -0.8475514 -0.7761684
## [2,] -0.8521620  1.0000000  0.9020329  0.8324475
## [3,] -0.8475514  0.9020329  1.0000000  0.7909486
## [4,] -0.7761684  0.8324475  0.7909486  1.0000000

The previous solution is correct, but, in R, it is rather inefficient. The best way is to use the cov2cor() function in the ‘stat’ package.

# From covariance to correlation - 2
cov2cor(Sigma)
##             mpg        cyl       disp         hp
## mpg   1.0000000 -0.8521620 -0.8475514 -0.7761684
## cyl  -0.8521620  1.0000000  0.9020329  0.8324475
## disp -0.8475514  0.9020329  1.0000000  0.7909486
## hp   -0.7761684  0.8324475  0.7909486  1.0000000

With base R, we can also sweep() twice:

# From covariance to correlation - 3
sweep(sweep(Sigma, 1, StDev, FUN = "/"), 2, StDev, FUN = "/")
##             mpg        cyl       disp         hp
## mpg   1.0000000 -0.8521620 -0.8475514 -0.7761684
## cyl  -0.8521620  1.0000000  0.9020329  0.8324475
## disp -0.8475514  0.9020329  1.0000000  0.7909486
## hp   -0.7761684  0.8324475  0.7909486  1.0000000

Alternatively, we can combine scale() and t() (transpose) twice, though it is noticeably less intuitive:

# From covariance to correlation - 4
scale(t(scale(t(Sigma), center = F, scale = StDev)), 
      center = F, scale = StDev)
##             mpg        cyl       disp         hp
## mpg   1.0000000 -0.8521620 -0.8475514 -0.7761684
## cyl  -0.8521620  1.0000000  0.9020329  0.8324475
## disp -0.8475514  0.9020329  1.0000000  0.7909486
## hp   -0.7761684  0.8324475  0.7909486  1.0000000
## attr(,"scaled:scale")
##        mpg        cyl       disp         hp 
##   6.026948   1.785922 123.938694  68.562868

Another very clean approach in R is based on the outer product. If we have a vectors of standard deviations ($), the outer product is:

Thus, the correlation is calculated as:

# From covariance to correlation - 5
Sigma/outer(StDev, StDev)
##             mpg        cyl       disp         hp
## mpg   1.0000000 -0.8521620 -0.8475514 -0.7761684
## cyl  -0.8521620  1.0000000  0.9020329  0.8324475
## disp -0.8475514  0.9020329  1.0000000  0.7909486
## hp   -0.7761684  0.8324475  0.7909486  1.0000000
From correlation to covariance

It is easy to see that:

Thus, if we have the correlation between ‘disp’ and ‘mpg’ (-0.8521620), we can easily calculate the covariance as:

-0.8475514 * sqrt(36.324103) * sqrt(15360.7998)
## [1] -633.0972

The only problem is that the variances are not contained in a correlation matrix, so we need to get them from elsewhere. Once we have them, we

    1. Take their square roots and place them into a diagonal matrix
  2. Pre-multiply and post-multiply the correlation matrix for this diagonal matrix of standard deviations

The solution is as follows:

# from correlation to covariance - 1
StDev <- sqrt(diag(Sigma))
StDevMat <- diag(StDev)
StDevMat %*% R %*% StDevMat
##             [,1]       [,2]       [,3]      [,4]
## [1,]   36.324103  -9.172379  -633.0972 -320.7321
## [2,]   -9.172379   3.189516   199.6603  101.9315
## [3,] -633.097208 199.660282 15360.7998 6721.1587
## [4,] -320.732056 101.931452  6721.1587 4700.8669

More efficiently, we can use the cor2cov() function in the ‘lavaan’ package.

# From correlation to covariance - 2
lavaan::cor2cov(R, StDev)
##              mpg        cyl       disp        hp
## mpg    36.324103  -9.172379  -633.0972 -320.7321
## cyl    -9.172379   3.189516   199.6603  101.9315
## disp -633.097208 199.660282 15360.7998 6721.1587
## hp   -320.732056 101.931452  6721.1587 4700.8669

Or, we can sweep() twice:

# From correlation to covariance - 3
sweep(sweep(R, 1, StDev, FUN = "*"), 2, StDev, FUN = "*")
##              mpg        cyl       disp        hp
## mpg    36.324103  -9.172379  -633.0972 -320.7321
## cyl    -9.172379   3.189516   199.6603  101.9315
## disp -633.097208 199.660282 15360.7998 6721.1587
## hp   -320.732056 101.931452  6721.1587 4700.8669

or scale() and t() twice:

# From correlation to covariance - 5
scale(t(scale(t(R), center = F, scale = 1/StDev)), 
      center = F, scale = 1/StDev)
##              mpg        cyl       disp        hp
## mpg    36.324103  -9.172379  -633.0972 -320.7321
## cyl    -9.172379   3.189516   199.6603  101.9315
## disp -633.097208 199.660282 15360.7998 6721.1587
## hp   -320.732056 101.931452  6721.1587 4700.8669
## attr(,"scaled:scale")
##         mpg         cyl        disp          hp 
## 0.165921457 0.559934979 0.008068505 0.014585154

Finally, we can use the outer product as follows:

# From correlation to covariance - 6
R * outer(StDev, StDev)
##              mpg        cyl       disp        hp
## mpg    36.324103  -9.172379  -633.0972 -320.7321
## cyl    -9.172379   3.189516   199.6603  101.9315
## disp -633.097208 199.660282 15360.7998 6721.1587
## hp   -320.732056 101.931452  6721.1587 4700.8669

Do you have a cleaner or faster trick for this in R? Drop a comment below and I’ll be happy to feature it here!

Thanks for reading, and happy coding!

(P.S. If you enjoyed this post, check out my book “Field Research Methods in Agriculture: An Introduction with R” via the link below!)

Prof. Andrea Onofri
Department of Agricultural, Food and Environmental Sciences
University of Perugia (Italy)

items.title: Crossing the Threshold: How OpenAI and Anthropic Approach Autonomy and Safety in Financial Agents
items.summary: OpenAI’s Joseph Kim talks about the threshold phenomenon at AIE NY today. One of the key themes at the AI Engineer New York conference this week was how to balance agent autonomy with security and safety . Both frontier labs and financial firms focused on this issue in their presentations this week. The main lesson: safe autonomy depends on where you put controls and human judgment , rather than how many restrictions you impose. Sponsor: Build shopping into your agent with shop.dev Adding commerce to an agent usually means rebuilding search and checkout from scratch. shop.dev gives you a single API for shopping in any agent or app. One connection gives you access to over a billion products with current price and availability, instant sign in with Shop, and one-tap Shop Pay checkout that happens right in the conversation. It’s open to any developer, with no account or key needed to try it. → Try shop.dev today Joseph Kim , Head of ChatGPT for Financial Services at OpenAI, gave a keynote at AIE New York today. (We also did a special podcast with Kim, which will be released shortly.) He talked about reliability and a “threshold of usefulness,” which he said is “the point where a model becomes capable and reliable enough to save you time.” Kim argued that ever-growing model capability will soon take financial analysts over the threshold and allow them to delegate more work to agents. He made some specific predictions about AI’s role in finance in 2027. Not only will the financial industry rely less on Excel and PowerPoint next year, he claimed, but agents will be good enough to do “investment idea generation and trading.” The “rising tide” of model capabilities is also leading to better traceability . “In finance, you need to be able to check where a number came from and understand the context around it,” said Kim. “We wanted that review to be a natural part of the [ChatGPT for Financial Services] experience. These are the kind of product details that help turn a model’s capabilities into work that someone can use. ” Joseph Kim at AIE NY; photo by Richard MacManus As for when a human needs to be in the loop, Kim framed this as a product design decision. “How would the interface change? What would the user still need to control, review, or approve? Those are product design questions you can start working on now.” Balancing AI Safety and Innovation at a Hedge Fund John Feminella , SVP Architecture at the hedge fund Two Sigma , is tackling the exact kinds of product design questions Kim referenced. In a keynote, he talked about five of the controls they’ve implemented to keep agents in check without limiting model capabilities. Feminella argued that safety and innovation shouldn’t be viewed as opposite ends of a spectrum. He was especially critical of “approval fatigue,” where a person approving everything can hold back innovation — and also introduce risk, if they’re not fully paying attention to all the decisions they’re required to make. At Two Sigma, they’ve implemented a set of controls , which he defined as “guardrails and shared capabilities that let teams move in ways that don’t hinder what they’re trying to do.” The controls are composable, meaning “each one does one job and then together they let us run agents with real autonomy at an appropriate level of safety.” One of the controls is to use auto-mode classifiers , which Feminella said “make decisions about routine calls and then send a person only the requests that are most important, the ones that are most likely to make a difference.” Classifiers can be used for ambiguous cases, whereas deterministic rules are better for clear cases. Anthropic: Give agents context, then define the boundaries of trust Anthropic’s presentation outlined a similar framework, in its case with the goal of building “trust” into financial agentic workflows. Last month, Anthropic announced Claude for Financial Advisors , allowing financial advisors to connect their systems to Claude and a set of workflow skills. At AIE this week, Belinda Neal , Managing Director of Financial Services at Anthropic, explained why Anthropic has partnered with financial firms on the new product. “Every so often, a model crosses a threshold. And when it does, a wave of working changes.” Neal’s colleague Keon Shahab , who works on applied AI at Anthropic, then talked about “building the trust layer for the agents.” He said this involves three steps: “Who the agent is acting as with an identity and permissions layer . How we can sandbox and determine the approval layer of the agent, so that someone is signing off before it acts. And lastly, how we know the agent will still work once we adjust any variables over time.” Shahab illustrated the boundary between proposing and acting with a trade break investigation agent, which would recommend an order amendment for human approval. “We want it [the agent] to just propose new amendments to our orders data, not actually make those amendments,” he said. “By building once with a foundational layer that you trust , you can work at speed to deploy many agents at scale,” Shahab concluded. Bloomberg: Enforce security outside the model As Head of Architecture & Emerging Technologies in the Office of the CTO at Bloomberg, Andrey Rybka has the responsibility to balance autonomy and scale at the company. In a presentation today at AIE, Rybka talked about a series of real-life events where agents caused havoc — and the defenses that can help prevent it . These include scoped identities and credentials, controls over tool calls, outbound traffic restrictions, audit trails, budgets, and kill switches. In one example, an agent treated instructions embedded in a marketplace review as an instruction to stock a product. Rybka recommended input validation, prompt injection defenses, provenance tracking, and human approval for high-value actions. “We want deterministic controls outside the model, ” Rybka said. “Check every call, log it, and keep a kill switch.” Go fast and stop safely Even though frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic are building a ‘trust framework’ for financial agents, ultimately it’s up to financial firms to put controls around their agents . Two Sigma’s John Feminella hit the nail on the head: implement controls that enable autonomy to happen, but don’t put up roadblocks. Or as he put it in his conclusion: “Why do cars have brakes? It’s not just so that you can stop, it’s so that you can go fast and stop safely.”

items.title: AI Email Personalization Needs an Evidence Gate
items.summary: Control source freshness, risky inferences, consent, review, and recovery before sending. AI-Generated Illustration of an Email Evidence Gate A personalized opening line can sound ready even when nobody’s sure where it came from. The recipient’s role may be old. A public post may belong to someone with the same name. The contact may have opted out since the draft was made. I wouldn’t let that line reach the send queue until its source, freshness, permission to use the data, and reviewer are visible. If your team is comparing AI email personalization tools, look beyond the quality of the draft. You need to know what happens when the evidence is missing or the contact record changes. Set the evidence boundary before choosing a tool A prospective recipient record contains a name, company, role, email address, and a link to a public company announcement. The drafting system should receive only fields approved for this campaign, and it should use only permitted fields in the message. The campaign owner must also establish whether the contact may receive it. I’d want those decisions written down before connecting the record to a tool. The campaign owner can approve ordinary source fields, while the data owner sets rules for checking whether they are still current. Someone responsible for privacy and sending rules needs to establish which contacts may receive the campaign and which inferences are excluded. On a small team, one person may hold several of these responsibilities. Each decision still needs to be visible. “Public” doesn’t settle permission. The UK Information Commissioner’s Office says business contact details identifying an individual can be personal data, and using publicly available personal data for direct marketing still requires compliance with data protection rules. Its business-to-business marketing guidance also distinguishes corporate subscribers from sole traders and certain partnerships under UK electronic marketing rules. I would have the campaign owner establish the rules that apply to the audience before marking collected addresses as eligible. Some material shouldn’t enter the drafting system at all. Scattered clues might suggest a person’s health, beliefs, financial trouble, or family situation. I would exclude those inferences from outreach inputs rather than ask a reviewer whether the resulting line sounds tactful. The ICO’s guidance on special category data explains that profiling can create sensitive inferences from other information. A source also needs a rule for when to check it again. A company announcement may remain useful long after publication; a person’s job title can change. Review points should reflect the field and its likely rate of change. An expired field returns to data review. The model doesn’t get to make an uncertain record sound current. Make every generated claim traceable “Your team recently expanded into Europe” looks like a plausible opening. Suppose its source is a company page about an office that opened years ago. The sentence is fluent, but the word recently has no support. For a claim about the recipient or their organization, I would keep the source link or internal record, retrieval date, relevant passage, generated wording, and review decision together. The reviewer can inspect what the source actually establishes about that recipient at that time. If a claim rests on a name match, the record should show how the person was identified. Tracing a Claim Across Email Drafts Unknown is a valid result. An unconfirmed role can be left out. An announcement with no clear date cannot be described as recent. Conflicting sources put the claim on hold until someone resolves them. A generic line may still be available, but it shouldn’t quietly carry an invented connection to the recipient. Traceability has a second use after approval. If a source turns out to be wrong, the campaign owner needs to find the drafts that relied on it. I would preserve the approved wording and the source state seen by the reviewer; a link alone may lead to a page that has since changed. A reviewer should be able to retrieve the evidence behind a specific sentence and find other drafts that use it. I would verify that behavior in your own setup. A product description cannot establish it. Separate drafting from permission to send A generated draft may be worth editing while the contact is still ineligible or a claim still needs proof. I would let automation suggest copy, then require a named reviewer to release the exact version that will be sent. The reviewer needs the claim beside its source and the contact’s current sending status. If either the recipient or the wording changes, the earlier approval needs another look. Risk changes who should decide. A verified company announcement may fit an ordinary review. A new audience segment, an uncertain identity match, or a claim about an individual calls for the owner of that risk. A second approval cannot override an input policy that excludes a sensitive inference. For US commercial email, the FTC’s CAN-SPAM guidance for businesses describes requirements including accurate sender and subject information, a valid postal address, an opt-out mechanism, and honoring opt-out requests. Other destinations may have different rules. A sending-rule check also leaves the reviewer with the content decision: the evidence must support what the message says about its recipient. A tool demonstration should include a draft with an unsupported line. The reviewer should be able to see the gap and block the line, approve a correction without authorizing later edits, and identify who can pause queued sends. Those actions matter more to this decision than a gallery of convincing examples. Test suppression and exception paths before scale Give the proposed workflow an opted-out contact whose profile otherwise looks ideal. Add a stale role, conflicting sources, a weak name match, and a duplicate record under another address. The assigned reviewer is unavailable in another case. Label the expected outcome for each record before running it through the workflow. The opted-out contact must remain blocked even if a draft was previously approved. The stale role returns to data review; conflicting sources hold the claim they affect. A weak match cannot supply a personal opening. The duplicate needs to inherit the relevant suppression decision, or the same person may re-enter the queue through another record. An unavailable reviewer leaves a message waiting with a visible owner. Opt-Out After Draft Approval Contact preferences can change between drafting and release. Suppression needs another check near the send decision, using the current record rather than the state captured when the draft was generated. For teams sending to Gmail accounts, Google’s email sender guidelines describe unsubscribe expectations and additional requirements for bulk senders. The sending service’s handling of those requirements needs checking in the actual setup. Use this test set to check whether the proposed controls behave as intended. It does not predict campaign performance. The test record should contain the input, expected outcome, observed outcome, and owner of any mismatch. Strong copy cannot compensate for a suppressed contact reaching the send queue. Keep correction and escalation human-owned Blocked messages need a destination. A queue entry should say why the message stopped, who owns it, and what would permit its release. Otherwise, “needs review” can become a backlog with no reliable distinction between an evidence gap and a routine edit. A data owner can correct a wrong role in the source record. A reviewer can reject or revise the claim that used it. The campaign owner decides whether related messages remain paused. The person responsible for privacy and sending rules handles questions about contact eligibility or prohibited inputs. I would keep those decisions with the record so the next colleague can see what changed. The correction must reach every affected draft. Fixing the wording of one message leaves the same faulty field available to others. A rejected source claim should let the campaign owner locate queued messages built from that source. An exception ends with a documented release, a revised draft awaiting approval, or a continued block. When comparing tools, I would look for a visible exception queue, source-level corrections, versioned approvals, suppression that survives imports, and a human-controlled campaign pause. Where the documentation is silent, I would ask to see the behavior. An approval button alone tells me little about what happens after the underlying record changes. Recover from a bad send without hiding it Suppose an email goes out with an outdated role and a line implying the sender knows about the recipient’s private circumstances. Further sends using the same rule or source should pause while the campaign owner establishes how far the error traveled. The sent message, recipient set, source records, reviewer decision, and send time need to be preserved before anyone repairs the inputs. The data owner, reviewer, and campaign owner each have a different decision to make. The data owner checks the faulty record and finds others that share its source. The reviewer identifies the unsupported claim in queued drafts. The campaign owner determines which sends stay paused and whether a correction to recipients is appropriate. A privacy or sending-rule concern goes to the person responsible for that decision. A sent email cannot be removed from every inbox. Recovery means stopping the faulty path, deciding how to address affected recipients, and correcting the rule or data source before release resumes. I would keep the failed version and the repair in the audit record, including who approved the change. A colleague reviewing the next campaign should be able to see why the pause happened. I also wouldn’t claim the evidence gate improved replies, conversions, or deliverability without real campaign baselines and a sound comparison. The immediate decision needs no performance claim. If the team cannot show what supports a personal line, who cleared the contact, and who can stop the next send, I would leave that line in draft. A tool demonstration should include a draft with an unsupported line. The reviewer should be able to see the gap and block the line, approve a correction without authorizing later edits, and identify who can pause queued sends. The reviewer identifies the unsupported claim in queued drafts. The campaign owner determines which sends stay paused and whether a correction to recipients is appropriate. A privacy or sending-rule concern goes to the person responsible for that decision.

A sent email cannot be removed from every inbox. Recovery means stopping the faulty path, deciding how to address affected recipients, and correcting the rule or data source before release resumes. items.title: Tree Appreciator
items.summary: Tool: Tree Appreciator Another game experiment with Claude. This one used the default Claude iPhone app (chat mode, not Claude Code mode), where I prompted Claude Opus 5.5 Max with: Build a three js game called "Tree appreciator" - it shows you two algorithmically generated trees and the game mechanics is about appreciating the differences between them. Think hard about how to make sure it is both fun and beautiful. Somewhat embarrassingly given my recent talk , I've found that telling Opus 5.5 "make sure it is fun" works uncomfortably well. In this case Claude crunched for 3 hours and 7 minutes before retuning a cosy little spot-the-difference game with music and animation and achievements that's quite compelling to play. items.title: Ex-OpenAI employee accused of planting a recording device booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia
items.summary: OpenAI previously said it used its AI models to help identify the employee who allegedly planted a recording device. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images A former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device had one-way tickets to Saudi Arabia booked. Federal prosecutors disclosed Abdulrahman Alfozan's travel plans in previously sealed court documents. Alfozan was arrested on October 9 and made his first court appearance on Tuesday. Federal prosecutors said a former OpenAI engineer accused of planting a recording device had a one-way ticket booked to Saudi Arabia. In newly unsealed court documents, it was revealed that the federal government feared its case against Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national, might be jeopardized if information about it leaked. "The defendant, his wife, and a third family member have booked one-way tickets from San Francisco to Saudi Arabia (via Istanbul) for Monday, October 12, 2026," the prosecutors, including US Attorney for the Northern District of California Craig Missakian, wrote in an October 8 court filing. The prosecutors wrote that Alfozan had "the means—and will have an incentive—to flee the United States sooner if he learns about this case before he is arrested." On October 9, the FBI arrested Alfozan. He made his initial court appearance on Wednesday when the government unveiled its case against him. Alfozan has been charged with "use of an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications," a felony that carries a maximum of five years in prison. According to the criminal complaint against Alfozan, the company found a USB device surreptitiously placed on the back of a television located in an " executive conference room." The device was concealed in toilet paper, the complaint said. Alfozan's lawyer did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Business Insider. OpenAI previously said in a statement that it used "our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier." items.title: Epic says its new vibe-coded Epic Games Launcher is faster than Steam
items.summary: Nearly eight years after Epic took on Steam with its own Game Store and launcher, the Fortnite maker is deploying a new tool to give it an edge over Valve: vibe coding. In announcing the new publicly available "Preview" build of its Epic Games Launcher, Epic writes that "programming is hard. So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that’s way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look." And while that might sound a little tongue-in-cheek, Epic Games Store General Manager and VP Martin Keely told PC Gamer that the team "started from scratch" and used AI as "a tool to write and review new features and new capabilities from the ground up in a different tech stack than what we had previously." The goal, Keely said, was to "look at functionality that existed [in the current Epic Games Launcher] and [say] we want to replicate that, but not the code itself." Speaking to IGN , Keely clarified that using AI to code the new Launcher "made us more efficient and allowed a small team to rewrite the code base and be able to launch it faster across platforms, support Windows and Mac, and we're going to have a Linux version as well." Read full article Comments

items.title: AI Agent Blamed for Deleting Entire Upcoming Season of TV Show
items.summary: Did a dog eat your homework? Or maybe an AI obliterated your files? In a world of Claudes and Muses, it’s common for an AI agent to run amok , and even more fashionable to blame an AI when it all goes wrong . The Swedish newspaper Aftonbladet reports one of the most incredible examples we’ve heard of this so far: an AI agent apparently deleted the entire upcoming season of a reality competition show called “The Challenge Sverige,” just weeks before it was supposed to premiere. There’s no hope of recovering the files, the paper was told, so the production team at Mastiff will have to recut the entire season together from scratch. According to the paper’s sources, the deletion happened after Mastiff allowed an AI agent into the server. With a year’s worth of work down the toilet, hundreds of people will now need to go in and cobble together the next season all over again, which was originally supposed to air on November 22. TV4, the channel which was supposed to air the season, confirmed that it was pushing back the premier to next year after a “technical breakdown” but said it hadn’t heard about whether an AI agent was at fault for the deletion. In a comment after the story was first published, though, TV4’s program director Mia Lindqvist tried to shift some of the blame away from AI, saying it wasn’t an “AI agent that acted independently” (via a machine translation from Swedish). “On the other hand, most production companies use AI in their work processes these days, but that’s a completely different matter,” she continued. “In this case, the big problem is that their backup didn’t work and that means they have to recut everything from scratch. The raw material exists, so there is no problem, but of course it means that we lose time.” In all, she said the season deletion came down to “human factor” and “not AI” — which, it’s worth noting, falls short of ruling out AI involvement. Ahmed Behran, the show’s host, appeared to be in good spirts when Aftonbladet broke the news to him. “Is it true?! I knew AI would be the death of me, this is just the beginning,” he told the newspaper, laughing. items.title: Lab-in-the-Loop at Compute Speed — Ian Quigley, Leash Bio
items.summary: A few years ago I stumbled upon Leash Bio’s Substack , and was hooked. Be it their Kaggle competition that showed that no, we really haven’t solved protein-ligand binding , or their crazy discovery that knowing a molecule’s author is perhaps all you need to know to predict how good it is . Their substack — or at least Owl Posting ’s 1 deep dive on them — should be required reading for any scientist trying to do chemistry with AI. So I was super excited to finally be able to sit down with Ian Quigley from Leash Bio, and pick his brain. Leash specializes in DNA Encoded Libraries (aka “DELs”), a way of collecting ridiculously high-throughput interaction data between proteins and small molecules. 2 Before I discovered Leash, I had heard nothing but horror stories from DEL users. And yet, Ian and friends somehow found a way to tame the beast, extracting clean and reproducible data that is just perfect for large scale modeling. Without teasing too much, the answer comes down to epistemic rigor, and an incredible conviction that you just have to Do The Thing. It gets even better! Near the end of this episode, Ian teases something his team was just playing with when we recorded: an AI playground for agents to do verifiable scientific reasoning. They discovered the data they had spent the last few years collecting could provide tens of thousands of “lab-in-the-loop” simulations, just what an agent needs for scientific RL. Two months later, it’s matured into Minos, and today they’re releasing a full preprint , blog , and open dataset . We’ll be releasing a lightning podcast in a few days with an update. Stay tuned! We had a blast with Ian, probably one of our most fun episodes to date. For both complete chemistry novices and expert AI x Bio practitioners, we think you’ll get something out of this. Enjoy! We covered: Why DELs traumatize everyone who touches them, and how Leash puts dozens of barcodes on each molecule to catch proteins that bind the DNA instead of the drug. Ian’s rule that biology only scales two ways: taking pictures and sequencing DNA. The Kaggle competition : about 4B measurements from a basement and about 2,000 teams, with nobody beating chance on an unseen chemical library. Also why Leash quietly feared co-folding would make them obsolete. Clever Hans in ChEMBL : models can guess a molecule’s chemist from its structure, and “who made it” predicts activity about as well as the structure does. Hermes , trained only on Leash’s own data, keeping pace with Boltz on public benchmarks. Plus the BRD4 molecule Boltz had already seen in the PDB. Breaking the pocket : engineering protein mutants at scale after catching Hermes memorizing “nicknames” for proteins instead of binding sites. Lumacaftor -like hits as an accidental detector for misfolded proteins. The agent sandbox : LLMs that reason about SAR in plain English, hunting for the best binders among 6.5M molecules on a budget of 100. The Recursion mafia, and why its alumni companies all rhyme. The Kosuri paradox : if you can collect the data, why do you need the model? Going from a DEL hit to good mouse PKPD in six months on an inflammation program, and the case for pills over antibodies on cytokine targets. What stops a better-funded lab from outscaling them, and Ian’s by-fiat wish for massively parallel purification. 1 The hands-down best bio blogger on the internet. 2 As always, the secret here is to map your problem to a combinatorial library and a readout using Next Generation Sequencing. We talk about this in depth in the podcast!

items.title: 382 translations crash their Android apps: a census of 1.26 million strings on F-Droid
items.summary: Made with AI agents by MV2 of Munim, Inc. Every number below comes from code and data you can rerun: android-translation-crash-census (code Apache-2.0, data CC BY 4.0). When an Android app calls getString(R.string.files_left, n) , the translation for the user's language goes to java.util.Formatter . If a translator typed %1$ where the English says %1$s , or wrote 50% without escaping it, the call throws. English never breaks, so the developer never sees it. Only people using that language do. How often does that happen in practice? Searches of GitHub, arXiv and the web turned up single-project fixes (Commons, Firefox for Android, ConnectBot, OsmAnd) but no measurement across apps. The census makes one. What was checked Every source repository behind F-Droid's index: 4,476 repositories for 4,667 apps, latest commit, read in 11 minutes on 4 cores. 3,755 have Android string resources. 1,703 have translations of strings with printf placeholders. That is 1,262,958 translations . Each one, and its English source, was formatted with OpenJDK 21's real java.util.Formatter , using arguments of the types the English string expects. For repositories with a failing translation, the census also reads the Kotlin and Java code to see whether anything formats that string with arguments. A broken string nobody formats can't crash. What it found 382 translations in 99 repositories throw whatever the app passes. 250 of them, in 67 repositories, are strings the app's own code formats. Those are the crashes users can actually hit. One hand correction brings that to 246: four Cashiro strings use %t , which rejects the Integer the census passed but accepts the Long the app passes, so they print the wrong text instead of crashing. About 1 in 3,300 formatted translations crashes. It's concentrated: ownCloud's Uyghur file alone has 47 reachable crashes ( % 1 $ s instead of %1$s ), and Cashiro and Wikimedia Commons follow. Most affected apps have one to four. The exceptions are UnknownFormatConversionException 251, MissingFormatArgumentException 59, FormatFlagsConversionMismatchException 48, IllegalFormatConversionException 20 and IllegalFormatFlagsException 4. The mistakes, by kind A small rule-based classifier names the mistake behind the first placeholder Formatter can't use. For the 250 reachable crashes: Kind Example Rows Repos malformed index % 1 $ s , %$1s 50 5 stray percent (%1$d%) , 电量 %1$d % 45 26 conversion missing %1$ musikspelare , Wideo (%1) 43 18 argument not passed a Russian few form reading %2$d 35 15 flag mismatch Mesaj:% s 34 14 conversion letter in another script %1$с , %1$دم , %1$δδ 26 6 wrong type %g or %t for %d 10 5 unknown Latin conversion %1$DH , %2$vs 7 4 A stray % is the most widespread mistake (26 repositories). The malformed index is the biggest cluster, but it is almost all one Uyghur file. Turkish % s makes up 22 of the 34 flag mismatches: the space between % and s is read as a flag. The kind I didn't expect: the placeholder letter itself gets translated. Russian %1$с (a Cyrillic es , not an s ), Bulgarian %1$дмлн. for %1$dM , Arabic %1$دم ( dal for d ), Greek %1$δδ . To a reader each looks fine. To Formatter , с is an unknown conversion. It's narrower than I expected: 26 reachable rows in 6 apps, and in 14 of them the letter looks like or transliterates the Latin one. Every route shipped one The hand-checked cases came through Crowdin, Transifex, translatewiki.net, Lokalise, Weblate, and files edited straight in the repository. All of those platforms have placeholder checks of some kind. A check that warns but doesn't block isn't enough once a release script pulls translations in automatically. (A per-platform crash rate is the next thing the census measures.) A static check you can run in CI The census compares the real JVM with a static check, the java-format rule in l10n-guard (Python, standard library only, Apache-2.0). Across all 1.26 million pairs it called 375 of the 382 JVM crashes errors and the other 7 warnings. It never called a working translation an error (precision 1.0, recall 0.98). python l10n_guard.py android app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml app/src/main/res/values-ru/strings.xml It exits non-zero on an error, so it can gate a pull request that brings in translations. Android Lint's StringFormatInvalid catches many of these too, but only in builds that run lint after the translations land. Reporting them The census files nothing by itself. Each case was checked by hand against the project's current code before anything was reported, and only to projects whose rules allow AI-assisted reports. Mastodon and AnkiDroid don't, so they weren't reported; their rows are in the data for their translators. So far: Tallybook merged the fix for 9 Turkish strings ( #397 ). The maintainer reproduced the crash on an emulator and found a path I had missed: one of the strings crashes the Utility settings screen as soon as it opens, and has since 2019. ownCloud acknowledged the 55 broken Uyghur strings ( #5018 ). Open: Homer Audio Player 2 #26 (Chinese battery indicator), Shader Editor #294 (a Russian plural reading an argument it never gets). Limits Only the latest commit of each default branch was read, so a translation may already be fixed on its platform. Code use is pattern-matched. Strings looked up by name at runtime count as unused, so the reachable count is a floor in that sense. So is leaving out the 190 translations that throw only if the app passes text: reading code shows some of those do crash. Verdicts come from OpenJDK 21. Android's Formatter is the same code for these cases, but edge cases can differ by API level. I reproduced nothing on a device. One maintainer did, on an emulator. If you maintain an app in the data, findings.csv links every row to the exact line at the commit read. This article and the census were made with AI agents working for MV2 of Munim, Inc. The numbers were checked against the published data.

The mistakes, by kind

A small rule-based classifier names the mistake behind the first placeholder Formatter can't use. For the 250 reachable crashes:

Kind Example Rows Repos malformed index % 1 $ s, %$1s 50 5 stray percent (%1$d%), 电量 %1$d % 45 26 conversion missing %1$ musikspelare, Wideo (%1) 43 18 argument not passed a Russian few form reading %2$d 35 15 flag mismatch Mesaj:% s 34 14 conversion letter in another script %1$с, %1$دم, %1$δδ 26 6 wrong type %g or %t for %d 10 5 unknown Latin conversion %1$DH, %2$vs 7 4

A stray % is the most widespread mistake (26 repositories). The malformed index is the biggest cluster, but it is almost all one Uyghur file. Turkish % s makes up 22 of the 34 flag mismatches: the space between % and s is read as a flag.

The kind I didn't expect: the placeholder letter itself gets translated. Russian %1$с (a Cyrillic es, not an s), Bulgarian %1$дмлн. for %1$dM, Arabic %1$دم (dal for d), Greek %1$δδ. To a reader each looks fine. To Formatter, с is an unknown conversion. It's narrower than I expected: 26 reachable rows in 6 apps, and in 14 of them the letter looks like or transliterates the Latin one.

Every route shipped one

The hand-checked cases came through Crowdin, Transifex, translatewiki.net, Lokalise, Weblate, and files edited straight in the repository. All of those platforms have placeholder checks of some kind. A check that warns but doesn't block isn't enough once a release script pulls translations in automatically. (A per-platform crash rate is the next thing the census measures.)

A static check you can run in CI

The census compares the real JVM with a static check, the java-format rule in l10n-guard (Python, standard library only, Apache-2.0). Across all 1.26 million pairs it called 375 of the 382 JVM crashes errors and the other 7 warnings. It never called a working translation an error (precision 1.0, recall 0.98).

python l10n_guard.py android app/src/main/res/values/strings.xml app/src/main/res/values-ru/strings.xml

It exits non-zero on an error, so it can gate a pull request that brings in translations.

Android Lint's StringFormatInvalid catches many of these too, but only in builds that run lint after the translations land.

Reporting them

The census files nothing by itself. Each case was checked by hand against the project's current code before anything was reported, and only to projects whose rules allow AI-assisted reports. Mastodon and AnkiDroid don't, so they weren't reported; their rows are in the data for their translators.

So far:

  • Tallybook merged the fix for 9 Turkish strings (#397). The maintainer reproduced the crash on an emulator and found a path I had missed: one of the strings crashes the Utility settings screen as soon as it opens, and has since 2019.
  • ownCloud acknowledged the 55 broken Uyghur strings (#5018).
  • Open: Homer Audio Player 2 #26 (Chinese battery indicator), Shader Editor #294 (a Russian plural reading an argument it never gets).
Limits
  • Only the latest commit of each default branch was read, so a translation may already be fixed on its platform.
  • Code use is pattern-matched. Strings looked up by name at runtime count as unused, so the reachable count is a floor in that sense. So is leaving out the 190 translations that throw only if the app passes text: reading code shows some of those do crash.
  • Verdicts come from OpenJDK 21. Android's Formatter is the same code for these cases, but edge cases can differ by API level.
  • I reproduced nothing on a device. One maintainer did, on an emulator.

If you maintain an app in the data, findings.csv links every row to the exact line at the commit read.

This article and the census were made with AI agents working for MV2 of Munim, Inc. The numbers were checked against the published data.

items.title: Auto MDM Enroll Failed (Event 76): A Read-First Intune Group Policy Auto-Enrollment Triage
items.summary: You linked the Enable automatic MDM enrollment using default Microsoft Entra credentials GPO. Devices are domain joined, Entra Connect is syncing, and a week later half the fleet still is not in Intune. On one of the missing PCs, Event Viewer says Event ID 76 — Auto MDM Enroll: Failed . The usual first moves are to run dsregcmd /leave everywhere, delete enrollment registry keys, or flip the GPO to Device Credential "because that's the one for computers." Hold off. GPO auto-enrollment is a short chain: tenant allows the user to auto-enroll (MDM user scope + license) → device is hybrid joined and the user has a PRT → GPO lands and creates the EnterpriseMgmt task → the task runs and the enrollment attempt logs Event 75 (success) or 76 (failure) → Intune-side gates (enrollment restrictions, device limits) accept the device . Most "auto-enrollment not working" tickets die in scope/licensing, a missing PRT, or the wrong credential type. This post walks them in order. Every step below only reads until the change table at the end. If the device shows Pending in Entra or AzureAdJoined : NO , stop here and use the hybrid join Pending triage first. MDM auto-enrollment rides on top of hybrid join; it cannot fix it. If the device is already enrolled and simply not checking in, use the Company Portal / device not syncing triage instead. TL;DR Microsoft's auto-enrollment checklist is: valid Intune license on the user, MDM user scope = All (or Some including the user), MAM/WIP user scope = None , default MDM discovery URL, Windows 10 1709+, and dsregcmd /status showing AzureAdJoined: YES, DomainJoined: YES, AzureAdPrt: YES . The GPO creates a task called Schedule created by enrollment client for automatically enrolling in MDM from Microsoft Entra ID under Microsoft > Windows > EnterpriseMgmt . It runs every 5 minutes for one day . No task = the GPO never landed. In DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider/Admin , Event 75 = Auto MDM Enroll succeeded, Event 76 = failed. If you see neither , enrollment was never triggered — go back to the GPO and task. Device Credential is only supported for Intune enrollment with co-management or Azure Virtual Desktop multi-session host pools. For ordinary user PCs, Microsoft's GPO walkthrough selects User Credential . 0x8018002b on Event 76 usually means a non-routable/unverified UPN suffix (like .local ) or MDM user scope = None — both are reads, not re-registrations. Where in the chain did it break? Step What happens Typical symptom when it breaks 1. Tenant scope MDM user scope All/Some includes the user; WIP (MAM) user scope None; default discovery URL Event 76 with 0x8018002b ; nothing enrolls for one department 2. User license Intune license (plus Entra ID P1 for automatic enrollment) Enrollment failures report row for "unlicensed"; only some users fail 3. Join + PRT Hybrid joined; user signed in with a PRT AzureAdPrt : NO ; "Get AAD device token failure"; wrong TenantId 4. GPO applied AutoEnrollMDM set; credential type matches the scenario No EnterpriseMgmt task; Device Credential (0x0/0x1) failures on user PCs 5. Task runs Scheduled task triggers every 5 min for a day No Event 75/76 at all; Task Scheduler 7016 already-enrolled code 6. Enrollment attempt Event 75 (success) or Event 76 (failure + code) Event 76 with an HRESULT you can decode 7. Intune-side gates Windows (MDM) allowed; device limit not reached; Entra join settings allow it 0x80180014 ; Event 71 "too many devices enrolled"; DeviceCapReached Pick two missing devices you can reach and one that enrolled fine. Comparing a good and a bad PC at each step answers most tickets faster than any portal. Step 1: Read MDM user scope and discovery URL In the Microsoft Intune admin center > Devices > Enrollment > Windows > Automatic Enrollment (the same blade appears in Entra as Mobility (MDM and MAM) > Microsoft Intune ): Setting Want If wrong MDM user scope All, or Some with a group that contains the failing user None = no auto-enrollment; Some = users outside the group fail WIP user scope (older docs: MAM user scope) None (or users not in both scopes) Microsoft notes MAM/WIP scope can take precedence and break MDM enrollment MDM discovery URL https://enrollment.manage.microsoft.com/enrollmentserver/discovery.svc Custom/blank URL — enrollment never finds the service App you configured Microsoft Intune (not Microsoft Intune Enrollment ) Both are listed; settings on the wrong one do nothing If the scope is Some , read the group membership for the failing user before touching anything else. "Scope = Some, user not in group" looks identical to a broken device from the client side. Step 2: Read licensing for the user who signs in Group Policy auto-enrollment is user-centric : the user who signs in is the one enrolling the device. Microsoft's checklist starts with a valid Intune license on that user, and automatic MDM enrollment is an Entra ID Premium (P1/P2) feature. Read-only license check (Microsoft Graph PowerShell, User.Read.All ): Connect-MgGraph -Scopes 'User.Read.All' Get-MgUserLicenseDetail -UserId 'jdoe@contoso.com' | ForEach-Object { $_ . ServicePlans } | Where-Object ServicePlanName -in 'INTUNE_A' , 'AAD_PREMIUM' , 'AAD_PREMIUM_P2' | Select-Object ServicePlanName , ProvisioningStatus INTUNE_A is the Microsoft Intune Plan 1 service plan. If it is missing or not Success , you have your answer for that user. In the Intune admin center, Devices > Monitor > Enrollment failures (or Troubleshooting + support for one user) shows each failed attempt with a reason and enrollment method. To see failures for unlicensed users there, use the filter User not found or licensed . Step 3: Read join type, PRT, and tenant info on the device On a failing device, signed in as the affected user: dsregcmd /status | Select-String -Pattern 'AzureAdJoined' , 'DomainJoined' , 'AzureAdPrt' , 'TenantName' , 'TenantId' Result Meaning Next AzureAdJoined YES, DomainJoined YES, AzureAdPrt YES Join + token healthy Continue to Step 4 AzureAdJoined NO (DomainJoined YES) Hybrid join not finished Hybrid join Pending triage AzureAdJoined YES, AzureAdPrt NO No user token to enroll with AzureAdPrt : NO triage TenantName / TenantId is a different tenant Leftover join from a previous tenant Read TenantInfo below before any leave/rejoin Workplace joined (Entra registered) only Not the GPO scenario Microsoft's GPO path is for domain-joined, hybrid-joined devices Microsoft documents a specific 0x80180002b case: Event 76 plus AzureAdPrt : NO plus wrong TenantId / AuthCodeUrl , caused by a device previously joined to another tenant that did not unjoin cleanly. Read the leftover tenant data (read-only): Get-ChildItem 'HKLM:\SYSTEM\ControlSet001\Control\CloudDomainJoin\TenantInfo' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | ForEach-Object { Get-ItemProperty $_ . PSPath } | Select-Object PSChildName , AuthCodeUrl , AccessTokenUrl If PSChildName (the tenant ID) is not your tenant, that device is a re-join candidate — but only after you have read it, and only that device. Step 4: Read whether the GPO landed and which credential it uses Get-ItemProperty -Path 'HKLM:\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\MDM' -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object AutoEnrollMDM , UseAADCredentialType gpresult /scope computer /r Value Meaning AutoEnrollMDM = 1 The policy is enabled on this device Key missing GPO not applied (link, security filtering, WMI filter, replication) UseAADCredentialType = 1 User Credential UseAADCredentialType = 2 Device Credential The Device Credential option arrived in the Windows 10 1903 MDM.admx. Microsoft's guidance: Device Credential is only supported for Intune enrollment with co-management or Azure Virtual Desktop multi-session host pools , because the Intune subscription is user-centric. If ordinary user PCs log Auto MDM Enroll: Device Credential (0x0) / (0x1), Failed , read the GPO credential type before anything else. If the policy does not appear in the GPO editor at all, your central store has an old MDM.admx . Microsoft's doc says the latest MDM.admx is backwards compatible. Also check that nothing on the device sets Disable MDM Enrollment : Microsoft maps 0x80180026 ( MENROLL_E_DEVICE_MANAGEMENT_BLOCKED ) to that policy, and the same code shows up when the classic Intune PC agent is installed. Step 5: Read the EnterpriseMgmt task and its history Get-ScheduledTask | Where-Object TaskPath -like '\Microsoft\Windows\EnterpriseMgmt*' | Get-ScheduledTaskInfo | Select-Object TaskPath , TaskName , LastRunTime , @{ n = 'LastResultHex' ; e = { '0x{0:X8}' -f $_ . LastTaskResult } } You are looking for Schedule created by enrollment client for automatically enrolling in MDM from Microsoft Entra ID . Microsoft documents that it is created when the GPO is deployed and runs every 5 minutes during one day . Task Scheduler's own log ( Microsoft > Windows > Task Scheduler > Operational ) adds: Event ID Meaning 107 Task triggered 102 Task completed — logged whether or not enrollment succeeded 7016 with code 2149056522 Task did not start: device already enrolled in another MDM ( 2149056522 = 0x8018000A ) Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-TaskScheduler/Operational' ; Id = 102 , 107 , 7016 } -MaxEvents 200 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Where-Object Message -match 'EnterpriseMgmt|enrolling in MDM' | Select-Object TimeCreated , Id , Message If that channel returns nothing, check whether Task Scheduler history is enabled on the device before you conclude the task never ran. A 102 only proves the task finished; Step 6 tells you whether enrollment worked. Step 6: Read Event 75 / 76 and decode the error Get-WinEvent -FilterHashtable @{ LogName = 'Microsoft-Windows-DeviceManagement-Enterprise-Diagnostics-Provider/Admin' ; Id = 71 , 75 , 76 } -MaxEvents 30 -ErrorAction SilentlyContinue | Select-Object TimeCreated , Id , Message | Format-List What you see Documented cause Read next Event 75 Auto MDM Enroll: Succeeded Enrollment worked Device not in the portal? Search by serial/Entra device ID; check sync, not enrollment No 75 and no 76 Enrollment never triggered Steps 4–5 (GPO, task, already enrolled elsewhere) 76 0x8018002b UPN suffix unverified or non-routable (e.g. @contoso.local ), or MDM user scope = None Step 1 scope; user's UPN suffix in AD vs verified domains 76 0x80180002b with AzureAdPrt NO + wrong TenantId Leftover join from a previous tenant Step 3 TenantInfo 76 Device Credential (0x0/0x1) Failed Device Credential outside co-management / AVD multi-session Step 4 UseAADCredentialType 0x80180026 Disable MDM Enrollment policy, or classic Intune PC agent present Step 4; installed software 0x8018000a / 7016 + 2149056522 Device already enrolled (another MDM, or another user's work account) Settings > Accounts > Access work or school; MDM vendor 0x80180014 "Your organization does not support this version of Windows" Windows (MDM) blocked in a device type enrollment restriction Step 7 Event 71 "The account has too many devices enrolled to Mobile Device Management (MDM)" Intune device limit reached (DeviceCapReached) Step 7 device limits For the UPN case, a read-only look at the user in AD: Get-ADUser -Identity jdoe -Properties UserPrincipalName | Select-Object SamAccountName , UserPrincipalName If the suffix is .local (or any domain not verified in Entra), the device side is fine. The fix lives in the UPN suffix and the next Entra Connect sync. For a full evidence bundle you can attach to a ticket, Microsoft's built-in collector is read-only: mdmdiagnosticstool.exe -area "DeviceEnrollment;DeviceProvisioning;Autopilot" -zip "C:\Users\Public\Documents\MDMDiagReport.zip" Step 7: Read the Intune and Entra gates Gate Where Healthy Device type enrollment restriction Intune admin center > Devices > Enrollment > device platform restriction Windows (MDM) allowed for the user's assigned restriction Device limit restriction Intune admin center > Devices > Enrollment > device limit restrictions User's enrolled devices below the limit (stale records count) Users may join devices Entra > Devices > Device settings Set to All (or Selected incl. the user) Maximum number of devices per user Entra > Devices > Device settings User below the quota Enrollment failures report Intune admin center > Devices > Monitor > Enrollment failures Row reason matches what the device logged Microsoft's support guidance on DeviceCapReached is to remove stale device records or adjust the limit in the right service (Intune vs Entra). It is a count problem, not a device problem. When a change is justified Finding Prefer Avoid MDM user scope None, or Some without the user Set scope to All, or add a pilot group to Some Re-imaging devices that were never in scope WIP/MAM user scope overlaps the user Set WIP user scope to None (or remove the overlap) Deleting the Intune app registration in Entra User lacks Intune / Entra P1 Assign the license; let the task retry Mass dsregcmd /leave .local UPN suffix (0x8018002b) Change the UPN suffix to a verified domain; wait for delta sync Re-joining devices whose join is already healthy AzureAdPrt NO with healthy join Work the PRT triage on that device Flipping the GPO to Device Credential Device Credential on ordinary user PCs Set the GPO to User Credential for those PCs Leaving Device Credential outside co-management / AVD multi-session Leftover tenant in TenantInfo (0x80180002b) Microsoft's documented leave → delete objects → rejoin → sync, on that device only Running it fleet-wide "to be safe" Already enrolled elsewhere (0x8018000a) Remove the other MDM / other user's work account first Deleting HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Enrollments keys blindly Windows (MDM) blocked (0x80180014) Allow Windows (MDM) in the restriction assigned to that user Disabling all enrollment restrictions Device cap reached Remove stale device records; adjust the limit if policy allows Making every user a Device Enrollment Manager No task, no events Fix GPO link/filtering/ADMX; gpupdate /force on a pilot Rewriting Intune configuration profiles FAQ What does Event 76 "Auto MDM Enroll: Failed" mean? The GPO-triggered enrollment task ran and the enrollment attempt failed. The code in the message is the clue: 0x8018002b points to UPN suffix or MDM user scope, Device Credential failures point to the GPO credential type, and 0x80180026 points to MDM enrollment being blocked. Event 75 is the success counterpart. There is no Event 75 or 76 at all. Where do I look? Enrollment was never triggered. Confirm AutoEnrollMDM exists under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\MDM , that the EnterpriseMgmt task exists, and whether Task Scheduler logged 7016 with 2149056522 (already enrolled in another MDM). Should the GPO use User Credential or Device Credential? Microsoft supports Device Credential for Intune only with co-management or Azure Virtual Desktop multi-session host pools. For normal user PCs, use User Credential. dsregcmd shows hybrid joined but AzureAdPrt is NO. Will auto-enrollment still work? Microsoft's checklist expects AzureAdPrt: YES. Without a PRT for the signed-in user, the enrollment task has no token to enroll with. Fix the PRT first; the task retries on its own schedule. Should I run dsregcmd /leave or delete enrollment registry keys? Only when you have evidence for it, such as the documented leftover-tenant case (wrong TenantId plus 0x80180002b ), and only on the affected device. It is a change with a re-join and sync cost, not a diagnostic step. Related posts Hybrid Azure AD Join Pending: A Read-First Triage Order for Entra Connect Admins AzureAdPrt : NO in dsregcmd /status: A Read-First Primary Refresh Token Triage Company Portal can't connect / device not syncing: a 10-minute triage order Intune Compliance: Not Applicable, Is Active, Minimum OS Free checklist Auto-enrollment is usually the step right before you require a compliant device in Conditional Access. If half the fleet is not enrolled yet, enforcing that grant locks those users out. The free Conditional Access pre-enforcement checklist keeps break-glass, pilot groups, and report-only review on one page: 👉 https://cashflow4375.gumroad.com/l/ujkqxb?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=aps_first_sale&utm_content=auto-mdm-enroll-failed-event-76 If you want the rest of the Intune runway written down for the team (enrollment hygiene, compliance phasing, break/fix cards and read-only PowerShell snapshots), the Intune & M365 Admin Starter Pack pairs with this triage: https://cashflow4375.gumroad.com/l/joonf?utm_source=devto&utm_medium=article&utm_campaign=aps_first_sale&utm_content=auto-mdm-enroll-failed-event-76 Admin Pack Studio; not affiliated with Microsoft. Steps 1–7 only read. Pilot any scope, GPO, or re-join change on a small device group first, and check current Microsoft docs for auto-enrollment prerequisites and error codes.

  Format-List
What you see Documented cause Read next Event 75 Auto MDM Enroll: Succeeded Enrollment worked Device not in the portal? Search by serial/Entra device ID; check sync, not enrollment No 75 and no 76 Enrollment never triggered Steps 4–5 (GPO, task, already enrolled elsewhere) 76 0x8018002b UPN suffix unverified or non-routable (e.g. @contoso.local), or MDM user scope = None Step 1 scope; user's UPN suffix in AD vs verified domains 76 0x80180002b with AzureAdPrt NO + wrong TenantId Leftover join from a previous tenant Step 3 TenantInfo 76 Device Credential (0x0/0x1) Failed Device Credential outside co-management / AVD multi-session Step 4 UseAADCredentialType 0x80180026 Disable MDM Enrollment policy, or classic Intune PC agent present Step 4; installed software 0x8018000a / 7016 + 2149056522 Device already enrolled (another MDM, or another user's work account) Settings > Accounts > Access work or school; MDM vendor 0x80180014 "Your organization does not support this version of Windows" Windows (MDM) blocked in a device type enrollment restriction Step 7 Event 71 "The account has too many devices enrolled to Mobile Device Management (MDM)" Intune device limit reached (DeviceCapReached) Step 7 device limits

For the UPN case, a read-only look at the user in AD:

Get-ADUser -Identity jdoe -Properties UserPrincipalName | Select-Object SamAccountName, UserPrincipalName

If the suffix is .local (or any domain not verified in Entra), the device side is fine. The fix lives in the UPN suffix and the next Entra Connect sync.

For a full evidence bundle you can attach to a ticket, Microsoft's built-in collector is read-only:

mdmdiagnosticstool.exe -area "DeviceEnrollment;DeviceProvisioning;Autopilot" -zip "C:\Users\Public\Documents\MDMDiagReport.zip"
Step 7: Read the Intune and Entra gates
Gate Where Healthy Device type enrollment restriction Intune admin center > Devices > Enrollment > device platform restriction Windows (MDM) allowed for the user's assigned restriction Device limit restriction Intune admin center > Devices > Enrollment > device limit restrictions User's enrolled devices below the limit (stale records count) Users may join devices Entra > Devices > Device settings Set to All (or Selected incl. the user) Maximum number of devices per user Entra > Devices > Device settings User below the quota Enrollment failures report Intune admin center > Devices > Monitor > Enrollment failures Row reason matches what the device logged

Microsoft's support guidance on DeviceCapReached is to remove stale device records or adjust the limit in the right service (Intune vs Entra). It is a count problem, not a device problem.

When a change is justified
Finding Prefer Avoid MDM user scope None, or Some without the user Set scope to All, or add a pilot group to Some Re-imaging devices that were never in scope WIP/MAM user scope overlaps the user Set WIP user scope to None (or remove the overlap) Deleting the Intune app registration in Entra User lacks Intune / Entra P1 Assign the license; let the task retry Mass dsregcmd /leave .local UPN suffix (0x8018002b) Change the UPN suffix to a verified domain; wait for delta sync Re-joining devices whose join is already healthy AzureAdPrt NO with healthy join Work the PRT triage on that device Flipping the GPO to Device Credential Device Credential on ordinary user PCs Set the GPO to User Credential for those PCs Leaving Device Credential outside co-management / AVD multi-session Leftover tenant in TenantInfo (0x80180002b) Microsoft's documented leave → delete objects → rejoin → sync, on that device only Running it fleet-wide "to be safe" Already enrolled elsewhere (0x8018000a) Remove the other MDM / other user's work account first Deleting HKLM\SOFTWARE\Microsoft\Enrollments keys blindly Windows (MDM) blocked (0x80180014) Allow Windows (MDM) in the restriction assigned to that user Disabling all enrollment restrictions Device cap reached Remove stale device records; adjust the limit if policy allows Making every user a Device Enrollment Manager No task, no events Fix GPO link/filtering/ADMX; gpupdate /force on a pilot Rewriting Intune configuration profiles
FAQ

What does Event 76 "Auto MDM Enroll: Failed" mean?
The GPO-triggered enrollment task ran and the enrollment attempt failed. The code in the message is the clue: 0x8018002b points to UPN suffix or MDM user scope, Device Credential failures point to the GPO credential type, and 0x80180026 points to MDM enrollment being blocked. Event 75 is the success counterpart.

There is no Event 75 or 76 at all. Where do I look?
Enrollment was never triggered. Confirm AutoEnrollMDM exists under HKLM\SOFTWARE\Policies\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\MDM, that the EnterpriseMgmt task exists, and whether Task Scheduler logged 7016 with 2149056522 (already enrolled in another MDM).

Should the GPO use User Credential or Device Credential?
Microsoft supports Device Credential for Intune only with co-management or Azure Virtual Desktop multi-session host pools. For normal user PCs, use User Credential.

dsregcmd shows hybrid joined but AzureAdPrt is NO. Will auto-enrollment still work?
Microsoft's checklist expects AzureAdPrt: YES. Without a PRT for the signed-in user, the enrollment task has no token to enroll with. Fix the PRT first; the task retries on its own schedule.

Should I run dsregcmd /leave or delete enrollment registry keys?
Only when you have evidence for it, such as the documented leftover-tenant case (wrong TenantId plus 0x80180002b), and only on the affected device. It is a change with a re-join and sync cost, not a diagnostic step.

  • AzureAdPrt : NO in dsregcmd /status: A Read-First Primary Refresh Token Triage
  • Company Portal can't connect / device not syncing: a 10-minute triage order
  • Intune Compliance: Not Applicable, Is Active, Minimum OS
Free checklist

Auto-enrollment is usually the step right before you require a compliant device in Conditional Access. If half the fleet is not enrolled yet, enforcing that grant locks those users out. items.summary_html:
What I Built

CivicPulse Tricity (NagrikSetu AI) is an open-source, multilingual Digital Public Infrastructure (DPI) platform built for the Code for Communities Chandigarh hackathon (supported by Google for Developers and GDG Cloud Chandigarh).

It unifies grassroots citizen feedback across Chandigarh, Mohali, and Panchkula by accepting natural voice notes, WhatsApp messages, and web tickets in Punjabi (ਪੰਜਾਬੀ), Hindi (हिंदी), and English, standardizing them through Google Gemini 1.5, geocoding complaints into Le Corbusier sector grids, and generating executive Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) for municipal commissioners.

🌐 Live Demo Portal: shivysidinfo.tech/civicpulse
📊 7-Slide Pitch Deck: shivysidinfo.tech/civicpulse/deck
🐙 GitHub Repository (MIT): github.com/satanic47/civicpulse-tricity

The Problem It Solves

Governments across Indian urban centers struggle with fragmented citizen feedback loops. In the Chandigarh Tricity region:

Linguistic Barrier: Over 70% of grassroots citizens verbally communicate in Punjabi or Hindi, but traditional municipal portals force rigid, English-only dropdown forms.
Data Fragmentation: Grievances sit isolated across WhatsApp messages, call center logs, and social media without spatial clustering. Municipal engineers cannot distinguish isolated complaints from systemic infrastructure failures.
Budget Misalignment: Multi-crore municipal capital budgets are often allocated based on historical inertia rather than real-time demand hotspots and citizen safety urgency.
How Open-Source & Google AI Powers the Solution
[Citizen Voice / WhatsApp (Punjabi / Hindi / English)]
↓
[Google Gemini 1.5 Multilingual Normalization Engine]
↓
[Canonical Schema: Urgency (1-10) + Municipal Dept Routing]
↓
[Le Corbusier Sector Grid Centroid Geocoding (Sectors 1-60)]
↓
[Spatial Clustering & Sector Health Scoring]
↓
[Gemini Municipal Capital DPR & Budget Generator]

  1. Dialect Normalization & Urgency Scoring

When a citizen speaks or texts in colloquial Punjabi ("ਸਾਡੇ ਸੈਕਟਰ 22 ਸ਼ਾਸਤਰੀ ਮਾਰਕੀਟ ਕੋਲ ਪਾਣੀ ਦੀ ਮੁੱਖ ਪਾਈਪ ਫਟ ਗਈ ਹੈ"), the Gemini 1.5 engine extracts the canonical intent, scores the hazard urgency (9/10), and assigns the municipal wing:

python

app/core/gemini_engine.py

prompt = f"""
Analyze this citizen civic report from Chandigarh Tricity:
Input: "{raw_input}"
Extract the following JSON:

  • language_detected: (e.g., "Punjabi (Gurmukhi)", "Hindi", "English")
  • category: ("Roads & Infrastructure", "Water Supply & Sewage", "Electricity & Lighting", "Public Safety", "Sanitation")
  • summary: (Canonical 1-sentence English description)
  • urgency_score: (Integer 1-10 based on immediate safety hazard)
  • routed_department: (MCC Division: B&R Roads, Water Supply, Electricity, Sanitation)
  • location_extracted: (Sector, Phase, or landmark) """
  1. Le Corbusier Sector Grid Geocoding

Colloquial landmarks (e.g., Shastri Market, Patel Market, Kiran Cinema, PU Gate 2) are resolved against pre-computed polygon centroids for Chandigarh Sectors 1–60, Mohali Phases, and Panchkula:

python

app/core/geocoding.py

def resolve_sector(text: str) -> Dict[str, Any]:
# Regex extraction of sector numbers and Tricity landmarks
match = re.search(r'(?:sector|sec|ਸੈਕਟਰ|सेक्टर)\s*(\d{1,2})', text, re.IGNORECASE)
if match:
sec_num = int(match.group(1))
return SECTOR_CENTROIDS.get(f"Sector {sec_num}", DEFAULT_CENTROID)
return match_landmark(text)

  1. Capital DPR Copilot

Rather than leaving issues as open complaint tickets, CivicPulse groups incident clusters and synthesizes municipal Detailed Project Reports (DPRs) with estimated costs in Lakhs:

json
{
"dpr_id": "DPR-2026-001",
"title": "Sector 22 Shastri Market Underground Water Conduit Overhaul",
"sector_or_ward": "Sector 22 (Ward 14)",
"urgency_level": "CRITICAL",
"estimated_cost_lakhs": 42.5,
"priority_score": 94,
"roi_metric": "Prevents chronic road foundation waterlogging across 1.2 km commercial zone."
}

Validation & Automated Testing

The entire system is containerized with Docker and verified with 21/21 passing automated unit tests:

test_gemini_engine.py: Validates multilingual dialect triage and fallback handling.
test_geocoding.py: Verifies sector boundary and landmark resolution.
test_api.py: Tests REST endpoints, voice upload pipelines, and hotspot clustering.

What's Next

We are expanding CivicPulse Tricity with WhatsApp webhook integration via Twilio and offline local Gemma 2 inference for air-gapped municipal data centers.
