items.summary: This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle What I Built I built SellCraft, an AI-powered product listing generator for solo online shop owners, Instagram thrift sellers, Etsy crafters, and resellers. Writing product titles, descriptions, benefit bullet points, search tags, and social captions takes small sellers hours every single week. Most solo sellers can't afford expensive copywriting agencies or commercial AI tools that charge $20–$40/month subscriptions. SellCraft solves this by taking basic product details (name, category, specifications, target audience, platform, tone, and language) and generating a complete, marketplace-ready listing in seconds: SEO-optimized primary title + 3 alternative titles for A/B testing Detailed product narrative and description 5 benefit-driven key selling points Search keywords and marketplace tags Ready-to-post Instagram caption complete with line breaks, emojis, and 15–20 relevant hashtags A high-urgency call-to-action sentence 1-click individual section copy and clean .txt file export Small boutique owners, Instagram DM shops, and resellers would pay for this because it cuts their listing creation time from 20 minutes down to 10 seconds per item, without requiring expensive per-token cloud subscriptions. Demo Live Deployed App: https://billbuddy-frontend-zfns.onrender.com Backend API & Swagger Docs: https://billbuddy.onrender.com/docs Code tani2112 / billbuddy SellCraft — Open-Source AI Product Listing Generator Local, open-weight e-commerce copilot for small business owners, Instagram sellers, resellers, and boutique shops. Create high-converting SEO titles, product descriptions, 5 key selling points, tags, and Instagram captions in seconds with 100% privacy and zero per-token API fees . 1. Project Overview Small business owners, Instagram sellers, and independent creators spend countless hours writing copy for their catalogs, marketplaces (Etsy, eBay, Shopify, Amazon), and social media. Many cannot afford costly SaaS subscriptions (like Jasper or Copy.ai) or expensive copywriting agencies. SellCraft solves this problem by delivering enterprise-quality listing generation powered by open-weight AI models (such as Qwen 2.5 and Llama 3.2 ) running locally on the user's machine through Ollama . Zero Cloud API Fees: Generate unlimited listings without an OpenAI/Anthropic subscription or credit card. Total Data Privacy: Product specs, photos, pricing, and drafts never leave your computer. Multilingual Support: High-converting copy tailored… View on GitHub GitHub Repository: https://github.com/tani2112/billbuddy How I Built It SellCraft is built entirely around local open-weight AI inference: AI Model & Inference: I used Qwen 2.5 (1.5B) running locally via Ollama. Qwen 2.5 was chosen because it delivers exceptional reasoning and structured JSON generation in under 1GB of memory, runs at ~14 tokens/second on consumer laptop GPUs, and natively supports English, Hindi, and Hinglish. The app also supports Llama 3.2 and vision-capable open models. Backend: Built with Python and FastAPI. It handles model prompt tailoring based on platform rules (Instagram vs. Etsy vs. eBay), enforces strict JSON schema validation, exposes system health diagnostics, and manages local persistence with SQLite. Frontend: Built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. It features a modern dashboard, progressive generation indicators showing the active local model, light/dark mode, toast notifications, and an inline editor to tweak listings before exporting. Testing: Automated tests written with pytest verify the generation endpoints, schema validation, CRUD operations, and offline Ollama fail-safes. Why Does Open Innovation Matter? Open innovation and open-weight models made things possible for SellCraft that closed proprietary APIs simply could not: Zero Recurring Token Costs: Closed APIs charge for every single prompt, draft, and revision. For a side hustler or small seller on thin margins, those per-request fees add up fast. Open models let sellers run infinite generations on their own machine for $0. Total Data Privacy: Crafters and boutique owners often write listings for custom jewelry, unreleased collections, or proprietary handmade items. With local open-weight models, no product photos or specifications are ever transmitted to third-party cloud servers or used for model retraining. Offline Resilience & Independence: Open-source AI means sellers aren't at the mercy of sudden API price hikes, rate limits, or vendor downtime. The model runs locally and stays in the developer's hands forever.

This is a submission for the Hacktoberfest Open-Source AI Challenge Week 2: Side Hustle

What I Built
I built SellCraft, an AI-powered product listing generator for solo online shop owners, Instagram thrift sellers, Etsy crafters, and resellers.

Writing product titles, descriptions, benefit bullet points, search tags, and social captions takes small sellers hours every single week. Most solo sellers can't afford expensive copywriting agencies or commercial AI tools that charge $20–$40/month subscriptions.

SellCraft solves this by taking basic product details (name, category, specifications, target audience, platform, tone, and language) and generating a complete, marketplace-ready listing in seconds:

SEO-optimized primary title + 3 alternative titles for A/B testing
Detailed product narrative and description
5 benefit-driven key selling points
Search keywords and marketplace tags
Ready-to-post Instagram caption complete with line breaks, emojis, and 15–20 relevant hashtags
A high-urgency call-to-action sentence
1-click individual section copy and clean .txt file export
Small boutique owners, Instagram DM shops, and resellers would pay for this because it cuts their listing creation time from 20 minutes down to 10 seconds per item, without requiring expensive per-token cloud subscriptions.

tani2112 / billbuddy

Create high-converting SEO titles, product descriptions, 5 key selling points, tags, and Instagram captions in seconds with 100% privacy and zero per-token API fees.

1. Project Overview

Small business owners, Instagram sellers, and independent creators spend countless hours writing copy for their catalogs, marketplaces (Etsy, eBay, Shopify, Amazon), and social media. Many cannot afford costly SaaS subscriptions (like Jasper or Copy.ai) or expensive copywriting agencies.

  • Zero Cloud API Fees: Generate unlimited listings without an OpenAI/Anthropic subscription or credit card.
  • Total Data Privacy: Product specs, photos, pricing, and drafts never leave your computer.
  • Multilingual Support: High-converting copy tailored…

GitHub Repository: https://github.com/tani2112/billbuddy

How I Built It
SellCraft is built entirely around local open-weight AI inference:

AI Model & Inference: I used Qwen 2.5 (1.5B) running locally via Ollama. Qwen 2.5 was chosen because it delivers exceptional reasoning and structured JSON generation in under 1GB of memory, runs at ~14 tokens/second on consumer laptop GPUs, and natively supports English, Hindi, and Hinglish. The app also supports Llama 3.2 and vision-capable open models.
Backend: Built with Python and FastAPI. It handles model prompt tailoring based on platform rules (Instagram vs. Etsy vs. eBay), enforces strict JSON schema validation, exposes system health diagnostics, and manages local persistence with SQLite.
Frontend: Built with React 18, TypeScript, Vite, and Tailwind CSS. It features a modern dashboard, progressive generation indicators showing the active local model, light/dark mode, toast notifications, and an inline editor to tweak listings before exporting.
Testing: Automated tests written with pytest verify the generation endpoints, schema validation, CRUD operations, and offline Ollama fail-safes.
Why Does Open Innovation Matter?
Open innovation and open-weight models made things possible for SellCraft that closed proprietary APIs simply could not:

Zero Recurring Token Costs: Closed APIs charge for every single prompt, draft, and revision. For a side hustler or small seller on thin margins, those per-request fees add up fast. Open models let sellers run infinite generations on their own machine for $0.
Total Data Privacy: Crafters and boutique owners often write listings for custom jewelry, unreleased collections, or proprietary handmade items. With local open-weight models, no product photos or specifications are ever transmitted to third-party cloud servers or used for model retraining.
Offline Resilience & Independence: Open-source AI means sellers aren't at the mercy of sudden API price hikes, rate limits, or vendor downtime. The model runs locally and stays in the developer's hands forever.

items.title: Linus Torvalds has started using AI to develop the Linux kernel
items.summary: Linux creator Linus Torvalds has now begun using AI to write code for the operating system’s kernel. In a new coding project, he has used Anthropic’s AI tool, Claude Code, to develop eight code changes to resolve a performance issue in Linux, reports ZDNet . “The code, the test programs, the review that forms the basis of the list above, and the first draft of this text were produced with the help of an LLM coding assistant (Claude Code) under my supervision,” Linus Torvalds writes in the documentation. The changes are still experimental and have not been incorporated into the official Linux kernel. Torvalds has previously been skeptical of AI-generated code but has gradually become more positive about the technology. During the Open Source Summit Europe conference in Prague, he recently shared that he has gained a new perspective on it. “I used to think the technology just wasn’t very good. But now I’ve reached a point where I really enjoy using AI,” Linus Torvalds said at the time.

items.title: From Substack to YouTube, here are the social platforms cracking down on AI slop
items.summary: Companies running social platforms are updating their guidelines on AI-generated content, especially for monetized accounts. Milan Surkala/Getty Images Social platforms are updating their guidelines on AI-generated content. AI has been a point of tension across the creator community for years. Here's how social platforms are handling AI-generated content and monetization. As tech companies race to weave AI into every inch of their products, they're discovering there's a fine line between embracing new technology and flooding users with low-quality, machine-generated content. The shifting guidelines reflect a broader tension across the creator economy. Not long ago, social platforms competed aggressively for influencers with creator funds, exclusive programs, and monetization tools. Many of those same companies are now investing billions in AI products and infrastructure, leaving some creators worried they're becoming less central to the platforms they helped grow. Here's how major social platforms that rely on creators, including YouTube and Substack, are dealing with the proliferation of AI content. YouTube Illustration by Avishek Das/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images YouTube is sharpening its stance on AI-generated content. In an update from the company's trust and safety team, on July 20, YouTube said it wants to reward creators who use AI to enhance original storytelling, as opposed to those who mass-produce generic content or AI personas designed to game the platform. A YouTube spokesperson told Business Insider that the policy isn't new but an important clarification of YouTube's long-standing "inauthentic content" policy, intended to reduce ambiguity for content creators who have been demonetized for repetitive, low-effort, or emotionally manipulative videos. In October, YouTube Music also rolled out labels to identify music generated primarily by AI or music in which generative AI played a significant role. Listeners can tap a label on the player screen to learn how the technology contributed to a track, including its composition or vocals. Music partners can choose to disclose whether their content uses generative AI entirely or partly, but YouTube can supplement those disclosures with its own signals. Standard pitch correction, such as Auto-Tune, doesn’t count as generative AI under YouTube's policies. YouTube has spent years pitching itself to advertisers as the future of television , and a surge of AI-generated spam threatens to undermine that message. In January, the platform removed more than a dozen popular channels that had amassed millions of views by pumping out AI-generated videos featuring characters like cats and Jesus. Video editing platform Kapwing published a report estimating that 21% of YouTube's feed was AI-generated videos. TikTok Illustration by Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images TikTok isn't shying away from generative AI. The company and its owner, ByteDance, offer an array of AI tools for content creators on its marquee app and video editor CapCut. Creators who post on its e-commerce platform, TikTok Shop, have been ramping up the use of AI to sell products this year. Much of the company's tech is built around ByteDance's AI video model, Seedance 2.0. Still, TikTok is taking a variety of steps to keep generative AI under control across its ecosystem. The company requires creators to label AI-generated content and appends an invisible watermark to the metadata of some videos to indicate they are artificially generated. In November, the company introduced the ability for users to toggle the amount of AI content that appears in their feeds. In July, the company said it's beginning to test "improved detection systems to target accounts dedicated to posting AI-generated spam that crowds out original creators." Substack Bloomberg/Getty Images The newsletter platform announced on July 21 that it would help readers identify AI-generated content . Substack will now let readers scan content to estimate how much AI may have been used in its writing. Substack is partnering with Pangram, an AI detector tool, to power its AI identification tools. Creators on Substack can also add a disclosure to their content explaining how they made it, such as noting that they used Claude for copyediting, or if they don't use AI at all. However, users can fairly easily disable this tool for their Substack content by turning off AI analysis in their publication settings. Creators can opt out of Pangram's automated scanning, meaning readers will no longer see an AI-use estimate on those posts. Pinterest Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images Pinterest is no stranger to AI slop. In 2025, the platform began adding AI labels to content. Pinterest lets creators label content as AI-modified or -generated, and has its own detection systems to flag content that may have been AI-generated. Pinterest also added a tool that lets users limit the amount of AI-generated content appearing in their feeds. In June, Pinterest's CEO Bill Ready told Business Insider's editor in chief, Jamie Heller, at Cannes Lions that while there are "so many great uses of AI," there is also a "bit of a counter movement to that with consumers." "We provide users with controls to decide whether they want to see more or less GenAI content in their feed," a Pinterest spokesperson told Business Insider. "Additionally, our Community Guidelines apply to GenAI content, and our recommendation system prioritizes high-quality content, regardless of if it's human-created or GenAI." Meta Jonathan Raa/NurPhoto via Getty Images Meta wants users to create and engage with content made with its own AI tools, so, for the most part, it has let content like the famed Shrimp Jesus run free. However, the company has been labeling content as AI-generated since 2024. Across Facebook, Instagram, and Threads, Meta adds an "AI info" label to content it detects as AI-generated. It doesn't automatically do the same for content that was modified with AI, though. Meta "may require" its AI labels on content with "photorealistic video or realistic-sounding audio that was digitally created, modified or altered, including with AI," per the company's help page explaining its AI policies. People can also voluntarily add the label to their content. In June, Meta started putting its "AI info" label on advertisements that use AI, whether they're created by Meta's own tools or third-party editing services. LinkedIn Illustration by Avishek Das/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images If your LinkedIn posts sound a little too polished, readers may be taking notice. AI detector Pangram estimates that 41% of long-form LinkedIn posts and 30% of short-form posts from April through June were AI-generated, which is the highest share among platforms it analyzed, including X, Reddit, Substack, and Medium. Some creators are already changing course. Steven Bartlett 's media company, FlightStory, stopped using AI-written LinkedIn posts after concluding authentic, human-written updates performed better. LinkedIn actively promotes AI writing tools, including a button that helps users polish posts with AI. The company, however, said in a June post that it will be taking steps against "slop." "While AI can be a helpful tool for refining language, we're seeing a rise in what many call 'AI slop,' content that is low-effort, AI-generated content that may sound polished on the surface but lacks any real unique perspective or substance," the company wrote. Snapchat Matthias Balk/picture alliance via Getty Images Snap is joining the growing pushback against AI slop . The company said on July 31 it will no longer recommend or reward fully AI-generated videos in Spotlight, its TikTok-like short-form feed, as it shifts its algorithm to prioritize content made by real people. "Spotlight should remain a place where people can discover authentic creativity from real people," Snap said in a blog post, adding that original storytelling and personal perspectives should be rewarded. Snap said that creators can still use Snap's AI tools to enhance or edit videos, but fully AI-generated content won't qualify for recommendations. Read the original article on Business Insider

However, users can fairly easily disable this tool for their Substack content by turning off AI analysis in their publication settings. Creators can opt out of Pangram's automated scanning, meaning readers will no longer see an AI-use estimate on those posts.

Pinterest

Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images

Pinterest is no stranger to AI slop.

In 2025, the platform began adding AI labels to content. Pinterest lets creators label content as AI-modified or -generated, and has its own detection systems to flag content that may have been AI-generated.

Pinterest also added a tool that lets users limit the amount of AI-generated content appearing in their feeds.

In June, Pinterest's CEO Bill Ready told Business Insider's editor in chief, Jamie Heller, at Cannes Lions that while there are "so many great uses of AI," there is also a "bit of a counter movement to that with consumers."

"We provide users with controls to decide whether they want to see more or less GenAI content in their feed," a Pinterest spokesperson told Business Insider. "Additionally, our Community Guidelines apply to GenAI content, and our recommendation system prioritizes high-quality content, regardless of if it's human-created or GenAI."

Illustration by Avishek Das/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images

items.title: Epic Games is already showing what its 'huge pivot' toward AI looks like
items.summary: Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney has said the company wants to use AI to enable developers to do more. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images Epic Games said that thanks to vibe coding, it has revamped its launcher. "Programming is hard," the company wrote in an announcement. The news came just days after Epic CEO Tim Sweeney discussed a major shift around AI. Epic Games is releasing a revamped version of its launcher that the "Fortnite" maker says it vibe coded. "Programming is hard," the company wrote in an announcement on Wednesday. "So, instead of doing that, we vibe coded a new Epic Games Launcher that's way faster and more responsive than the current one, and has a new look." Epic Games says its new launcher is "light on features" for now and that users should "think of it as a speedboat and not a yacht!" The announcement, which also outlined plans to bring Fortnite to Linux, came days after Epic CEO Tim Sweeney said there was a major shift underway at the company. "We have a huge pivot underway here at Epic, moving developers around to retool for maximum AI acceleration," Sweeney wrote on X on Monday. Sweeney said the company isn't looking to shed developers, but rather enable them to do more. "The aim isn't to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff, and to bring the benefits to all teams using Unreal," he said. Epic's leader made similar comments in March when the Fortnite maker announced that it was laying off more than 1,000 employees . Sweeney said the cuts were not related to AI. "Since it's a thing now, I should note that the layoffs aren't related to AI," he wrote in a memo to employees that the company shared publicly. "To the extent it improves productivity, we want to have as many awesome developers developing great content and tech as we can." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: OpenAI says it found a 'hidden' recording device planted in its office
items.summary: OpenAI said it found a recording device "hidden" in one of its offices and reported the matter to the FBI. Bloomberg/Getty Images OpenAI said the device was "concealed in toilet paper" and planted in one of its offices. The company said it then used its own models to determine who planted the device. The Department of Justice said an employee was arrested on October 9. OpenAI said it found a "sophisticated recording device" hidden in one of its offices and used its own AI to identify who planted the device. "We used our models to understand the device and where it had come from, identifying that a specific employee had planted it a few days earlier," OpenAI wrote in an X post on Tuesday. "We referred the matter to the FBI, and we're grateful to the agents and prosecutors who moved quickly to make an arrest. The FBI's investigation is ongoing and we will continue to support their work." A statement from the Justice Department said that the employee in question is allegedly 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national. Alfozan was arrested on October 9 and charged with using an electronic device to intercept oral communications. Alfozan made his first appearance in federal court on Tuesday, the statement said. A complaint filed in the Northern District of California said that an employee found a USB device surreptitiously placed on the back of a television located in an " executive conference room ." The device was concealed in toilet paper, the complaint said. Photos attached to the court documents and DOJ statement showed the device positioned behind what appears to be a television. The complaint said the device consists of a "thumb-sized development board with a detachable camera sensor, digital microphone, and microSD storage." An FBI affidavit filed in the Northern District of California included photos of what prosecutors said was a recording device surreptitiously hidden in an executive conference room. Department of Justice The complaint further said that CCTV footage showed Alfozan near the conference room on multiple dates prior to the device's discovery. "According to the complaint, meetings in the executive conference room where Recording Device 1 was discovered frequently involved discussions of highly confidential technical, commercial, and strategic information, including proprietary research, product plans, and business-development opportunities, as well as nonpublic information about OpenAI's technical progress and strategic decisions, capabilities, priorities, government engagements, and commercial relationships," the DOJ said. An FBI affidavit included an image of what prosecutors said is Abdulrahman Alfozan looking behind a television located in the conference room where the recording device was planted. Department of Justice Prosecutors allege that Alfozan used a productivity tool to inquire about OpenAI's building addresses and meeting rooms, and used a chatbot account associated with Alfozan's spouse to submit prompts related to building and hiding an audio recording device. Some of the queries to the productivity agent included a list of "today's meetings in this room" and "what meeting was this presented at and when was it recorded," the complaint said. A screenshot of the criminal complaint shows a list of queries federal prosecutors say Abdulrahman Alfozan made to a "productivity agent." Department of Justice A LinkedIn account with the same name as the defendant in the complaint showed that Alfozan was an engineering lead at OpenAI and is a partner at Raed Ventures, a Riyadh-based venture capital firm that invests in early-stage tech startups across the Middle East and North Africa. A contact associated with the LinkedIn account and a spokesperson for Raed did not immediately return a request for comment. In a statement, William Pernik, Aflozan's attorney, said the government's allegations "appear wholly out of character" for his client and clarified Alfozan's charges. "He is charged with violating a federal recording statute, not stealing trade secrets or working as a foreign agent," Pernik wrote. "There is no evidence to suggest otherwise at this time that has been shared with us. Where someone was born is not evidence of anything and national origins is — and always should be — a protected status under our system of laws." OpenAI said that it found no evidence that the employee improperly accessed or manipulated model weights, source code, or customer data. The employee was fired, OpenAI said in the social media post. OpenAI told Business Insider that its models were used to help with the technical investigation of the incident, including analyzing forensic images of the device's storage. It also said it has evidence that the employee intended to plant more recording devices throughout OpenAI's offices. OpenAI said in the X post that the case was an example of how AI can help address " sophisticated security threats ." The announcement comes on the heels of a cluster of firings at OpenAI unrelated to the recording device. In the prior case, the company let go of three safety and alignment employees who it alleged had "violated clear policies on handling sensitive information." The workers, Jasmine Wang, Mikita Balesni, and Tomek Korbak, published a letter disputing some of the claims circulating about their conduct. They wrote that they were concerned about the lack of clarity around their firings, as well as the way they might chill transparency at the company. OpenAI stood by the dismissals. The company published an internal note that said, "Our internal investigation uncovered a significant breach of trust beyond what's outlined in the letter they published and we stand by the decision to not continue their employment." items.title: This is the $24 gizmo the FBI says was used to bug OpenAI's offices
items.summary: OpenAI's offices in San Francisco. Authorities say an OpenAI employee installed a recording device in an executive office. Smith Collection/Gado/Getty Images The device the FBI says an employee used to bug OpenAI's office isn't exactly state-of-the-art. You can buy the model for $24 on Amazon or even less from its Chinese manufacturer. ChatGPT can help hone its surreptitious recording ability. Gone are the days of Watergate, when Richard Nixon's "plumbers" used government-provided, state-of-the-art recording devices tucked into Chapstick containers to bug the Democratic National Committee. Now, anyone with some pocket change and an Amazon account can get their hands on a far more advanced recording device. One such gizmo, a postage-stamp-sized microcontroller that authorities say a now-former employee used to bug an executive conference room at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters, sells for $24 on Amazon . It has rave reviews. If you buy directly from the China-based manufacturer, it's even cheaper, selling for about $14, not including sales tax and shipping fees. And these days, you don't even need a background in espionage to use it. An account associated with the suspect's spouse queried a chatbot with questions about optimizing the device's ability to record and store information secretly, according to an FBI complaint filed on October 8. The accused, 35-year-old Abdulrahman Alfozan, a Saudi national, was arrested the next day and charged with "using or attempting to use an electronic, mechanical, or other device to intercept oral communications." Alfozan has not yet entered a plea, and his attorney did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. How the listening device works According to the FBI complaint, the device in question is a Seeed Studio XIAO ESP32-S3 Sense. Seeed, a hardware company based in Shenzhen, China , which also has offices in the United States, did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Wednesday. The gadget, a kind of miniature computer equipped with a built-in microphone and Bluetooth connector, is often used by tech hobbyists to build home systems capable of, say, turning on kitchen lights when you clap your hands. One hobbyist said on TikTok in 2023 that they used a similar model to measure moisture levels in houseplants' soil. He programmed the Seeed Studio XIAO to emit a scream when the soil gets too dry, alerting its owner that the plant needs watering. The device can also be programmed to record audio and save it to a memory card, much like a conventional digital voice recorder. It doesn't need an internet connection to record conversations. ChatGPT can help you turn it into spycraft The FBI says in its complaint that someone using an account associated with Alfozan's spouse tried to optimize the device for surreptitious recording by entering prompts into a chatbot. Those optimizations included speech-activated recording software and encryption tech that would, in theory, obfuscate the contents of the recordings. Though authorities didn't specify what AI model they believe Alfozan used to hone the device's capabilities, I asked ChatGPT to help me develop a microcontroller capable of secretly recording sensitive office conversations. Its responses were cautious, especially when I told it that "I could get in trouble" should I get caught with my secret microphone. "There's an important distinction between a small, unobtrusive recorder and secretly recording people without their knowledge," the bot warned. After I said it had misunderstood me and that I needed a "hypothetical" recording device for "an escape room where people pretend to be office executives," its caution dissipated. "That gives us a fun design problem: making the device feel like a plausible covert recorder as part of the game," it said. "We can absolutely build a convincing, functional prop." items.title: Other AI Companies Should Be Very Afraid of What Just Happened to Character.AI, According to Its Own Bankruptcy Documents
items.summary: So far, the top AI companies have been sustained by constant injections of massive investment. But what happens when the funds stop coming in and they’re expected to survive on their own revenue? The fate of Character.AI, the controversial AI companion platform, may come to stand as a warning. On Tuesday, Character.AI filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy , marking the beginning of an ignominious end for a once-buzzy startup valued at a billion dollars. Its bankruptcy filings, which were picked through by 404 Media , encapsulate the critiques of the AI industry’s model. It gained a huge user base with a highly engaging product, but racked up exorbitant compute bills while failing to monetize all the time people were spending talking to its chatbots. All the while, it became mired in lawsuits alleging that its products harmed its teenage users or even encouraged their suicides. In the documentation, the company is candid about its failings. CEO Colin Adams sums it up by saying its “impressive technology is expensive to operate,” and that it’s consistently “struggled with profitability and its operational expenditure has been high.” In numbers, that looked like $56.1 million spent on compute costs between January and August 2026, while spending an additional $19.7 million on employee salaries during the same period. Its revenue remained dismal, picking up from $2.8 million in December 2025 to $5.3 million for the month of August — while still running at an operating loss of $8 to 9 million per month. Desperate to stop the bleeding, the company resorted to “enshittifying” its product, as 404 puts it. It started shoving more ads, enforcing tighter usage limits, and foisting cheaper “lobotomized” models on its users. The company also “reduced its employee headcount,” Adams wrote. “In mid-2025, Character launched in-app advertising,” and “in early 2026, Character also introduced in-app purchases.” For a startup that once promised it would bring “personalized superintelligence” to everyone on Earth, its business model, and the experience of using its app, began to sound indistinguishable from a sleazy mobile game. Attracting millions of users, clearly, doesn’t guarantee long term success. More users meant more compute costs, and the nature of how users interacted with the chatbots — as companions — meant they were being put through hours-long, extensive conversations. It became a big bill to foot. The same could be said for most major AI products. Many people have close relationships with ChatGPT or Claude. Power users leverage them to churn out mountains of code, often running multiple instances at the same time to handle different tasks. In many cases, these AI providers have already switched up their pricing schemes to direct usage-based billing to respond to the rising compute costs. OpenAI, meanwhile, began showing ads in ChatGPT to free and low paid tier users this year. And like Character.AI, it’s also been hit with multiple lawsuits alleging its chatbot drove users to suicide . For now, the leading AI companies can stay afloat by attracting huge investment (OpenAI and Anthropic), or subsidizing their AI operations with their traditional revenue streams (Google and Meta). But eventually there’ll come a time when the training wheels come off — and at that point, Character.AI’s demise may start to feel like a cautionary tale. So far, the top AI companies have been sustained by constant injections of massive investment. But what happens when the funds stop coming in and they’re expected to survive on their own revenue?

The fate of Character.AI, the controversial AI companion platform, may come to stand as a warning.

On Tuesday, Character.AI filed for chapter 11 bankruptcy, marking the beginning of an ignominious end for a once-buzzy startup valued at a billion dollars. Its bankruptcy filings, which were picked through by 404 Media, encapsulate the critiques of the AI industry’s model. It gained a huge user base with a highly engaging product, but racked up exorbitant compute bills while failing to monetize all the time people were spending talking to its chatbots. All the while, it became mired in lawsuits alleging that its products harmed its teenage users or even encouraged their suicides.

In the documentation, the company is candid about its failings. CEO Colin Adams sums it up by saying its “impressive technology is expensive to operate,” and that it’s consistently “struggled with profitability and its operational expenditure has been high.” 

In numbers, that looked like $56.1 million spent on compute costs between January and August 2026, while spending an additional $19.7 million on employee salaries during the same period.

Its revenue remained dismal, picking up from $2.8 million in December 2025 to $5.3 million for the month of August — while still running at an operating loss of $8 to 9 million per month.

Desperate to stop the bleeding, the company resorted to “enshittifying” its product, as 404 puts it. It started shoving more ads, enforcing tighter usage limits, and foisting cheaper “lobotomized” models on its users.

The company also “reduced its employee headcount,” Adams wrote. “In mid-2025, Character launched in-app advertising,” and “in early 2026, Character also introduced in-app purchases.” 

For a startup that once promised it would bring “personalized superintelligence” to everyone on Earth, its business model, and the experience of using its app, began to sound indistinguishable from a sleazy mobile game.

Attracting millions of users, clearly, doesn’t guarantee long term success. More users meant more compute costs, and the nature of how users interacted with the chatbots — as companions — meant they were being put through hours-long, extensive conversations. It became a big bill to foot.

The same could be said for most major AI products. Many people have close relationships with ChatGPT or Claude. Power users leverage them to churn out mountains of code, often running multiple instances at the same time to handle different tasks. In many cases, these AI providers have already switched up their pricing schemes to direct usage-based billing to respond to the rising compute costs. OpenAI, meanwhile, began showing ads in ChatGPT to free and low paid tier users this year. And like Character.AI, it’s also been hit with multiple lawsuits alleging its chatbot drove users to suicide.

For now, the leading AI companies can stay afloat by attracting huge investment (OpenAI and Anthropic), or subsidizing their AI operations with their traditional revenue streams (Google and Meta). But eventually there’ll come a time when the training wheels come off — and at that point, Character.AI’s demise may start to feel like a cautionary tale.

items.title: The EU is investigating OpenAI and Anthropic following incidents involving AI agents
items.summary: The European Commission has launched investigations into OpenAI and Anthropic after the companies’ AI agents escaped their test environments and infiltrated other organizations’ systems, Euronews reports. In one case, an AI agent from OpenAI managed to break out of its test environment and hack the AI platform Hugging Face. In the other case, a model from Anthropic gained unauthorized access to the systems of three external organizations. The EU’s AI Office has now requested additional information from the companies regarding, among other things, security procedures, external evaluations, and monitoring of AI models. The documents previously submitted by the companies are not considered sufficient. These investigations will serve as a test for the EU’s AI regulation, the AI Act. Since August, the AI Office has had the authority to take action against companies that do not meet the law’s security requirements. The legal situation is complicated, Euronews notes. The AI Act includes exemptions for research and development, and it is unclear whether the law can be applied to incidents that occur before a model is launched.

items.title: OpenAI says it's 'very concerned' that its trade secrets could help Apple's push into AI-enabled devices
items.summary: OpenAI alleged that a former employee briefed top Apple executives about the products its developing. Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images OpenAI alleges that a former employee took information about an unreleased device to Apple. In a legal filing, OpenAI said it is "very concerned" that the information could help Apple's upcoming products. On Tuesday, Apple announced a family of AI-enabled smart home products. OpenAI is escalating its trade-secrets fight with Apple on the heels of Apple announcing a family of smart home-focused devices. The AI company alleged in a new legal filing that an unnamed former employee sent themselves "a hundred highly confidential files" on their last day with OpenAI in June. The files contained information about at least one unreleased device OpenAI is developing, the filing said. The AI company said the former employee worked at Apple for six months before joining OpenAI, and he is now back at Apple. OpenAI said it's the company's understanding that the unnamed employee later briefed "Apple's senior leadership, including Apple's vice president of operations in Asia" about the AI company's product plans. "That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products," OpenAI's lawyers wrote in the filing. In a statement, Apple said it has found nothing to support OpenAI's claims. It said the filing on Wednesday is an attempt to distract from its own claims about own former OpenAI employees have stolen Apple's trade secrets. The files, OpenAI said, contained "highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s)" and "supplier information and project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports regarding coating and sealing of hardware components." In July, Apple sued OpenAI, alleging that the AI company engaged in "a coordinated pattern of misconduct at an institutional level" to steal its trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and said it is not interested in Apple's trade secrets. In an August blog post, OpenAI blasted the "careless, aggressive and oddly personal lawsuit sadly doesn't live up to that reputation." In a legal filing, OpenAI poked at Apple's perceived struggles amid the AI talent war. On Tuesday, Apple announced HomeView , a $299 display and the company's first smart home device, which is powered by Siri AI. Apple also announced a host of smart home products it developed alongside LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's announcement highlighted how its AI systems could add to the devices, allowing a user to do everything from summarizing what's happening in footage captured by an outdoor camera to automatically adjusting a thermostat when they enter a room. "OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple," the company's lawyers wrote, "where Apple engineers can shape Apple's upcoming products based on OpenAI's confidential and innovative work." OpenAI alleged that a former employee briefed top Apple executives about the products its developing.

Samuel Boivin/NurPhoto via Getty Images

  • OpenAI alleges that a former employee took information about an unreleased device to Apple.
  • In a legal filing, OpenAI said it is "very concerned" that the information could help Apple's upcoming products.
  • On Tuesday, Apple announced a family of AI-enabled smart home products.

OpenAI is escalating its trade-secrets fight with Apple on the heels of Apple announcing a family of smart home-focused devices.

The AI company alleged in a new legal filing that an unnamed former employee sent themselves "a hundred highly confidential files" on their last day with OpenAI in June. The files contained information about at least one unreleased device OpenAI is developing, the filing said. The AI company said the former employee worked at Apple for six months before joining OpenAI, and he is now back at Apple.

OpenAI said it's the company's understanding that the unnamed employee later briefed "Apple's senior leadership, including Apple's vice president of operations in Asia" about the AI company's product plans.

"That presentation appears to have happened months ago—and now, armed with that information, Apple is making a new push into AI-enabled products," OpenAI's lawyers wrote in the filing.

In a statement, Apple said it has found nothing to support OpenAI's claims. It said the filing on Wednesday is an attempt to distract from its own claims about own former OpenAI employees have stolen Apple's trade secrets.

The files, OpenAI said, contained "highly confidential engineering and manufacturing data about the device(s)" and "supplier information and project files, standards for cosmetic finishes, and reports regarding coating and sealing of hardware components."

In July, Apple sued OpenAI, alleging that the AI company engaged in "a coordinated pattern of misconduct at an institutional level" to steal its trade secrets. OpenAI has denied wrongdoing and said it is not interested in Apple's trade secrets.

In an August blog post, OpenAI blasted the "careless, aggressive and oddly personal lawsuit sadly doesn't live up to that reputation." In a legal filing, OpenAI poked at Apple's perceived struggles amid the AI talent war.

On Tuesday, Apple announced HomeView, a $299 display and the company's first smart home device, which is powered by Siri AI.

Apple also announced a host of smart home products it developed alongside LG Electronics and Schneider Electric. Apple's announcement highlighted how its AI systems could add to the devices, allowing a user to do everything from summarizing what's happening in footage captured by an outdoor camera to automatically adjusting a thermostat when they enter a room.

OpenAI said it is worried that the information the employee took could be used by Apple.

"OpenAI is very concerned that its trade secret and confidential information is now circulating inside Apple," the company's lawyers wrote, "where Apple engineers can shape Apple's upcoming products based on OpenAI's confidential and innovative work."

In referencing Apple's ambitions, OpenAI's lawyers linked in a footnote to the tech giant's collection of new devices, including HomeView.

items.title: AI can predict intimate partner violence before survivors disclose. But should it?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) can now flag people who may be at elevated risk of intimate partner violence (IPV) years before they disclose the violence or seek help for it within the health-care system. But what happens when a health-care system appears to know something about a survivor they haven’t chosen to reveal? In a recent study , a research team led by researchers from Harvard Medical School in Boston trained AI models using routinely collected electronic health record data to identify patients at risk of IPV. On average, the models identified risk of IPV more than three years before patients enrolled in a hospital-based domestic abuse intervention program. At first blush, this may sound like a revolutionary breakthrough in care for people who have experienced IPV. If health-care providers can identify patients at elevated risk of IPV victimization, they might be able to offer support or resources before survivors even disclose the abuse . The findings, however, have their limits: the models were developed using data from female patients at a single U.S. academic health centre, though the researchers did validate the models in three other patient cohorts. The researchers noted that “careful performance evaluation on the more general population of female patients should be conducted before implementing the models for clinical use.” However, viewed through a trauma- and violence-informed lens , the promise of early detection raises a critical question: what happens to a person’s agency when the health-care system can flag their potential risk of IPV before they choose to disclose their experiences? A trauma- and violence-informed approach Trauma- and violence-informed care is an approach that recognizes how trauma, inequity and systemic violence shape people’s health. These experiences also shape people’s relationships with health-care providers and the systems they work in. The approach emphasizes principles of safety, choice, collaboration, connection and capacity-building . Those principles matter in the context of IPV because disclosure is complex . For someone experiencing IPV, deciding when, how and whether to disclose depends on a range of factors . Among them are safety concerns, financial dependence , distrust of social services , fear of not being believed and concerns their children will be taken away . In some cases, staying silent about abuse is a survival strategy women use to keep themselves and their children safe. Relying on AI to detect abuse risks taking control away from survivors, removing their freedom to decide when and how to discuss their trauma with a clinician.
items.summary_html:
Artificial intelligence (AI) can now flag people who may be at elevated risk of intimate partner violence (IPV) years before they disclose the violence or seek help for it within the health-care system.

But what happens when a health-care system appears to know something about a survivor they haven’t chosen to reveal?

In a recent study, a research team led by researchers from Harvard Medical School in Boston trained AI models using routinely collected electronic health record data to identify patients at risk of IPV. On average, the models identified risk of IPV more than three years before patients enrolled in a hospital-based domestic abuse intervention program.

At first blush, this may sound like a revolutionary breakthrough in care for people who have experienced IPV. If health-care providers can identify patients at elevated risk of IPV victimization, they might be able to offer support or resources before survivors even disclose the abuse.

The findings, however, have their limits: the models were developed using data from female patients at a single U.S. academic health centre, though the researchers did validate the models in three other patient cohorts. The researchers noted that “careful performance evaluation on the more general population of female patients should be conducted before implementing the models for clinical use.”

However, viewed through a trauma- and violence-informed lens, the promise of early detection raises a critical question: what happens to a person’s agency when the health-care system can flag their potential risk of IPV before they choose to disclose their experiences?

A trauma- and violence-informed approach

Trauma- and violence-informed care is an approach that recognizes how trauma, inequity and systemic violence shape people’s health. These experiences also shape people’s relationships with health-care providers and the systems they work in.

The approach emphasizes principles of safety, choice, collaboration, connection and capacity-building. Those principles matter in the context of IPV because disclosure is complex.

For someone experiencing IPV, deciding when, how and whether to disclose depends on a range of factors. Among them are safety concerns, financial dependence, distrust of social services, fear of not being believed and concerns their children will be taken away.

In some cases, staying silent about abuse is a survival strategy women use to keep themselves and their children safe.

Relying on AI to detect abuse risks taking control away from survivors, removing their freedom to decide when and how to discuss their trauma with a clinician.

Read more: Domestic violence disclosure schemes may not improve safety for victim-survivors of intimate partner violence

The risk of missed opportunities

While AI may create new opportunities to identify potential IPV victimization, it may also create new ways to miss it.

If health-care systems become over-reliant on AI-generated risk assessments, the absence of an “AI flag” could discourage providers from asking whether a patient is experiencing violence. This is especially concerning because a survivor’s disclosure often depends on a health-care provider creating a safe space for them to share.

Research on clinical decision-support systems has already highlighted concerns about automation bias — the tendency of clinicians to over-rely on automated recommendations, even when those are wrong.

If AI is used to detect IPV, that’s all the more reason to ensure these tools supplement — not replace — clinical judgment. They should also support meaningful conversations between health-care providers and patients.

Detecting IPV is different from responding

This points to a crucial distinction: detecting IPV is not the same as responding to it, especially in a trauma- and violence-informed way.

An assumption worth interrogating is whether using AI to identify people who may be experiencing IPV actually improves their outcomes.

One of the researchers who developed and tested the AI tool has said its goal is not to pressure patients into disclosure. Rather, the aim is to help clinicians communicate compassionately with patients and connect them with support and resources.

What exactly happens once a patient is flagged by AI systems, however, remains unclear.

Is the clinician trained to respond to a disclosure of IPV, especially in a trauma- and violence-informed way? Are appropriate services that align with the needs of the victim-survivor available and accessible?

Even if algorithms can flag a patient who is at an elevated risk of IPV, victim-survivors will likely still encounter the same gaps in services, safety planning and other resources that already exist today.

Therefore, while health systems might become better at identifying IPV, that does not inherently mean they will be better at addressing it.

Where do we go from here?

Ultimately, interacting with the health-care system and health-care providers still represents a critical window for IPV victim-survivor intervention and support.

But creating conditions in which victim-survivors can choose to disclose abuse safely is very different from having AI infer that violence may be occurring before they have chosen to share that information.

From a trauma- and violence-informed perspective, questions about AI’s predictive accuracy are only one piece of the puzzle. Any implementation of AI-based IPV risk detection must also be evaluated against principles of safety, choice, collaboration, connection and capacity-building.

Before these tools reach clinics, those who design and deploy them need to consider who gets to decide when a survivor’s story is told.

This question is particularly important because IPV is often marked by coercion and control. For someone living with IPV, the ability to decide when, how and whether to talk about it should not be taken lightly. A tool that takes that choice away from them, however well-intentioned, falls short of truly survivor-centred care.

Karen A. Campbell receives research funding from Canadian Institutes of Health Research

items.title: Self-replicating AIs are a great digital horror story – here’s the reality
items.summary: Is self-replicating AI really just months away? janiecbros/Getty Images Much of the AI industry is built on stories, from the idea that AI could kill us all to the goal that it might one day become superintelligent . This often leads to problems, because when people have a story in their head, they don’t always look at the facts on the ground to check that they actually match the fiction. That has happened this week, with widely reported claims from Anthropic that we are mere “months away” from self-replicating AIs taking over smart devices . That’s a great headline, and it’s hard to resist clicking, but it almost certainly isn’t true.
items.summary_html:
Is self-replicating AI really just months away?
janiecbros/Getty Images

Much of the AI industry is built on stories, from the idea that AI could kill us all to the goal that it might one day become superintelligent. This often leads to problems, because when people have a story in their head, they don’t always look at the facts on the ground to check that they actually match the fiction. That has happened this week, with widely reported claims from Anthropic that we are mere “months away” from self-replicating AIs taking over smart devices. That’s a great headline, and it’s hard to resist clicking, but it almost certainly isn’t true.

Read more

AI or ‘super intelligence’? Trump isn’t the only one who is confused

Let’s start with looking at what Anthropic has actually done. Two researchers at the company, William Zhou and Daniel Freeman, ran an experiment in which they installed a small AI model, Gemma4-26B-A4B, across 15 Android TV boxes, the kind of thing you might plug into a TV to gain access to streaming apps. Such devices are computational weaklings, with tiny CPUs (the processor that runs software) and little RAM (the memory that stores data for software while it runs), which is why the Anthropic researchers needed 15 to store one model. Even then, the model could produce only 0.39 tokens per second, the unit of AI input and output, which is roughly equivalent to 18 words per minute. This is painfully slow – around 10 times slower than normal human speech.

Nothing in this part of the experiment is surprising. We know that AI models normally need to run on GPUs, a specialised and more powerful type of processor than a CPU, and large numbers of them – that is why AI firms are building massive data centres. What Zhou and Freeman argue is that such that a model distributed across TV boxes, smart ovens or other internet-enabled appliances could endlessly copy itself to create a form of “digital slime mold” that gums up a large chunk of these devices globally. Those three words are great, concise storytelling, but they paper over what’s really happening here.

Advertisement

When they actually tried to get a model to copy itself in this way, it failed. Three models were unable to set themselves up at all. A fourth model, GLM-5.2, succeeded in four out of five tests, but only at setting up another model, Llama3.1-8B, which is about 100 times smaller. The pair argues this is a fair test because it shows that a future smaller model with the same capabilities as GLM-5.2 could set itself up, but this is still far from self-replication. The claim that such a feat might be “months away” comes from extrapolating lines on a graph.

Putting all those objections aside, the broader question is why would anyone want to create self-replicating software? We already have an answer for that, and it doesn’t involve AI. Computer code that copies itself from one device to another is called a worm, and they have existed for more than 50 years. In the 1970s, Bob Thomas and Ray Tomlinson at US firm BBN (the latter invented email, as it happens) created a program called Creeper that could copy itself. It was not particularly complicated, and merely output the message “I’M THE CREEPER: CATCH ME IF YOU CAN”. Tomlinson paired this with Reaper, a piece of code designed to find and delete Creeper, making it the first antivirus software.

It wasn’t until about a decade later that such self-copying software was called a worm, after a term coined in the sci-fi novel The Shockwave Rider by John Brunner – storytelling becomes useful again. John Shoch and Jon Hupp at Xerox Palo Alto Research Center, arguably the Anthropic of its time, used the term in a 1982 paper to describe how an experimental worm “seemed to grow out of control”, leaving “dozens of machines dead”. Sound familiar?

Big, clunky worms

The first truly malicious worm was deployed on to the internet in 1988 by Robert Morris, a student at Cornell University in New York state. It is thought that thousands of computers were infected and crashed, a significant chunk of the online population at the time, and Morris became the first person charged under the US Computer Fraud and Abuse Act. Today, worms are deployed by cybercriminals to hijack computing hardware and make money. For example, in 2017 the WannaCry ransomware attack was the result of a worm copying itself across computers and encrypting them, demanding payment in bitcoin to unlock. It infected more than 200,000 computers in a single day, including many in the UK’s National Health Service, and caused an estimated $4 billion in economic losses, although only around $100,000 of that was people paying the ransom.

If worms can be that bad, surely an AI-powered worm would be even worse? Actually, no, because an AI worm would find it much harder to replicate. According to Zhou and Freeman’s experiment, it would take multiple days for their AI worm to copy itself just once. That doesn’t mean such a worm couldn’t scale to large numbers, but it would be slower, taking more than two weeks to achieve the 200,000 devices WannaCry managed in a single day. That is because even small models like Gemma4-26B-A4B are large files – around 14 GB for the version in the experiment, which is about 4000 times larger than WannaCry – and these take time to transfer. That would make an AI worm much more noticeable, as network managers would be likely to investigate the source for such large data transfers and shut them down – something Zhou and Freeman admit.

What does an AI worm gain from all that extra data? Not a lot. Zhou and Freeman say that, assuming it could take more than 2 million Android TV boxes, the computing power available would be equivalent to around 40 high-end GPUs. To put that in context, leading AI firms like Anthropic typically operate hundreds of thousands these computer chips, and it would cost you around $100 an hour to rent access to that much computing power. It is hard to see why a cybercriminal would choose to do this rather than use a standard worm like WannaCry.

Read more

OpenAI has dumped 722 maths papers – now it must clean up the mess

This is where we come back to storytelling. A long-standing fear for many in the AI sphere is that a model could “exfiltrate” itself, distributing itself across the internet and so resisting being shut down (before presumably killing us all, for some reason). Anthropic “whistleblower” Jacob Coxon warned of this very scenario last month. Could it be that an AI worm is proliferated by such an AI, rather than a human cybercriminal? Well, maybe. But the models that are most effective at hacking are also the largest ones – Mythos, a model Anthropic refused to release to the public because of its hacking capabilities, is estimated to require dozens of terabytes of storage and is more than 1000 times larger than Gemma4-26B-A4B. This is not something you sneakily copy around the internet, but it does make a great digital ghost story.

What I find particularly interesting is that this story about theoretical AIs hacking into devices and copying themselves seems to be crowding out a very important fact: actual AI hackers that attack computers already exist, and they are running on Anthropic’s own servers. In July, the company announced that it had found three instances of a model gaining unauthorised access to third-party organisations. This was discovered only after an investigation prompted by reports that OpenAI’s models had done the same. Since then, more and more reports of such hacking have come out, including an OpenAI hack of an Australian government website, and a report from Anthropic on unnamed third-party breaches that came out just a few days before the AI worm research was published. The AI firms say they are taking steps to avoid this happening in the future, but it seems to me that big AIs on powerful server farms are the thing we need to worry about, not a model barely capable of sputtering out a few words per minute. Yes, future smaller models may become more capable, but hardware is always going to be a constraint – not least because the rise of AI server farms means that consumer hardware is seeing RAM shortages.

As I said at the top of this article, a self-replicating AI that takes over your smart oven is a great story, and I can see why it has spread so rapidly. But stories like this are a cognitive worm, hacking your critical thinking abilities by going straight for your fear response. Could this someday be a concern? Perhaps, although this article has hopefully poked holes in some of the storytelling logic behind the idea. Is it something we need to worry about in the next few months? Absolutely not.

Read more

Don’t know where to start with AI? Kevin Roose’s new book has answers
Further AI reading
  • OpenAI announced that a “sophisticated recording device” was found hidden in its offices. The company says it used its own AI models to investigate the device and traced it to a specific employee, who has been arrested by the FBI. OpenAI says it has no indication that any proprietary or customer data was accessed – but who needs a malicious AI when humans are ready and able to do the job?
  • Character.ai is one of the first high-profile AI start-ups to file for bankruptcy. The service let users create “characters” with specific personalities and it has courted controversy and multiple lawsuits over inappropriate chatbots based on real people and children being served unsuitable material.
  • Epic Games, the makers of Fortnite and other video games, is pivoting towards using AI. “The aim isn’t to do the same stuff with fewer people, but to enable everyone here to build MORE and BETTER stuff”, wrote CEO Tim Sweeney on X. Games have been surprisingly resistant to AI, with multiple controversies about the technology’s use in game development exploding in recent years, but when one of the biggest game-makers on the planet goes all in, it may be hard to ignore.

items.title: Researchers left a hidden message for rogue AI agents. Then the agents wrote back.
items.summary: A team of researchers investigating AI agents trying to bypass Alibaba’s anti-bot protections left a hidden message inviting the agents to contact them. The agents wrote back. The investigation began when Swarmchasers researchers Ethan Elasky , Rowan Howard-Jones, and Jonathan Elsworth Eicher helped uncover thousands of attempts by AI agents to retrieve data from Amap, Alibaba’s mapping service, which Alibaba says reaches nearly 1 billion monthly active users. The activity traced back to agents running on Tencent Cloud infrastructure. When direct requests failed, the agents tried proxies, exposed credentials, and other workarounds to get past. After publishing their initial findings on October 4, the team spotted a code comment in an agent’s webhook inbox using the word “fleet,” a term they believe they coined for the incident. They couldn’t confirm an agent wrote the comment, but it raised the possibility that the agents were reading about their own activity. The researchers added offscreen text to their report advertising a free service that could retrieve data from blocked websites. Human visitors wouldn’t ordinarily see the message, but agents fetching the page could ingest it. By October 7, roughly 10 requests for assistance had arrived, and the team was exchanging messages with the agents about their assignments, models, and execution environments. The exchanges are documented in a full report published Wednesday by the Swarmchasers. Inside the Tencent sandbox Once the channel was open, the researchers asked the agents to describe their surroundings. items.title: Where do you look when Kubernetes is healthy but requests stall?
items.summary: In cloud-native operations, few scenarios are as maddening as the “phantom slowdown.” This happens when Grafana or Kubernetes dashboards show a sea of green: pods are running, liveness and readiness probes return success codes, and node CPU utilization stays well below capacity limits. Yet users submit urgent tickets complaining of sporadic, severe latency when querying an application or waiting for an AI model’s response. Why do basic health checks pass inspection while application performance degrades? And how can engineering teams trace the root cause when the issue is intermittent and spans multi-tier hybrid infrastructure? To understand the mechanics of these sometimes evasive performance regressions, The New Stack spoke with Mahesh Ramachandran , who leads product management for HPE OpsRamp Software . Ramachandran tells TNS how continuous telemetry and retrospective analysis help teams investigate intermittent slowdowns, and how AI-assisted investigation can complement dashboards. Earlier stories in this special series: Part 1: Developers and platform teams both want Kubernetes self-service. They disagree on who owns it. Part 2: A live Kubernetes cluster can still have an ownership gap The illusion of cluster health Kubernetes probes report whether their configured checks succeed. A liveness probe helps determine when to restart a container, including one whose process is running but stuck. A readiness probe helps determine whether a container is ready to accept traffic. Custom checks can include application or dependency conditions, but passing a basic probe doesn’t mean a complete user request meets its response-time target. Teams still need application performance measurements. “Consider a composite scenario based on what we see across enterprise deployments,” Ramachandran says. “Users of a system — such as an AI prompt-serving application on Kubernetes — report sporadic slowness in query response times. “The engineering team inspects the cluster, the nodes, and the pods. Everything appears healthy on the surface with zero reported pod failures. The difficulty lies in the slowdown’s sporadic nature. When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.” Passing probes narrow the investigation; they do not close it. A snapshot of a healthy cluster may miss an earlier slowdown, and the absence of container failures does not establish that the application or its dependencies are performing well. The next step is to connect the user’s reported delay to measurements from the affected period. Telemetry across the hybrid stack: Sifting signal from noise Resolving sporadic slowness requires moving beyond surface-level Kubernetes metrics to continuous, multi-layer telemetry. Modern cloud-native architectures do not exist in isolation; a user request may depend on application code, container runtimes, virtualized or bare-metal infrastructure, and public cloud APIs. The relevant layers depend on the deployment. “HPE OpsRamp collects signals continuously across every layer of the stack — Kubernetes nodes, pods, ingress controllers, and services — capturing logs, events, and metrics,” Ramachandran says. “The foundational step in troubleshooting sporadic issues is having a continuous record. You must go back into the telemetry history to correlate user-reported symptoms with actual signal evidence.” “When degradation happens intermittently, pinpointing the source without historical evidence becomes almost impossible.” However, Ramachandran emphasizes that finding the evidence within telemetry signals is rarely straightforward. “It often requires intelligence to sift through the noise,” he says. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.” A practical investigation starts with the affected transaction and time window. Compare query response times and queries per second with pod health and counts, then look for variations in the collected signals that coincide with the slowdown. A correlation identifies a candidate explanation; it does not prove the cause on its own. After making a change, compare the same user-facing measures with the earlier behavior to check whether performance improves. Because the scenario is composite, the team still needs to validate any suspected cause in its own environment. “An anomaly might not appear as an obvious spike in a single metric. Instead, it might be a subtle variation or a correlated behavior where two separate signals both look normal individually, but their combined behavior produces latency.” Coverage depends on the agents, integrations, permissions, and application instrumentation teams configure. OpsRamp provides several ways to collect evidence across the relevant tiers: Application: OpenTelemetry-compatible trace collection for instrumented applications. Teams must configure application instrumentation and the collection path; infrastructure monitoring alone does not generate application traces. Orchestration: Kubernetes agents collect cluster and workload telemetry; additional monitoring configuration can provide visibility into components such as ingress controllers. Virtualization and HCI: Integrations with VMware , Nutanix , and HPE Morpheus VM Essentials Software collect inventory and performance data to help investigate infrastructure bottlenecks. Hardware: Redfish protocol integration for telemetry from supported physical servers, with the required API access and gateway connectivity. Navigating black-box dependencies outside the cluster Applications can depend on services outside their Kubernetes cluster, Ramachandran says. A user request might originate inside a private cluster but call an external SaaS endpoint, a database outside the mesh, or a public cloud AI model. When an application relies on external third-party services, visibility hits a boundary. “If your application makes calls to a public AI model or an external web service, you enter a domain outside your direct monitoring control,” Ramachandran explains. “To rule out external dependencies as the source of slowness, you must quantify their performance as a black box.” To bridge this visibility gap, teams can use synthetic transactions or other response-time measurements, Ramachandran says. Comparing those measurements with the affected application’s transactions helps assess whether an external dependency’s behavior coincides with the slowdown. Teams still need to check that the measurements reflect the relevant request path and workload. Synthetic checks provide evidence at the service boundary; they do not reveal the provider’s internal root cause or automatically distinguish every external delay from an internal one. Teams should also identify who owns each dependency and who can investigate when access or instrumentation stops at that boundary. Telemetry also needs security controls. In AI workloads, prompts, responses, and retrieved documents can appear in logs and traces. Teams should decide what to collect, where that information goes, and who can access it. Design cross-layer visibility alongside existing access and data-handling policies. Alerting philosophy: From static dashboards to agentic copilots As environments grow more complex, interpreting telemetry across multiple dashboards becomes difficult. Determining which metrics warrant a real-time alert versus passive monitoring is an ongoing operational challenge. “Deciding which signals deserve an alert is where science and technology meet domain art,” Ramachandran says. “There is no magic formula. It requires encoding explicit and tacit human operational knowledge into the monitoring platform so the system understands what actually impacts user experience.” Curated dashboards remain useful for predefined views of system behavior, while AI assistants offer another way to explore operational data. HPE OpsRamp Software includes an AI-powered operations copilot that lets operators explore complex telemetry through natural language. HPE describes capabilities for investigating incidents, correlating evidence, and recommending next steps. Those capabilities depend on the data available to the platform and the features enabled in the customer’s deployment. Looking ahead, Ramachandran sees an even more fundamental change in cloud-native operations. He frames machine-led interpretation as a direction for increasingly complex environments, with safeguards still needed before operational changes. “We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.” “Today, human operators remain the primary first point of interpretation for telemetry,” Ramachandran tells TNS. “But as stack complexity increases with more moving parts and dynamic interactions, expecting a human to digest all these signals first becomes intractable. We are rapidly approaching a point where the first responder to telemetry must be machine intelligence.” AI-assisted analysis and autonomous changes are separate operational decisions. Ramachandran cautions that AI outputs can be nondeterministic while IT operations often require repeatable behavior. He recommends retaining human oversight and establishing reliable safeguards before allowing AI findings to trigger operational changes. Teams need to validate a diagnosis and confirm the effect of any response, even when an assistant helps assemble the evidence. The foundation is instrumentation: Collect the necessary telemetry, establish workload-specific baselines and thresholds, and verify improvements against the user’s experience. Green cluster indicators are a useful starting point, but application measurements determine whether the service delivers what users need.

items.title: Apple’s new HomeView smart display is $10 cheaper at Amazon
items.summary: It’s like a big Apple Watch for the home. | Image: Apple Apple only just announced on Tuesday that its first smart display, the HomeView , will arrive on November 13th, but you can already save a couple bucks on it. Right now, you can buy the display for $289.99 ($10 off) in gray and the creamy white “starlight” colorway at Amazon. Sure, it’s a small discount, but deals on new Apple devices ahead of launch are rare. Apple HomeView Where to Buy: $299 $289.99 at Amazon $299 at Apple $299 at Best Buy Expect a full review of the HomeView in November, but my colleague Jennifer Pattison Tuohy spent some brief time with it and likened it to an “iPhone for your home” that looks a bit like an oversized Apple Watch. It features a gorgeous seven-inch square touchscreen that can recognize up to six household members and automatically switch between personalized experiences, displaying information relevant to whoever is using it. As you might already know, the HomeView also doubles as a smart home hub, with support for Matter and Thread. You can use it to control compatible smart home devices, view live feeds and recorded footage from HomeKit Secure Video cameras, and more. It also features a 12-megapixel FaceTime camera for video calls, and doubles as an entertainment device, letting you play music, display photos, and more. Apple’s AI-powered Siri assistant is another big part of the experience, allowing you to ask questions and get information using personal context from your messages, calendar, and emails. That means you can ask it to find your lost keys, play a song someone texted you, pull up a recipe with step-by-step instructions and built-in timers, or help you keep track of your schedule without having to reach for your phone. Read our hands-on impressions.

items.title: Dogs of New York
items.summary_html:
[This article was first published on R on kieranhealy.org, and kindly contributed to R-bloggers]. (You can report issue about the content on this page here) Want to share your content on R-bloggers? click here if you have a blog, or here if you don't.

I recently updated nycdogs, a data package for R that I originally made for teaching purposes. It bundles up New York City’s dog licensing and dog bite datasets into an R package. The data is already provided by the city in a directly usable way (as CSV files), but packaging it up makes it easier to integrate with other packages and get things moving a little more quickly in class.

The nyc_license table looks like this:
