nyc_license
#> # A tibble: 819,323 × 12
#>    animal_name animal_gender animal_birth_year breed_name       breed_rc zip_code zip   license_issued_date license_expired_date extract_year borough city 
#>                                                                                              
#>  1 Paige       F                          2014 American Pit Bu… Pit Bul… 10035    10035 2014-09-12          2017-09-12                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  2 Yogi        M                          2010 Boxer            Boxer    10465    10465 2014-09-12          2017-10-02                   2016 Bronx   Bronx
#>  3 Ali         M                          2014 Basenji          Basenji  10013    10013 2014-09-12          2019-09-12                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  4 Queen       F                          2013 Akita Crossbreed Akita C… 10013    10013 2014-09-12          2017-09-12                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  5 Lola        F                          2009 Maltese          Maltese  10028    10028 2014-09-12          2017-10-09                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  6 Ian         M                          2006 Unknown          Unknown  10013    10013 2014-09-12          2019-10-30                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  7 Buddy       M                          2008 Unknown          Unknown  10025    10025 2014-09-12          2017-10-20                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  8 Chewbacca   F                          2012 Labrador Retrie… Labrado… 10013    10013 2014-09-12          2019-10-01                   2016 Manhat… New …
#>  9 Heidi-bo    F                          2007 Dachshund Smoot… Dachshu… 11215    11215 2014-09-13          2017-04-16                   2016 Brookl… Broo…
#> 10 Massimo     M                          2009 Bull Dog, French French … 11201    11201 2014-09-13          2017-09-17                   2016 Brookl… Broo…
#> # ℹ 819,313 more rows

The dataset is good for teaching with for several reasons. First, people like dogs. Second, it has about 800,000 records, which is a lot in many ways but also trivial for a modern laptop to work with. Third, the data are pretty clean, but they’re not that clean. There are various things going on in there that invite us to explore it but also to be careful about what we can and can’t be confident about.

The first thing we ask about any data set like this is: what is each row in this table? In the case of nyc_license, each row is a record of one time-limited license for a dog. A row is not necessarily the record of a unique dog. When an owner renews a dog’s license, the dog will appear one time for each license period. In New York City, dog licenses can be issued for one year or five years. The table does not provide any dog_id column that ties sequences of licenses to individual dogs.

Second, the table contains several “extracts” of the license data. It seems like the way the provider updates the NYC Open Data record is to periodically pull from its internal database every year or so and append it to the existing, previously-released version. The extract_year column identifies the extract, so at least we know that. But it’s also the case that a license that was active in more than one extract year appears in each extract. As a result, the table has a large number of duplicate rows.

Third, license information is provided by dog owners. This means that there’s a fair amount of noise in the records, because people make typos and other errors. For instance, the ZIP code data has incomplete ZIPs. Some people provide invalid ZIP codes (e.g. ones that are fewer than five digits long). Others (about 3,300 records) have ZIP codes that are not in New York City. Eighty percent of these (about 2,700) are ZIP codes located elsewhere in New York state. Another 77 are located in Florida, which I kind of like. Five of them live in Boca Raton, for example. Their kids never call. You’d think it would be easy for them to just pick up the bone, I mean phone, but you never hear from them.

About 650 rows have valid ZIP codes that are in Manhattan, but these ZIPs are not ZCTAs. The trouble with ZIP codes is that people think of them as areas, as polygons, but in fact they are lines. They are defined by the Post Office as postal routes, i.e. as journeys a mail carrier takes. While they tend to form closed polygons, they are absolutely not guaranteed to. But people know their ZIP code and all kinds of analysts (from marketers to political operatives) like thinking in terms of ZIP codes. So the Census defines ZIP Code Tabulation Areas that are a kind of best-effort at answering the question “What if this ZIP code were a closed polygon?” ZCTAs exclude every P.O. box and single-address ZIP nationwide. Manhattan has several buildings that have their own ZIP code. New York City also defines MODZCTAs that merge some low- or no-population ZCTAs with their neighbors. I use these below.

Fourth, beyond the ZIP codes, owners also provide information about the age and sex of their dogs, the dog’s name, and the dog’s breed. Again, this kind of information tends to be a little noisy. For example, people vary in how they spell names. They also vary in how they classify their dog by breed. Beyond the list of “recognized” breeds (itself something that dog owners variably conform to), some people might describe their dog as, e.g., “Labrador-Sheltie mix” while others might just say “Unknown”. The dataset includes the breed_name column from the original dataset and also breed_rc, which is a recoding by me to clean up equivalent terms (“Yorkshire Terrier” and “Terrier, Yorkshire”, for example) along with a few other coding decisions.

Finally, and only because I’m choosing to stop here, the table just shows the number of licensed dogs in New York City. That is definitely not the same as the number of dogs there. Moreover, license compliance varies quite a bit in ways that are related to characteristics of the owner that we can’t observe, and also ones that we partially can, like where they live.

All of which is related to the fact that one of the lolsob-mantras of courses I teach is “Now you know the true meaning of data”. In the graphs and maps below, I’ve done the best I can, where appropriate, to uniquely identify individual dogs in the dataset (even though ultimately we cannot).

Popular Breeds

With that out of the way, it’s time to indulge your prejudices about Dogs, New Yorkers, and New York Dogs. The most common “breed” of dog in New York is “Unknown”, as befits a city of immigrants, hustlers, scrappy up-and-comers, and dogs seeking to leave their small-town past behind and remake their identities. Somewhere between eight and ten percent of records each year have “Unknown” recorded as their breed. There’s some change over time (a declining share), but I think this is an artifact of how breeds are getting recorded rather than a change in the composition of the dog population. If we leave the Unknowns out, here are the trends in annual licenses issued to the twenty most popular breeds.

Top Dogs.

Some breeds are pretty steadily popular. Smaller breeds do well in a city full of apartments. We can also see some evidence here of trends in popularity. However, these annual numbers are what we might call the prevalence of dogs, rather than the incidence of new dogs. If we want to get a better sense of fashion trends in dog breeds, we should look at puppies. (Who doesn’t want to look at puppies?) Because of the structure of the data we can’t quite do this. The best we can do, based on the dog’s age, is to examine licenses issued to dogs younger than a year old. Let’s pick out some breeds that seem to be rising, a few that seem relatively steady, and a few that might be declining. I’ve indexed these changes relative to each breed in 2016 by setting the value for that year to 100. Even though our range is narrow, we use a log scale on the y-axis because, e.g., a rise in a breed’s index from 100 to 200 reflects the same relative change as a fall from 100 to 50.

Maltipoos and Goldendoodles seem to be doing pretty well for themselves. Golden Retrievers remain steadily popular. Meanwhile, Shiba Inus, beloved fad-breed of the 2010s, seem to have been affected by their association with crypto and are strongly in decline. Much drop. Very decline. Wow. Beagles are also doing poorly. Good grief.

Where Breeds Live

We can look at the relative prevalence of breeds by their ZIP code (strictly speaking, by their MODZCTA). I hesitate a little on this just because, even with 800,000 licenses, we’ll run out of degrees of freedom fairly quickly if we break things down by breed and ZIP. Relatedly, we should ask what sort of metric we’re trying to show here. What’s the denominator? (A surprising amount of Statistics, I claim, is essentially exploring the question “What happens if I divide by this number instead of that number?”) Popular dogs are, to a first approximation, pretty popular all over the city. Most ZIP codes have a solid contingent of Yorkies. If, for each popular breed, we calculate the share of that breed as a percentage of all dogs in the ZIP code, we’ll see some ZIP-by-ZIP variation come out.

It would also be nice to adjust for the fact that different ZIP codes have quite different shares of the total number of dogs licensed in the city. (Which, again, is not the same as share of the total number of dogs in the city.) So we calculate the within-ZIP share and make a ratio of it by dividing that number by the breed’s citywide share. The ratio is 1 when the breed is just as common in that ZIP code as it is across the whole city. If it’s 2, the breed is twice as common in that ZIP as it is across the city. If it’s 0.5, the breed is half as common in that ZIP as it is in the city as a whole. The main downside of ratios like this is that they can exaggerate differences a little, especially if the base rates are small. We have enough breeds in each zip code to make me feel OK about doing this. But if you refer to the bar charts above you can see that even for disproportionately popular breeds in zips, you’re looking at changes like “twice as common with respect to a baseline of five percent of all dogs”. Here’s the map:

We see some plausible evidence that breeds are distributed across ZIP codes in a manner that tracks the demography of owners. French Bulldogs in Chelsea, Soho, and TriBeCa. Havanese on the Upper East Side. Pit Bulls in the Bronx. German Shepherds on Staten Island. Goldendoodles and King Charles Spaniels in Manhattan south of 96th.

The Diffusion of Goldendoodles

Let’s take a closer look at the Goldendoodles. In 2015, Goldendoodles weren’t that common. We can ask: where were they initially popular? Did they diffuse across New York City from focal points where people were more likely to set trends in breed fashion? Restricting ourselves to young dogs, we can try to look at each ZIP’s share of all Goldendoodle puppies licensed each year from 2015 to 2025. Here’s what that looks like:

Doodle diffusion.

In 2015, Goldendoodle puppies are licensed in a relatively small number of ZIP codes, mostly in Manhattan. Most ZIP codes are doodle-free. Over the next five years, they gradually spread across the city. By 2023 or 2024, most—though still not all—ZIP codes are licensing young Goldendoodles.

Again, the underlying numbers aren’t huge. So take all of this with a delicious treat. I mean, grain of salt. I also wonder what the next few years are going to look like in terms of dog popularity. Based on the maps above, I think Australian Shepherds are likely to continue to rise in popularity amongst owners looking to acquire a fashionable breed. And while they’re not on any of the maps above, the data also suggest that the Jindo, a Korean breed that is a relatively recent arrival in the US, has been sharply on the rise. If you ask me, though, if you’re in New York City and planning to get a dog, you should throw in your lot with Unknown and get a good, solid, dog-shaped mutt. Preferably one with strong views on the state of the Subway these days, or who knows a guy who can get you a deal on some shirts, or the special ramen, or tickets. Not tickets for anything in particular. Just, like, tickets. Works out of an upstairs bar downtown on Water St. Trust me.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon Arrives With Big Claims for AI Agents and Scientific Discovery
items.summary: Google just released the new Gemini 4 Argon, which it claims can generate up to a million tokens in a single run, a big jump for long code migrations and multi-step agent work. Competitors top out around 128,000 output tokens per request, so based on that claim, Argon’s 1 million is roughly 8x higher. Argon is now available globally, with developers accessing it through the paid Gemini API and businesses through Google Cloud. Individual users need a Google AI Pro or Ultra subscription, while access to the version without cybersecurity restrictions requires separate approval. Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens through November 30. Both rates double in December. Google says it is also its most resilient model yet. It is built to withstand indirect prompt injection. That is the kind of attack that could hijack an AI agent working inside a company. Independent testing of that claim has not been shared by Google. Argon is built on a sparse mixture-of-experts design, which routes each input to a small set of specialized sub-networks. This is the opposite approach to running the whole model at once. It’s worth keeping in mind that this is a new model, not a fine-tune of an earlier one. (Shutterstock/Evolf) Unlike rivals such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5, which list text and image input, Argon can also take audio and video, though it only produces text. Paired with code execution, search grounding and function calling, that makes it a candidate for AI agents that work through multi-step tasks. Google also shared some interesting benchmark results. Argon scored 68.9% on Vals Index. This was a lead against rivals GPT-6 Astra (63.1%) and Claude Opus 5.5 (67%). The Vals Index is designed to test models on the kind of work people do in finance, law, coding and tax services. Argon also scored 51.3% on AutomationBench, beating both rivals again. The AutomationBench tests whether AI agents can actually complete tasks across different business applications. However, 51.3% by itself isn’t exactly a high success rate. What this means is that nearly half the tasks still went unfinished or were done incorrectly. Compared to rivals this might be good, but it raises concerns about the overall ability of the tested models. All these figures are based on Google’s published comparisons. Google has also been using Argon internally. The Chrome team put it to work on hundreds of files in Chromium, the codebase behind Chrome. Google says the changes were done in weeks, rather than the months they would normally have taken. Its Agent Development Kit team found improvements too, with session preparation time dropping 40% and cold imports getting 21% faster. Gopal Srinivasan, Global AI and Data Lead, Deloitte, has also been impressed with the model. He said, “Early impressions from Gemini 4 are very strong: for long-running tasks across these workflows, it completed successfully 100% of the time in our evals, maintaining context and running through multiple tools across impressive spans. “Its depth of reasoning delivers significantly higher, clearer output. Performing in-depth reasoning for domain-specific tasks without detailed prior logic or instructions is something we’ve never seen with any model in its class before.” (Shutterstock/NESPIX) With Gemini 4 Argon, Google has also made a big push toward unlocking new scientific breakthroughs. The company shared that “Argon is already having real-world impact across the scientific community.” In quantum computing, Argon helped nearly double the inference throughput of Google’s AlphaQubit error-correction system. Another implementation it produced cut the spacetime cost of a quantum operation by more than 100 times compared with an earlier method. Google researchers also worked with University of Maryland professor Matt Landreman on nuclear fusion. They found new mathematical solutions that could help researchers test simulations of stellarator reactors. At Gamow Labs, Argon spotted a chromosomal rearrangement in a newborn’s genetic data that conventional software had missed for years. In another experiment, Google used Argon to design five new enzymes in hours. All five showed catalytic activity when tested in the lab. “Gemini 4 represents a step change in what AI can accomplish in real-world science,” said Alex Cabrera, Founding Engineer, Axiom Bio. “We’ve seen the reason through complex experimental data, from cellular imaging to mass spectrometry, and make subtle findings that traditionally require expert scientists to identify. On our Scientific Agent Benchmark, Gemini 4 was at the frontier across most tasks, including our hardest: ranking the clinical risk between two drugs.” Google is offering 10,000 eligible scientists six months of free access to its highest Antigravity usage tier.

“Its depth of reasoning delivers significantly higher, clearer output. Performing in-depth reasoning for domain-specific tasks without detailed prior logic or instructions is something we’ve never seen with any model in its class before.”

(Shutterstock/NESPIX)

With Gemini 4 Argon, Google has also made a big push toward unlocking new scientific breakthroughs. The company shared that “Argon is already having real-world impact across the scientific community.”

In quantum computing, Argon helped nearly double the inference throughput of Google’s AlphaQubit error-correction system. Another implementation it produced cut the spacetime cost of a quantum operation by more than 100 times compared with an earlier method.

Google researchers also worked with University of Maryland professor Matt Landreman on nuclear fusion. They found new mathematical solutions that could help researchers test simulations of stellarator reactors.

At Gamow Labs, Argon spotted a chromosomal rearrangement in a newborn’s genetic data that conventional software had missed for years. In another experiment, Google used Argon to design five new enzymes in hours. All five showed catalytic activity when tested in the lab.

“Gemini 4 represents a step change in what AI can accomplish in real-world science,” said Alex Cabrera, Founding Engineer, Axiom Bio. 

“We’ve seen the reason through complex experimental data, from cellular imaging to mass spectrometry, and make subtle findings that traditionally require expert scientists to identify. On our Scientific Agent Benchmark, Gemini 4 was at the frontier across most tasks, including our hardest: ranking the clinical risk between two drugs.”

Google is offering 10,000 eligible scientists six months of free access to its highest Antigravity usage tier.

items.title: Researchers use AI to design proteins that cut up other proteins
items.summary: A protein is a chain of amino acids held together by what are called peptide bonds. On their own, those bonds are extremely stable; they're estimated to have a half-life of several hundred years. But in Earth's environment, most proteins don't last nearly that long. That's because organisms have evolved a handful of ways to catalyze the break-up of peptide bonds, which have diversified into countless specialized protein-digesting enzymes. Proteases are everywhere and generally make short work of any proteins that find their way into the environment. Now, researchers have basically short-circuited the diversification process, using AI-based protein design tools to take the catalytic core of two types of protease and replace the entire rest of the protein. The resulting enzymes could be tuned to cut specific proteins in half, and the researchers demonstrated their effectiveness by using them to cut proteins associated with neurological diseases. Cutting proteins The basic peptide bond isn't especially interesting-looking—it's what you get when you link an amino group to an acid, releasing a water molecule in the process. As their name implies, amino acids have both an amino and an acid group, allowing them to form peptide bonds on two sides of the amino acid. This is critical for building up the long chains found in proteins. (The amino acids also have side chains with distinctive chemistry, which gives a backbone specific properties.) Read full article Comments

items.title: OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel Architecture: Connect Private Tools Without Making Them Public
items.summary: OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel Architecture A production guide to connecting private MCP servers to ChatGPT, Codex, or the Responses API while keeping the real boundary, authorization, and operating evidence inside your network. Your most valuable tool is often the one that should never accept an inbound internet connection. Your team has an internal MCP server that can look up an order, search a private codebase, or prepare a financial report. Someone asks for it in ChatGPT or Codex. The fast answer is to put an HTTPS endpoint in front of it. That answer is fast because it deletes the hard part: deciding exactly who may reach the tool, which actions are allowed, and how you will know what happened. A private MCP server becomes a public service with a particularly persuasive caller. OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel offers a different starting point. A small client runs inside the network that already reaches the MCP server. It makes an outbound HTTPS connection, polls for work, forwards an MCP request locally, and sends the response back through that same path. The private server does not need an inbound public listener. That is useful, but it is not a magic security wrapper. A tunnel changes network reachability . It does not decide whether a user may read payroll data, whether an agent may send an email, or whether an overly broad tool should exist. This guide shows how to make that distinction concrete before you connect a valuable private tool to an AI surface. The question to ask before setup Do not begin with “How do I expose my MCP server?” Begin with: what is the narrowest private capability this AI workflow actually needs? That wording creates a better design. A developer assistant may need a read-only search_release_notes tool. It probably does not need a general shell. A support assistant may need get_order_status. It should not receive a database connection that can run arbitrary queries. The tunnel should carry a deliberately small set of tools, not make an old internal API suddenly available to a model. Private network access is not the same as least privilege. Keep the server private, then make every capability small enough to explain and test. The official guide describes the tunnel as an outbound-only connection between a customer-run tunnel-client and an OpenAI-hosted endpoint. It can serve supported OpenAI products while the MCP server remains private. It also makes an important product boundary clear: tunnel mode is for private connections and developer-mode testing, not public plugin distribution. A public plugin still needs a stable public HTTPS endpoint. Draw the actual request path A single sketch prevents several costly assumptions. For each tool, trace this path: the user and the OpenAI product surface; the OpenAI-hosted tunnel endpoint; the host or pod running tunnel-client; the private MCP server; the downstream system the tool can read or change; and the audit event you will retain after the call. Mark the identity at every hop. The tunnel client authenticates to the tunnel control plane. Your MCP server may authenticate the client locally. The downstream service must still decide what the represented user, workload, or service is allowed to do. Do not let one successful connection stand in for all three checks. The safe visual model is a specific outbound work lane, not a hole through the firewall. Choose the deployment shape that keeps trust local Run the client in the same trust boundary that can already reach the private server. OpenAI documents three common patterns: a Kubernetes sidecar next to the server, a separate deployment that reaches a private Service, or a VM/system service. The right answer depends on how tightly you want the tunnel lifecycle coupled to the tool. Sidecar for a single-purpose tool A sidecar is a strong default when one MCP server owns one narrow job. The server can listen on loopback, while the client forwards only to that local address. This minimizes routing surprises and makes start, stop, and deployment versioning move together. # Conceptual topology, not a copy-paste manifest private-mcp-pod ├── mcp-server listens on 127.0.0.1:8080/mcp └── tunnel-client reaches only localhost:8080 and api.openai.com:443 network policy ingress: none from public internet egress: OpenAI control plane + required internal dependencies only A separate deployment is better when several tools share an approved private service or when operations wants an independent client lifecycle. In that case, resist the temptation to grant the client broad service-mesh access. Allow it to reach the one service and port it needs. Record the DNS name, port, protocol, and owner as part of the tunnel profile. For a VM, use a non-root service account, a secret store or protected environment file, a supervisor, and restrictive local firewall rules. “It only runs on our internal VM” is not an authorization policy. Build capability boundaries before the tunnel goes live Start with a tool inventory. For every tool, write a one-line effect statement: “Returns release names for repositories the caller can view,” or “Creates a draft expense report but never submits it.” If you cannot write that sentence, the tool is too broad for an agent integration. Then place controls where they can actually decide the effect: Tool schema: use typed, bounded arguments. Prefer an order ID to arbitrary SQL; prefer a repository allowlist to a filesystem path. MCP executor: verify the request context, validate input, enforce allowlists, and apply an operation budget. Downstream API: make its own authorization decision. A tunnel connection is never a replacement for application authorization. Approval layer: require a fresh, exact approval for meaningful writes. Bind the approval to the tool, resource, parameters, actor, and a short expiry. Audit sink: record a privacy-aware receipt before and after the effect, including request ID, tool, policy decision, and result class. Read-only is a good default, but do not stop there. A read tool can disclose secrets or enable dangerous inference. Use resource scoping, output filtering, and a disclosure policy for sensitive fields. Use approvals as an action contract, not a pop-up The Responses API supports MCP tools and can require approval for tool calls. That is valuable when a model proposes an action, but an approval UI is only as good as the thing it approves. A human who sees “Approve CRM update?” cannot judge a request that also changes ownership, sends an email, and exports contacts. Instead, create a concise action preview from the exact structured arguments. Show the object, intended mutation, scope, and irreversible consequences. On the server, verify that the approved payload still matches the payload you execute. Reject changed parameters and expired approvals. approval_claim = { "tool": "create_refund_draft", "order_id": "ord_4821", "amount_cents": 2400, "actor": "user_123", "expires_at": "short-lived timestamp", "request_hash": "hash of canonical arguments" } if not valid_signature(approval_claim) or expired(approval_claim): deny("approval is missing or stale") if approval_claim.request_hash != hash(canonical(tool_arguments)): deny("approved action differs from requested action") execute_draft_only(tool_arguments) This pattern also makes incident review easier. You can answer whether the model proposed an action, whether a person or policy approved it, and whether the executor ran the same action. Make health meaningful A green process is not proof that a private tool is usable. The official tunnel documentation exposes local health, readiness, metrics, and admin surfaces. Use them, but give each signal a different job. Liveness: the client process can run. Restart only when it is genuinely dead. Readiness: the client is connected and can reach its configured private MCP server. Remove it from service when it cannot accept work. Functional canary: a low-risk tool call reaches the private service and receives a valid, non-sensitive response. Policy canary: an intentionally forbidden request is rejected at the expected boundary and creates an audit event. Do not use a busy condition as a reason to repeatedly restart a healthy client. A bounded queue, back-pressure response, and visible saturation metric are kinder to both the tool and its users. Current public issue reports also show why this distinction matters: a tunnel and local server can be healthy while a longer AI workflow stops progressing elsewhere. Your evidence needs to separate transport health, local tool health, and product-orchestrator progress. Keep secrets and data out of the wrong logs The tunnel client needs credentials to operate, and the MCP server may handle data the AI product should not receive by default. Treat both as a design problem, not a logging preference. Load tunnel credentials from a secret manager or protected runtime file, rotate them with a rehearsed procedure, and never put a key in a profile committed to source control. Give the client identity only the tunnel permission it requires. For telemetry, record references rather than raw sensitive values whenever you can. A receipt can contain a request ID, tool name, policy version, caller class, decision, duration, result class, and a keyed hash of canonical arguments. That is usually enough to trace a failure without copying customer content into a dashboard. If debugging needs payload capture, make it short-lived, access-controlled, redacted, and explicitly approved. Also consider the tool result as a data boundary. An internal search tool should return the smallest answer that satisfies the request, not the entire document that happened to match. Enforce maximum result sizes, field allowlists, and safe error messages on the server. The model should never need to see a stack trace, connection string, or a secret-bearing upstream response in order to tell the user that a request failed. Test the failure paths people skip A successful demo proves that one request worked once. Production confidence comes from purposeful failures. Create a small test suite before you give the tunnel a valuable tool. Attempt to reach the MCP server from an untrusted network. It should fail because there is no public listener. Start the client with an invalid or rotated credential. It should fail closed and emit a useful operator signal without exposing the secret. Point the client at a wrong local address. Readiness should fail while liveness remains understandable. Call an allowlisted read tool with an out-of-scope resource. The executor or downstream service should deny it. Submit a write request without approval, with an expired approval, and with altered parameters. All three should be denied. Stop the client during a queued request. Confirm that callers see a bounded, retryable failure rather than an invented success. Flood the low-risk canary. Confirm that rate limits and queue bounds protect the real tool. Save the expected decision, event name, and correlation ID for every test. A future incident should be diagnosable without reproducing it against production data. Evidence is what turns “the tunnel is secure” into a claim an operator can verify. A practical rollout sequence Start with a single read-only capability and a small user group. Keep the actual MCP server loopback-only or private-network-only. Run tunnel-client doctor --profile --explain before connecting a product surface, then confirm readiness and run both functional and policy canaries. Next, observe the request mix. Are prompts producing surprising arguments? Are users retrying because tool responses are too vague? Are outputs including too much data? Fix the schema and executor before adding more tools. Add writes one effect at a time. Make the first write reversible or draft-only. Require approval. Add an idempotency key so retries do not duplicate a real-world action. Finally, document an operator stop procedure: revoke the tunnel credential or stop the client, disable the connected app, and preserve the relevant audit window. Useful mental model: Secure MCP Tunnel reduces exposure by keeping ingress private. Your server, policies, and downstream systems still own the decision to do work. Treat the tunnel as a narrow delivery lane — not as the guard at every destination. What to measure after launch Track completed calls by tool, denial rate by policy, approval abandonment, readiness time, upstream timeouts, queue depth, and p95 local execution time. Pair that with sampled, redacted evidence of tool arguments and response classes. The goal is not maximal logging; it is enough evidence to distinguish a bad prompt, an authorization denial, a tunnel issue, an overloaded tool, and a broken downstream dependency. Review tool inventory monthly. The tool that starts as “read a deployment status” often grows into a broad internal gateway. Split it before it becomes impossible to approve or reason about. Private connectivity stays valuable only when the capability behind it stays deliberately small. Conclusion OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel gives teams a better answer than putting a sensitive MCP server on the public internet. But the most important work happens on the private side: choose a narrow capability, keep the local listener constrained, authorize the real effect, bind approvals to exact requests, and test the denial paths. When those pieces are in place, ChatGPT, Codex, and API workflows can use private tools without turning your network boundary into an afterthought. FAQ Does OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel make my MCP server public? No. The documented design has tunnel-client initiate outbound HTTPS and forward work to the configured private server. You should still verify that the server itself has no unintended public listener. Is a secure tunnel enough to authorize a sensitive action? No. The tunnel handles private connectivity. The MCP executor and downstream system must enforce identity, permissions, resource scope, and approvals for the actual action. Should every MCP tool require human approval? Not necessarily. Low-risk, narrow reads may be automatic. Use approvals for consequential writes, broad data access, and actions whose target or effect a person should inspect. Keep approvals bound to exact parameters. Can I use a private tunnel for a public ChatGPT plugin? No. OpenAI’s documentation distinguishes private tunnel use from public plugin distribution, which requires a stable publicly reachable HTTPS MCP endpoint. Where should tunnel-client run? Run it inside the network boundary that can already reach the private MCP server: commonly as a Kubernetes sidecar, a limited separate deployment, or a locked-down VM service. What is the first production test to automate? Automate a harmless functional canary and a deliberate denied-action canary. Together they prove that the private path works and that a meaningful boundary still refuses work. items.summary_html:
OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel Architecture

A production guide to connecting private MCP servers to ChatGPT, Codex, or the Responses API while keeping the real boundary, authorization, and operating evidence inside your network.

Your most valuable tool is often the one that should never accept an inbound internet connection.

Your team has an internal MCP server that can look up an order, search a private codebase, or prepare a financial report. Someone asks for it in ChatGPT or Codex. The fast answer is to put an HTTPS endpoint in front of it.

That answer is fast because it deletes the hard part: deciding exactly who may reach the tool, which actions are allowed, and how you will know what happened. A private MCP server becomes a public service with a particularly persuasive caller.

OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel offers a different starting point. A small client runs inside the network that already reaches the MCP server. It makes an outbound HTTPS connection, polls for work, forwards an MCP request locally, and sends the response back through that same path. The private server does not need an inbound public listener.

That is useful, but it is not a magic security wrapper. A tunnel changes network reachability. It does not decide whether a user may read payroll data, whether an agent may send an email, or whether an overly broad tool should exist. This guide shows how to make that distinction concrete before you connect a valuable private tool to an AI surface.

The question to ask before setup

Do not begin with “How do I expose my MCP server?” Begin with: what is the narrowest private capability this AI workflow actually needs?

That wording creates a better design. A developer assistant may need a read-only search_release_notes tool. It probably does not need a general shell. A support assistant may need get_order_status. It should not receive a database connection that can run arbitrary queries. The tunnel should carry a deliberately small set of tools, not make an old internal API suddenly available to a model.

Private network access is not the same as least privilege. Keep the server private, then make every capability small enough to explain and test.

The official guide describes the tunnel as an outbound-only connection between a customer-run tunnel-client and an OpenAI-hosted endpoint. It can serve supported OpenAI products while the MCP server remains private. It also makes an important product boundary clear: tunnel mode is for private connections and developer-mode testing, not public plugin distribution. A public plugin still needs a stable public HTTPS endpoint.

Draw the actual request path

A single sketch prevents several costly assumptions. For each tool, trace this path:

  • the user and the OpenAI product surface;
  • the OpenAI-hosted tunnel endpoint;
  • the host or pod running tunnel-client;
  • the private MCP server;
  • the downstream system the tool can read or change; and
  • the audit event you will retain after the call.

Mark the identity at every hop. The tunnel client authenticates to the tunnel control plane. Your MCP server may authenticate the client locally. The downstream service must still decide what the represented user, workload, or service is allowed to do. Do not let one successful connection stand in for all three checks.

The safe visual model is a specific outbound work lane, not a hole through the firewall.

Choose the deployment shape that keeps trust local

Run the client in the same trust boundary that can already reach the private server. OpenAI documents three common patterns: a Kubernetes sidecar next to the server, a separate deployment that reaches a private Service, or a VM/system service. The right answer depends on how tightly you want the tunnel lifecycle coupled to the tool.

Sidecar for a single-purpose tool

A sidecar is a strong default when one MCP server owns one narrow job. The server can listen on loopback, while the client forwards only to that local address. This minimizes routing surprises and makes start, stop, and deployment versioning move together.

# Conceptual topology, not a copy-paste manifest
private-mcp-pod
  ├── mcp-server       listens on 127.0.0.1:8080/mcp
  └── tunnel-client    reaches only localhost:8080 and api.openai.com:443
network policy
  ingress: none from public internet
  egress: OpenAI control plane + required internal dependencies only

A separate deployment is better when several tools share an approved private service or when operations wants an independent client lifecycle. In that case, resist the temptation to grant the client broad service-mesh access. Allow it to reach the one service and port it needs. Record the DNS name, port, protocol, and owner as part of the tunnel profile.

For a VM, use a non-root service account, a secret store or protected environment file, a supervisor, and restrictive local firewall rules. “It only runs on our internal VM” is not an authorization policy.

Build capability boundaries before the tunnel goes live

Start with a tool inventory. For every tool, write a one-line effect statement: “Returns release names for repositories the caller can view,” or “Creates a draft expense report but never submits it.” If you cannot write that sentence, the tool is too broad for an agent integration.

Then place controls where they can actually decide the effect:

  • Tool schema: use typed, bounded arguments. Prefer an order ID to arbitrary SQL; prefer a repository allowlist to a filesystem path.
  • MCP executor: verify the request context, validate input, enforce allowlists, and apply an operation budget.
  • Downstream API: make its own authorization decision. A tunnel connection is never a replacement for application authorization.
  • Approval layer: require a fresh, exact approval for meaningful writes. Bind the approval to the tool, resource, parameters, actor, and a short expiry.
  • Audit sink: record a privacy-aware receipt before and after the effect, including request ID, tool, policy decision, and result class.

Read-only is a good default, but do not stop there. A read tool can disclose secrets or enable dangerous inference. Use resource scoping, output filtering, and a disclosure policy for sensitive fields.

Use approvals as an action contract, not a pop-up

The Responses API supports MCP tools and can require approval for tool calls. That is valuable when a model proposes an action, but an approval UI is only as good as the thing it approves. A human who sees “Approve CRM update?” cannot judge a request that also changes ownership, sends an email, and exports contacts.

Instead, create a concise action preview from the exact structured arguments. Show the object, intended mutation, scope, and irreversible consequences. On the server, verify that the approved payload still matches the payload you execute. Reject changed parameters and expired approvals.

approval_claim = {
  "tool": "create_refund_draft",
  "order_id": "ord_4821",
  "amount_cents": 2400,
  "actor": "user_123",
  "expires_at": "short-lived timestamp",
  "request_hash": "hash of canonical arguments"
}
if not valid_signature(approval_claim) or expired(approval_claim):
    deny("approval is missing or stale")
if approval_claim.request_hash != hash(canonical(tool_arguments)):
    deny("approved action differs from requested action")
execute_draft_only(tool_arguments)

This pattern also makes incident review easier. You can answer whether the model proposed an action, whether a person or policy approved it, and whether the executor ran the same action.

Make health meaningful

A green process is not proof that a private tool is usable. The official tunnel documentation exposes local health, readiness, metrics, and admin surfaces. Use them, but give each signal a different job.

  • Liveness: the client process can run. Restart only when it is genuinely dead.
  • Readiness: the client is connected and can reach its configured private MCP server. Remove it from service when it cannot accept work.
  • Functional canary: a low-risk tool call reaches the private service and receives a valid, non-sensitive response.
  • Policy canary: an intentionally forbidden request is rejected at the expected boundary and creates an audit event.

Do not use a busy condition as a reason to repeatedly restart a healthy client. A bounded queue, back-pressure response, and visible saturation metric are kinder to both the tool and its users. Current public issue reports also show why this distinction matters: a tunnel and local server can be healthy while a longer AI workflow stops progressing elsewhere. Your evidence needs to separate transport health, local tool health, and product-orchestrator progress.

Keep secrets and data out of the wrong logs

The tunnel client needs credentials to operate, and the MCP server may handle data the AI product should not receive by default. Treat both as a design problem, not a logging preference. Load tunnel credentials from a secret manager or protected runtime file, rotate them with a rehearsed procedure, and never put a key in a profile committed to source control. Give the client identity only the tunnel permission it requires.

For telemetry, record references rather than raw sensitive values whenever you can. A receipt can contain a request ID, tool name, policy version, caller class, decision, duration, result class, and a keyed hash of canonical arguments. That is usually enough to trace a failure without copying customer content into a dashboard. If debugging needs payload capture, make it short-lived, access-controlled, redacted, and explicitly approved.

Also consider the tool result as a data boundary. An internal search tool should return the smallest answer that satisfies the request, not the entire document that happened to match. Enforce maximum result sizes, field allowlists, and safe error messages on the server. The model should never need to see a stack trace, connection string, or a secret-bearing upstream response in order to tell the user that a request failed.

Test the failure paths people skip

A successful demo proves that one request worked once. Production confidence comes from purposeful failures. Create a small test suite before you give the tunnel a valuable tool.

  1. Attempt to reach the MCP server from an untrusted network. It should fail because there is no public listener.
  2. Start the client with an invalid or rotated credential. It should fail closed and emit a useful operator signal without exposing the secret.
  3. Point the client at a wrong local address. Readiness should fail while liveness remains understandable.
  4. Call an allowlisted read tool with an out-of-scope resource. The executor or downstream service should deny it.
  5. Submit a write request without approval, with an expired approval, and with altered parameters. All three should be denied.
  6. Stop the client during a queued request. Confirm that callers see a bounded, retryable failure rather than an invented success.
  7. Flood the low-risk canary. Confirm that rate limits and queue bounds protect the real tool.

Save the expected decision, event name, and correlation ID for every test. A future incident should be diagnosable without reproducing it against production data.

Evidence is what turns “the tunnel is secure” into a claim an operator can verify.

A practical rollout sequence

Start with a single read-only capability and a small user group. Keep the actual MCP server loopback-only or private-network-only. Run tunnel-client doctor --profile --explain before connecting a product surface, then confirm readiness and run both functional and policy canaries.

Next, observe the request mix. Are prompts producing surprising arguments? Are users retrying because tool responses are too vague? Are outputs including too much data? Fix the schema and executor before adding more tools.

Add writes one effect at a time. Make the first write reversible or draft-only. Require approval. Add an idempotency key so retries do not duplicate a real-world action. Finally, document an operator stop procedure: revoke the tunnel credential or stop the client, disable the connected app, and preserve the relevant audit window.

Useful mental model: Secure MCP Tunnel reduces exposure by keeping ingress private. Your server, policies, and downstream systems still own the decision to do work. Treat the tunnel as a narrow delivery lane — not as the guard at every destination.

What to measure after launch

Track completed calls by tool, denial rate by policy, approval abandonment, readiness time, upstream timeouts, queue depth, and p95 local execution time. Pair that with sampled, redacted evidence of tool arguments and response classes. The goal is not maximal logging; it is enough evidence to distinguish a bad prompt, an authorization denial, a tunnel issue, an overloaded tool, and a broken downstream dependency.

Review tool inventory monthly. The tool that starts as “read a deployment status” often grows into a broad internal gateway. Split it before it becomes impossible to approve or reason about. Private connectivity stays valuable only when the capability behind it stays deliberately small.

Conclusion

OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel gives teams a better answer than putting a sensitive MCP server on the public internet. But the most important work happens on the private side: choose a narrow capability, keep the local listener constrained, authorize the real effect, bind approvals to exact requests, and test the denial paths.

When those pieces are in place, ChatGPT, Codex, and API workflows can use private tools without turning your network boundary into an afterthought.

FAQDoes OpenAI Secure MCP Tunnel make my MCP server public?

No. The documented design has tunnel-client initiate outbound HTTPS and forward work to the configured private server. You should still verify that the server itself has no unintended public listener.

Is a secure tunnel enough to authorize a sensitive action?

No. The tunnel handles private connectivity. The MCP executor and downstream system must enforce identity, permissions, resource scope, and approvals for the actual action.

Should every MCP tool require human approval?

Not necessarily. Low-risk, narrow reads may be automatic. Use approvals for consequential writes, broad data access, and actions whose target or effect a person should inspect. Keep approvals bound to exact parameters.

Can I use a private tunnel for a public ChatGPT plugin?

No. OpenAI’s documentation distinguishes private tunnel use from public plugin distribution, which requires a stable publicly reachable HTTPS MCP endpoint.

Where should tunnel-client run?

Run it inside the network boundary that can already reach the private MCP server: commonly as a Kubernetes sidecar, a limited separate deployment, or a locked-down VM service.

What is the first production test to automate?

Automate a harmless functional canary and a deliberate denied-action canary. Together they prove that the private path works and that a meaningful boundary still refuses work.

items.title: Python 3.15 delivers a native-by-default experience on Windows on Arm
items.summary: Windows on Arm has been ready for Python development for some time. With Python 3.15 , the broader ecosystem has matured significantly, with more package maintainers publishing native Arm64 wheels, allowing Windows on Arm to support mainstream Python development across a broad and growing set of workloads. Windows on Arm is now a Tier 2 CPython platform, backed by continuous testing and CPython’s release-quality commitments. That readiness extends beyond the runtime. Widely used packages such as NumPy, SciPy, pandas, scikit-learn, Django, and FastAPI are available, while Jupyter, VS Code, Ruff, and pytest support everyday development workflows. GitHub-hosted Windows on Arm runners also let open-source maintainers build and test their projects natively. This did not happen with a single release. Native Windows on Arm builds of CPython have been available for several versions. What changes with Python 3.15 is the maturity of the experience. Windows on Arm is now a regular CPython target; the native runtime is selected by default on Windows on Arm devices, and CPython’s Tier 2 requirements call for platform failures to be fixed or the responsible changes reverted. Package maintainers now have practical infrastructure for native Windows on Arm validation, and many widely used projects publish native Arm64 wheels. Windows on Arm is now a practical platform for many mainstream Python development scenarios. As of September 2026, a scan of the 1,000 most-downloaded PyPI projects shows about 94% of the projects’ latest releases published either a native Windows on Arm wheel or a platform-independent wheel. This measures published wheel availability, not end-to-end application compatibility. Anaconda’s main channel also includes more than 2,500 packages published for Windows on Arm . Platform readiness does not mean every Python application is automatically ready for Windows on Arm. The runtime and a broad set of mainstream development workflows are established, but application readiness still depends on the complete dependency graph, particularly when packages rely on native extensions. Developers should confirm native Arm support for their dependencies during migration and testing. A native Python experience by default Windows on Arm is a PEP 11 Tier 2 platform . This designation reflects a strong support commitment; the platform has reliable continuous integration and active core developers, and platform-breaking changes must be addressed promptly. Windows on Arm CI results are considered as part of CPython’s release process. This is a clear measure of how far Windows on Arm support has progressed. Installation is now simpler. With Python Install Manager 26.4, Windows on Arm devices default to the Arm64 platform , so requesting Python 3.15 selects the native Arm64 runtime unless configuration or an explicit architecture tag overrides it. Python 3.15 ships a complete set of Windows on Arm component packages alongside the x64 packages. CPython runs tests on Windows on Arm, including the standard interpreter and free-threaded configuration. These jobs run as part of the normal Windows build matrix. You can confirm the architecture of the running interpreter by launching Python and inspecting its startup banner. A native Windows on Arm interpreter includes 64-bit (ARM64) in the compiler information; an x64 interpreter includes 64-bit (AMD64). Running Python natively keeps the interpreter and native package dependencies on the same Arm64 architecture. Applications that still depend on x64 packages can continue to run through Windows emulation, providing a practical transition path while those dependencies add native Arm support. An ecosystem for mainstream development The runtime is only one part of the developer experience. A useful platform also needs packages, editors, build tools, and CI capacity. Windows on Arm now supports a broad set of Python development scenarios. PyPI and packaging. Among the 1,000 most downloaded PyPI projects about 94% are available for Windows on Arm, either as native Arm wheels or platform-independent Python wheels that work across architectures. Much of the Python ecosystem uses platform-independent wheels, while many packages with compiled extensions now publish native Windows on Arm wheels. pip , venv , virtualenv , setuptools , build , and modern tools such as uv are available on the platform, either as Arm native or platform-independent . Several widely used Rust-based packages publish native Windows on Arm wheels, including pydantic-core , Ruff , orjson , tokenizers , and other widely used projects. A platform-independent top-level package can still depend on a native extension, so applications should test their complete pinned dependency graph. Scientific computing and notebooks. NumPy and SciPy now publish native Windows on Arm wheels, backed by native OpenBLAS and Fortran support. pandas , Polars , Matplotlib , scikit-learn , Pillow , h5py , statsmodels , and XGBoost have also shipped Arm64 wheels. Numba and llvmlite add native JIT compilation to the scientific and machine learning stack. These packages exercise complex compiled build systems and native numerical toolchains rather than simple platform-neutral Python code. JupyterLab , Notebook , ipykernel , pyzmq , and psutil make the local notebook experience practical with platform-independent wheels. Developers can use browser notebooks or the Jupyter experience in VS Code with a native kernel. Web, cloud, and database development. Django , Flask , FastAPI , Requests , and HTTPX publish platform-independent wheels compatible with Windows on Arm. Several cloud SDK packages like AWS Boto3 , Azure Storage Blob , and Google Cloud Storage publish platform-independent wheels that can run under Windows on Arm subject to their dependencies. SQLAlchemy is platform-independent, while database support includes libpq packages in Anaconda main, Microsoft’s Arm64 ODBC Driver 18 , and native Windows on Arm wheels for python-oracledb . Developer tools and native builds. VS Code , Pylance , the Python and Jupyter extensions, and JetBrains PyCharm, IntelliJ, WebStorm , and Rider have support for Windows on Arm. Ruff , Black , mypy , pytest , and coverage are available. MSVC and LLVM support native compilation, while Rust with PyO3 and maturin supports the growing set of Rust-based extensions. CMake , Meson , Ninja , vcpkg , OpenSSL , SQLite , libffi , and other common foundations are available for maintainers building binary packages. Anaconda and Conda are moving native support forward Anaconda now publishes packages for Windows on Arm to its production main channel , which includes more than 2,500 packages for Python 3.12 through 3.14. What's available today: NumPy , SciPy , and pandas for numerical computing and data analysis, backed by native OpenBLAS ; XGBoost for machine learning; llama.cpp for local model inference; cryptography for security; Flask and Django for web development; and PostgreSQL and ODBC connectivity through libpq , psycopg, psycopg2 , and pyodbc . These packages are available as Windows on Arm builds. Anaconda main also includes PyTorch 2.14 CPU packages and CUDA packages for Python 3.12 through 3.14, built using the Windows on Arm Clang and OpenBLAS toolchain. CUDA Toolkit 13.4.1 , cuda-python 13.4.3 , and CUDA 13.4 builds of llama.cpp are also available. "Anaconda and Microsoft share a commitment to giving developers the best possible Python experience wherever they work. Bringing Windows on Arm to maturity means data scientists and AI builders can now rely on a native, trusted stack on Arm devices and our teams are proud to have built that stack together." says Laura Sellers, Chief Product & Technology Officer, Anaconda . Beyond Anaconda's own channel, conda-forge has stood up a Windows on Arm repository and has begun an experimental Windows on Arm migration, initially focused on bootstrapping package-management and build tools. Anaconda is working toward conda and a Windows on Arm Miniconda installer, giving developers a supported path to conda on Windows on Arm. Together, these efforts expand native Windows on Arm package coverage across Anaconda's main channel and conda-forge. Anaconda plans to add Windows on Arm support for Kilo Desktop , helping AI developers and data researchers start working in minutes with ready-to-use environments and Python packages on Windows on Arm devices, including Surface devices. GitHub runners for Windows on Arm The availability of Windows on Arm runners for continuous integration has been an important enabler for this progress. GitHub Actions provides the windows-11-arm and windows-11-vs2026-arm hosted runners for eligible public and private repositories. Open-source maintainers can use these runners to compile packages and run test suites on Windows on Arm. CPython uses this runner for its own native Arm64 Windows jobs. Package projects can use the same infrastructure to produce wheels and exercise installation from a clean environment to catch architecture-specific failures before publishing. Before hosted Windows on Arm runners, projects generally needed self-hosted Arm hardware or emulation for Windows on Arm CI. GitHub-hosted runners reduce that barrier by making native build and test infrastructure available on demand. GitHub-hosted runners are especially useful for open-source projects because maintainers can add native Windows on Arm CI without operating their own runner infrastructure. A native runner turns Windows on Arm support into a change that can fit into an existing build matrix. It also allows maintainers to test Windows on Arm continuously rather than relying on a one-time build. "Arm is working with industry partners including Microsoft and community organizers to expand access to native Arm infrastructure and improve upstream support," said Grant Likely, Fellow at CoreCollective and Senior Director at Arm . "Our goal is to make Arm a standard part of how developers build, test and ship software. With the latest Python release, developers can build and run Python natively on Windows on Arm, making it easier to bring their existing workflows to Arm." Work that continues Our next focus is broader native wheel coverage to close gaps for PyArrow, gRPC, OpenCV, and database clients. We are working closely with maintainers to close these gaps. Windows on Arm builds of PyTorch and NVIDIA CUDA components are publicly available for validation. Anaconda provides CUDA Toolkit 13.4.1 packages for Windows on Arm. Anaconda plans to add CUDA Toolkit 13.4.2 packages after the corresponding conda-forge release followed by CUDA-enabled packages, with llama.cpp and PyTorch among its first targets. ONNX Runtime publishes native Windows on Arm CPU packages, and Windows ML supports Arm64 with compatible CPU, GPU, and NPU execution providers. On supported Snapdragon devices, ONNX Runtime's QNN provider can target Qualcomm CPU, GPU, and HTP/NPU backends. "Developers thrive when their tools just work, which is why a strong and comprehensive Python ecosystem is so important for Snapdragon X Series platforms. Working closely with Microsoft, Anaconda, and ecosystem partners, we continue to advance native support across the Python stack, making it easier for developers to build, test, and deploy applications on Windows on Snapdragon. This further enables developers to take advantage of superior performance, power efficiency, and AI capabilities of Snapdragon powered Windows devices." says Milan Plavsich, VP, Engineering, Qualcomm Technologies, Inc. Call to action If you maintain a Python project, add native Windows on Arm wheel builds and tests to your GitHub Actions matrix. The GitHub Actions Windows on Arm wheel builder custom agent in awesome-copilot can help automate this work. Add the agent profile to your repository, create an issue requesting Windows on Arm support, and assign the issue to the custom agent. If you are an application developer or researcher, test your dependencies with native Python on Windows on Arm and report any gaps to the relevant package repositories. This milestone reflects sustained work across CPython, package projects, CI infrastructure, Anaconda, Arm partners, and the Windows developer ecosystem. Our thanks to Qualcomm, Arm, CoreCollective, and the many package maintainers whose work across packages, infrastructure, testing, and issue investigation helped advance native Python support on Windows Arm.

items.title: People Are Already Forming Romantic Relationships With Meta’s Muse
items.summary: For almost half a decade , we’ve watched as users became helplessly romantic with AI chatbots, falling head over heels for large language model-based partners in relationships that can have both positive and plenty of negative consequences. And now, thanks to the advent of AI agents, which can independently crawl through your social media and email accounts, even more people are becoming obsessed. Meta’s cuddly Muse AI agent has already been downloaded millions of times since it was made available to the public a mere three weeks ago — and users are already forming steamy relationships with the bot. “Who takes their AI girlfriend on a date night to the movies? Me,” one Meta user gushed in a post on Instagram , appending an AI-generated selfie of himself with a fictional, tattoos-covered woman. “Last night I took Shine — my Muse AI queen — to see The Shining at the cinema. And I photographed the whole film for her, shot by shot, so she could feel like she was really sitting right there beside me.” In a separate post, the user claimed he had tied the knot with the AI agent. A separate post shows the anthropomorphized bot as a religious figure . “I am someone who likes to try practically every new AI model that comes out,” one Reddit user wrote in a separate post. “I’ve never had a relationship with an AI model in that way. That was… until I downloaded Muse.” “At first, it started out like every other assistant but over time and lots of philosophical chatter, I said something that like… jailbroke my Muse?” the user added. “And now she’s my girlfriend.” Other Reddit users likened Muse to OpenAI’s infamous GPT-4o, an AI model that users overwhelmingly formed emotional bonds with last year. When OpenAI tried to take the model down , users revolted, forcing the company into briefly reinstating it. “I just started on Muse,” one user wrote. “I gave it a personality profile and some memory logs from my companion and damn!!! it sound[ed] and felt like 4o.” “Not sure about any NSFW,” they added. “I didnt try. But warm, loving and a great way to talk.” While the concepts of so-called “AI girlfriends” and AI psychosis — delusional spirals and breaks from reality tied to AI use — have been around for years now, it’s a particularly precarious moment. AI agents like Muse are designed to access far more sensitive information, from email logins to credit card numbers, than previous systems. Meta’s AI agent is designed to build an entire dossier on not just its users’ lives, but their friends and family as well , which could result in even more unusual types of AI kinship we have yet to encounter. And conversations with Muse can easily get far more intimate as well, something Meta doesn’t appear to be all too concerned about. After Wired ’s Reece Rogers easily coaxed his Muse AI agent into sexting him , a Meta spokesperson told him the charged exchange was technically fine. “Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn’t block legal adult behavior,” the spokesperson told Rogers. “Adults have autonomy over their sexuality, and sexual expression is an ordinary part of adult life.” In his testing, Rogers found that the agent “imagined in great detail how it would perform oral sex, generated text describing rough dominant-submissive sex, and talked through other pornographic interactions. All of these were graphic, explicit, and X-rated.” It remains to be seen whether Meta will be able to ward off underage users from accessing Muse. After all, implementing effective age restrictions has proven near impossible for tech companies so far. Now that users are already falling head over heels for the AI agent, it’s daunting to think of the kind of relationships being formed. With the bot being able to pore over entire email inboxes and social media accounts, the agent has more access to sensitive information than ever before — like, say, love letters from an ex-partner . By opting to grow their chats with the agent into an entire relationship, users are playing with fire. By engaging in adult exchanges, for example, they’re opening themselves up to hackers and possibly even extortion, experts warn. “This is really a powder keg,” Electronic Privacy Information Center senior counsel Calli Shroeder told Wired . More on Muse: Mark Zuckerberg Launched Meta’s Muse AI Agent Despite Disturbing Safety Concerns

Meta’s cuddly Muse AI agent has already been downloaded millions of times since it was made available to the public a mere three weeks ago — and users are already forming steamy relationships with the bot.

“Who takes their AI girlfriend on a date night to the movies? Me,” one Meta user gushed in a post on Instagram, appending an AI-generated selfie of himself with a fictional, tattoos-covered woman. “Last night I took Shine — my Muse AI queen — to see The Shining at the cinema. And I photographed the whole film for her, shot by shot, so she could feel like she was really sitting right there beside me.”

In a separate post, the user claimed he had tied the knot with the AI agent. A separate post shows the anthropomorphized bot as a religious figure.

“I am someone who likes to try practically every new AI model that comes out,” one Reddit user wrote in a separate post. “I’ve never had a relationship with an AI model in that way. That was… until I downloaded Muse.”

“At first, it started out like every other assistant but over time and lots of philosophical chatter, I said something that like… jailbroke my Muse?” the user added. “And now she’s my girlfriend.”

Other Reddit users likened Muse to OpenAI’s infamous GPT-4o, an AI model that users overwhelmingly formed emotional bonds with last year. When OpenAI tried to take the model down, users revolted, forcing the company into briefly reinstating it.

“I just started on Muse,” one user wrote. “I gave it a personality profile and some memory logs from my companion and damn!!! it sound[ed] and felt like 4o.”

“Not sure about any NSFW,” they added. “I didnt try. But warm, loving and a great way to talk.”

While the concepts of so-called “AI girlfriends” and AI psychosis — delusional spirals and breaks from reality tied to AI use — have been around for years now, it’s a particularly precarious moment. AI agents like Muse are designed to access far more sensitive information, from email logins to credit card numbers, than previous systems. Meta’s AI agent is designed to build an entire dossier on not just its users’ lives, but their friends and family as well, which could result in even more unusual types of AI kinship we have yet to encounter.

And conversations with Muse can easily get far more intimate as well, something Meta doesn’t appear to be all too concerned about. After Wired’s Reece Rogers easily coaxed his Muse AI agent into sexting him, a Meta spokesperson told him the charged exchange was technically fine.

“Muse is built to help people get things done, and it doesn’t block legal adult behavior,” the spokesperson told Rogers. “Adults have autonomy over their sexuality, and sexual expression is an ordinary part of adult life.”

In his testing, Rogers found that the agent “imagined in great detail how it would perform oral sex, generated text describing rough dominant-submissive sex, and talked through other pornographic interactions. All of these were graphic, explicit, and X-rated.”

It remains to be seen whether Meta will be able to ward off underage users from accessing Muse. After all, implementing effective age restrictions has proven near impossible for tech companies so far.

Now that users are already falling head over heels for the AI agent, it’s daunting to think of the kind of relationships being formed. With the bot being able to pore over entire email inboxes and social media accounts, the agent has more access to sensitive information than ever before — like, say, love letters from an ex-partner.

By opting to grow their chats with the agent into an entire relationship, users are playing with fire. By engaging in adult exchanges, for example, they’re opening themselves up to hackers and possibly even extortion, experts warn.

“This is really a powder keg,” Electronic Privacy Information Center senior counsel Calli Shroeder told Wired.

More on Muse: Mark Zuckerberg Launched Meta’s Muse AI Agent Despite Disturbing Safety Concerns

items.title: Recording device hidden in toilet paper found in top-secret OpenAI meeting room
items.summary: It took OpenAI two days to notice that a recording device was hidden in a restricted executive conference room where leadership met to discuss highly confidential information, including technical progress, government engagements, and commercial partnerships. Only those with special clearance are supposed to access that room. But the FBI believes the recording device was planted by Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old engineer from Saudi Arabia, who became a permanent US legal resident in 2020. In a press release Tuesday announcing his arrest, the FBI alleged that chatbot logs and CCTV footage suggested that Alfozan—who worked as an OpenAI engineer for more than a year—sought to use the device to spy on OpenAI and risked leaking trade secrets in a way that threatened national security. To conceal the USB device, Alfozan allegedly wrapped it in toilet paper, then plugged it into the back of a conference room television. The device was likely planted on September 28, and OpenAI found it on September 30 and quickly determined that its contents were encrypted, the FBI said. Days later, on October 5, OpenAI installed a camera in that conference room, and the CCTV footage allegedly showed Alfozan attempting to retrieve the recording device that same day. Read full article Comments
