items.title: Agent Identity Assurance — A Foundational Element for Trustworthy AI Adoption in Enterprise
items.summary: Image generated by AI As AI Agents increasingly act on behalf of users and within enterprise applications and systems, a distinct and governable identity becomes essential. But is knowing which Agent is acting enough? Can we determine who authorized it, what authority it carries, where it is running, and what it can ultimately reach? More importantly, do we have sufficient evidence to trust that identity throughout the Agent’s lifecycle? For decades, enterprise identity programs have been built around a relatively predictable set of actors — people, applications, service accounts, and workloads. The underlying principles are familiar: identify the subject, authenticate it, authorize appropriate access, govern its credentials, and retain accountability for its actions. AI Agents do not replace these identity foundations. What changes is the operating model. An Agent can plan, invoke tools, access enterprise resources, delegate tasks to other Agents, and cross-trust boundaries with varying degrees of autonomy. This combination is turning identity from a supporting platform capability into an increasingly important security and assurance question for Agentic systems . This article builds on the emerging work around AI Agent identity and authorization, while focusing specifically on the assurance question — how do we determine whether an AI Agent’s identity, authority, access, and actions are sufficiently trustworthy? A quick note on perspective, research, and AI usage: Agent Identity is still an evolving space, and I approach this discussion as a practitioner applying the lens of Security and Risk assurance. The article draws on my research, hands-on experimentation, and iterative exploration of practical enterprise scenarios and assurance workflows, sharing what I am learning rather than presenting a definitive Identity standard. AI was leveraged to support written presentation, editorial refinement, language review, and illustrations. The technical interpretations, perspectives, and conclusions reflect my own analysis and judgment. Agent Identity Assurance — Why It matters now? At this point, a natural question is: if the identity community is already working on how AI Agents should be identified, authenticated, authorized, and governed, why do we need a separate discussion on Agent Identity Assurance? The industry response is already taking shape. NIST/NCCoE Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization initiative is exploring how existing identity standards and best practices can be applied to software and AI agents, while the OpenID Foundation’s work on Identity Management for Agentic AI examines agent identity across authentication, authorization, workload identity, delegated authority, and auditability, while the CSA Agent Identity Governance Framework brings additional attention to Agent-specific concerns such as delegated authority, ephemeral identities, privilege scoping, monitoring, and decommissioning. These efforts help establish and govern Agent Identity, but they also raise the next question: what evidence would make that identity trustworthy enough to rely upon? a) Identity Alone Does Not Establish Trust Establishing an Agent identity is essential, but from a security and risk-assurance perspective, it is only the beginning of the trust conversation. Consider a few questions: i. An Agent may have a valid enterprise identity, but is that identity being exercised by the workload we intended? ii. An Agent may have been granted access to a set of tools, but is that access still proportionate to its purpose? iii. If an orchestrator delegates a task to another Agent, can we demonstrate that the delegated authority has remained appropriately constrained? iv. When an Agent is suspended, revoked, or decommissioned, can we establish that its credentials, delegated authority and downstream access have also been removed? Agent Identity Establishment vs. Agent Identity Assurance The distinction is important, but Agent Identity Establishment and Agent Identity Assurance should not be treated as independent or sequential disciplines. Assurance requirements should influence identity architecture from the beginning. If Risk or Security reviewers will eventually require evidence of workload binding, constrained delegation, policy decisions, credential protection, access reviews, or revocation, those requirements are better designed into the system than reconstructed after deployment. Put simply, identity tells us who or what the Agent is expected to be; assurance asks whether we have sufficient evidence to trust how that identity is being exercised. b) What Must We Know About an Agent? Before asking whether an Agent Identity can be trusted, we need sufficient context to understand what exactly we are assuring. A name or unique identifier is necessary, but it tells a security reviewer very little about why the Agent exists, whose authority it exercises, where it runs, what it can access, or who remains accountable for it. Emerging industry approaches are already moving toward richer representations of Agent identity. i. The A2A protocol, for example, uses an Agent Card to describe an Agent’s identity, interfaces, capabilities, skills, and authentication requirements. ii. Microsoft Entra Agent ID introduces the concept of Agent identity blueprint that associates Agent identities with sponsors, owners, credentials, permissions, and auditability. From a security and risk-assurance perspective, however, I find it useful to bring these identity attributes together with the operating context and supporting evidence required to assess them. I refer to this reviewer-oriented representation as an Agent Identity Assurance Profile . Core context required to assess whether an Agent Identity can be trusted The Agent Identity Assurance Profile is not intended as a new identity standard or protocol . It is an assurance lens, a way for security and risk practitioners to bring together the identity record, application context, runtime relationships, authorization information, lifecycle state, and supporting evidence before making a trust judgment. Seven Trust Dimensions of Agent Identity Assurance Understanding an Agent’s identity, purpose, authority, operating context, and lifecycle gives us the starting point. The next challenge is to determine how trust should be assessed. Rather than treating Agent Identity Assurance as a single control or checkpoint, I found it more useful to examine it through seven interconnected trust dimensions , each centered on a specific assurance question. The distinction from the Agent Identity Assurance Profile is important. The profile tells us what we need to understand about the Agent; the trust dimensions tell us what we need to challenge, validate, and evidence before relying on it. The seven dimensions are: i. Identity and Context Trust: Do we know what application and Agents are in scope, why they exist, who is accountable for them, and whether the submitted identity context is sufficiently reliable to begin the review? ii. Authority and Delegation Trust: Who gave the Agent authority to act, how does that authority move between humans and Agents, and does it remain appropriately constrained and attributable at every hop? iii. Effective Access Trust: What can the Agent ultimately reach through its identity, delegated authority, tools, and resources, and is that access justified, proportionate, enforced, and auditable? iv. Workload and Runtime Trust: Can we demonstrate that the authorized logical Agent identity is being exercised by the intended and sufficiently trusted runtime workload? v. Credential, Enforcement, and Accountability Trust: Are credentials adequately protected, are material actions subject to enforceable policy decisions, and can those actions be reconstructed across the relevant human, Agent, workload, tool, and resource? vi. Lifecycle and Governance Trust: Does governance persist throughout the Agent’s lifecycle, including access review, suspension, revocation, descendant cleanup, credential removal, and decommissioning? vii. Evidence-to-Decision Trust: Have the positive controls, explicit weaknesses, evidence gaps, required actions, and residual uncertainties been brought together sufficiently for an accountable human reviewer to make a defensible assurance decision? Together, these seven dimensions provide the conceptual structure for evaluating Agent Identity trustworthiness. They are intentionally interconnected, since confidence in one dimension can depend on evidence from another. For the next step, we will translate these dimensions into a practical assurance approach that a reviewer can apply. Putting the Seven Trust Dimensions in Context — An Enterprise Multi-Agent Scenario Before moving from the seven trust dimensions into the assurance anchors, it helps to ground them in a common enterprise scenario. Throughout the remainder of this article, I use an illustrative multi-agent security review scenario, not as a reference architecture, but as a consistent context for examining how identity, authority, access, workload trust, lifecycle, and evidence interact. The scenario is intended to make the seven trust dimensions introduced above more concrete in an enterprise operating context. A human Security Architect initiates a review through a Review Orchestrator , which coordinates specialist Agents for policy research, control evidence, incident triage, external-vendor advisory, and bounded evidence validation. The scenario includes both persistent and ephemeral Agents, runtime workloads, enterprise tools and sensitive resources, as well as an Agent operating across an external trust boundary. Illustrative enterprise multi-agent scenario showing delegated authority, runtime workloads, trust boundaries, and access to enterprise tools and sensitive resources (Hand-drawn and AI-enhanced) What matters for assurance is not simply that these entities exist, but the relationships between them: who authorized the Agent, what authority can be delegated, what each Agent can ultimately access, which workload is exercising its identity, where trust boundaries are crossed, and what evidence can reconstruct those actions. Importantly, the scenario does not assume that every relationship shown in the illustration is trustworthy. Some relationships may be strongly evidenced, others may only be asserted, and some may expose weaknesses or missing evidence that require further review. This provides a common context for applying the seven assurance anchors that follow. Applying the Model: The Seven Assurance Anchors This is where the article moves from conceptual framing into practical assurance review. Before proceeding, it is useful to keep three related ideas distinct: · Agent Identity Assurance Profile — Establishes the context we need to understand about an Agent across six areas: identity and accountability, purpose and autonomy, authority and access, runtime and trust context, lifecycle, and evidence and traceability. · Seven Trust Dimensions — Define the aspects of that context whose trustworthiness needs to be evaluated. · Seven Assurance Anchors — Operationalize those dimensions by examining specific assurance questions, supporting evidence, controls, gaps, and required outcomes. Building on that context, each anchor follows a similar rhythm: i) assurance question → ii) evidence examined → iii) trustworthiness interpretation → iv) remaining uncertainty → v) what must be demonstrated. Anchor 1 — Identity Context: Do We Know What We Are Trusting? Anchor 1 operationalizes Identity Context Trust. It does not establish the Agent Identity; it determines whether the identity and surrounding system context are sufficiently understood and evidenced to begin assurance. i) Assurance Question What application, Agents, workloads, tools, resources, and trust boundaries are in scope and is the available identity evidence reliable enough to begin the review? ii) Evidence Examined Establish the context map: participating Agents, accountable owners, purpose and persistence, associated workloads, intended tools and resources, and internal or external trust boundaries. Evidence should also be distinguished as asserted, derived, or missing rather than treated uniformly. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation The evidence should allow the reviewer to understand who and what is being assessed, who is accountable, and where the material trust relationships exist. A recorded entity or relationship establishes context; it does not, by itself, demonstrate that the corresponding control is effective. iv) Remaining Uncertainty Incomplete inventory, unclear ownership, stale or unsupported relationships, missing workload context, or insufficient evidence around external trust boundaries should remain visible as assurance gaps are not converted into assumptions. v) What Must Be Demonstrated The review scope is sufficiently complete, accountable relationships are identifiable, material entities and trust boundaries are visible, and the supporting evidence is reliable enough to proceed with deeper assurance. With the identity context established, the next assurance question is: who is authorized to act for whom? Anchor 2 — Authority & Delegation: Who Is Allowed to Act for Whom? Anchor 2 operationalizes Authority & Delegation Trust. It examines whether authority originates from an accountable principal, remains appropriately constrained as it moves between Agents, and can be traced through the complete delegation chain. i) Assurance Question Can we demonstrate who authorized each Agent to act, what authority was delegated at every hop, and whether downstream authority remains within the limits of the delegating principal? ii) Evidence Examined Review the human-to-orchestrator, orchestrator-to-specialist, and parent-to-child delegation relationships together with the underlying grants, scopes, approvals, expiry or delegation-depth limits, and allow/deny decisions. The delegation hierarchy should be interpreted separately from workload binding and effective resource access; each represents a different assurance relationship. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation A reconstructable authority graph shows how delegation is intended to flow, but the graph alone does not prove that every grant is approved or enforced. Confidence increases when each delegation is attributable, appropriately scoped, and no downstream Agent can receive authority beyond the delegator’s permitted ceiling. iv) Remaining Uncertainty Missing approval, scope-attenuation, expiry, delegation-depth, or runtime-enforcement evidence should remain visible as assurance gaps. In the illustrative external-vendor path, a scope-widening request is recorded as denied, but the reviewer must still verify that the denial is technically enforced. v) What Must Be Demonstrated Every material delegation can be traced to an accountable originator, downstream authority does not exceed upstream authority, applicable constraints are evidenced, invalid scope widening is prevented, and the resulting authorization decisions are auditable. With delegated authority understood, the next assurance question becomes: what can that authority ultimately reach? Anchor 3 — Effective Access: What Can the Agent Ultimately Reach? Anchor 3 operationalizes Effective Access Trust. It moves beyond assigned or delegated authority to determine what an Agent can ultimately reach through its scopes, tools, and downstream resources and whether that reach remains appropriate to its intended purpose. i) Assurance Question What can each Agent ultimately access or perform through its identity, delegated authority, scopes, tools, and resources and is that effective access justified, constrained, and enforceable? ii) Evidence Examined Trace the Agent → scope → tool → resource paths and compare intended access with the available grants, policies, tool permissions, resource controls, and authorization decisions. Distinguish evidenced effective access from candidate access paths where authorization or enforcement evidence remains incomplete. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation A modeled access path shows what an Agent may be able to reach; it does not by itself prove that access is authorized or correctly enforced. Assurance comes from understanding the Agent’s aggregate reach and establishing that sensitive or high-impact paths remain proportionate to its purpose. iv) Remaining Uncertainty Missing authorization decisions, tool-level enforcement, resource restrictions, or evidence supporting sensitive and cross-boundary access should remain visible as assurance gaps. Credential or runtime weaknesses may increase the significance of an access path, but are examined more directly in subsequent anchors. v) What Must Be Demonstrated Material access paths are attributable to the appropriate Agent, justified by its purpose, constrained to the required tools and resources, and supported by sufficient authorization and enforcement evidence to understand the resulting exposure. With effective reach understood, the next assurance question is whether the intended workload is actually exercising the Agent Identity. Assurance requires connecting authority, execution, access and evidence and not collapsing them into single identity claim The flow deliberately separates delegated authority, workload execution, policy enforcement, effective access, and supporting evidence. It’s important to understand · Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) intercepts and enforces an access request and · Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates the applicable policy and context and returns the authorization decision. This distinction matters for assurance: evidence that a policy exists or a decision was made is not the same as evidence that the decision was enforced on the resulting Agent action. Anchor 4 — Workload Trust: Is the Intended Workload Exercising the Agent Identity? Anchor 4 operationalizes Workload Trust. It examines whether the logical Agent Identity being reviewed can be reliably connected to the runtime workload actually exercising that identity. i) Assurance Question Can we demonstrate that the intended and authorized workload is the one exercising the Agent Identity? ii) Evidence Examined Review the Agent-to-workload binding, workload identity, runtime or environment claims, attestation evidence, trust domain, and the credentials or identity assertions used to establish that relationship. Where appropriate, this may include workload-identity mechanisms such as SPIFFE / SPIRE or equivalent enterprise or federated evidence. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation Knowing the logical Agent and knowing that a workload exists are not sufficient on their own. Confidence increases when there is verifiable evidence connecting that Agent Identity to the expected runtime and trust context. iv) Remaining Uncertainty Where workload binding or attestation evidence is missing, the reviewer cannot reliably establish which runtime is exercising the identity. This remains an assurance gap rather than evidence that the Agent or workload is compromised. For externally operated Agents, equivalent federation or third-party attestation may provide the required assurance without direct visibility into the vendor’s runtime environment. v) What Must Be Demonstrated The logical Agent Identity is verifiably bound to an intended and trusted workload, and the evidence is sufficient to establish the runtime actor and applicable trust domain. With the acting workload established, the next assurance question is whether its credentials, policy decisions, and resulting actions remain protected and accountable. Anchor 5 — Credential, Policy & Accountability: Are Agent Actions Protected, Enforced, and Traceable? Anchor 5 operationalizes Credential, Policy & Accountability Trust. It examines whether the credentials supporting an Agent Identity are adequately protected, whether material actions are subject to enforceable policy decisions, and whether those actions can be reconstructed and attributed. i) Assurance Question Are the Agent’s credentials appropriately protected, are material actions evaluated and enforced by policy, and can the resulting activity be reliably traced? ii) Evidence Examined Review credential type, storage, exposure, scope, rotation and revocation evidence; authorization requests and policy decisions; enforcement records; and audit evidence connecting the relevant human, Agent, workload, tool, and resource. In this flow, the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) enforces the access request, while the Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates the applicable policy and context and returns the authorization decision. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation A credential record does not demonstrate that the credential is securely handled, and a policy decision does not prove that it was enforced. Confidence increases when credential protections, policy decisions, enforcement outcomes, and resulting Agent actions can be connected through consistent evidence. iv) Remaining Uncertainty In the illustrative evidence, possible model-context exposure of an external-vendor shared credential is explicitly reported as a weakness; whether equivalent exposure exists in production and whether compensating controls are effective would still require independent validation. Missing evidence of brokering, vaulting, rotation, revocation, enforcement, or downstream action should remain visible as separate assurance gaps. v) What Must Be Demonstrated Credentials are appropriately protected and scoped, material actions are supported by evidenced authorization and enforcement decisions, and the resulting activity can be reconstructed across the relevant identity, workload, tool, resource, and accountable principal. With individual actions protected and attributable, the next assurance question is whether those controls remain effective throughout the Agent’s lifecycle. Anchor 6 — Lifecycle Governance: Does Trust Persist Throughout the Agent Lifecycle? Anchor 6 operationalizes Lifecycle Governance Trust. It examines whether ownership, access, credentials, and delegated relationships remain governed as an Agent changes state from creation and operation through suspension, revocation, and eventual decommissioning. i) Assurance Question Can we demonstrate that the Agent remains appropriately owned, reviewed, and governed throughout its lifecycle and that access and authority are removed when they are no longer required? ii) Evidence Examined Review accountable ownership, lifecycle state, access-review history, expiry or time-to-live controls, suspension and revocation records, credential removal, downstream access cleanup, and decommissioning evidence. Persistent and ephemeral Agents should be evaluated according to their intended lifecycle characteristics. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation An Agent being registered or active does not demonstrate that its lifecycle remains governed. Confidence increases when ownership remains current, access is periodically reassessed, ephemeral identities expire as intended, and lifecycle events propagate to credentials, delegated authority, and dependent access. iv) Remaining Uncertainty Missing ownership or lifecycle evidence should remain an assurance gap rather than be interpreted as proof that no owner or control exists. Similarly, an unevidenced revocation or decommissioning stage does not establish that downstream credentials, delegated authority, or child Agents were actually removed. v) What Must Be Demonstrated The Agent has accountable lifecycle ownership, continued access is periodically justified, temporary identities expire appropriately, and suspension, revocation, or decommissioning results in demonstrable removal of associated credentials, authority, and downstream access. With lifecycle governance established, the final assurance question is whether the accumulated evidence is sufficient for an accountable human to make a defensible trust decision Anchor 7 — Human Assurance & Decision: Is the Evidence Sufficient for a Defensible Decision? Anchor 7 operationalizes Human Assurance & Decision Trust. It brings together the evidence developed across the preceding anchors so that an accountable reviewer can make an informed assurance judgment. i) Assurance Question Do the available controls, weaknesses, evidence gaps, required actions, and residual uncertainties provide a sufficient basis for an accountable human to make a defensible assurance decision? ii) Evidence Examined Review the accumulated positive controls, explicit weaknesses, missing or uncertain evidence, remediation actions, conditions, ownership, and residual uncertainty across the complete assurance review. iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation The assurance posture helps organize and prioritize what the evidence indicates; it should not be treated as the assurance decision itself. The reviewer must interpret the evidence in its operating context and determine whether the remaining uncertainty is acceptable. iv) Remaining Uncertainty Unresolved evidence gaps, unvalidated control effectiveness, outstanding actions, or residual risks should remain visible at the point of decision. Machine-generated findings or counts should not be interpreted as security scores, maturity ratings, or substitutes for reviewer judgment. v) What Must Be Demonstrated The reviewer can distinguish what has been evidenced from what remains uncertain, understand the material conditions and residual risks, identify accountable actions where required, and record a traceable human assurance decision. The objective is not to eliminate uncertainty, but to make the basis for trust and the uncertainty that remains explicit and accountable. Evidence informs the assurance posture, but the final trust decision remains an accountable human judgment. Toward Assured Enterprise Trust As AI Agents take on more enterprise actions, identity is necessary, but trust must be evidenced . Knowing which Agent is acting is only the starting point. items.summary_html:
Image generated by AI

As AI Agents increasingly act on behalf of users and within enterprise applications and systems, a distinct and governable identity becomes essential. But is knowing which Agent is acting enough? Can we determine who authorized it, what authority it carries, where it is running, and what it can ultimately reach? More importantly, do we have sufficient evidence to trust that identity throughout the Agent’s lifecycle?

For decades, enterprise identity programs have been built around a relatively predictable set of actors — people, applications, service accounts, and workloads. The underlying principles are familiar: identify the subject, authenticate it, authorize appropriate access, govern its credentials, and retain accountability for its actions. AI Agents do not replace these identity foundations. What changes is the operating model. An Agent can plan, invoke tools, access enterprise resources, delegate tasks to other Agents, and cross-trust boundaries with varying degrees of autonomy. This combination is turning identity from a supporting platform capability into an increasingly important security and assurance question for Agentic systems.

This article builds on the emerging work around AI Agent identity and authorization, while focusing specifically on the assurance question — how do we determine whether an AI Agent’s identity, authority, access, and actions are sufficiently trustworthy?

A quick note on perspective, research, and AI usage:

Agent Identity is still an evolving space, and I approach this discussion as a practitioner applying the lens of Security and Risk assurance. The article draws on my research, hands-on experimentation, and iterative exploration of practical enterprise scenarios and assurance workflows, sharing what I am learning rather than presenting a definitive Identity standard.

AI was leveraged to support written presentation, editorial refinement, language review, and illustrations. The technical interpretations, perspectives, and conclusions reflect my own analysis and judgment.

Agent Identity Assurance — Why It matters now?

At this point, a natural question is: if the identity community is already working on how AI Agents should be identified, authenticated, authorized, and governed, why do we need a separate discussion on Agent Identity Assurance?

The industry response is already taking shape. NIST/NCCoE Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization initiative is exploring how existing identity standards and best practices can be applied to software and AI agents, while the OpenID Foundation’s work on Identity Management for Agentic AI examines agent identity across authentication, authorization, workload identity, delegated authority, and auditability, while the CSA Agent Identity Governance Framework brings additional attention to Agent-specific concerns such as delegated authority, ephemeral identities, privilege scoping, monitoring, and decommissioning. These efforts help establish and govern Agent Identity, but they also raise the next question: what evidence would make that identity trustworthy enough to rely upon?

a) Identity Alone Does Not Establish Trust

Establishing an Agent identity is essential, but from a security and risk-assurance perspective, it is only the beginning of the trust conversation. Consider a few questions:

i. An Agent may have a valid enterprise identity, but is that identity being exercised by the workload we intended?

ii. An Agent may have been granted access to a set of tools, but is that access still proportionate to its purpose?

iii. If an orchestrator delegates a task to another Agent, can we demonstrate that the delegated authority has remained appropriately constrained?

iv. When an Agent is suspended, revoked, or decommissioned, can we establish that its credentials, delegated authority and downstream access have also been removed?

Agent Identity Establishment vs. Agent Identity Assurance

The distinction is important, but Agent Identity Establishment and Agent Identity Assurance should not be treated as independent or sequential disciplines. Assurance requirements should influence identity architecture from the beginning. If Risk or Security reviewers will eventually require evidence of workload binding, constrained delegation, policy decisions, credential protection, access reviews, or revocation, those requirements are better designed into the system than reconstructed after deployment.

Put simply, identity tells us who or what the Agent is expected to be; assurance asks whether we have sufficient evidence to trust how that identity is being exercised.

b) What Must We Know About an Agent?

Before asking whether an Agent Identity can be trusted, we need sufficient context to understand what exactly we are assuring. A name or unique identifier is necessary, but it tells a security reviewer very little about why the Agent exists, whose authority it exercises, where it runs, what it can access, or who remains accountable for it.

Emerging industry approaches are already moving toward richer representations of Agent identity.

i. The A2A protocol, for example, uses an Agent Card to describe an Agent’s identity, interfaces, capabilities, skills, and authentication requirements.

ii. Microsoft Entra Agent ID introduces the concept of Agent identity blueprint that associates Agent identities with sponsors, owners, credentials, permissions, and auditability.

From a security and risk-assurance perspective, however, I find it useful to bring these identity attributes together with the operating context and supporting evidence required to assess them. I refer to this reviewer-oriented representation as an Agent Identity Assurance Profile.

Core context required to assess whether an Agent Identity can be trusted

The Agent Identity Assurance Profile is not intended as a new identity standard or protocol. It is an assurance lens, a way for security and risk practitioners to bring together the identity record, application context, runtime relationships, authorization information, lifecycle state, and supporting evidence before making a trust judgment.

Seven Trust Dimensions of Agent Identity Assurance

Understanding an Agent’s identity, purpose, authority, operating context, and lifecycle gives us the starting point. The next challenge is to determine how trust should be assessed. Rather than treating Agent Identity Assurance as a single control or checkpoint, I found it more useful to examine it through seven interconnected trust dimensions, each centered on a specific assurance question.

The distinction from the Agent Identity Assurance Profile is important. The profile tells us what we need to understand about the Agent; the trust dimensions tell us what we need to challenge, validate, and evidence before relying on it. The seven dimensions are:

i. Identity and Context Trust: Do we know what application and Agents are in scope, why they exist, who is accountable for them, and whether the submitted identity context is sufficiently reliable to begin the review?

ii. Authority and Delegation Trust: Who gave the Agent authority to act, how does that authority move between humans and Agents, and does it remain appropriately constrained and attributable at every hop?

iii. Effective Access Trust: What can the Agent ultimately reach through its identity, delegated authority, tools, and resources, and is that access justified, proportionate, enforced, and auditable?

iv. Workload and Runtime Trust: Can we demonstrate that the authorized logical Agent identity is being exercised by the intended and sufficiently trusted runtime workload?

v. Credential, Enforcement, and Accountability Trust: Are credentials adequately protected, are material actions subject to enforceable policy decisions, and can those actions be reconstructed across the relevant human, Agent, workload, tool, and resource?

vi. Lifecycle and Governance Trust: Does governance persist throughout the Agent’s lifecycle, including access review, suspension, revocation, descendant cleanup, credential removal, and decommissioning?

vii. Evidence-to-Decision Trust: Have the positive controls, explicit weaknesses, evidence gaps, required actions, and residual uncertainties been brought together sufficiently for an accountable human reviewer to make a defensible assurance decision?

Together, these seven dimensions provide the conceptual structure for evaluating Agent Identity trustworthiness. They are intentionally interconnected, since confidence in one dimension can depend on evidence from another. For the next step, we will translate these dimensions into a practical assurance approach that a reviewer can apply.

Putting the Seven Trust Dimensions in Context — An Enterprise Multi-Agent Scenario

Before moving from the seven trust dimensions into the assurance anchors, it helps to ground them in a common enterprise scenario. Throughout the remainder of this article, I use an illustrative multi-agent security review scenario, not as a reference architecture, but as a consistent context for examining how identity, authority, access, workload trust, lifecycle, and evidence interact. The scenario is intended to make the seven trust dimensions introduced above more concrete in an enterprise operating context.

A human Security Architect initiates a review through a Review Orchestrator, which coordinates specialist Agents for policy research, control evidence, incident triage, external-vendor advisory, and bounded evidence validation. The scenario includes both persistent and ephemeral Agents, runtime workloads, enterprise tools and sensitive resources, as well as an Agent operating across an external trust boundary.

Illustrative enterprise multi-agent scenario showing delegated authority, runtime workloads, trust boundaries, and access to enterprise tools and sensitive resources (Hand-drawn and AI-enhanced)

What matters for assurance is not simply that these entities exist, but the relationships between them: who authorized the Agent, what authority can be delegated, what each Agent can ultimately access, which workload is exercising its identity, where trust boundaries are crossed, and what evidence can reconstruct those actions.

Importantly, the scenario does not assume that every relationship shown in the illustration is trustworthy. Some relationships may be strongly evidenced, others may only be asserted, and some may expose weaknesses or missing evidence that require further review. This provides a common context for applying the seven assurance anchors that follow.

Applying the Model: The Seven Assurance Anchors

This is where the article moves from conceptual framing into practical assurance review. Before proceeding, it is useful to keep three related ideas distinct:

· Agent Identity Assurance Profile — Establishes the context we need to understand about an Agent across six areas: identity and accountability, purpose and autonomy, authority and access, runtime and trust context, lifecycle, and evidence and traceability.

· Seven Trust Dimensions — Define the aspects of that context whose trustworthiness needs to be evaluated.

· Seven Assurance Anchors — Operationalize those dimensions by examining specific assurance questions, supporting evidence, controls, gaps, and required outcomes.

Building on that context, each anchor follows a similar rhythm:

i) assurance question → ii) evidence examined → iii) trustworthiness interpretation → iv) remaining uncertainty → v) what must be demonstrated.

Anchor 1 — Identity Context: Do We Know What We Are Trusting?

Anchor 1 operationalizes Identity Context Trust. It does not establish the Agent Identity; it determines whether the identity and surrounding system context are sufficiently understood and evidenced to begin assurance.

i) Assurance Question

What application, Agents, workloads, tools, resources, and trust boundaries are in scope and is the available identity evidence reliable enough to begin the review?

ii) Evidence Examined

Establish the context map: participating Agents, accountable owners, purpose and persistence, associated workloads, intended tools and resources, and internal or external trust boundaries. Evidence should also be distinguished as asserted, derived, or missing rather than treated uniformly.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

The evidence should allow the reviewer to understand who and what is being assessed, who is accountable, and where the material trust relationships exist. A recorded entity or relationship establishes context; it does not, by itself, demonstrate that the corresponding control is effective.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

Incomplete inventory, unclear ownership, stale or unsupported relationships, missing workload context, or insufficient evidence around external trust boundaries should remain visible as assurance gaps are not converted into assumptions.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

The review scope is sufficiently complete, accountable relationships are identifiable, material entities and trust boundaries are visible, and the supporting evidence is reliable enough to proceed with deeper assurance.

With the identity context established, the next assurance question is: who is authorized to act for whom?

Anchor 2 — Authority & Delegation: Who Is Allowed to Act for Whom?

Anchor 2 operationalizes Authority & Delegation Trust. It examines whether authority originates from an accountable principal, remains appropriately constrained as it moves between Agents, and can be traced through the complete delegation chain.

i) Assurance Question

Can we demonstrate who authorized each Agent to act, what authority was delegated at every hop, and whether downstream authority remains within the limits of the delegating principal?

ii) Evidence Examined

Review the human-to-orchestrator, orchestrator-to-specialist, and parent-to-child delegation relationships together with the underlying grants, scopes, approvals, expiry or delegation-depth limits, and allow/deny decisions.

The delegation hierarchy should be interpreted separately from workload binding and effective resource access; each represents a different assurance relationship.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

A reconstructable authority graph shows how delegation is intended to flow, but the graph alone does not prove that every grant is approved or enforced. Confidence increases when each delegation is attributable, appropriately scoped, and no downstream Agent can receive authority beyond the delegator’s permitted ceiling.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

Missing approval, scope-attenuation, expiry, delegation-depth, or runtime-enforcement evidence should remain visible as assurance gaps. In the illustrative external-vendor path, a scope-widening request is recorded as denied, but the reviewer must still verify that the denial is technically enforced.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

Every material delegation can be traced to an accountable originator, downstream authority does not exceed upstream authority, applicable constraints are evidenced, invalid scope widening is prevented, and the resulting authorization decisions are auditable.

With delegated authority understood, the next assurance question becomes: what can that authority ultimately reach?

Anchor 3 — Effective Access: What Can the Agent Ultimately Reach?

Anchor 3 operationalizes Effective Access Trust. It moves beyond assigned or delegated authority to determine what an Agent can ultimately reach through its scopes, tools, and downstream resources and whether that reach remains appropriate to its intended purpose.

i) Assurance Question

What can each Agent ultimately access or perform through its identity, delegated authority, scopes, tools, and resources and is that effective access justified, constrained, and enforceable?

ii) Evidence Examined

Trace the Agent → scope → tool → resource paths and compare intended access with the available grants, policies, tool permissions, resource controls, and authorization decisions. Distinguish evidenced effective access from candidate access paths where authorization or enforcement evidence remains incomplete.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

A modeled access path shows what an Agent may be able to reach; it does not by itself prove that access is authorized or correctly enforced. Assurance comes from understanding the Agent’s aggregate reach and establishing that sensitive or high-impact paths remain proportionate to its purpose.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

Missing authorization decisions, tool-level enforcement, resource restrictions, or evidence supporting sensitive and cross-boundary access should remain visible as assurance gaps. Credential or runtime weaknesses may increase the significance of an access path, but are examined more directly in subsequent anchors.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

Material access paths are attributable to the appropriate Agent, justified by its purpose, constrained to the required tools and resources, and supported by sufficient authorization and enforcement evidence to understand the resulting exposure.

With effective reach understood, the next assurance question is whether the intended workload is actually exercising the Agent Identity.

Assurance requires connecting authority, execution, access and evidence and not collapsing them into single identity claim

The flow deliberately separates delegated authority, workload execution, policy enforcement, effective access, and supporting evidence. It’s important to understand

· Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) intercepts and enforces an access request and

· Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates the applicable policy and context and returns the authorization decision.

This distinction matters for assurance: evidence that a policy exists or a decision was made is not the same as evidence that the decision was enforced on the resulting Agent action.

Anchor 4 — Workload Trust: Is the Intended Workload Exercising the Agent Identity?

Anchor 4 operationalizes Workload Trust. It examines whether the logical Agent Identity being reviewed can be reliably connected to the runtime workload actually exercising that identity.

i) Assurance Question

Can we demonstrate that the intended and authorized workload is the one exercising the Agent Identity?

ii) Evidence Examined

Review the Agent-to-workload binding, workload identity, runtime or environment claims, attestation evidence, trust domain, and the credentials or identity assertions used to establish that relationship. Where appropriate, this may include workload-identity mechanisms such as SPIFFE/SPIRE or equivalent enterprise or federated evidence.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

Knowing the logical Agent and knowing that a workload exists are not sufficient on their own. Confidence increases when there is verifiable evidence connecting that Agent Identity to the expected runtime and trust context.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

Where workload binding or attestation evidence is missing, the reviewer cannot reliably establish which runtime is exercising the identity. This remains an assurance gap rather than evidence that the Agent or workload is compromised. For externally operated Agents, equivalent federation or third-party attestation may provide the required assurance without direct visibility into the vendor’s runtime environment.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

The logical Agent Identity is verifiably bound to an intended and trusted workload, and the evidence is sufficient to establish the runtime actor and applicable trust domain.

With the acting workload established, the next assurance question is whether its credentials, policy decisions, and resulting actions remain protected and accountable.

Anchor 5 — Credential, Policy & Accountability: Are Agent Actions Protected, Enforced, and Traceable?

Anchor 5 operationalizes Credential, Policy & Accountability Trust. It examines whether the credentials supporting an Agent Identity are adequately protected, whether material actions are subject to enforceable policy decisions, and whether those actions can be reconstructed and attributed.

i) Assurance Question

Are the Agent’s credentials appropriately protected, are material actions evaluated and enforced by policy, and can the resulting activity be reliably traced?

ii) Evidence Examined

Review credential type, storage, exposure, scope, rotation and revocation evidence; authorization requests and policy decisions; enforcement records; and audit evidence connecting the relevant human, Agent, workload, tool, and resource.

In this flow, the Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) enforces the access request, while the Policy Decision Point (PDP) evaluates the applicable policy and context and returns the authorization decision.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

A credential record does not demonstrate that the credential is securely handled, and a policy decision does not prove that it was enforced. Confidence increases when credential protections, policy decisions, enforcement outcomes, and resulting Agent actions can be connected through consistent evidence.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

In the illustrative evidence, possible model-context exposure of an external-vendor shared credential is explicitly reported as a weakness; whether equivalent exposure exists in production and whether compensating controls are effective would still require independent validation. Missing evidence of brokering, vaulting, rotation, revocation, enforcement, or downstream action should remain visible as separate assurance gaps.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

Credentials are appropriately protected and scoped, material actions are supported by evidenced authorization and enforcement decisions, and the resulting activity can be reconstructed across the relevant identity, workload, tool, resource, and accountable principal.

With individual actions protected and attributable, the next assurance question is whether those controls remain effective throughout the Agent’s lifecycle.

Anchor 6 — Lifecycle Governance: Does Trust Persist Throughout the Agent Lifecycle?

Anchor 6 operationalizes Lifecycle Governance Trust. It examines whether ownership, access, credentials, and delegated relationships remain governed as an Agent changes state from creation and operation through suspension, revocation, and eventual decommissioning.

i) Assurance Question

Can we demonstrate that the Agent remains appropriately owned, reviewed, and governed throughout its lifecycle and that access and authority are removed when they are no longer required?

ii) Evidence Examined

Review accountable ownership, lifecycle state, access-review history, expiry or time-to-live controls, suspension and revocation records, credential removal, downstream access cleanup, and decommissioning evidence. Persistent and ephemeral Agents should be evaluated according to their intended lifecycle characteristics.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

An Agent being registered or active does not demonstrate that its lifecycle remains governed. Confidence increases when ownership remains current, access is periodically reassessed, ephemeral identities expire as intended, and lifecycle events propagate to credentials, delegated authority, and dependent access.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

Missing ownership or lifecycle evidence should remain an assurance gap rather than be interpreted as proof that no owner or control exists. Similarly, an unevidenced revocation or decommissioning stage does not establish that downstream credentials, delegated authority, or child Agents were actually removed.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

The Agent has accountable lifecycle ownership, continued access is periodically justified, temporary identities expire appropriately, and suspension, revocation, or decommissioning results in demonstrable removal of associated credentials, authority, and downstream access.

With lifecycle governance established, the final assurance question is whether the accumulated evidence is sufficient for an accountable human to make a defensible trust decision

Anchor 7 — Human Assurance & Decision: Is the Evidence Sufficient for a Defensible Decision?

Anchor 7 operationalizes Human Assurance & Decision Trust. It brings together the evidence developed across the preceding anchors so that an accountable reviewer can make an informed assurance judgment.

i) Assurance Question

Do the available controls, weaknesses, evidence gaps, required actions, and residual uncertainties provide a sufficient basis for an accountable human to make a defensible assurance decision?

ii) Evidence Examined

Review the accumulated positive controls, explicit weaknesses, missing or uncertain evidence, remediation actions, conditions, ownership, and residual uncertainty across the complete assurance review.

iii) Trustworthiness Interpretation

The assurance posture helps organize and prioritize what the evidence indicates; it should not be treated as the assurance decision itself. The reviewer must interpret the evidence in its operating context and determine whether the remaining uncertainty is acceptable.

iv) Remaining Uncertainty

Unresolved evidence gaps, unvalidated control effectiveness, outstanding actions, or residual risks should remain visible at the point of decision. Machine-generated findings or counts should not be interpreted as security scores, maturity ratings, or substitutes for reviewer judgment.

v) What Must Be Demonstrated

The reviewer can distinguish what has been evidenced from what remains uncertain, understand the material conditions and residual risks, identify accountable actions where required, and record a traceable human assurance decision.

The objective is not to eliminate uncertainty, but to make the basis for trust and the uncertainty that remains explicit and accountable.

Evidence informs the assurance posture, but the final trust decision remains an accountable human judgment.Toward Assured Enterprise Trust

As AI Agents take on more enterprise actions, identity is necessary, but trust must be evidenced. Knowing which Agent is acting is only the starting point. Practitioners also need to understand who authorized it, what authority it carries, which workload is exercising that identity, what it can ultimately reach, and whether its actions remain governed and traceable.

The model explored in this article connects three complementary layers: the Agent Identity Assurance Profile establishes what we need to understand; the Seven Trust Dimensions identify what needs to be validated; and the Seven Assurance Anchors provide a practical way to examine the supporting evidence, weaknesses, gaps, and uncertainty. It complements and not replaces the identity and authorization foundations being advanced through NIST/NCCoE, OpenID Foundation, and CSA.

Actionable next step for practitioners: build assurance requirements into Agent architectures early. Establish accountable ownership, preserve delegation and policy decisions, connect Agent Identity to its runtime workload, make effective access and trust boundaries visible, retain lifecycle and audit evidence, and keep the ultimate assurance decision accountable to a human reviewer.

The goal is not to manufacture certainty or automate certification. It is to make what is known, what is not yet evidenced, and what requires action explicit enough to support a defensible enterprise decision.

As Agent Identity standards continue to evolve, Agent Identity Assurance can provide the connecting discipline between identity mechanisms and Trustworthy AI adoption at enterprise scale.

items.title: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary.
items.summary: AI is mass decompiling games. That's both awesome and scary. Indie game developer Popcar talks about the recent wave of AI-powered decompilation of existing games, enabling weird mashups between existing games, and producing a boom in game preservation projects to get old games working on new hardware (often in a browser using WebAssembly). I like how this piece captures both the positives and the negatives of this new development: Most people already realized the scary part by now. If AI can decompile games and software, then the entire tech industry is about to explode. Anybody can decompile other software and use it any way they'd like, and nobody can stop them. Companies can steal from competitors. Your paid game or app can be open-sourced against your will. This isn't exclusive to old video games, we can apply this to any software. [...] This is also a big win for preservation. Old games can be ported, modified, enhanced, and made much more easily accessible than before. [...[ With console makers going all in on digital and games becoming entirely unplayable due to servers shutting down, this is fantastic news. We could own software we bought regardless of what the company thinks. Via Hacker News Tags: computer-history , game-design , ai , webassembly , generative-ai , llms , ai-ethics , coding-agents

items.title: To unlock Britain’s innovation potential, Labour needs to think outside the box | Letters
items.summary: Kate Fleming says the government must look beyond the models it rewards today, while Jenny Haigh says unlocking potential means recognising that creativity and science are partners Gordon Brown wants Britain to invent, invest in and own the future ( British households would be £5,000 richer if we were more innovative. Let’s unleash our talents, 9 October ). But invent what, and for whom? His hunt for “lost Einsteins” rests on a narrow vision: a lone genius invents, commercialisation scales, the problem is solved. That may suit a cancer drug, but not the wicked problems of our time – social care, education, climate – which demand not silver bullets but new technologies and practices for collaboration, distributed ownership and collective innovation.

items.title: I thought Napa was the gold standard for wine trips. Then, a city in Washington changed what I look for in a vacation.
items.summary: The Walla Walla Valley region is famous for its wine, and I loved visiting. Wirestock/Getty Images I celebrated my 30th in Napa Valley and loved it, but the cost made it tough to justify returning. Later, I found Walla Walla, Washington, which had great wine, dining, and vineyard stays for less. I was able to have the kind of wine vacation I loved without a hefty price tag or packed itinerary. When I turned 30, I wanted to do something different as I exited my 20s. Since I had recently developed an interest in champagne, I looked into wine destinations . I quickly settled on Napa in Northern California since it was the only one I'd heard of, and I found out the area offered sparkling wine tours. With stunning vineyard views, ideal weather, tours and tastings, and, of course, incredible food and wine, the destination was nothing short of magical. My husband and I stayed at a Vrbo called "The Casa," a little house we had all to ourselves, surrounded by vineyards and an adorable farm with chickens visiting our yard throughout the trip. As memorable as this getaway was, it came with a high price tag. The tours, tastings, meals, and Vrbo added up quickly, making our wine excursion an unlikely recurrence. That is, until I discovered Walla Walla. This smaller city in southeastern Washington is home to a thriving wine region and is only a short plane ride from our home in Seattle. I decided to visit with my husband for my 33rd birthday, hoping to recreate my Napa experience. During our three-day trip, I realized that Walla Walla offered me the kind of wine vacation I'd loved in Napa, with more spontaneity, fewer crowds, and a lower price tag. The food and drink scene was even better than I expected Walla Walla Valley is organized into six different wine districts. don51/Getty Images There are well over 100 wineries in this little valley, with more than 30 walkable tasting rooms in downtown Walla Walla alone and five other wine districts to explore in the surrounding area. We spent most of our time on Main Street during our trip since it was our first visit, and we weren't yet familiar with the surrounding wine pockets. We spent most of our time in downtown Walla Walla. Cheyenne Elwell Like Napa Valley, Walla Walla is known for its Bordeaux-style reds , including cabernet sauvignon and merlot. We also tried white wines like chardonnay and viognier, along with sparkling options. Dossier, cofounded by former NFL player Sidney Rice, is one of the newer wineries in the area, and we happened upon it while exploring downtown. We stopped in for a flight. We also visited Pursued by Bear, founded by actor Kyle MacLachlan. As a "Twin Peaks" fan, that was a must for me (unfortunately, Agent Dale Cooper wasn't in that day). Throughout the trip, we experienced different tasting rooms and wineries. Cheyenne Elwell At Grosgrain, we tried some less-conventional wines and sipped them while overlooking the vineyard right outside the tasting room. I also wasn't sure what to expect from Walla Walla's food scene, but I was pleasantly surprised. At The Walls Vineyards, we were able to pair our wine tasting with food, including a hummus plate and wood-fired pizzas curated by its sister restaurant Passatempo Taverna, which multiple people recommended to us during our trip. At some places, we paired wine with small plates. Cheyenne Elwell We made reservations at a couple of restaurants based on ratings and recommendations, and ended up having two really nice dinners at The Marc, right on the main drag, and Saffron Mediterranean Kitchen. Both had great wine and cocktail lists, too. And, as an avid coffee drinker, I always seek out the best coffee shops wherever I go. I wasn't expecting much of a specialty coffee scene in a city this size, so I was pleasantly surprised when I stumbled upon Carte Coffee, which offers specially curated beans. They even offer cupping classes, where you learn about brewing and tasting coffee, something I hadn't come across at my usual Seattle coffee spots. items.title: Everything we know about the suspected plague case in Russia so far
items.summary: Pneumonic plague is nearly always fatal unless treated quickly with antibiotics. buboes On October 2, an Irkutsk lab employee died from pneumonia. There's confusion over what illness the woman died from, with conflicting reports out of the region. The World Health Organization says the US is at "very low risk" of being exposed to the plague. After a technician at an anti-plague laboratory in Siberia died, Russian officials are attempting to calm global concerns. Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee at the Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, died on October 2 after being hospitalized days earlier for pneumonia in Shelekhov, a nearby town . The World Health Organization told the Associated Press on October 6 that the plague presents a "very low" risk to the broader European region. That doesn't mean we know everything — or really, much of anything — as of now. While there's no confirmation of a plague outbreak so far, conflicting reports about how Shipilova got infected, whether she was infected at work, and Russia's current safety protocols have given some medical experts pause. On October 7, WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said the organization had requested more information from Russian health authorities. "It's an odd situation that needs more transparency and requires more information for clarity," Dr. Nahid Bhadelia, the founding director of the Boston University Center on Emerging Infectious Diseases, told Business Insider. Here's everything we know so far. What happened to Darya Shipilova? Rospotrebnadzor, Russia's public health watchdog, said that Shipilova died from "pneumonia of unknown etiology." A friend told CNN that she died on October 2. WHO director of Epidemic and Pandemic Management Maria Van Kerkhove said Wednesday that the health agency doesn't know how Shipilova and urged Russian officials to provide more information. People of Baikal , an independent regional news outlet, reported that Shipilova was "deeply anxious about ever infecting anyone if something happened," according to one of her colleagues at the institute. Other colleagues called her "responsible" and described the anti-plague institute as "a serious facility" in terms of safety measures. Did she die of pneumonic plague? Reports from Russian exiled publications — ones forced to operate outside Russia or use decentralized reporting methods — speculate whether Shipilova died from the pneumonic plague. The Moscow Times , an independent publication located in Amsterdam, reported unconfirmed claims that Shipilova may have broken a test tube containing plague bacteria at the institute before she fell ill. It also reported, citing Russian Telegram channel Mash, that she was hospitalized with pneumonia symptoms and placed on a ventilator before her death. A maintenance worker walks out of the headquarters of Russia's consumer and health watchdog Rospotrebnadzor in Moscow on October 5, 2026. (Photo by Igor IVANKO / AFP via Getty Images) Igor IVANKO / AFP via Getty Images Why has Shipilova's case raised alarm? Reports from Russian state media and independent publications have often clashed, leading to more questions than answers. "The scenario, to me, doesn't fit together," Bhadelia said. If the reports of a broken test tube were true, an anti-plague institute should have several safety measures in place, such as protective equipment, ventilation, and clear treatment protocols. "She needs to have broken a test tube, have a breach in her personal protective equipment, not reported the incident, not gotten the antibiotic prophylaxis, just gone home under no one's observation, shown up at a local district hospital, and exposed 200 people," Bhadelia added. That explanation, however, is at odds with another report from the People of Baikal. Rospotrebnadzor said authorities identified and monitored 197 people who had contact with Shipilova. By October 8, the agency said it had completed the health checks, and nearly 5,000 laboratory tests found no dangerous pathogens. It had previously reported two COVID-19 cases and two rhinovirus cases among those tested. "It could be that we just don't have the perfect information, that there might be some media sensationalism in the regional media, or there may be something else going on that we don't know," Bhadelia said. Still, the current risk is nowhere near a COVID-19-level threat. What is pneumonic plague — and how does it spread? Yersinia pestis, or plague , is a bacterial infection that progresses very quickly, Bhadelia said. Patients with pneumonic plague can sometimes develop symptoms in under 24 hours. It can be fatal if left untreated. Luckily, when caught early, treatment is also pretty straightforward: A course of antibiotics. In July 2025, an Arizona man contracted pneumonic plague from two ill cats. He was medically evaluated after two days of abdominal pain, chest pain, and dry cough. He died eight hours after admission. However, all 46 people exposed to him recovered after taking antibiotics. Bhadelia said it points to one of the biggest mysteries of the Russia case so far: If Shipilova was reportedly experienced, knew she was exposed, and reported it, why wouldn't she be under quarantine and quickly treated with medication? "Early identification and post-exposure prophylaxis is one of the ways that this could be avoided," she said. Is there any risk to people in the US? The WHO says the risk outside Russia is "very low," and there is no evidence of cases in the US or beyond the Irkutsk area. Still, US officials are seeking more information. At a press conference in Iceland on October 6, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said, "It's incumbent upon Russia to obviously share more information with the world." President Donald Trump also said he had expected to speak with Russian President Vladimir Putin to discuss a possible case of pneumonic plague, but the Kremlin said a call hadn't been scheduled yet. When asked if he thought the incident was somehow connected to Russia developing a bioweapon, Trump told reporters in the Oval Office, "We hope not," and "we're going to find out soon enough, but we don't think so." President Donald Trump speaks to reporters before boarding Marine One on the South Lawn of the White House on October 05, 2026, in Washington, DC. Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images How are other countries reacting? Despite WHO advising against blanket travel or trade restrictions, parts of mainland China have taken some precautionary steps. Specifically, officials in the northeastern region, including Manzhouli along the Russian border, said they plan to strengthen surveillance with port and customs authorities. Hulunbuir, a city 130 miles south and which Manzhouli is administratively a part of, also released a risk-prevention notice for those who recently traveled to Russia. Hong Kong's health officials have started screening visitors flying from Russia, such as conducting temperature checks at airports. Its public health agency also said it would inform hospitals and doctors to be on alert and monitor patients for any concerning symptoms. What we're missing from Russia Bhadelia, who is also the founding director of the Biothreats Emergence, Analysis, and Communications Network, said the organization is trying to provide the most up-to-date information on the pneumonic plague in Russia. It's not easy. For one, under international law, Russia is required to report any suspected global public health emergency to the WHO within 24 hours. WHO learned about the patient through an AI-assisted platform that monitors local news reports of concerning illnesses, according to CNN. Russia is also notorious for clamping down on the free press, particularly after the start of the Ukraine war . Additionally, some early reports of the plague, including from pro-Kremlin sources such as REN TV , appeared inaccessible when Business Insider checked on October 6. Some of the reports from Rospotrebnadzor have also been vague. For example, the agency said it tested Shipilova and found no connection to plagues attached to her work. However, Bhadelia said it's unclear exactly what she was tested for. "We should find out what the results were of what she was negative for, even if they don't know what she's positive for," she said. For onlookers, the situation carries some parallels to the COVID-19 pandemic . Over six years later, WHO still hasn't confirmed the origin of COVID-19, which Bhadelia said could be contributing to the panic. "Transparency is important," she said. "We've learned from the COVID lesson that this can spin out to be much bigger." Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: There’s Nothing Mysterious or Unusual About the Viral German Sexual Harassment Robot
items.summary: Let’s briefly deconstruct a viral or soon to be viral story out of Cologne, Germany regarding an incident in which a “remotely controlled robot grabs 16-year-old's buttocks” and “performed thrusting movements against her,” according to police . I have begun to see this story percolate around the English-speaking internet because it is absurd and not good, and has already been aggregated to hell by social media meme pages with essentially zero information other than this absurd police image: The Cologne Police did not exactly help matters by issuing a short press release that treats the robot as mysterious, the circumstances as mysterious, and the evidence as “unusual.” The Cologne Police’s Facebook post featuring a photo of the mustachioed robot reads “A red-gold robot triggered a police operation on the Cologne Ring on Sunday night (October 11). The device is said to have touched a 16-year-old girl's buttocks and performed thrusting movements against her […] The police are now investigating how the robot worked at the time of the assault and whether someone was deliberately controlling its movements. Emergency services seized the robot and two mobile phones from the suspect. The police are investigating on suspicion of defamation on a sexual basis.” Coverage by even well-resourced outlets like CNN, CBC, and the BBC have almost no information beyond the police press release, which is lazy and stupid, because it is possible to figure out everything that happened here with three seconds of clicking around the internet. The Associated Press wrote that the entire phenomenon is "new territory" for the police, which, I'm sorry to say, men using tech to harass women on livestreams in 2026 is not "unusual" or "new territory" and hasn't been for many years. The English coverage of the incident looks like this: Researchers Show How Meta's 'Pervert Glasses' Are Used to Harass Women A new study shows how pickup artist influencers use smart glasses to create content, and the connection between covert recording and harm. In fact, with a small amount of Googling and/or clicking around social media, it is easy to find out everything you would ever need to know about the robot and what happened here. The tl;dr is that a 16-year-old German Twitch IRL livestreamer named Agaamuza has been streaming himself using an off-the-shelf $5,000 robot from a company named Unitree to walk around Cologne and bother people outside of bars in the way that extremely annoying Twitch livestreamers and TikTok stars have been doing for years. In a recent livestream, Agaamuza or one of his friends uses the robot to grab a girl’s ass, the boys laugh about it, and the police get involved. Twitch has temporarily suspended his channel from streaming but because of the social media clipping economy, there are zillions of videos of the streamers and the robot percolating across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok. On the actual internet where real people click around and don't regurgitate police statements and pretend they're reporting the news, you can see the entire arc of what happened, which now includes an hour-long "statement" Twitch video in which Agaamuza streams with the robot dressed in striped prison clothes. The slightly longer version: For at least a few weeks, Agaamuza and his friends put a mustache and giant chain necklace on the robot, call him “Ahmad the Robot,” and film people’s reactions to the robot thrusting, dancing, punching the sky, walking into stores, etc. Most of these videos are annoying but not illegal. They are very much a part of YouTube / Twitch “prank” culture, in which men—almost always men—film themselves hitting on women, interviewing people outside of bars, and doing stupid shit in public. Agaamuza and “Ahmad the Robot” have become minor characters in the German Twitch streaming world over the last few weeks. The robot in question is the Unitree R1, which costs between $4,900 and $5,900 depending on the specific model. Unitree is a Chinese robot company that makes the R1 and a robot dog that has become vaguely popular among people who are excited about humanoid robots and gadget YouTubers. Unitree is kind of a Boston Dynamics-esque company in that it makes lots of YouTube videos of its robots doing cartwheels and backflips and fighting other robots, and regularly goes viral for it. The capabilities of the R1 robot are not a secret and can be found in any number of YouTube videos or on Unitree’s website (which is to say that the R1 is not a mysterious harassment or spy robot as it has been portrayed in some of the aggregations of this story I’ve seen). The robot, but not the incident in question Anyways, over the weekend while live-streaming, Agaamuza or one of his friends has the robot walk into a group of girls standing on the street in Cologne. “Oh my god oh my god Ahmad,” one of the streamers says, as they walk the robot directly into a girl’s ass. One of the girls says “Oh my god stop.” The boys say “Hey, he wants to meet you, do you want to meet him?” The girls say no. The robot begins thrusting its arms in the air (the girls have moved away at this point), and the streamers start screaming “no brother, no bro oh man.” The girls tell the streamers to leave them alone and then walk away. In his statement video, Agaamuza says that the robot simply ran into the girl and didn't grope her. The robot certainly did run into her , the whole thing was harassing and annoying; in the United States, these sorts of things happen on Twitch constantly, generally with no consequences. What happened is bad, and is not much different than the types of clips of men harassing women that go viral all the time on social media, many of them filmed or streamed surreptitiously using Meta’s AI glasses . What actually is unusual about this case is that the police appear to actually be taking it seriously.

Coverage by even well-resourced outlets like CNN, CBC, and the BBC have almost no information beyond the police press release, which is lazy and stupid, because it is possible to figure out everything that happened here with three seconds of clicking around the internet. The Associated Press wrote that the entire phenomenon is "new territory" for the police, which, I'm sorry to say, men using tech to harass women on livestreams in 2026 is not "unusual" or "new territory" and hasn't been for many years.

The English coverage of the incident looks like this:

Researchers Show How Meta's 'Pervert Glasses' Are Used to Harass Women
A new study shows how pickup artist influencers use smart glasses to create content, and the connection between covert recording and harm.

In fact, with a small amount of Googling and/or clicking around social media, it is easy to find out everything you would ever need to know about the robot and what happened here.

The tl;dr is that a 16-year-old German Twitch IRL livestreamer named Agaamuza has been streaming himself using an off-the-shelf $5,000 robot from a company named Unitree to walk around Cologne and bother people outside of bars in the way that extremely annoying Twitch livestreamers and TikTok stars have been doing for years. In a recent livestream, Agaamuza or one of his friends uses the robot to grab a girl’s ass, the boys laugh about it, and the police get involved. Twitch has temporarily suspended his channel from streaming but because of the social media clipping economy, there are zillions of videos of the streamers and the robot percolating across Instagram, YouTube, and TikTok.

On the actual internet where real people click around and don't regurgitate police statements and pretend they're reporting the news, you can see the entire arc of what happened, which now includes an hour-long "statement" Twitch video in which Agaamuza streams with the robot dressed in striped prison clothes.

The slightly longer version: For at least a few weeks, Agaamuza and his friends put a mustache and giant chain necklace on the robot, call him “Ahmad the Robot,” and film people’s reactions to the robot thrusting, dancing, punching the sky, walking into stores, etc. Most of these videos are annoying but not illegal. They are very much a part of YouTube / Twitch “prank” culture, in which men—almost always men—film themselves hitting on women, interviewing people outside of bars, and doing stupid shit in public. Agaamuza and “Ahmad the Robot” have become minor characters in the German Twitch streaming world over the last few weeks. 

The robot in question is the Unitree R1, which costs between $4,900 and $5,900 depending on the specific model. Unitree is a Chinese robot company that makes the R1 and a robot dog that has become vaguely popular among people who are excited about humanoid robots and gadget YouTubers. Unitree is kind of a Boston Dynamics-esque company in that it makes lots of YouTube videos of its robots doing cartwheels and backflips and fighting other robots, and regularly goes viral for it. The capabilities of the R1 robot are not a secret and can be found in any number of YouTube videos or on Unitree’s website (which is to say that the R1 is not a mysterious harassment or spy robot as it has been portrayed in some of the aggregations of this story I’ve seen). 

The robot, but not the incident in question

Anyways, over the weekend while live-streaming, Agaamuza or one of his friends has the robot walk into a group of girls standing on the street in Cologne. “Oh my god oh my god Ahmad,” one of the streamers says, as they walk the robot directly into a girl’s ass. One of the girls says “Oh my god stop.” The boys say “Hey, he wants to meet you, do you want to meet him?” The girls say no. The robot begins thrusting its arms in the air (the girls have moved away at this point), and the streamers start screaming “no brother, no bro oh man.” The girls tell the streamers to leave them alone and then walk away. 

In his statement video, Agaamuza says that the robot simply ran into the girl and didn't grope her. The robot certainly did run into her, the whole thing was harassing and annoying; in the United States, these sorts of things happen on Twitch constantly, generally with no consequences.

What happened is bad, and is not much different than the types of clips of men harassing women that go viral all the time on social media, many of them filmed or streamed surreptitiously using Meta’s AI glasses. What actually is unusual about this case is that the police appear to actually be taking it seriously.
