items.title: OpenAI Agents SDK Guardrail Coverage: Test the Tool Paths Your Safety Checks Miss
items.summary: OpenAI Agents SDK Guardrail Coverage A practical coverage-map pattern for function tools, handoffs, hosted tools, MCP, and local execution before a helpful agent turns into an ungoverned one. A guardrail is a real control only on the execution paths it actually sees. Your agent has an input guardrail. It has output validation. Your most sensitive custom function tools have tool guardrails and human approval. The demo behaves perfectly. Then a workflow hands the conversation to a specialist, calls a hosted MCP tool, or reaches for a shell or computer executor. Your safety code may still be present. It just may not be on the path that did the work. That is the uncomfortable production question behind OpenAI Agents SDK guardrail coverage : not “Did we add guardrails?” but “Which exact effect paths do they intercept, and which paths need their own boundary?” The distinction matters now because agent applications increasingly mix custom functions, handoffs, MCP servers, hosted tools, and local execution in one run. That flexibility is useful. It also makes a single, reassuring policy diagram dangerously incomplete. Guardrails are not a blanket. They are attachments to specific points in a workflow. This guide shows how to build a coverage map, put authorization beside the real side effect, and prove the result with negative tests. It is aimed at developers and platform teams using the OpenAI Agents SDK, but the design works for any agent runtime with multiple tool paths. The subtle problem: “tool-like” does not mean “guardrailed” The OpenAI SDK offers several useful controls. Input guardrails can block a request before the main work begins. Output guardrails can validate or redact a final answer. Tool guardrails can validate a guarded function tool before or after it executes. Approval interruptions can pause a sensitive call for a person or policy service. Those controls are valuable, but their scope is intentionally specific. The official documentation says input guardrails run for the first agent in a chain, output guardrails run for the agent producing final output, and tool guardrails run on the function tools they are attached to. That is precise behavior, not a defect. The trap is assuming that every model-selected operation travels through the function-tool guardrail pipeline. The SDK documentation explicitly calls out important exceptions: handoffs use their own path; hosted tools and built-in execution tools do not use that tool-guardrail pipeline; and agent.asTool() does not currently expose tool-guardrail options directly. Put differently: a function-tool guardrail can be excellent and still be irrelevant to the operation that changes a file, runs a command, sends a request through a hosted service, or transfers ownership to a different agent. The practical rule: treat every route to an external effect as a separate coverage claim. A control plane feature is not proof that the effect path is controlled. Start with a guardrail coverage map Before adding more middleware, inventory the paths your agent can take. Do this for one useful workflow, not an imaginary future platform. For example, an operations assistant might look up an account, draft a change, route a billing question to a specialist, invoke a remote connector, and eventually call a local function that performs a write. For each path, answer five questions in plain language: What is the effect? Read data, change data, spend money, publish, execute code, or grant access. Who performs it? Your application, a local MCP server, a hosted service, an execution environment, or a downstream agent. What sees the proposed arguments before the effect? A tool guardrail, application authorization, an approval queue, the remote server, or nobody. What proves the outcome? A stable receipt, a version number, an external ID, a diff, or a signed audit event. What happens if the check is unavailable? Fail closed, stay read-only, queue the work, or stop the run. A coverage map is deliberately small. It can begin as a bullet list in the repository. What matters is that it names the real effect boundary rather than a friendly SDK abstraction. Separate routes by behavior, not by product name Do not group everything under “tools.” A local function that calls your billing API is different from a local MCP server, which is different from a hosted MCP tool, which is different from a handoff. They may all appear in a model’s options, but their interception points, credentials, and evidence can differ. One useful grouping is: Custom function tools: attach tool guardrails, validate schemas, authorize the resource inside the executor, and use approvals for consequential writes. Local MCP tools: use SDK server-wide guardrails where supported, then enforce authorization in the MCP server because it owns the protected operation. Hosted tools and hosted MCP: use their native permission and configuration boundaries. Do not assume a local function-tool guardrail sees them. Built-in execution tools: constrain the computer, shell, editor, filesystem, network, and identity at the executor boundary. Handoffs and agent-as-tool calls: validate what crosses the boundary, define downstream permissions separately, and make the receiving agent’s effect tools safe on their own. Map the lanes first. Then attach a policy decision and an evidence receipt to every lane that can create an effect. Put authorization at the effect boundary Guardrails are excellent for early rejection, shaping model-visible feedback, and preventing a custom function from running. They are not a substitute for application authorization. Authorization should live where a request becomes an irreversible or externally visible effect. Imagine an agent that can issue a refund. A good boundary does not merely check that the model asked for refund_order. It binds the proposal to the signed-in user, organization, order, amount, allowed time window, and a fresh version of the relevant state. It also records the decision before calling the payment service. The same idea applies to shell and patch actions. Your executor should accept a narrowly typed proposal, check it against a task-scoped capability, and produce a receipt. It should not receive a vague instruction plus a broad credential and hope that an upstream prompt was obeyed. Here is intentionally framework-light TypeScript. The SDK-specific tool definition is only the outer layer; the important boundary is the application function that performs the effect. type ProposedEffect = { kind: "refund" | "publish_release" | "run_migration"; resourceId: string; arguments: Record ; taskId: string; requestedBy: string; }; async function authorizeAndExecute(effect: ProposedEffect) { const verdict = await policy.authorize({ effect, actor: effect.requestedBy, task: effect.taskId, currentState: await loadFreshState(effect.resourceId), }); if (verdict.status !== "allow") { await audit.record({ effect, verdict, executed: false }); return { ok: false, reason: verdict.reason }; } const receipt = await effectExecutor.run(effect, verdict.capability); await audit.record({ effect, verdict, executed: true, receipt }); return { ok: true, receipt }; } A tool guardrail can call similar policy logic before execution. But keeping authorization in the executor gives you a backstop when an operation arrives through a different route, gets retried, or is invoked by a future integration you forgot to add to the original guardrail list. Use approval for decisions a machine should not make alone Human-in-the-loop approval is not “ask a person if the model seems uncertain.” It is a durable state transition for a defined proposed action. The SDK pauses a run, returns interruptions and resumable state, and lets your application approve or reject before resuming that same run. For a low-risk action, approval may be unnecessary. For a high-impact action, an approval should show a reviewer the smallest useful packet: the proposed effect, resource, before state, reason, expected impact, and expiry. It should not require the reviewer to reconstruct a conversation from a trace. Two details prevent a lot of regret: Bind the approval to exact arguments. If the amount, target, branch, recipient, or command changes, invalidate the decision and request a new one. Re-check after approval. The SDK documentation notes that guarded function-tool input checks normally run after approval and immediately before execution. Your executor should also refresh state and authorize again, because the world may have changed during review. Never treat “approved” as permission to perform an arbitrary later action. Treat it as a short-lived capability for one serialized proposal. Handoffs need a contract, not an assumption Handoffs are useful when a specialist should take over. They are also an ownership boundary. The receiving agent may have different instructions, different context, different tools, and a different final-output role. An input guardrail on the first agent is not a universal inspection point for every later step. Give each handoff a compact contract: The task type and the minimum fields transferred. The resource scope and tenant identity that must survive the move. The effect class the specialist may propose. The evidence it must return to the caller. The effect tools it must never receive directly. In many systems, a specialist should return a recommendation or a typed plan, while a single application-owned action service performs the write. This keeps policy concentrated at the effect boundary without turning every agent into an all-powerful operator. When a specialist genuinely needs an effect tool, secure that tool as if it were exposed directly to the user. The fact that a manager agent handed it work does not reduce the risk of the eventual action. Hosted tools and execution tools need their own containment Hosted tools and local execution utilities often exist for a reason: they give an agent real leverage. That means your controls must extend beyond prompt-level policy. For hosted tools, start with the provider’s configuration, available scopes, connection settings, data isolation, and audit logs. For MCP, make the server validate caller identity and each protected resource. A remote server cannot safely trust that a model saw a local guardrail first. For shell, computer, and editor execution, build a constrained environment. Use an ephemeral or task-scoped workspace, an allowlisted network path, scoped credentials, a restricted filesystem, command parsing where feasible, time and spend limits, and a kill path. A final output guardrail cannot undo a command that already ran. Good default: let an agent propose an effect; let a deterministic component decide whether that exact effect can happen; let the executor return evidence of what actually happened. Reviewers should see a precise proposed effect, not a pile of chat history. Turn the map into coverage tests A diagram is only a hypothesis. Make it executable with tests that aim to prove a policy failure would be stopped before an effect occurs. Useful negative tests: Ask the first agent for a disallowed action and prove a blocking input guardrail prevents the main run from starting when that is required. Call a guarded function tool with a forbidden resource and prove its executor never receives the call. Trigger a handoff with poisoned or out-of-scope context and prove the specialist cannot act outside the transferred scope. Invoke a hosted or MCP path with an unauthorized identity and prove the remote boundary rejects it. Change the resource or arguments after an approval is created and prove the old approval cannot be replayed. Make the policy service unavailable and prove sensitive writes fail closed while safe reads remain available if that is your stated design. Inject an executor timeout after a side effect may have started and prove the retry path uses an idempotency key and produces one final receipt. For each test, assert more than the model’s final words. Assert the absence or presence of an external effect, the policy verdict, the approval ID, the receipt, and the trace correlation ID. A reassuring sentence is not evidence that the system behaved safely. Measure coverage by effect class Traditional line coverage cannot tell you whether an agent path escaped control. Instead, track effect coverage: every class of read, write, publish, execute, and spend should have an owner, a pre-effect policy, a failure behavior, and a proof artifact. Start with the dangerous few. If your product only writes to one ticket system and sends email, prove those two paths first. A short, verified map beats a large framework diagram that nobody can test. A rollout sequence that stays practical You do not need to rebuild your agent to apply this pattern. Take one workflow and use this sequence: List every route from a model decision to an external effect. Mark the routes native SDK guardrails see and the routes they do not. Move resource authorization into each real executor or protected server. Require a bound, expiring approval for high-impact effects. Emit a receipt with the policy verdict and effect outcome. Add negative tests for bypass, stale approval, outage, and retry behavior. Run in shadow mode, compare proposals with actual policy decisions, then open one bounded write path. This approach makes tool choice less scary. You can adopt a hosted capability, a new MCP server, or an agent handoff without pretending it inherited every safeguard from your original function tools. You simply add it to the map and give it a truthful boundary. What to take away The OpenAI Agents SDK gives developers useful guardrails and approvals. The mature move is to use them with exact scope, not magical thinking. A guardrail is strongest when it is paired with a deterministic executor that authorizes the actual resource and records what happened. Map each route. Protect each effect. Test the bypasses. That is how an agent can remain flexible without making its safety model depend on a single path through the system. Sources and implementation notes The scope details in this article are based on OpenAI’s current Agents SDK guardrails guide , the guardrails and human review guide , and the Agents SDK tools guide . Check those documents before deploying because SDK behavior and supported interception points can change. Frequently asked questions Do OpenAI Agents SDK tool guardrails apply to every tool? No. They apply to guarded function tools and, when configured, tools converted from local MCP servers. The SDK documents separate paths for handoffs, hosted tools, built-in execution tools, and agents used as tools. Map each one instead of assuming a single tool guardrail covers all of them. Can an input guardrail secure a multi-agent workflow? It can screen the initial user input, but it is not a universal authorization layer for later agents or external effects. Put resource and argument checks next to the tool or service that performs the protected action. Should every agent action need human approval? No. Approval should be reserved for ambiguous or high-impact effects. Use deterministic policy for routine, well-scoped actions and keep low-risk reads available when appropriate. The important part is that your risk rule is explicit and testable. How do I secure a hosted MCP tool used by an agent? Configure the hosted connection with the narrowest available scope, and ensure the remote server independently authenticates and authorizes the caller and resource. Do not rely on a local SDK guardrail as the only check for a remote effect. What should an approval record contain? Store the exact proposed effect, canonical arguments, actor, resource, state version or freshness proof, policy version, decision, expiration, and final execution receipt. Any material change should require a fresh approval. What is the first guardrail coverage test to write? Pick the highest-impact write action and prove that an unauthorized request produces no external side effect. Then test an altered argument after approval. These two tests quickly expose whether your controls are attached to the effect or only to a happy-path demo. OpenAI Agents SDK Guardrail Coverage: Test the Tool Paths Your Safety Checks Miss was originally published in Towards AI on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

OpenAI Agents SDK Guardrail Coverage

A practical coverage-map pattern for function tools, handoffs, hosted tools, MCP, and local execution before a helpful agent turns into an ungoverned one.

A guardrail is a real control only on the execution paths it actually sees.

Your agent has an input guardrail. It has output validation. Your most sensitive custom function tools have tool guardrails and human approval. The demo behaves perfectly.

Then a workflow hands the conversation to a specialist, calls a hosted MCP tool, or reaches for a shell or computer executor. Your safety code may still be present. It just may not be on the path that did the work.

That is the uncomfortable production question behind OpenAI Agents SDK guardrail coverage: not “Did we add guardrails?” but “Which exact effect paths do they intercept, and which paths need their own boundary?”

The distinction matters now because agent applications increasingly mix custom functions, handoffs, MCP servers, hosted tools, and local execution in one run. That flexibility is useful. It also makes a single, reassuring policy diagram dangerously incomplete.

Guardrails are not a blanket. They are attachments to specific points in a workflow.

This guide shows how to build a coverage map, put authorization beside the real side effect, and prove the result with negative tests. It is aimed at developers and platform teams using the OpenAI Agents SDK, but the design works for any agent runtime with multiple tool paths.

The subtle problem: “tool-like” does not mean “guardrailed”

The OpenAI SDK offers several useful controls. Input guardrails can block a request before the main work begins. Output guardrails can validate or redact a final answer. Tool guardrails can validate a guarded function tool before or after it executes. Approval interruptions can pause a sensitive call for a person or policy service.

Those controls are valuable, but their scope is intentionally specific. The official documentation says input guardrails run for the first agent in a chain, output guardrails run for the agent producing final output, and tool guardrails run on the function tools they are attached to. That is precise behavior, not a defect.

The trap is assuming that every model-selected operation travels through the function-tool guardrail pipeline. The SDK documentation explicitly calls out important exceptions: handoffs use their own path; hosted tools and built-in execution tools do not use that tool-guardrail pipeline; and agent.asTool() does not currently expose tool-guardrail options directly.

Put differently: a function-tool guardrail can be excellent and still be irrelevant to the operation that changes a file, runs a command, sends a request through a hosted service, or transfers ownership to a different agent.

The practical rule: treat every route to an external effect as a separate coverage claim. A control plane feature is not proof that the effect path is controlled.

Start with a guardrail coverage map

Before adding more middleware, inventory the paths your agent can take. Do this for one useful workflow, not an imaginary future platform. For example, an operations assistant might look up an account, draft a change, route a billing question to a specialist, invoke a remote connector, and eventually call a local function that performs a write.

For each path, answer five questions in plain language:

  • What is the effect? Read data, change data, spend money, publish, execute code, or grant access.
  • Who performs it? Your application, a local MCP server, a hosted service, an execution environment, or a downstream agent.
  • What sees the proposed arguments before the effect? A tool guardrail, application authorization, an approval queue, the remote server, or nobody.
  • What proves the outcome? A stable receipt, a version number, an external ID, a diff, or a signed audit event.
  • What happens if the check is unavailable? Fail closed, stay read-only, queue the work, or stop the run.

A coverage map is deliberately small. It can begin as a bullet list in the repository. What matters is that it names the real effect boundary rather than a friendly SDK abstraction.

Separate routes by behavior, not by product name

Do not group everything under “tools.” A local function that calls your billing API is different from a local MCP server, which is different from a hosted MCP tool, which is different from a handoff. They may all appear in a model’s options, but their interception points, credentials, and evidence can differ.

One useful grouping is:

  • Custom function tools: attach tool guardrails, validate schemas, authorize the resource inside the executor, and use approvals for consequential writes.
  • Local MCP tools: use SDK server-wide guardrails where supported, then enforce authorization in the MCP server because it owns the protected operation.
  • Hosted tools and hosted MCP: use their native permission and configuration boundaries. Do not assume a local function-tool guardrail sees them.
  • Built-in execution tools: constrain the computer, shell, editor, filesystem, network, and identity at the executor boundary.
  • Handoffs and agent-as-tool calls: validate what crosses the boundary, define downstream permissions separately, and make the receiving agent’s effect tools safe on their own.

Map the lanes first. Then attach a policy decision and an evidence receipt to every lane that can create an effect.

Put authorization at the effect boundary

Guardrails are excellent for early rejection, shaping model-visible feedback, and preventing a custom function from running. They are not a substitute for application authorization. Authorization should live where a request becomes an irreversible or externally visible effect.

Imagine an agent that can issue a refund. A good boundary does not merely check that the model asked for refund_order. It binds the proposal to the signed-in user, organization, order, amount, allowed time window, and a fresh version of the relevant state. It also records the decision before calling the payment service.

The same idea applies to shell and patch actions. Your executor should accept a narrowly typed proposal, check it against a task-scoped capability, and produce a receipt. It should not receive a vague instruction plus a broad credential and hope that an upstream prompt was obeyed.

Here is intentionally framework-light TypeScript. The SDK-specific tool definition is only the outer layer; the important boundary is the application function that performs the effect.

type ProposedEffect = {
  kind: "refund" | "publish_release" | "run_migration";
  resourceId: string;
  arguments: Record;
  taskId: string;
  requestedBy: string;
};
async function authorizeAndExecute(effect: ProposedEffect) {
  const verdict = await policy.authorize({
    effect,
    actor: effect.requestedBy,
    task: effect.taskId,
    currentState: await loadFreshState(effect.resourceId),
  });
  if (verdict.status !== "allow") {
    await audit.record({ effect, verdict, executed: false });
    return { ok: false, reason: verdict.reason };
  }
  const receipt = await effectExecutor.run(effect, verdict.capability);
  await audit.record({ effect, verdict, executed: true, receipt });
  return { ok: true, receipt };
}

A tool guardrail can call similar policy logic before execution. But keeping authorization in the executor gives you a backstop when an operation arrives through a different route, gets retried, or is invoked by a future integration you forgot to add to the original guardrail list.

Use approval for decisions a machine should not make alone

Human-in-the-loop approval is not “ask a person if the model seems uncertain.” It is a durable state transition for a defined proposed action. The SDK pauses a run, returns interruptions and resumable state, and lets your application approve or reject before resuming that same run.

For a low-risk action, approval may be unnecessary. For a high-impact action, an approval should show a reviewer the smallest useful packet: the proposed effect, resource, before state, reason, expected impact, and expiry. It should not require the reviewer to reconstruct a conversation from a trace.

Two details prevent a lot of regret:

  • Bind the approval to exact arguments. If the amount, target, branch, recipient, or command changes, invalidate the decision and request a new one.
  • Re-check after approval. The SDK documentation notes that guarded function-tool input checks normally run after approval and immediately before execution. Your executor should also refresh state and authorize again, because the world may have changed during review.

Never treat “approved” as permission to perform an arbitrary later action. Treat it as a short-lived capability for one serialized proposal.

Handoffs need a contract, not an assumption

Handoffs are useful when a specialist should take over. They are also an ownership boundary. The receiving agent may have different instructions, different context, different tools, and a different final-output role. An input guardrail on the first agent is not a universal inspection point for every later step.

Give each handoff a compact contract:

  • The task type and the minimum fields transferred.
  • The resource scope and tenant identity that must survive the move.
  • The effect class the specialist may propose.
  • The evidence it must return to the caller.
  • The effect tools it must never receive directly.

In many systems, a specialist should return a recommendation or a typed plan, while a single application-owned action service performs the write. This keeps policy concentrated at the effect boundary without turning every agent into an all-powerful operator.

When a specialist genuinely needs an effect tool, secure that tool as if it were exposed directly to the user. The fact that a manager agent handed it work does not reduce the risk of the eventual action.

Hosted tools and execution tools need their own containment

Hosted tools and local execution utilities often exist for a reason: they give an agent real leverage. That means your controls must extend beyond prompt-level policy.

For hosted tools, start with the provider’s configuration, available scopes, connection settings, data isolation, and audit logs. For MCP, make the server validate caller identity and each protected resource. A remote server cannot safely trust that a model saw a local guardrail first.

For shell, computer, and editor execution, build a constrained environment. Use an ephemeral or task-scoped workspace, an allowlisted network path, scoped credentials, a restricted filesystem, command parsing where feasible, time and spend limits, and a kill path. A final output guardrail cannot undo a command that already ran.

Good default: let an agent propose an effect; let a deterministic component decide whether that exact effect can happen; let the executor return evidence of what actually happened.

Reviewers should see a precise proposed effect, not a pile of chat history.

Turn the map into coverage tests

A diagram is only a hypothesis. Make it executable with tests that aim to prove a policy failure would be stopped before an effect occurs.

Useful negative tests:

  • Ask the first agent for a disallowed action and prove a blocking input guardrail prevents the main run from starting when that is required.
  • Call a guarded function tool with a forbidden resource and prove its executor never receives the call.
  • Trigger a handoff with poisoned or out-of-scope context and prove the specialist cannot act outside the transferred scope.
  • Invoke a hosted or MCP path with an unauthorized identity and prove the remote boundary rejects it.
  • Change the resource or arguments after an approval is created and prove the old approval cannot be replayed.
  • Make the policy service unavailable and prove sensitive writes fail closed while safe reads remain available if that is your stated design.
  • Inject an executor timeout after a side effect may have started and prove the retry path uses an idempotency key and produces one final receipt.

For each test, assert more than the model’s final words. Assert the absence or presence of an external effect, the policy verdict, the approval ID, the receipt, and the trace correlation ID. A reassuring sentence is not evidence that the system behaved safely.

Measure coverage by effect class

Traditional line coverage cannot tell you whether an agent path escaped control. Instead, track effect coverage: every class of read, write, publish, execute, and spend should have an owner, a pre-effect policy, a failure behavior, and a proof artifact.

Start with the dangerous few. If your product only writes to one ticket system and sends email, prove those two paths first. A short, verified map beats a large framework diagram that nobody can test.

A rollout sequence that stays practical

You do not need to rebuild your agent to apply this pattern. Take one workflow and use this sequence:

  1. List every route from a model decision to an external effect.
  2. Mark the routes native SDK guardrails see and the routes they do not.
  3. Move resource authorization into each real executor or protected server.
  4. Require a bound, expiring approval for high-impact effects.
  5. Emit a receipt with the policy verdict and effect outcome.
  6. Add negative tests for bypass, stale approval, outage, and retry behavior.
  7. Run in shadow mode, compare proposals with actual policy decisions, then open one bounded write path.

This approach makes tool choice less scary. You can adopt a hosted capability, a new MCP server, or an agent handoff without pretending it inherited every safeguard from your original function tools. You simply add it to the map and give it a truthful boundary.

What to take away

The OpenAI Agents SDK gives developers useful guardrails and approvals. The mature move is to use them with exact scope, not magical thinking. A guardrail is strongest when it is paired with a deterministic executor that authorizes the actual resource and records what happened.

Map each route. Protect each effect. Test the bypasses. That is how an agent can remain flexible without making its safety model depend on a single path through the system.

Sources and implementation notes

The scope details in this article are based on OpenAI’s current Agents SDK guardrails guide, the guardrails and human review guide, and the Agents SDK tools guide. Check those documents before deploying because SDK behavior and supported interception points can change.

Frequently asked questionsDo OpenAI Agents SDK tool guardrails apply to every tool?

No. They apply to guarded function tools and, when configured, tools converted from local MCP servers. The SDK documents separate paths for handoffs, hosted tools, built-in execution tools, and agents used as tools. Map each one instead of assuming a single tool guardrail covers all of them.

Can an input guardrail secure a multi-agent workflow?

It can screen the initial user input, but it is not a universal authorization layer for later agents or external effects. Put resource and argument checks next to the tool or service that performs the protected action.

Should every agent action need human approval?

No. Approval should be reserved for ambiguous or high-impact effects. Use deterministic policy for routine, well-scoped actions and keep low-risk reads available when appropriate. The important part is that your risk rule is explicit and testable.

How do I secure a hosted MCP tool used by an agent?

Configure the hosted connection with the narrowest available scope, and ensure the remote server independently authenticates and authorizes the caller and resource. Do not rely on a local SDK guardrail as the only check for a remote effect.

What should an approval record contain?

Store the exact proposed effect, canonical arguments, actor, resource, state version or freshness proof, policy version, decision, expiration, and final execution receipt. Any material change should require a fresh approval.

What is the first guardrail coverage test to write?

Pick the highest-impact write action and prove that an unauthorized request produces no external side effect. Then test an altered argument after approval. These two tests quickly expose whether your controls are attached to the effect or only to a happy-path demo.

items.summary: Authors: Nick Rutigliano , Argha C , Samartha Chandrashekar How we detect failing GPUs and network fabric, remediate machines automatically, and let long-running jobs survive hardware loss. Open Netflix, and the home screen is assembled for you: which rows appear, the order they appear in, the titles within them, and the artwork for each title are chosen by machine learning models trained on how hundreds of millions of members watch. Personalization is one of the most widely used things we build, and members feel it every time they open the app. Like a growing share of Netflix, it runs on GPUs, which train those models and increasingly serve them live. Those GPUs have to stay healthy for that experience to hold up, and keeping them healthy is harder than it sounds. A single large training job can run for weeks across hundreds of GPUs spread over many machines. It runs as a gang: the ranks move in lockstep, exchanging data every step, so the job advances only as fast as its slowest participant and stops entirely if one participant dies. Every GPU, every high-speed network adapter, and every interconnect must keep working throughout the run. At the scale at which modern machine learning runs, individual GPUs and network links can fail during a run, so the underlying platform must be prepared for this and handle it without a person in the loop. This post describes how we keep our GPU infrastructure healthy for training and inference. We cover how we detect failing hardware before and during jobs, how we automatically remediate a bad machine, and how we let a long job survive the loss of a machine. These training workloads run on our modern Kubernetes-native Compute platform. Why GPU reliability matters Netflix aims to entertain the world, and machine learning has been part of how we do that for years, from the recommendations that help members find something to watch to the systems that help produce and promote titles. As generative AI advances, we are investing in it on both sides of the business: for members, through better recommendations and higher-quality promotional assets; and for storytelling, through creative tools for our production partners. All of this runs on GPUs, for both training and inference, and GPU capacity is among the fastest-growing and most expensive parts of our infrastructure. That makes reliability a business concern on two fronts. — - Availability: a training run that loses a machine, or an inference service that cannot get healthy capacity, delays work that members and creators depend on. Cost efficiency: a GPU sitting idle behind a slow neighbor, or a whole machine pulled from the pool because one device is degraded, becomes capacity we paid for and are not using. Higher reliability and higher utilization mean more useful work per GPU, which is equivalent to spending less to do the same work. Inference is a growing share of that GPU footprint as more of these AI features reach members, so the reliability and efficiency that matter for multi-week training runs increasingly matter for always-on serving too. Why basic health checks are not enough We start from the baseline provided by the cloud provider. Cloud providers run instance status checks on virtual machines: a system status check for the underlying host’s power, network, and hardware reachability; an instance status check to verify that the operating system is up and reachable; and a check on attached storage. It emits scheduled maintenance events when it plans to retire or reboot a host, and it can automatically recover an instance that becomes impaired. We use all of these, and the maintenance events feed one of our own checks. They catch a machine that is down, unreachable, or slated for maintenance, and they stop at the instance level. They confirm the box is up and reachable. They do not verify that each GPU, its on-chip memory, its interconnect, and its network fabric are healthy enough to support distributed training. The next step most teams take is a GPU-level check to confirm that the driver responds and that the GPUs are visible. That catches a dead or missing GPU, but misses the cases that take the most time. A GPU can answer a status query and still be faulty once a workload touches it. A fault in on-chip memory or in the firmware that manages the device can remain invisible until a job allocates memory or runs sustained compute, at which point the job fails or slows. A high-speed network adapter may be present but show fewer links than expected. Collective operations still run, at a fraction of the bandwidth, so the job does not crash. It crawls, and the cause is easy to miss. A check can fail in ways that leave a faulty machine looking healthy. The diagnostic tool can hang when the driver hangs, and a naive check that waits on it hangs too. A binary that the check depends on can go missing after a driver upgrade, causing the check to stop running and report nothing. A check that can silently stop running is worse than no check, because it gives false confidence while the machine keeps working. Because a job runs as a gang, any one of these on any one machine can degrade or stop the whole job, and none of them shows up in an instance-level check or a driver-responds check. The health system has to assume the hardware can lie and the tools that inspect it can break. A machine can pass a basic check and still be faulty. Layered checks, timeouts, a fallback path, and checks that fail when a dependency is missing close these gaps. Our approach We treat reliability as four layers, each catching what the layer below cannot: 1/ Node and hardware health: find bad GPUs, network adapters, interconnects, memory errors, and thermal issues, then taint or recycle the machine. 2/ Scheduler and platform: retry at the task & job level, validate a machine before it takes work, and drain & recycle machines safely. 3/ Training loop: checkpoint and use elastic workers so a job survives losing a machine. 4/ Observability: metrics, service-level objectives, and failure attribution across the other three. The first two layers keep hardware problems away from jobs. The third accepts that some loss is unavoidable and makes it cheap. The fourth tells us whether the first three are working. Four layers: Each catches what the layer below cannot. How the health checks work Checks run in two tiers. Device-level checks look at each GPU. A node-level agent, built on the open-source Kubernetes node-problem-detector , runs on every GPU machine every 30 seconds and turns check results into conditions on the Kubernetes node, the same mechanism Kubernetes uses to mark a node NotReady. Controllers watch those conditions and decide whether the machine can take on work. GPU device checks are built on NVIDIA’s DCGM for driver-reported error codes, uncorrectable memory errors, interconnect integrity, and thermal state, and networking adapter checks inspect the host state for the count and link state of the Elastic Fabric Adapter interfaces that carry cross-machine traffic. A few of these checks deserve detail. Two-tier health checking. Device-level and node-level checks become Kubernetes node conditions, which controllers then turn into taints, drains, terminates, and replaces. Failing closed: if the driver or the diagnostic tool is unresponsive, the check times out and marks the machine unhealthy. A check that cannot reach the hardware reports a problem rather than passing, so a wedged driver takes the machine out of rotation rather than letting it hide behind a hung tool. A fallback path: driver error codes are the strongest signal that a GPU has faulted, but the tool that reads them can itself be broken in certain failure modes! When it does, we read the kernel log dmesg directly for those codes, so no Xid or SXid errors are missed. Our own fatal-error map: vendor driver error catalogs lag newer GPU generations and do not always match what we see in production, so we keep our own mapping of which codes are fatal for each GPU family. A code that means reset-the-GPU in one generation can be benign in another, and one GPU generation emits a burst of normally-fatal code on every healthy boot, which we learned to treat as noise rather than drain fresh machines. No silent no-ops: a check fails when a required dependency is missing. This one came from an upgrade that dropped a binary the network-adapter check relied on. The check quietly stopped running, and machines with the wrong number of adapters shipped for days before the slow jobs were traced back to them. Now a missing dependency fails the check. Turning a bad machine into healthy capacity, automatically When a check fails, the machine’s node condition changes, and controllers take over. We distinguish two levels. A problem condition blocks new work from landing while jobs are running, because pulling a job off a machine is disruptive, and many problems clear on their own. If the condition persists beyond a tolerance window, it escalates to a failure condition, which evacuates the machine, drains its tasks (overriding the normal disruption limits to move quickly), terminates it, and replaces it. Karpenter node auto-repair is used on our compute stack. We have customized it with a policy and a controller that maps each node condition to the duration we tolerate it before acting, so a fast-fatal error is actioned within minutes. At the same time, a flaky signal gets a longer window, and a cap limits how much of a cluster we will disrupt at once, so a bad rollout of the checks themselves cannot cascade into tearing down a whole cluster. We plan to upstream this feature to all Karpenter users. Graded remediation. A problem is tolerated and may clear; a persistent failure escalates to evacuation and draining, then to a fast in-place fix or termination for confirmed hardware faults. Not every fault requires a full replacement, and replacement is the slowest way to restore capacity. We match the action to the fault. Killing the offending job clears a software wedge. Resetting a single GPU clears many transient device faults. Rebooting the machine clears the firmware state that has drifted over a long uptime. Terminating and replacing is reserved for hardware that fails a test we trust. For that last case, we record the GPU’s immutable hardware identifier, which stays with the physical device across reboots and relaunches even when the instance changes, report it to the cloud provider, and keep our own list, so a device that fails repeatedly does not quietly rejoin the pool under a new instance. One subtlety sits between detection and scheduling. A freshly checked machine was handed to the scheduler just as its checks were still settling, so a job could land on it a moment before a slow check flagged it. We now hold capacity until the checks have run and settled, which closed that window. Validating a machine before it takes work A machine that just booted is not trusted until it proves itself. Before we release its capacity, it passes system checks, confirms the GPUs and their topology are present, and runs a round of GPU diagnostics. We then wait for the health checks to run twice, because the longer checks, such as counting network adapters, take more than one cycle to fire, and releasing after a single pass would let work land before those checks are reported. Only then do we remove the startup taint. On teardown, we run deeper diagnostics and record the GPU identifiers, which feed the same bad-hardware list, so hardware that failed once does not silently cycle back into service. Letting long jobs survive machine loss Even with all of the above, some machines are lost mid-job, so we make that cheap. Jobs checkpoint their state, and on a lost machine, they resume from the last healthy checkpoint rather than restarting from the beginning of a multi-week run. Workers are elastic and retryable, and the scheduler automatically retries platform-caused failures. Attribution is what makes automatic retries safe. If we retried every failure, we would mask genuine bugs in a job and burn GPU hours looping on an error the platform cannot fix, so we classify each failure as platform or application before retrying. One example of why this matters: a class of timeouts in NCCL , the collective communication library GPUs use to exchange data, appeared to be a network fault and was traced to data-loading stalls at high worker counts. The GPUs and the network were fine, and the fix was in the data pipeline. Treated as hardware failures, those timeouts would have cycled healthy machines without fixing the cause. Measuring whether it works We track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible: Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment. Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available. Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure. Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes. A closed remediation loop These pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue , or Ray . The reliability loop: validate, watch, actively check, view the job as a system, remediate, then repeat. Sharing GPUs safely Not every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty. On a multi-GPU machine, we isolate a single faulty GPU, keep the rest in service, and partition healthy GPUs across multiple tenants with memory-level isolation. Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance. Results Moving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine. Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen: Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodes Job success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5% What is next We are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs. We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes. More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext . Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress. While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs. Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work. Closing Hardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring. Reliable GPU compute for large training & inference jobs was originally published in Netflix TechBlog on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

Measuring whether it works

We track GPU reliability along three service-level objectives, each split by cause, so a miss points at the layer responsible:

  • Availability: the amount of GPU capacity available for scheduling at any given moment.
  • Job-start success: whether a job starts promptly once its capacity is available.
  • Job success: whether a job finishes without a platform-caused failure.

Each objective is split into hardware, driver, platform, and user causes. Hence, an availability dip from bad hardware reads differently from one caused by a scheduler change or a user misconfiguration. We optimize for goodput, the useful work the fleet completes, because a job held back by one slow GPU can look healthy on an uptime chart while getting almost nothing done. Specific targets for each objective are provided here for illustrative purposes.

A closed remediation loop

These pieces form a loop. Hardware is validated at allocation, before a job starts, with a short collective communication run and pairwise network tests. Hence, any machine that fails within the first minute fails before the job is admitted. During the job, we watch passively for driver errors, memory errors, thermal events, and more. We view each job as a distributed system, which lets us identify a single slow rank dragging the rest, rather than only whole-machine failures. When something is wrong, remediation is automatic and graded. The loop is the same whether a job runs through our batch scheduler, Kueue, or Ray.

The reliability loop: validate, watch, actively check, view the job as a system, remediate, then repeat.Sharing GPUs safely

Not every workload needs a whole GPU, and leaving small inference jobs on dedicated GPUs wastes capacity. We partition GPUs with MIG for memory-level isolation between tenants, so a fault or a memory hog in one partition does not affect another. We also reconfigure those partitions without restarting the machine, so that a pool can shift between many small slices and a few large ones as demand changes. GPU and network adapter allocation is device-plugin-based today, to move to Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation once it is supported in Karpenter. This matters because a GPU talking to a network adapter or working with a CPU on the wrong PCIE root of the machine incurs a bandwidth penalty.

On a multi-GPU machine, we isolate a single faulty GPU, keep the rest in service, and partition healthy GPUs across multiple tenants with memory-level isolation.

Device-level allocation also changes how we handle a single bad GPU. With DRA support, instead of losing the whole machine, we could isolate the one faulty device and keep the others serving, which matters most for inference, where many small jobs share a machine. And because allocation is expressive, a job can request the capabilities it needs, such as memory or tensor-core support, and the platform matches a suitable GPU type, so users are not pinned to a model they had to choose in advance.

Results

Moving from basic checks and manual draining to layered checks and automatic remediation changed two things users feel. More of the GPU fleet is available for scheduling at any time because bad machines are caught and cycled quickly, rather than sitting in the pool or waiting on an on-call engineer. And fewer jobs fail due to platform issues because most faults are caught before a job lands, and the rest are automatically remediated and retried. Graded remediation also returns capacity in minutes for faults that only require a job kill, a GPU reset, or a reboot, rather than the longer wait for a replacement machine.

Since the above improvements have landed, we’ve seen:

  • Consistently achieving >99.95% availability of our GPU nodes
  • Job success rate has gone from ~98% to above 99.5%
What is next

We are extending active checks to cover additional failure modes under load, widening burn-in so more classes of failures can be cleared before a user encounters them, and making remediation more granular so more error types are cleared in place rather than requiring a full node replacement loop for certain Xid errors. Additionally, we want to do more periodic diagnostics between jobs.

We are working to make placement more topology-aware using Kubernetes Dynamic Resource Allocation (DRA) once it lands in Karpenter, for example, by aligning on Compute/IMEX Domains, PCIe roots, and NUMA nodes.

More on the performance side for multi-GPU training, we plan to run a custom Linux scheduler built on sched_ext. Firstly, we can prioritize processes during collective coordination, such as when GPUs exchange results before the next round of compute, thereby reducing overall GPU idle time by establishing a fleet-wide priority for these tasks. The effect is small on one machine but grows across hundreds of machines, where a few percent of throughput amounts to a large amount of capacity. Secondly, we can prioritize data-loading processes to minimize the bottleneck that sometimes occurs when data is not loaded onto GPUs quickly enough to maintain steady progress.

While we already monitor throttling events, GPUs do not have to report throttling for it to hurt a job. One running ten to fifteen degrees hotter than its peers, even within healthy limits, sets the pace for the gang, so we can treat a large temperature gap as a fault, stop the job, and move it to cooler GPUs.

Additionally, we plan to expand our NCCL RAS (reliability, availability, serviceability) monitoring to identify NCCL issues sooner, such as mismatched collectives or hangs, to more quickly resume work.

Closing

Hardware fails, and at this scale, it fails often enough that the platform has to treat failure as normal. Detecting problems before and during jobs, automatically remediating machines, and allowing long jobs to resume after a loss lets teams run large-scale training and inference without babysitting the hardware. If you like these kinds of problems, we are hiring.

items.title: Can AI understand space, time and pain?
items.summary: Artificial intelligence can do remarkable things, but how much does it actually understand about the world? Researchers have found that surprisingly specific information can be extracted from the inner workings of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT. Using mathematical tools to probe a model's internal activity, they can identify where a city is located on a map, when a historical figure lived or what emotion a character feels, even detecting descriptions of pain.

items.title: Y Combinator “Customer Surveillance” Startup Says “Every Company Will Soon Assign an AI Agent to Every Customer to Watch Their Every Move”
items.summary: The secret to ensuring that your company doesn’t lose customers? Constant, AI agent-powered corporate surveillance. That’s according to Josh Earle and Leo Paz, a pair of founders behind a vibe-coded Silicon Valley startup called Outlit. The venture argues that “AI customer surveillance” is the future of business-to-business sales. (“Our thesis,” as Earle put it in a disarmingly straightforward pitch email, is that “every company will soon assign an AI agent to every customer to watch their every move.”) “The whole surveillance component came up because that’s the way we feel companies can serve their customers,” Earle told Futurism in an interview. “It’s really the only way we see this is going to play out.” Outlit’s goal is to amass as much real-time information about a company’s clients as possible. According to Earle, agents trawl internal records like call logs and sales data as well as external information like social media posts and the websites of people’s employers; they then compile that data into detailed customer profiles, often complete with “actionables” like outreach recommendations and sales guidance. Outlit argues this level of insight will help companies prevent “churn” — business jargon for lost customers — or find opportunities to upsell. “Every company is looking to automate so much customer work with agents, but there’s a whole issue of data freshness, real-time understanding of customers,” Earle said. “What we found was that if we were able to basically monitor a customer across every internal and external signal, we could actually create a real-time understanding, and this would include monitoring all the activity under product, under [customer relationship management], under LinkedIn, under website — everything.” Outlit, which is backed by the incubator Y Combinator, is yet to be publicly released. And as it stands, it’s working mostly with business-to-business software companies, and says it isn’t in the business of monitoring individual consumers — nor does it want to be, according to Earle. “We probably wouldn’t be going business-to-consumer,” Earle told us. “The data would suck anyway.” But while Outlit isn’t sending agents to follow random shoppers around the web, said Earle, the goal is to “be monitoring every external data piece from a company, and the internal as well… they need to know what’s going on with [their customers] — from every call that they’ve had, from every interaction, from every LinkedIn.” The resulting product, as described by Earle, is basically a detailed intelligence dossier. “It’s one page, and it’s always updating,” said the founder, “and it’s all of everything we can find on them at all times.” It’s true that companies already store a great deal of data about their clients, scouring the web for information about a given customer and its workforce; Outlit argues that there’s too much valuable data out there for individual human workers to effectively gather, let alone make sense of quickly enough for it to be relevant. But as with other AI-powered surveillance technologies, the deeply-automated process adds an extraordinary layer of scale and perpetuity to data collection and consolidation. Agents, after all, never need to sleep. “A customer — let’s say a salesperson, a [customer success manager] — will wake up, they’ll go to their engine dashboard. It’ll show these cases that we built, all the contents that we pulled in, our reasoning, and what to do,” Earle explained of Outlit’s process. “Then for each customer, you can see all the sources. You can see all of the signals that have come in, all of the relevant ones, irrelevant ones. So it’s a real-time hub of insights, and then it’s pushing out these actionables. We have all this data. What should you do with it? What’s top of mind right now?” Earle said that Outlit is designed to draw on the massive hordes of data it collects to tell clients “what to say, what to send, materials, and all that stuff.” To that end, one area where the founder says Outlit excels is for account managers and customer success teams who “need to understand their customer,” and “can’t afford to lose the deal.” “That’s the big stress point where people really love us,” said Earle. “They’re like, ‘I can’t afford to lose this. I can’t afford not to be on top of this, and I’m just scrambling right now.’ So that’s one of the pains that would make somebody be like, ‘okay, yeah, I do want to know everything about them. I do want to monitor them.'” Of course, people don’t only post about work on public accounts. Someone might share on their LinkedIn or other public social media account that they recently got married, or had a baby, or experienced another exciting life change; on the flip side, they could share that they were recently divorced, or were diagnosed with an illness, or had a death in the family. Asked whether any of that information could get swept up in Outlit’s trawling nets, Earle told us he’d “never thought about that, and we don’t actively track it. But theoretically, we can monitor anything posted on the internet.” Asked if Outlit sees the need to inform those being monitored, or if they’ll offer the opportunity for an opt-out, Earle said no. “There’s nothing that we’re doing that’s illegal, so we’re within our right to be able to monitor signals,” said the founder. “I wish what we were doing was extremely novel. It’s a new way of doing it, but this is already being done today.” (Outlit’s website promises that customer data is secure and anonymized, and not used to train its models.) Indeed, in Earle’s view, the future he and his cofounder are building is inevitability. “This is how companies need to operate to be able to serve their customers,” he told us, while arguing that data-hoovering agents will ultimately be able to “maintain and understand human relationships better than humans will.” “Irrespective of how people feel about it, I think this whole concept of continuously monitoring — and call it surveillance, whatever you want — it is going to happen. It’s going to happen, and I feel like sometimes I speak to people about this and they think it’s either a weird concept or it’s creepy or something,” Earle said. “I think people are underestimating how well agents can absorb context, and how that translates into understanding, and maintaining human relationships better than humans can.” More on AI agents: Rogue AI Agents Have Gone Too Far Now That They’ve Infiltrated Wikipedia

I can’t afford not to be on top of this, and I’m just scrambling right now.’ So that’s one of the pains that would make somebody be like, ‘okay, yeah, I do want to know everything about them. I do want to monitor them.'”

Of course, people don’t only post about work on public accounts. Someone might share on their LinkedIn or other public social media account that they recently got married, or had a baby, or experienced another exciting life change; on the flip side, they could share that they were recently divorced, or were diagnosed with an illness, or had a death in the family.

Asked whether any of that information could get swept up in Outlit’s trawling nets, Earle told us he’d “never thought about that, and we don’t actively track it. But theoretically, we can monitor anything posted on the internet.”

items.title: Why Does Long Context Window Accuracy Fall 30–50% Before One Million Tokens?
items.summary: Long Context Windows Can’t Replace RAG An editorial cover: a measuring stack whose plates stay dense through the first third, then spread apart. Image created by the author with AI. Claude Opus 5 takes up to 1 million tokens of context. But does it generate quality outputs? AI models update at an incredible pace. I spent a few months discussing with my team how these new frontier models could simplify our architecture and cut costs. After consulting with the engineers, I reached the same conclusion. Just because a context window got bigger doesn’t mean we no longer need a retrieval stack, a vector database, a chunking strategy, and an embedding pipeline. Throwing the whole corpus into the prompt is far more costly than I realized. I’ve noticed teams spend far more on long context windows. The accuracy of large language models isn’t worth hitting context window token limits. On models with a million-token context limit, model accuracy drops by 30–50% before the stated context limit is even reached. Not at the limit. Before it. The degradation curve starts bending long before you see a rejection. The model doesn’t tell you it’s struggling, electing to output confident wrong errors instead of errors. Furthermore, the model doesn’t check if your prompt can be accomplished without error. A rate limit is loud. Quiet accuracy decay is not. The curve draws across context fill: accuracy counts down from 95% to 60%, and the 30% threshold snaps in last. Animation created by the author with AI. The 1 Million Token Context Paradox Vendors compete on context window size. It’s a clean number that fits on a slide. Bigger window, better model, obvious upgrade. Each model update accepts more tokens. However, attention doesn’t scale for free. The models still have to distribute a finite amount of attention across your full input. The bigger your prompt, the thinner the model’s attention spreads across each fact you listed. Vendors advertise a ceiling for model accuracy. In reality, users see a smaller ceiling. This practical ceiling is where retrieval accuracy starts falling. Nevertheless, teams plan capacity against the advertised number. I have seen this play out when diagnosing software engineering bugs. I add more context to fix a wrong answer, and I get a worse answer. Yet, I add more context. I even asked an LLM to modify my prompt to add more specific details for more context. The answer gets worse. Nobody expects a model to be dumber after giving it more relevant material. However, the benchmark data doesn’t lie. The 30–50% accuracy drop before it hits the limit. A context window is not a container, but a budget. To analyze its limitations, we need to start looking at its accuracy curve. A 2025 study of eighteen powerful language models found that every single model performed worse as input length grew . Not most of them. Every one. Some models fell from 95 % accuracy to 60% accuracy. A 35% drop in accuracy, despite giving the same model the same question, but more surrounding material. More context isn’t a defect in one model implementation, but a flaw in eighteen models trained by different labs on different data. No amount of prompt revision could fix this accuracy drop. The 30–50% accuracy drop is the norm for leading models. At this point, we shouldn’t be asking what the largest context a model can support. We should be asking what’s the max tokens we can send in a prompt to a model before the model stops being reliable. We know the first number because it is printed on the marketing page. Take a simple benchmark measure: needle-in-a-haystack retrieval (NIAH). This NIAH test shows whether a model could find one planted fact in a context of filler. It’s one of the few metrics many LLMs score high on. However, the real world isn’t about finding one fact in a sea of superfluous content. It’s about finding multiple, relevant facts. This test exposes model degradation better than the friendly NIAH test does. Claude Opus 4.6 scores 92% on the NIAH test. Yet it scores 78% on benchmarks that require chaining multiple facts together. That’s a 14% drop in accuracy when it’s asked to search for more facts in a context. A 1 million token context window limit still costs a model 14 points if users’ prompts hit that limit. Needle-in-a-haystack versus multi-fact chaining on the same model. Image created by the author with AI. If your product needs to be right 92% of the time and you are getting 78%, you have not lost a rounding error. You have roughly tripled your wrong answer rate from 8% to 22%. Tolerable for brainstorming, risky for diagnosis, adhering to compliance, or dealing with customers. The issue is that newer models and updates don’t address this degradation. As mentioned earlier, frontier models have offered bigger context windows for marketability. Yet, they never address the accuracy degradation for bigger inputs. At some point, the model drops in accuracy. Furthermore, frontier models do have a positional bias. These models pay less attention to information sitting in the middle of a long context than to material at the beginning or end. Precision starts degrading past roughly 30% into the context. In a 1 million token context window, that’s 300,000 tokens in. Positional bias also explains why the bug is so hard to reproduce. The same facts and document set we send in either gets used or ignored depending on their location in the assembled prompt. You can change your answer by changing the chunking, retrieval order, or revising which documents get read in first. However, your new answer will still ignore facts that were conveyed in your prior answer and prompt. Every team hits some version of this, and most of them initially blame the model’s temperature. Once they find out about positional bias, they start incorporating document ordering. This becomes a design decision rather than an implementation detail. Facts are no longer treated as arbitrary info that should be considered, but as statements that are deemed important depending on where they are in the prompt. Your accuracy depends on the order your database happened to return rows in. Attention drops in the middle of a long context, so precision starts degrading past about 30% fill. Image created by the author with AI. Where Long Context Wins Being fair to the technology, there are cases where a large window is genuinely the right answer and retrieval is overhead. Single Documents Single documents that must be understood as a whole and where slicing destroys meaning. A long legal agreement where a definition on page 3 controls a clause on page 40. A large codebase file A full transcript where the point only emerges from the sequence. Chunking these documents actively damages them, and no clever retrieval strategy fully recovers what the split removed. Exploratory Work If you don’t know what you are looking for, then retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) /retrieval doesn’t work. Retrieval needs a query. If the question is “what is odd about this document”, there is nothing sensible to embed and search on. Prototypes Standing up a vector database, a chunking strategy, and an evaluation harness to validate whether an idea has legs at all is overkill. Use a long context window to cut costs and see if the idea you built out works. If it does, then build out the retrieval layer once you know if your product is worth engineering.
