items.summary_html:
Long Context Windows Can’t Replace RAGAn editorial cover: a measuring stack whose plates stay dense through the first third, then spread apart. Image created by the author with AI.

Claude Opus 5 takes up to 1 million tokens of context. But does it generate quality outputs?

AI models update at an incredible pace. I spent a few months discussing with my team how these new frontier models could simplify our architecture and cut costs.

After consulting with the engineers, I reached the same conclusion. Just because a context window got bigger doesn’t mean we no longer need a retrieval stack, a vector database, a chunking strategy, and an embedding pipeline.

Throwing the whole corpus into the prompt is far more costly than I realized. I’ve noticed teams spend far more on long context windows. The accuracy of large language models isn’t worth hitting context window token limits.

On models with a million-token context limit, model accuracy drops by 30–50% before the stated context limit is even reached. Not at the limit. Before it.

The degradation curve starts bending long before you see a rejection. The model doesn’t tell you it’s struggling, electing to output confident wrong errors instead of errors. Furthermore, the model doesn’t check if your prompt can be accomplished without error.

A rate limit is loud. Quiet accuracy decay is not.

The curve draws across context fill: accuracy counts down from 95% to 60%, and the 30% threshold snaps in last. Animation created by the author with AI.The 1 Million Token Context Paradox

Vendors compete on context window size. It’s a clean number that fits on a slide. Bigger window, better model, obvious upgrade. Each model update accepts more tokens.

However, attention doesn’t scale for free. The models still have to distribute a finite amount of attention across your full input. The bigger your prompt, the thinner the model’s attention spreads across each fact you listed.

Vendors advertise a ceiling for model accuracy. In reality, users see a smaller ceiling. This practical ceiling is where retrieval accuracy starts falling. Nevertheless, teams plan capacity against the advertised number.

I have seen this play out when diagnosing software engineering bugs. I add more context to fix a wrong answer, and I get a worse answer. Yet, I add more context. I even asked an LLM to modify my prompt to add more specific details for more context. The answer gets worse.

Nobody expects a model to be dumber after giving it more relevant material. However, the benchmark data doesn’t lie. The 30–50% accuracy drop before it hits the limit.

A context window is not a container, but a budget. To analyze its limitations, we need to start looking at its accuracy curve.

A 2025 study of eighteen powerful language models found that every single model performed worse as input length grew. Not most of them. Every one.

Some models fell from 95 % accuracy to 60% accuracy. A 35% drop in accuracy, despite giving the same model the same question, but more surrounding material.

More context isn’t a defect in one model implementation, but a flaw in eighteen models trained by different labs on different data. No amount of prompt revision could fix this accuracy drop. The 30–50% accuracy drop is the norm for leading models.

At this point, we shouldn’t be asking what the largest context a model can support. We should be asking what’s the max tokens we can send in a prompt to a model before the model stops being reliable. We know the first number because it is printed on the marketing page.

Take a simple benchmark measure: needle-in-a-haystack retrieval (NIAH). This NIAH test shows whether a model could find one planted fact in a context of filler. It’s one of the few metrics many LLMs score high on.

However, the real world isn’t about finding one fact in a sea of superfluous content. It’s about finding multiple, relevant facts. This test exposes model degradation better than the friendly NIAH test does.

Claude Opus 4.6 scores 92% on the NIAH test. Yet it scores 78% on benchmarks that require chaining multiple facts together. That’s a 14% drop in accuracy when it’s asked to search for more facts in a context. A 1 million token context window limit still costs a model 14 points if users’ prompts hit that limit.

Needle-in-a-haystack versus multi-fact chaining on the same model. Image created by the author with AI.

If your product needs to be right 92% of the time and you are getting 78%, you have not lost a rounding error. You have roughly tripled your wrong answer rate from 8% to 22%. Tolerable for brainstorming, risky for diagnosis, adhering to compliance, or dealing with customers.

The issue is that newer models and updates don’t address this degradation. As mentioned earlier, frontier models have offered bigger context windows for marketability. Yet, they never address the accuracy degradation for bigger inputs. At some point, the model drops in accuracy.

Furthermore, frontier models do have a positional bias. These models pay less attention to information sitting in the middle of a long context than to material at the beginning or end. Precision starts degrading past roughly 30% into the context. In a 1 million token context window, that’s 300,000 tokens in.

Positional bias also explains why the bug is so hard to reproduce. The same facts and document set we send in either gets used or ignored depending on their location in the assembled prompt. You can change your answer by changing the chunking, retrieval order, or revising which documents get read in first. However, your new answer will still ignore facts that were conveyed in your prior answer and prompt.

Every team hits some version of this, and most of them initially blame the model’s temperature. Once they find out about positional bias, they start incorporating document ordering. This becomes a design decision rather than an implementation detail. Facts are no longer treated as arbitrary info that should be considered, but as statements that are deemed important depending on where they are in the prompt. Your accuracy depends on the order your database happened to return rows in.

Attention drops in the middle of a long context, so precision starts degrading past about 30% fill. Image created by the author with AI.Where Long Context Wins

Being fair to the technology, there are cases where a large window is genuinely the right answer and retrieval is overhead.

Single Documents

Single documents that must be understood as a whole and where slicing destroys meaning.

  • A long legal agreement where a definition on page 3 controls a clause on page 40.
  • A large codebase file
  • A full transcript where the point only emerges from the sequence.

Chunking these documents actively damages them, and no clever retrieval strategy fully recovers what the split removed.

Exploratory Work

If you don’t know what you are looking for, then retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) /retrieval doesn’t work. Retrieval needs a query. If the question is “what is odd about this document”, there is nothing sensible to embed and search on.

Prototypes

Standing up a vector database, a chunking strategy, and an evaluation harness to validate whether an idea has legs at all is overkill.

Use a long context window to cut costs and see if the idea you built out works. If it does, then build out the retrieval layer once you know if your product is worth engineering.

Prototype architectures are different from production architectures. Transitioning from one to another uncovers more pains and different problems.

What This Means For Your RAG Versus Long Context Decision

Long context isn’t useless. It’s not a replacement for retrieval, for it doesn’t solve the problem that retrieval-augmented generation solves.

Retrieval is a relevance filter. Its job is to put a small amount of highly relevant material in front of the model.

A big window is a capacity increase. Teams assume they can skip building the filter with this window, but they instead obscure ways to debug why their LLMs are returning more incorrect answers.

From what I and my team of engineers tested out, we concluded that there are different use cases when retrieval/RAG works over long context windows, and vice versa.

I recommend using retrieval/RAG in the following:

  • The corpus is bigger than the context window.
  • You need to cite which source produced an answer.
  • Accuracy has a significant cost attached.
  • You want to control what the model sees rather than hoping the model looks in the right place.

I recommend using long context windows in the following:

  • Material is one coherent artifact that cannot be sliced.
  • The task needs the whole data at once.
  • You’ve measured the accuracy at your actual fill level as opposed to assuming it, and can tolerate the cost of some errors.

The strongest production systems I have seen do both. The context window is a buffer instead of an infrastructure strategy.

A short decision rule: retrieval is a relevance filter, long context is a capacity buffer. Image created by the author with AI.

Retrieve aggressively, keep the prompt small, and treat unused window capacity as a safety margin instead of space that needs filling.

Furthermore, context distillation helps tremendously. Summarise or compress retrieved material so that what reaches the model is dense rather than merely voluminous.

If you want the full architecture rather than the decision rule, I wrote a production RAG architecture guide that covers chunking, reranking, and evaluation in more depth.

Finally, it’s crucial to test your accuracy at several context fill levels as opposed to one. If you only evaluate at 10% context fill and then ship at 60% context fill, then you evaluated a system that isn’t in production.

The Takeaway

Long context windows are a real capability and a genuine convenience. They are not a retrieval replacement.

What frontier models market is not an accuracy guarantee. You still need to test out this accuracy at different context fill levels.

By doing so, you can see when your model stops being reliable for a specific task. You can design your system to stay under that fill level and cut costs.

I guarantee you that the token limit at which your accuracy peaks is a lot lower than a million tokens.

Frequently Asked Questions

Does a larger context window improve LLM accuracy?

Not by itself, and often the opposite. A larger window increases how much the model will accept, while accuracy on a given task tends to fall as you use more of it. Across leading models, accuracy declines of 30 to 50 percent show up before the stated limit is reached. Treat window size as capacity, and measure accuracy separately at the fill level you actually plan to run at.

What is the lost-in-the-middle problem?

It is a positional bias effect. Models attend less to information placed in the middle of a long context than to information near the start or the end, so facts in that middle region get underweighted or missed. Precision begins degrading past roughly 30 percent fill, which means it is a live concern long before you approach the model’s limit.

Do frontier models handle million token contexts reliably?

Reliably enough for some tasks and not for others. Claude Opus 4.6 drops from 92 percent to 78 percent accuracy in the 1M token range on reasoning tasks that require chaining several facts. That is a frontier model performing well relative to the field and still losing 14 points. Whether it counts as reliable depends on what a wrong answer costs you.

Syed Ali is cofounder of Echonos, an audio-aware AI music video pipeline for indie artists, managers, and small labels. He was previously COO at Tabler (1M+ users, $50K+ MRR, exit) and a data science consultant at Deloitte, Booz Allen Hamilton, and Accenture. He writes about the economics of music release at the intersection of streaming, AI tooling, and indie artist strategy.

items.title: One to Watch - nolabs on sandboxes and securing agents
items.summary: Welcome to The Stack’s One To Watch. Every week we pick out a notable startup and go deep on what they’re building, why they’re building it, and the trials behind it all. Throughout the current AI boom, security has been a major concern, but OpenAI’s disclosure that one of its models had breached a sandbox during testing and hacked Hugging Face brought a whole new wave of attention to the issue, particularly as the capabilities and access of AI agents grows. After his success creating the open source software signing tool Sigstore to help address supply chain security, Luke Hinds turned his attention to agentic security and co-founded nolabs around the open source nono tool for agentic sandboxing. Since launching at the end of 2025 as Always Further, the company has raised $1.8 million and gained supporters in companies such as Datadog and Okta. CEO Hinds sat down with The Stack during Open Source Summit Europe in Prague to discuss nono’s different approach to sandboxing, designing easy-to-use tools for the complex topic of agentic security, and navigating industry misunderstandings.

items.title: Can AI help ‘humanise’ museums? New report reminds us why art matters in a changing world
items.summary: The cover of a new report on AI from a US museum thinktank restyles the Sistine Chapel’s Creation of Adam, with the hand of God replaced by a Terminator-style robotic one. So far so obvious. In Remuseum’s Five Ways AI Can Humanise Museums , AI has presumably replaced God as the enabler of all things. But who is Adam’s hand supposed to represent: the museum visitor or the museum worker? Or could it be the figure of the artist, being granted the power to create new worlds with AI? Creating worlds is exactly what artists can do, and paying attention to their creative and critical uses of AI is an urgent task for art museums today. This article is part of our State of the Arts series. These articles tackle the challenges of the arts and heritage industry – and celebrate the wins, too. Written by Remuseum’s founding director Stephen Reily , the report deftly introduces, by way of case studies from seven major American art museums, different ways in which the adoption of AI systems might enhance what they offer. From communicating with visitors (many museums now have chatbots) to streamlining curatorial tasks, the report shares knowledge from projects which have used AI to develop marketing programmes, aid in fundraising, build relationships with sponsors, facilitate access to collection records online, train staff in new technology, and offer new means of art interpretation. As a professor of museum studies, and a longtime curator of art that uses technology as both its medium and subject, my work has increasingly turned to consider AI . The report – which aims to inspire confidence by sharing practical examples – is interesting and useful, but I can’t help feel that it glosses over some of the more complex issues behind such innovations. Museums in a technological age It clearly calls out and thus aims to diminish resistance to AI from across the museum sector. “Avoidance is not an option,” the report declares – but much like the graphic on the cover, it risks oversimplifying some issues. There has been decades of research into how museums can better use technology , which suggests any resistance from museum staff to AI might be borne of something other than technophobia. The report names one possible factor dampening museum workers’ enthusiasm for AI: that it will result in potential museum job losses. It answers this worry about AI taking jobs stating: “The best way to preserve and increase museum employment is to make museums matter to more people.” While this doesn’t exactly address that concern, it introduces examples of how art museums have used AI to better connect with audiences, with all the tangible benefits that accrue from that increased brand visibility. Why do museums matter to people, and to whom do they matter exactly? Do they matter to me because they offer cutting-edge exhibitions and events, educational and even life-affirming experiences? Or do they matter to you because they do the difficult work of preserving our cultural heritage, warts and all? Art museums face a particular challenge, as how and why art matters to people is a much debated question. So knowing who art museums matter to and why, is the first step to developing more connected and personalised experiences for audiences, whether enabled by AI or not. Using AI art to explain our technological age I was drawn to the opening case study which talks encouragingly about hosting artists in residence to work with new technologies. One example is the Toledo Museum of Art, which in 2023 exhibited UK-based artist Alexandra Daisy Ginsberg’s work Machine Auguries , a sound and light installation made with AI (which I first co-commissioned in 2019 . Machine Auguries is a simulated dawn chorus of birdsong, inviting reflection on the relationship between technologies and nature. The report proposes this is a way of increasing the understanding of digital art and the creative potential of technology, which can help make museum staff more open to AI. Ideally the institution’s staff learn from these new artworks not just because they are made with new technologies such as AI, but because they are also often about new technology and its effects on society. Artists like Ginsberg are building new worlds for visitors to experience. Such works demonstrate that sometimes an art museum is a place where audiences can encounter not just new technologies as the medium for an artwork, but also, its subject. For AI that means not just a demonstration of what it can do (“this artwork is made with AI”), but an interrogation of how it works (“this artwork is about how AI systems are trained to act on our behalf and how they affect us”). The art museum then becomes, as I’ve long argued , a place where we all can take the time to think about – and through art, feel – what new technologies might mean for us in our world. This is a crucial way museums might “matter to more people” especially in times of technological change. Of course questions remain. Who is encouraging art museums to choose AI in their operations, who is benefiting and who is losing out? What constitutes “responsible reuse of a museum’s own assets”? Is my data, as a visitor, such an asset? How do we deploy proprietary technology to make “real” art museum experiences matter to a greater number of visitors, without glossing over the complex stack of ethical and legal concerns that sit behind the rollout of any new technology? This last question is one the report doesn’t quite get to, focused as it is on offering positive and useful examples of the successful deployment of AI in customer-facing activities. But maybe we should pause and think about how we feel about the potential trade-offs, such as whose data is being shared, and with whom. Museums might want to do too, when it comes to their use of AI beyond the art they display in their galleries. Sarah Cook receives funding from WASP-HS.

items.title: Pope Leo XIV has been diagnosed with lung cancer. Here's what to know about the first American pope.
items.summary: Pope Leo XIV announced he was to undergo surgery during the Sunday Angelus prayer on October 11, 2026. Elisabetta Trevisan - Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images In May 2025, Pope Leo XIV was elected as the current pope. Hailing from Chicago, he has been outspoken about the impact of AI on society during his papacy. Pope Leo XIV was recently diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery. Pope Leo XIV was elected pope in May 2025. Born Robert Francis Prevost, Pope Leo XIV has since made his mark on the papacy, writing his first encyclical about the impact of artificial intelligence on society and making key appointments to the Vatican. He's the first pope from the US and the 267th pope overall. Most recently, Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer after undergoing surgery to remove the lower lobe of his right lung. Here's what you need to know about Pope Leo XIV. Robert Prevost was born in Chicago in 1955. US Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost attends the funeral of Pope Francis in 2025. Franco Origlia/Getty Images He's 71 years old and was ordained to the priesthood in 1982. He has two brothers. He's also a citizen of Peru , where he was first assigned in 1985, and later served as the Bishop of Chiclayo. He has a doctorate and is multilingual. Pope Leo XIV, Robert Francis Prevost, celebrates a Mass in 2025. Franco Origlia/Getty Images He studied at Villanova University and the Catholic Theological Union of Chicago. In 1984, he obtained his Canon Law licentiate, and in 1985, he defended his doctoral dissertation at the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas. Pope Leo XIV speaks English , Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French. Pope Francis appointed him to one of the Vatican's most influential positions. Pope Francis and Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost in 2023. Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images In 2023, the then-pope appointed then- Bishop Prevost as Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, which plays a key role in bishop nominations. In 2024, Pope Leo said in an interview with Vatican News that a "bishop is not supposed to be a little prince sitting in his kingdom, but rather called authentically to be humble, to be close to the people he serves, to walk with them and to suffer with them." A group of 133 cardinals elected him during the May 2025 conclave. Cardinals of the Catholic Church at the papal conclave in 2005. Arturo Mari - Vatican Pool/ Getty Images The process is known as the conclave . It took two days and four rounds of voting for the cardinals to agree on a new pope, per the AP . Before the conclave, the National Catholic Reporter wrote that it was unlikely the US cardinal would become pope because of political implications. Yet Cardinal Prevost was considered a contender by others, especially as the week went on, ABC News reported. Pope Leo XIV gave his first message on May 8, 2025. Pope Leo XIV, Robert Prevost, addresses the crowd from the balcony of the St Peter's Basilica in 2025. TIZIANA FABI/AFP via Getty Images Speaking from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Leo XIV said, "Peace be with all of you" in his first words in his new role. He spoke in Italian and then Spanish. "My experience of Cardinal Prevost was that he's not a showboat," Father Mark R. Francis, who worked with Pope Leo in the past, told CBS News in 2025. "He's very calm, but extremely intelligent, and extremely compassionate." Since becoming pope, he has begun putting his stamp on the Church. TOPSHOT - Pope Leo XIV is welcomed by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Presidential Palace in Ankara on November 27, 2025. (Photo by Andreas SOLARO / AFP via Getty Images) Andreas SOLARO / AFP via Getty Images He canonized Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati in September 2025, and made his first foreign trip to Turkey and Lebanon in November and December of that year. His first encyclical, a letter written by the Pope for guidance, addressed AI. Pope Leo XIV attends the presentation of his first Encyclical Letter, "Magnifica Humanitas," on May 25, 2026. Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty Images Business Insider's Joshua Nelken-Zitser identified three main takeaways from the encyclical: the power of AI should not be monopolized by a small group; AI developers should ensure that what they are cultivating "is a genuine good"; and warnings that AI could lead to mass unemployment. In addition to the encyclical, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about AI multiple times, including a recent address to artists and curators in which he said, "We urgently need to distinguish human art from what is produced by machines." Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer on October 13, 2026. Pope Leo XIV arriving at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital ahead of his surgery. Isabella Bonotto/Anadolu via Getty Images The pope underwent an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, the Holy See press office said in October. It added that the surgery was successful with no complications. The operation confirmed a previously suspected lung cancer diagnosis. On Wednesday, the Holy See press office said the "night passed calmly" for the pope . Read the original article on Business Insider

US Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost attends the funeral of Pope Francis in 2025.

He's 71 years old and was ordained to the priesthood in 1982. He has two brothers.

He's also a citizen of Peru, where he was first assigned in 1985, and later served as the Bishop of Chiclayo.

He has a doctorate and is multilingual.
Pope Leo XIV, Robert Francis Prevost, celebrates a Mass in 2025.

Franco Origlia/Getty Images

He studied at Villanova University and the Catholic Theological Union of Chicago. In 1984, he obtained his Canon Law licentiate, and in 1985, he defended his doctoral dissertation at the Pontifical University of Saint Thomas Aquinas.

Pope Leo XIV speaks English, Spanish, Portuguese, Italian, and French.

Pope Francis appointed him to one of the Vatican's most influential positions.
Pope Francis and Cardinal Robert Francis Prevost in 2023.

Vatican Media via Vatican Pool/Getty Images

In 2023, the then-pope appointed then-Bishop Prevost as Prefect of the Dicastery for Bishops and president of the Pontifical Commission for Latin America, which plays a key role in bishop nominations.

In 2024, Pope Leo said in an interview with Vatican News that a "bishop is not supposed to be a little prince sitting in his kingdom, but rather called authentically to be humble, to be close to the people he serves, to walk with them and to suffer with them."

A group of 133 cardinals elected him during the May 2025 conclave.
Cardinals of the Catholic Church at the papal conclave in 2005.

Arturo Mari - Vatican Pool/ Getty Images

The process is known as the conclave. It took two days and four rounds of voting for the cardinals to agree on a new pope, per the AP.

Before the conclave, the National Catholic Reporter wrote that it was unlikely the US cardinal would become pope because of political implications. Yet Cardinal Prevost was considered a contender by others, especially as the week went on, ABC News reported.

Pope Leo XIV gave his first message on May 8, 2025.
Pope Leo XIV, Robert Prevost, addresses the crowd from the balcony of the St Peter's Basilica in 2025.

TIZIANA FABI/AFP via Getty Images

Speaking from the balcony of St. Peter's Basilica, Pope Leo XIV said, "Peace be with all of you" in his first words in his new role. He spoke in Italian and then Spanish.

"My experience of Cardinal Prevost was that he's not a showboat," Father Mark R. Francis, who worked with Pope Leo in the past, told CBS News in 2025. "He's very calm, but extremely intelligent, and extremely compassionate."

Since becoming pope, he has begun putting his stamp on the Church.
TOPSHOT - Pope Leo XIV is welcomed by Turkey's President Recep Tayyip Erdogan at the Presidential Palace in Ankara on November 27, 2025. (Photo by Andreas SOLARO / AFP via Getty Images)

Andreas SOLARO / AFP via Getty Images

He canonized Carlo Acutis and Pier Giorgio Frassati in September 2025, and made his first foreign trip to Turkey and Lebanon in November and December of that year.

His first encyclical, a letter written by the Pope for guidance, addressed AI.
Pope Leo XIV attends the presentation of his first Encyclical Letter, "Magnifica Humanitas," on May 25, 2026.

Alberto PIZZOLI / AFP via Getty Images

Business Insider's Joshua Nelken-Zitser identified three main takeaways from the encyclical: the power of AI should not be monopolized by a small group; AI developers should ensure that what they are cultivating "is a genuine good"; and warnings that AI could lead to mass unemployment.

In addition to the encyclical, Pope Leo XIV has spoken about AI multiple times, including a recent address to artists and curators in which he said, "We urgently need to distinguish human art from what is produced by machines."

Pope Leo XIV was diagnosed with lung cancer on October 13, 2026.
Pope Leo XIV arriving at Agostino Gemelli University Hospital ahead of his surgery.

Isabella Bonotto/Anadolu via Getty Images

The pope underwent an operation to remove the lower lobe of his right lung, the Holy See press office said in October. It added that the surgery was successful with no complications.

The operation confirmed a previously suspected lung cancer diagnosis.

On Wednesday, the Holy See press office said the "night passed calmly" for the pope.

items.title: Researchers improve weather forecasts looking two to six weeks out
items.summary: In 2021, Texas suffered the worst energy infrastructure failure in state history, following three severe winter storms in February. At least 246 people were killed as a result of the disruptions, which led to food, water, heat and electricity shortages. If energy officials had had more time to prepare for the storms, for example by bringing in more trucks of natural gas to disrupted areas, damage from the event could have been mitigated. Unfortunately, weather forecasts beyond two weeks are notoriously unreliable, making for a tighter window for energy operators, farmers, and emergency response officials around the globe. A new technique by a team including researchers at MIT significantly improves weather forecasting beyond two weeks. The researchers developed a machine-learning model that learns to correct errors in existing forecasting models to improve their output over the two-to-six-week time frame. When applied to a gold-standard forecasting model, it doubled forecasting accuracy over that time frame, placing first in a prominent international forecasting competition. In a new paper in Nature , the researchers describe their approach and show how it enables forecasts that for the first time beat climatologic averages between two and six weeks. “Not only does this do better on time averaged forecasts for this range, which is already very useful for farmers and members of the energy industry trying to match supply with demand, but it also improves predictions of extreme weather events, whether it’s flooding or cold spells or something else,” co-author and MIT Research Scientist Judah Cohen says. “It’s really important to predict both, but extreme events might be the most impactful part of this for society.” Joining Cohen on the paper are lead authors Hannah Guan, a Harvard College undergraduate; Soukayna Mouatadid, a University of Toronto postdoc; Genevieve Flaspohler SM ’18, PhD ’22; Paulo Orenstein, an associate professor at Brazil’s National Institute for Pure and Applied Mathematics; Jeremy Berman of the data company DTN; Jakob Schloer and Joshua Talib, researchers with the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts; and Alex Lu, Haiyu Dong, Jonathan Weyn, Zekun Ni, and Lester Mackey, all researchers at Microsoft. Longer forecasts In the 1970s, longtime MIT Professor Edward Lorenz came up with the idea of chaos theory to describe how tiny changes in initial weather conditions lead to completely different outcomes. “He came up with this theoretical two-week limit where beyond that, we just can’t predict weather because the noise in the system grows so much that it overwhelms any signal you start with,” Cohen says. “That had a strong influence on the field that may have held people back from exploring forecasting beyond the two-week range. I never really believed that completely. In theory the atmosphere can create an infinite number of patterns, but it likes to fall into these favorite patterns over and over again. Once one thing happens, I think you can predict the domino that will fall after that, and the domino that will fall after that.” Today, the best weather forecasts come from either dynamical models, which numerically simulate how the atmosphere and oceans evolve over time, or artificial intelligence models, which learn to make predictions from historical weather data. AI models have shown improvements in predicting weather at short ranges, but they’re even worse than dynamical models at longer time ranges. Cohen, who is based in the MIT Department of Civil and Environmental Engineering, focuses on forecasting weather two to six weeks in advance, which is known as subseasonal forecasting. “That range is referred to as the ‘predictability desert,’ because in the short range you can capitalize on the initial conditions in the climate system and the atmosphere, and on the longer term you have these slow, varying boundary forces, like the super El Niño everyone’s focused on this winter,” Cohen says. “The subseasonal range can’t take advantage of either of those. In most cases forecasting in the subseasonal ranges is no different than going to a casino and rolling the dice.” Cohen credits his co-author Lester Mackey, whom he has been collaborating with for more than a decade, with the initial idea of using machine learning to reduce errors in forecasting models. “We built this wrapper — Lester calls it postprocessing,” Cohen says. “We know AI models have a lot of errors, so we thought maybe we can quantify those errors and remove them.” While other forecasting systems do more simplistic error correction, the research team’s postprocessing layer uses AI to learn from a forecasting system’s mistakes based on historic data and shifts its forecasts. In that time range, forecasters use so-called probabilistic forecasts, where the likelihood of a range of possibilities if given. “As more forecasts and data become available, our model adaptively improves its correction,” Cohen says. To build the model, the researchers used MIT Engaging, a supercomputing cluster hosted by MIT’s Office of Research Computing and Data, but the resulting model does not require a supercomputer to run. To put their model to the test, last year the research team submitted three models that included their post-processing layer to the European Center for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts (ECMWF), which is considered the best forecasting center in the world. Each season ECMWF holds forecasting competitions between models. The submission that won first place combined ECMWF’s forecasting model with another, and then applied the postprocessing correction on top. That approach ended up doubling the original model’s predictive power in the subseasonal range. For the first time, the model offered an improvement over relying on climatologic averages. “Up until now, no one had been able to show a model predicts weather better than long term averages for these subseasonal forecasts,” Cohen says. “They’ve pretty much all been worse than that — you could literally flip a coin and do better. People have questioned if it’s even worth investing in models at all for this time range. We consistently beat climatology averages with our models.” The model also showed a statistically significant improvement in the ability to predict extreme weather. “That’s one of the more important findings, because it’s so difficult to accomplish,” Cohen says. “When the ECMWF developed their own, non-AI, error-correction to their model, it got worse at predicting extreme weather. I think that’s because traditional error, or bias, correction is always trying to get to the mean, whereas extreme weather is on the fringe of probabilities.” Preparing for disaster In the Nature paper, the team showed their technique could be used to improve land forecasts in most regions across the globe. They also applied their bias correction technique to other models and showed it improved those as well, putting even lesser models on par with the ECMWF’s forecasts. “What’s nice about our model is it’s an add-on wrapper,” Cohen explains. “We used it with the ECMWF’s dynamical model because that was considered the best, but it can be used with any model. It even improves models that are already bias corrected using another AI algorithm. So it shows a robust improvement. And it’s open source and low cost.” Cohen says the meteorological office for the Republic of Kenya has already reached out about implementing the model to improve forecasting of the annual monsoon season to improve agricultural yields this winter. He hopes other groups will also use the model. “This could help you decide when to fertilize around rain, when there’s a freeze coming to protect crops during winter harvests, or help you avoid droughts,” Cohen says. “It could also be useful for energy and emergency management. I’ve talked to energy officials who say, ‘If I’m told two days before that an ice storm’s coming, I don’t have enough time, but if I had two weeks, that could be enough to make adequate preparations.” The work was supported, in part, by the U.S. National Science Foundation, the Carlos Chagas Filho Foundation for Research Support, and the European Union.

items.title: Your database decision could come back to haunt you
items.summary: When building AI prototypes, developers naturally want to get up and running as fast as possible. But move too fast, and those decisions can come back to haunt you if they lead you to make flippant decisions about data infrastructure. For smaller, less-regulated startups building SaaS or internal applications, the consequences may not be as dire. Wherever you start building, you can usually keep running there even when applications move into production. But for large-scale enterprises operating in highly regulated environments — think healthcare, finance, government — some developer-friendly database platforms simply can’t meet the security, compliance, deployment, availability, and reliability requirements that emerge when it’s time to shift into production . Yes, you can re-platform. But it’ll cost you in redevelopment work, labor, and operational overhead. Choosing a database that can support both prototyping and production from Day 1 could let you skip those headaches altogether. The cost of choosing a database you’ll outgrow Moving an application from one database platform to another as developers move prototypes into production may not seem like a particularly arduous transaction. After all, since nothing’s in production yet, there’s no real risk of downtime. That changes for teams that don’t discover the mismatch until after launch. But the risks lie elsewhere, largely in wasted time and money — and they usually don’t reveal themselves until it’s too late to change course cheaply. When asked what happens when enterprises prototype on developer-friendly platforms without production-ready security, compliance, and deployment flexibility, Phillip Merrick , co-founder and CEO of pgEdge , tells The New Stack they may be looking at significant, costly rework: “You’ve got to look at retargeting the whole application to a new compliant platform, where it can run on-premises in a tightly managed cloud environment. And that’s going to require some amount of rework.” “Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.” Besides the direct cost of technical work — which can get particularly gnarly if the application relies on proprietary capabilities from the original platform — Merrick cautions enterprises about the additional operational and administrative burdens of moving to and managing a new environment, including a second procurement cycle that few may plan for. It also takes time and resources to establish the necessary agentic operations strategy . Bottom line, he doesn’t see any way around the added expense: “Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.” More pgEdge coverage in The New Stack : Why developers are betting on Postgres for AI Scaling AI Inference at the Edge With Distributed PostgreSQL Why most AI projects fail: It’s infrastructure and people Moving AI apps from prototype to production requires enterprise-grade postgres infrastructure How Distributed Postgres Solves Cloud’s High-Availability Problem Why teams don’t realize the problem until it’s too late Many enterprises are drawn to fast, developer-friendly platforms because they’re snappy, easy to use, and often support agentic AI applications. That’s understandable. But Merrick tells The New Stack that too many developers default to these platforms without considering whether they match their enterprise’s specific production requirements — for example, whether they offer deployment choice. Security by default? High availability? In the end, that can leave a prototype stuck on infrastructure that just can’t support production in highly regulated industries. That’s because the prototyping platform and the production platform are often two different products, built by different teams for different buyers, not two tiers of the same thing. That’s because the prototyping platform and the production platform are often two different products, built by different teams for different buyers, not two tiers of the same thing. “If you prototyped in an environment that doesn’t match up with your enterprise production requirements, then you have no choice but to re-platform.” Being able to deploy in a tightly controlled cloud environment or on-premises, meet strict security and compliance requirements, and count on 99.99% uptime may not be an immediate priority for a small startup or less-regulated company. Still, it’s non-negotiable for many large enterprises. “If you prototyped in an environment that doesn’t match up with your enterprise production requirements, then you have no choice but to re-platform,” explains Merrick. From where he sits, that infrastructure mismatch likely plays an outsized role in why so many generative AI and agentic prototypes never make it into production or, when they do, only produce scant business value. And at this point, the tale of underwhelming AI returns is an old line: MIT NANDA reports 95% of organizations are getting “zero return” on Generative AI investments. At the same time, IDC research with Lenovo says that for every 33 AI proofs-of-concept developed, only four make it into production. What a database built for both stages looks like While data infrastructure missteps aren’t solely responsible for AI projects failing to reach production, choosing the right database from Day 1 can remove one obstacle. Per Merrick, that means finding a platform that does away with the longstanding trade-off between developer speed and enterprise requirements: “If you’re an enterprise developer, there has been a trade-off: ‘If I want developer speed, am I willing to relax my enterprise requirements for this prototype, knowing that I’m going to have to incur the cost later to re-platform the [application] into my production environment?’” Specifically, he says such a database platform needs enterprise-grade controls, deployment flexibility, high availability, and scalability — all on the same underlying platform. “It’s the comfort of knowing that it’s the same. If your application behaves one way on [the] cloud, it’s going to behave exactly the same way in your cloud or on-premises.” That consistency is the kicker, as Merrick says it’s what gives developers the ability to move between environments without having to take on excessive rework. As he explains to The New Stack : “It’s the comfort of knowing that it’s the same. If your application behaves one way on [the] cloud, it’s going to behave exactly the same way in your cloud or on-premises.” It’s possible to scale without re-platforming pgEdge aims to give developers that continuity with pgEdge Starfleet, a new Postgres cloud database platform designed to bridge the gap between AI prototypes and production. Merrick describes it to The New Stack as “the only 100% Postgres platform that combines a smooth developer experience and the AI tooling that developers want with the security, compliance, scalability, reliability, and deployment flexibility that the enterprise demands.” He also claims any developer can use it to get a database up and running in under two minutes, using the free 14-day trial to start building immediately and then deploy into different environments as production needs evolve. For smaller teams without strict requirements for deployment location or enterprise controls, that may simply mean going into production on pgEdge’s managed cloud, where developers can scale up instance sizes as needed. But what Merrick stresses as most important for larger enterprises is Starfleet’s ability to support other deployment models: “If, for your production environment, it needs to be your cloud, you can very easily migrate from Starfleet managed to Starfleet BYO Cloud.” There’s also the option for on-premises deployment via a simple migration to pgEdge Enterprise Postgres, the company’s self-hosted option. “But it’s the very same Postgres platform you’re running on Starfleet,” he points out. “So it is not a re-platform. You’re just moving to a different underlying infrastructure. When building AI prototypes, developers naturally want to get up and running as fast as possible. But move too fast, and those decisions can come back to haunt you if they lead you to make flippant decisions about data infrastructure. 

For smaller, less-regulated startups building SaaS or internal applications, the consequences may not be as dire. Wherever you start building, you can usually keep running there even when applications move into production. 

But for large-scale enterprises operating in highly regulated environments — think healthcare, finance, government — some developer-friendly database platforms simply can’t meet the security, compliance, deployment, availability, and reliability requirements that emerge when it’s time to shift into production. 

Yes, you can re-platform. But it’ll cost you in redevelopment work, labor, and operational overhead. Choosing a database that can support both prototyping and production from Day 1 could let you skip those headaches altogether. 

The cost of choosing a database you’ll outgrow

Moving an application from one database platform to another as developers move prototypes into production may not seem like a particularly arduous transaction. After all, since nothing’s in production yet, there’s no real risk of downtime. That changes for teams that don’t discover the mismatch until after launch.

But the risks lie elsewhere, largely in wasted time and money — and they usually don’t reveal themselves until it’s too late to change course cheaply. 

When asked what happens when enterprises prototype on developer-friendly platforms without production-ready security, compliance, and deployment flexibility, Phillip Merrick, co-founder and CEO of pgEdge, tells The New Stack they may be looking at significant, costly rework: 

“You’ve got to look at retargeting the whole application to a new compliant platform, where it can run on-premises in a tightly managed cloud environment. And that’s going to require some amount of rework.”

“Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.”

Besides the direct cost of technical work — which can get particularly gnarly if the application relies on proprietary capabilities from the original platform — Merrick cautions enterprises about the additional operational and administrative burdens of moving to and managing a new environment, including a second procurement cycle that few may plan for. It also takes time and resources to establish the necessary agentic operations strategy. 

Bottom line, he doesn’t see any way around the added expense: “Choose the wrong platform, and you are going to incur additional costs.”

Why teams don’t realize the problem until it’s too late

items.title: Creator of Free Adobe Suite Strikes Again, Reverse Engineers Microsoft Office
items.summary: As the fiery debate surrounding AI and copyright infringement continues to boil, the software world has run into its own controversy head first. Earlier this month, crafty software engineers used Anthropic’s Claude AI model to reverse-engineer Adobe’s expensive and widely-loathed Creative Cloud suite of apps, including Photoshop, Lightroom and Premiere. The resulting “ArtCraft” suite was a shot across the bow, highlighting how quickly industry-leading software can now be copied and redistributed for free. “We were shocked by how well they actually worked internally, so decided to open source them,” ArtCraft co-founder Michael Caffrey told Futurism . “Adobe has been notoriously scummy in the past, and when using it we were shocked that this wasn’t an alternative, it was better.” Now, ArtCraft developer Brandon Thomas has thrown down the gauntlet once more by announcing open-source clones of Microsoft’s widely used Office suite, including Excel, PowerPoint, and Word. The resulting apps — GridCraft, DeckCraft, and WordCraft, respectively — are already available to download for free on ArtCraft’s website. The startup will also happily sell you optional AI image and video generating credits, powered by Google’s Nano Banana Pro. And judging by the appended screenshots, they’re close to one-to-one carbon copies of the original apps, which cost anywhere from $19.99 to $199.99 a year when purchased from Microsoft directly. Neither Adobe nor Microsoft have done much to appease to their user base. Prices have skyrocketed over the years, while subscriptions have become increasingly limiting, requiring sign-ins, license activations, and active internet connections. Both companies have also been criticized for overcharging for features that most users never asked for (we’re looking at you, generative AI.) As Tom’s Hardware points out , ArtCraft’s latest tools also have an inherent advantage over Google’s Sheets, Docs, and Slides apps, which are available for free. Since they’re a standalone app, they work without an internet connection and aren’t at the whims of a tech giant looking to start charging for a subscription out of the blue. How long ArtCraft will be able to keep up its momentum — it’s presumably only a matter of time until their inboxes are flooded with cease and desist letters, if they haven’t already — it’s a satisfying win for those who’ve begrudgingly paid companies like Microsoft and Adobe extortionate amounts of money year after year. To the people behind the project, it’s also a win for the open source community after years of creatives being stuck with paying considerable monthly fees. “The tech industry has relied on the open source community for decades to keep their companies running,” Caffrey told Futurism . “Now models are being trained on open source code. So it’s kinda cosmic karma that open source bites back.” More on ArtCraft: Adobe in Trouble After Someone Reverse Engineered Adobe Creative Suite and Released It as Open Source

items.title: Why 88% of AI pilots never make it to production
items.summary: A joint IDC and Lenovo study reports that 88% of AI proof-of-concept (POC) projects fail to reach production because of unclear objectives, unprepared data, and a lack of in-house agentic AI expertise. These result in a build-vs.-run split, where the team that designed and deployed AI agents, often an agentic AI partner, doesn’t get to run them over the business processes. When the operating team, often experienced on demo, uses the agentic system without any external help, errors arise. Operational gaps can cause cascading failures and business catastrophes if a single agent deviates from normal behavior beyond the permissible range. When asked about estimating whether an agentic AI system is production-ready or limited to demos, Serhii Semenchenko, the CTO of Dedicatted , a Toronto-based AWS Premier Tier Partner for Agentic AI Specialization, tells The New Stack , “The demo is a clean environment where we have clean, prepared data. No edge cases, so everything is defined — input and output. “ He means the demo data is scripted with clean prompts, while the production environment is unpredictable. “Every single step should include the logging, tracing, monitoring, breakers, all the checks, and validation,” he adds. All these steps ensure failure preparedness. Semenchenko shares a basic production checklist: “every single agent should have a timeout and every single step that agents, like, generate some output should be logged for traceability.” Broadly, he believes agentic AI systems should self-assess in production, decide whether to continue after a particular event or reschedule tasks. Agent as a service Semenchenko then compares agentic AI systems to microservices architecture, where each agent has its own permissions rather than static or long-term broad access keys/tokens/credentials. He explains, “Agents use a specific set of permissions and the short-lived key that actually grants access to specific tools, which could be some other services or databases that act as a tool.” According to Semenchenko, preventing an agent from calling tools that it shouldn’t call prevents data leaks, unintended use, and prompt injection attacks. He adds, “Every single agent should be treated as a separate service.” To explain multi-agent orchestration, Semenchenko describes a handoff and offers this use case: “A router that gathers the inputs from the user, the system, and the platform — and decides what to do with the input data.” He further explains that the router can decide what to do with input data, such as escalating to specialist agents for documentation, analysis, video, audio, livestream, etc., each with its own tools, such as third-party APIs. He talks about the final agent, “that composes the outputs from all these tools and previous agents to provide the required output”. If the final step fails, the composer doesn’t invent the missing piece; it either retries or marks failure. This means that there’s a clean definition of who receives the work, what state survives a step, and what happens if it dies. What persists beyond POC? Between all of this, if something corrupts an agent’s memory — known as memory poisoning — he talks about “guardrails”. All documents and data undergo deterministic checks to ensure data validity or trace inconsistencies to records, databases, and duplicates. Need agentic AI that runs in production, not just in demos? Explore Dedicatted’s Custom Agentic AI Solutions . Semenchenko looks back on the multi-agent system they built for CASSEN Testing Laboratories , an established chemical environmental testing and occupational health laboratory in Canada, which faced multi-day turnaround times for their reliable reports due to manual regulatory testing and lengthy processing. The project had clear input and output expectations, but human-related edge cases emerged. He shared that the chemist group had a personal view of how the report and chemical compounds from their error-sample investigations should be presented. Things got even tougher in production when the report style was more in-house than domain-specific. To solve this problem, Semenchenko reveals, “We adjusted our flow, adjusted the agent that composed this report. So, everything in the final, after these adjustments, reports look the same as if chemists had manually prepared them.” Agentic AI projects must succeed in migration projects. Zivian Health, a U.S.-based compliance infrastructure for organizations managing NP/PA workforces across multiple states, migrated from AWS to Azure , a re-platforming under regulatory stakes. Semenchenko tells The New Stack how AWS and Azure use completely different access systems and where least-privilege permissions matter. “So, everything should be mapped, adjusted, and validated first”, he says. “The second thing is monitoring.” He reveals they “use cloud-agnostic tools to monitor and trace everything that happens on the agentic AI platform.” He also discusses models that are unavailable on both platforms during migration. Semenchenko adds, “We should go through a validation suite. You need a data set covering all cases the platform should handle and all requirements. After the migration, you could validate every single agent, use case, and user flow.” Semenchenko concludes the final stages of agentic AI projects: “Check if you achieve the same success rate, latency, and token cost.” If agentic AI projects succeed, they extend beyond the bubble to business use cases, as PwC’s AI survey found: about two-thirds (66%) of AI agents deliver value and improve productivity. Unexpected 3 a.m. call An agent misbehaves at 3 a.m. in a pipeline and does something outside its scope. Semenchenko describes a common scenario where, “An agent could use different tools, and at some moment it could decide that the output of one tool is not enough, and will try to call it, like, 2, 3, 5 more times. Every single time it will decide that it’s not enough; it should call again, maybe some new data will appear.” According to Semenchenko, certain breakers flag agent misbehavior. They use advanced monitoring to track anomalies; as he explains, “It will throw the error into the monitoring system.” The operator, based on the managed services contract — either the agentic AI partner or the client’s team — receives the alert. When the operator is an agentic AI partner, Semenchenko shares, “We have dashboards, alerts, and then it depends on the client and depends on our responsibility.” He adds, “We actively monitor the system, and we could actively react to such cases that appear during the night.” If the operator is the client team, he shares, “In other cases, the client will receive some error messages that we detected some anomalies, and something went wrong.” As a solution, the clients would use runbooks provided by the [partner] developers to tackle the 3 a.m. misbehavior themselves. The benefit of having a partner operate agentic projects is continuous monitoring, handling unexpected events, and reporting. The partner takes full recovery responsibility and reduces the burden on the in-house team by immediately stopping the agent or revoking access — without waiting for morning. Furthermore, partners investigate edge cases to prevent future issues. Commercial reality of agentic AI Denys Yermakov , the CEO of Dedicatted , believes agent failure is often quieter on the commercial side. “You will have to have in place a lot of monitors, regression tests, other tests, different prompts, and different behavior of the agents,” he says. According to Yermakov, how the company ships fixes matters as much as detection. He then points to outages caused by infrastructure issues or bad deployments. “The price of failure is going to be much higher compared to other platforms,” he says. For change management, Yermakov emphasizes “Flexibility for the [Agentic AI] solution and adaptability for all the future change requests you might have.” He then talks about questioning the agentic AI partner about the project scope and discussing ownership of the code and platform. This matters because the team will eventually have to handle incident response and maintenance. “The demo is a clean environment where we have clean, prepared data. No edge cases, so everything is defined — input and output.” Yermakov then opens some cards for verifying the right agentic AI partner’s expertise: “You can always start with some small piece of the POC concept or with a small piece of the demo environment, and the way the partner delivers that, that is crucial.” That would draw a fine line between a red flag service reseller and a green flag — real service provider. “Because this part has to be delivered on real data, with a real workflow and with real challenges you face in your business. Not based on some mock data,” as he believes a predefined demo scenario irrelevant to the client’s business case is usually a reseller. Yermakov gives a thumbs up to a partner who faces challenges on the client data layer during demos. “If the [agentic AI] partner comes with the right questions and approach, the right partner is here,” he adds. Security stones for agentic AI success According to a Modern Data Company survey, 75.9% of enterprise data leaders and practitioners across 66 nations cite data quality and trust as barriers to AI systems reaching production. When asked about sensitive data shared among partners, Yermakov shares the business perspective, “It’s so important that your data stay within your perimeter and not leave your secure perimeter, which you already have in your platform.” He explains that traditional businesses with large-scale on-premises data face a challenge in adopting agentic AI because providers might use their data to train public models. Semenchenko shows a technical picture of how they delivered a couple of healthcare projects where personally identifiable information (PII) around health is critical. He says, “The problem was that this PII shouldn’t be stored anywhere.” He explained how every agent would need this data to extract or process outputs. Solving this problem, he adds, “We have an additional layer that actually cleans all the PII data from the output of agents. The traceable data goes to the observability platform. So no PII data in logs and monitoring.” Build vs. hiring partners Yermakov emphasizes how new agentic AI is to enterprise systems. He tells TNS that enterprises are stuck on basic questions, like: “How do you have to set up everything? What should the platform look like? What are the benefits? What is the cost of users for this platform?” AI partners have experience shipping systems after overcoming challenges. “They know how to solve problems and how to build some of the platforms efficiently with pretty predictable scenarios”, he adds. “It’s quite important to build and architect all the platforms from the very beginning in the very right way, to not redo what you’ve implemented into the business processes.” The operational reality hits during platform maintenance, which, according to Yermakov, must be adaptable and adjustable. He believes it’s critical to avoid early failures in every agentic AI project. “It’s so important to build your team, to build your knowledge in-house,” he says, talking about future platform maturity. Further explaining whether to go in-house or outsource agentic AI projects, Yermakov says, “Once you figure out the area where you benefit the most from the AI, you have to think about this process from two different perspectives. From the business process of how the company operates on the business side and from the technical challenges you face.” Yermakov shares the key to agentic AI project success — staffing — “Always the team effort of the in-house resources and the outsourcing resources.” He warns enterprises, “Outsourcing everything is not going to work for you because the outsourcing partner can’t understand your business in a very detailed way.” Yermakov says SMEs and partners must engage from the start to achieve optimal knowledge transfer. The in-house team should own and safeguard the business process, while the partner architects and operates the core runtime.

He means the demo data is scripted with clean prompts, while the production environment is unpredictable. “Every single step should include the logging, tracing, monitoring, breakers, all the checks, and validation,” he adds. All these steps ensure failure preparedness.

Semenchenko shares a basic production checklist: “every single agent should have a timeout and every single step that agents, like, generate some output should be logged for traceability.” Broadly, he believes agentic AI systems should self-assess in production, decide whether to continue after a particular event or reschedule tasks.

Agent as a service

Semenchenko then compares agentic AI systems to microservices architecture, where each agent has its own permissions rather than static or long-term broad access keys/tokens/credentials. He explains, “Agents use a specific set of permissions and the short-lived key that actually grants access to specific tools, which could be some other services or databases that act as a tool.”

According to Semenchenko, preventing an agent from calling tools that it shouldn’t call prevents data leaks, unintended use, and prompt injection attacks. He adds, “Every single agent should be treated as a separate service.”

To explain multi-agent orchestration, Semenchenko describes a handoff and offers this use case: “A router that gathers the inputs from the user, the system, and the platform — and decides what to do with the input data.”

He further explains that the router can decide what to do with input data, such as escalating to specialist agents for documentation, analysis, video, audio, livestream, etc., each with its own tools, such as third-party APIs.

He talks about the final agent, “that composes the outputs from all these tools and previous agents to provide the required output”. If the final step fails, the composer doesn’t invent the missing piece; it either retries or marks failure. This means that there’s a clean definition of who receives the work, what state survives a step, and what happens if it dies.

What persists beyond POC?

Between all of this, if something corrupts an agent’s memory — known as memory poisoning — he talks about “guardrails”. All documents and data undergo deterministic checks to ensure data validity or trace inconsistencies to records, databases, and duplicates.

Need agentic AI that runs in production, not just in demos? Explore Dedicatted’s Custom Agentic AI Solutions.

Semenchenko looks back on the multi-agent system they built for CASSEN Testing Laboratories, an established chemical environmental testing and occupational health laboratory in Canada, which faced multi-day turnaround times for their reliable reports due to manual regulatory testing and lengthy processing.

The project had clear input and output expectations, but human-related edge cases emerged. He shared that the chemist group had a personal view of how the report and chemical compounds from their error-sample investigations should be presented. Things got even tougher in production when the report style was more in-house than domain-specific.

To solve this problem, Semenchenko reveals, “We adjusted our flow, adjusted the agent that composed this report. So, everything in the final, after these adjustments, reports look the same as if chemists had manually prepared them.”

Agentic AI projects must succeed in migration projects. Zivian Health, a U.S.-based compliance infrastructure for organizations managing NP/PA workforces across multiple states, migrated from AWS to Azure, a re-platforming under regulatory stakes.

Semenchenko tells The New Stack how AWS and Azure use completely different access systems and where least-privilege permissions matter. “So, everything should be mapped, adjusted, and validated first”, he says.

“The second thing is monitoring.” He reveals they “use cloud-agnostic tools to monitor and trace everything that happens on the agentic AI platform.” He also discusses models that are unavailable on both platforms during migration.

Semenchenko adds, “We should go through a validation suite. You need a data set covering all cases the platform should handle and all requirements. After the migration, you could validate every single agent, use case, and user flow.”

Semenchenko concludes the final stages of agentic AI projects: “Check if you achieve the same success rate, latency, and token cost.” If agentic AI projects succeed, they extend beyond the bubble to business use cases, as PwC’s AI survey found: about two-thirds (66%) of AI agents deliver value and improve productivity.

Unexpected 3 a.m. call

An agent misbehaves at 3 a.m. in a pipeline and does something outside its scope. Semenchenko describes a common scenario where, “An agent could use different tools, and at some moment it could decide that the output of one tool is not enough, and will try to call it, like, 2, 3, 5 more times. Every single time it will decide that it’s not enough; it should call again, maybe some new data will appear.”

According to Semenchenko, certain breakers flag agent misbehavior. They use advanced monitoring to track anomalies; as he explains, “It will throw the error into the monitoring system.” The operator, based on the managed services contract — either the agentic AI partner or the client’s team — receives the alert.

When the operator is an agentic AI partner, Semenchenko shares, “We have dashboards, alerts, and then it depends on the client and depends on our responsibility.” He adds, “We actively monitor the system, and we could actively react to such cases that appear during the night.”

If the operator is the client team, he shares, “In other cases, the client will receive some error messages that we detected some anomalies, and something went wrong.” As a solution, the clients would use runbooks provided by the [partner] developers to tackle the 3 a.m. misbehavior themselves.

The benefit of having a partner operate agentic projects is continuous monitoring, handling unexpected events, and reporting. The partner takes full recovery responsibility and reduces the burden on the in-house team by immediately stopping the agent or revoking access — without waiting for morning. Furthermore, partners investigate edge cases to prevent future issues.

Commercial reality of agentic AI

Denys Yermakov, the CEO of Dedicatted, believes agent failure is often quieter on the commercial side. “You will have to have in place a lot of monitors, regression tests, other tests, different prompts, and different behavior of the agents,” he says.

According to Yermakov, how the company ships fixes matters as much as detection. He then points to outages caused by infrastructure issues or bad deployments. “The price of failure is going to be much higher compared to other platforms,” he says.

For change management, Yermakov emphasizes “Flexibility for the [Agentic AI] solution and adaptability for all the future change requests you might have.” He then talks about questioning the agentic AI partner about the project scope and discussing ownership of the code and platform. This matters because the team will eventually have to handle incident response and maintenance.

“The demo is a clean environment where we have clean, prepared data. No edge cases, so everything is defined — input and output.”

Yermakov then opens some cards for verifying the right agentic AI partner’s expertise: “You can always start with some small piece of the POC concept or with a small piece of the demo environment, and the way the partner delivers that, that is crucial.” That would draw a fine line between a red flag service reseller and a green flag — real service provider.

“Because this part has to be delivered on real data, with a real workflow and with real challenges you face in your business. Not based on some mock data,” as he believes a predefined demo scenario irrelevant to the client’s business case is usually a reseller.

Yermakov gives a thumbs up to a partner who faces challenges on the client data layer during demos. “If the [agentic AI] partner comes with the right questions and approach, the right partner is here,” he adds.

Security stones for agentic AI success

According to a Modern Data Company survey, 75.9% of enterprise data leaders and practitioners across 66 nations cite data quality and trust as barriers to AI systems reaching production.

When asked about sensitive data shared among partners, Yermakov shares the business perspective, “It’s so important that your data stay within your perimeter and not leave your secure perimeter, which you already have in your platform.” He explains that traditional businesses with large-scale on-premises data face a challenge in adopting agentic AI because providers might use their data to train public models.

Semenchenko shows a technical picture of how they delivered a couple of healthcare projects where personally identifiable information (PII) around health is critical. He says, “The problem was that this PII shouldn’t be stored anywhere.” He explained how every agent would need this data to extract or process outputs.

Solving this problem, he adds, “We have an additional layer that actually cleans all the PII data from the output of agents. The traceable data goes to the observability platform. So no PII data in logs and monitoring.”

Build vs. hiring partners

Yermakov emphasizes how new agentic AI is to enterprise systems. He tells TNS that enterprises are stuck on basic questions, like: “How do you have to set up everything? What should the platform look like? What are the benefits? What is the cost of users for this platform?”

AI partners have experience shipping systems after overcoming challenges. “They know how to solve problems and how to build some of the platforms efficiently with pretty predictable scenarios”, he adds.

“It’s quite important to build and architect all the platforms from the very beginning in the very right way, to not redo what you’ve implemented into the business processes.”

The operational reality hits during platform maintenance, which, according to Yermakov, must be adaptable and adjustable. He believes it’s critical to avoid early failures in every agentic AI project. “It’s so important to build your team, to build your knowledge in-house,” he says, talking about future platform maturity.

Further explaining whether to go in-house or outsource agentic AI projects, Yermakov says, “Once you figure out the area where you benefit the most from the AI, you have to think about this process from two different perspectives. From the business process of how the company operates on the business side and from the technical challenges you face.”

Yermakov shares the key to agentic AI project success — staffing — “Always the team effort of the in-house resources and the outsourcing resources.” He warns enterprises, “Outsourcing everything is not going to work for you because the outsourcing partner can’t understand your business in a very detailed way.”

Yermakov says SMEs and partners must engage from the start to achieve optimal knowledge transfer. The in-house team should own and safeguard the business process, while the partner architects and operates the core runtime.
