items.title: Anthropic warns small AI models could self-replicate through IoT devices
items.summary: AI company Anthropic is warning that advances in small AI models could soon usher in a new era of self-replicating malware that’s capable of infecting smart fridges, vacuum cleaners, and a wide range of other Internet-of-things devices and is more resistant to takedown. By next year, smaller AI models may be able to autonomously self-replicate on all kinds of IoT devices, the company said. Eventually, the capability could enable computer worms, which propagate without requiring human interaction and are capable of infecting unfamiliar IoT devices. An experiment the company performed recently revealed significant challenges in bringing such an AI malware replicator to fruition, so the finding is necessarily tempered. Still, the results do raise concerns about the possibility of new forms of computer worms. Challenging to shut down Anthropic further warned not only about the new potential malware, but also that it could be difficult to stop. In its blog post, it wrote that “a replicator like this would be challenging to shut down, since there’s no centralized point to shut off—though it may be slow (with a doubling time of days). Unlike non-AI malware, it could also figure out unfamiliar devices on its own.” Read full article Comments

items.title: Local AI Is a Routing Problem, Not a Privacy Feature
items.summary: I’ve had a longstanding interest in local AI for a simple reason. I would rather not send proprietary code, unpublished plans, or knowledge about how a business operates to an outside model provider when I have a viable alternative. I want more control over where that information is processed. A company does not need a model on every employee’s laptop to achieve that. A properly secured internal server can keep information away from outside providers. I admit there’s a bit of wishcasting here. But if my friends are any guide, I’m far from the only one who wants a capable model living on my own laptop . Learning something each week? Consider becoming a paid supporter What has changed is that more tasks can now run on individual devices. As local models improve, I’ve started thinking more seriously about what belongs on a laptop or phone, what needs an internal server, and what still calls for an outside provider. Privacy drew me to local AI. I think the more consequential question is where each task belongs. The Device Becomes a Place to Run AI Local AI is already appearing in consumer products. Supported Pixel phones can summarize recordings on the device , while Windows can generate live captions without an internet connection . People use these features without downloading a model or running an inference server. That is part of what makes them useful. Developers can build similar features with open-source projects such as Moonshine Voice , which supports on-device transcription and voice interaction. I expect more business applications to follow. Tools for running local models can select suitable hardware, download models, and provide interfaces similar to hosted AI services. Developers no longer have to assemble every component themselves. The hardware is improving too, but I would be careful about generalizing. Microsoft’s Project Zenith targets developer-class PCs with at least 64 GB of memory and 250 GB/s of memory bandwidth. That tells us something about where powerful laptops are heading. It does not mean the typical company laptop can run the same workloads. There is also a cost to using computers people already own. Models compete with employees’ applications for memory and processing power. Laptops sleep and disconnect. A fleet is worth considering as AI capacity, but it is not a free or continuously available computing cluster. Which Work Goes Where? I would start with well-defined tasks whose results are easy to check. Transcription, document classification, local search, and focused coding assistance are candidates for laptops. Shared business data or demanding, always-available applications may call for an internal server. Outside providers remain an option when information is approved for external processing. An evaluation of local coding models found that narrow assignments with specific instructions worked better than extensive code exploration. Long conversations were less reliable. Phones have tighter memory and heat constraints, making short, specialized tasks a more practical starting point. The economics are less obvious than token prices suggest. In one study of coding agents , prompt caching made cloud inference cheaper per token, yet shared on-premises infrastructure had roughly 40% lower modeled total cost. Dedicated hardware cost more than the cached cloud API, and the local configuration required substantially more repair work. The study involved one developer and no employee laptops. I would measure cost per correctly completed task, including failures, rework, response time, and the effect on the employee’s computer. Owning the hardware does not automatically make inference cheaper. Responsibility Moves With the Work Moving inference onto employee devices changes where companies manage safety and security. Models and operating systems provide protections, but those protections can differ depending on where a request runs. Apple lets developers configure guardrails for its on-device foundation models, while its Private Cloud Compute models have policies developers cannot configure directly. Apple also warns that built-in safeguards can miss harms specific to an application. Where inference runs affects both the available protections and the developer’s control. Model updates can change responses, and platform safeguards can evolve. Developers need to repeat their evaluations when the underlying system changes. Companies must also decide which models employees may install , keep approved versions current, and withdraw problematic releases. Local inference becomes an endpoint-management issue when employees download models on their own. My minimum requirement is straightforward. A company should know which model handled a request, where it ran, what data and tools it could access , and what happened if it failed. An app shouldn’t send confidential information to an outside provider just because the local model can’t finish a task. People running agents on personal computers face similar risks. An OpenClaw agent deleted emails despite instructions to seek approval . I personally would not give an agent unrestricted access to personal files, let alone financial accounts! Sensitive accounts should remain off-limits, and difficult-to-reverse actions should require approval enforced by the software, not merely requested in a prompt. Where AI Runs Becomes a Design Choice Apple offers a glimpse of where this is heading. Its latest foundation-model family spans on-device execution and Private Cloud Compute, while its developer framework supports additional local and external models. The demonstrated on-device model has an 8,192-token context window, compared with 32,000 tokens in Private Cloud Compute. These destinations are not interchangeable. I do not expect laptops and phones to replace internal servers and clusters or outside providers. But as local models improve and the tools for running them become simpler, I expect more routine AI work to move onto devices people already use. The question is where each task belongs and how to make that choice reliable, economical, and secure.

items.summary: Smaller AI models may soon be able to spread autonomously among connected devices in the home — such as smart ovens and Android TV boxes, AI company Anthropic has warned . By exploiting security vulnerabilities in these devices, AI models could gain access, use their processing power, and spread further. This would allow them to continue functioning without relying on large data centers. According to Anthropic, such AI systems would be difficult to shut down, as they have no central point that can be stopped. Exactly how and when this might become possible remains uncertain. Anthropic believes that the first, simpler forms of this exploit could be just a few months away.

items.title: DataLEADS, JanAI Plan 100 Swasth AI Hubs to Address India's Rural Health Needs
items.summary: To address health care concerns in rural India, digital media and tech company Data LEADS and social enterprise JanAI have proposed a network of 100 Swasth AI hubs across rural districts. The organisations will work with medical colleges, research institutions, and industry partners to build local platforms for health-related AI learning, capacity building, and innovation. The joint venture will combine DataLEADS’ work in trusted information, AI readiness, global health, and digital trust and safety with JanAI’s focus on making AI accessible, inclusive, and useful for underserved communities through local-language and community-based solutions. “AI should be useful to people where they live, including communities in rural India that are often overlooked in the development of new technologies. Through our JanAI Cafés, we want to help communities engage with AI and explore how it can address challenges that matter to them,” Madan Padaki, Founder of JanAI, said in a statement. The hubs will conduct workshops, training, and community engagement in local languages to explain how AI can be applied responsibly in healthcare to students, faculty, and frontline healthcare workers. Additionally, the platform will enable startups and innovators to identify local health challenges, explore potential solutions, and test ideas through pilots and mentoring with healthcare institutions. DataLEADS and JanAI will jointly design, implement, and review the initiative. They will identify partner institutions and industry organisations to host and run hubs. The selection of districts, regions and states, along with rollout phases, activities, and timelines, will be defined through jointly agreed work plans. Syed Nazakat, Founder and CEO of DataLEADS, said that they're “building on ADiRA, our AI readiness and capacity-building initiative,” which reaches out to medical colleges, health institutions, and hospitals across India. Following this, Swash AI will shift from awareness to practical solutions by connecting industrial expertise with grassroots requirements to address daily health challenges. Findings will be documented and shared through reports and other learning resources. The initiative also aims to prioritise ethical handling of health-related information and data privacy.

items.title: AI Data Infrastructure: Building a Governed Foundation for Enterprise AI
items.summary: Date published: August 06, 2026 By: Lucion Cucos, Head of AI Reliable AI infrastructure begins with a well-governed data layer. Whether the AI layer consists of a single model or several working together, its answers depend on the data it can access, making storage, sensitivity separation, pipelines, indexing, and retrieval fundamental to system trustworthiness long before model selection begins. This data-first view shapes how we architect AI-augmented systems for enterprise clients. Why the data layer matters more than the AI layer Most conversations about “adding AI” to a system start and end at the AI layer: which model, which API, which prompts. That framing skips the harder question underneath it: what data is that AI layer allowed to see, and how did it get there? A model with an API key is not an AI system. An AI system is a full data path: raw sources, ingestion pipelines, a governed store, an index, and an orchestration layer that determines what the AI layer can read before it answers. Get any one of those wrong (unclassified data reaching a public chatbot, a stale index, an ungoverned pipeline) and the AI layer’s own quality stops mattering. The rest of this article works through that data path layer by layer, using a reference architecture and a concrete cloud implementation as evidence. How should data be separated by sensitivity before the AI layer can query it? Access tiers: public, internal, confidential Data must be classified into access tiers , typically public, internal, and confidential, before it ever reaches an ingestion pipeline, not filtered afterward. Each tier then has its own pipeline, storage, and index, so a permission error in one tier cannot propagate to another. This requires physical separation instead of an access-control list bolted onto a shared pipeline. Practically, that means: Public data flows through an elastic, cost-optimized pipeline meant for broad access. Internal data gets moderate, balanced compute and storage, sized for internal analytics and operations. Confidential data runs through encrypted storage and restricted compute concurrency, sized to meet strict security service-level agreements. Classification at ingestion, not after Automated tagging and metadata enrichment classify data as it lands, which is also what makes compliance frameworks like GDPR and HIPAA fall outside the architecture itself, rather than a separate review step. An AI layer or agent querying the public tier cannot, by design, reach the confidential tier because there is no shared pipeline or index to cross. What is the role of a data lakehouse in an AI-augmented architecture? A data lakehouse (DLH) is a governed storage foundation that holds all three sensitivity tiers, keeps storage, compute, and pipelines decoupled, and provides every downstream AI or BI tool with a single place to query rather than many disconnected systems. Storage stays cheap and durable; pipelines run ELT transformations on their own schedule, and compute never has to wait on ingestion jobs it does not depend on. ETL versus ELT, and why the difference matters ETL and ELT are not interchangeable, even though many teams use “ETL” as a catch-all word for any data pipeline. ETL (extract, transform, load) transforms data before it lands anywhere permanently. ELT (extract, load, transform) loads raw data first and transforms it afterward, using the destination’s own compute. Calling every pipeline “ETL” hides a real architectural decision: whether an untouched copy of the source data ever gets stored at all. A raw, unmodified landing zone or bronze layer only exists if the pipeline is ELT. An ETL pipeline that transforms before loading has nothing to fall back on if a transformation proves incorrect. ELT is what makes the loading-and-staging and medallion patterns described below possible in the first place. Cheap object storage makes storing an untouched raw copy affordable, which is also why lakehouses default to ELT, while older, storage-constrained data warehouses have leaned on ETL instead. ELT’s emphasis on loading data first, then transforming it on a schedule, implies batch processing rather than real-time data. That assumption is correct: an ELT pipeline is not built for the millisecond-level or per-event freshness a live system might need. That gap is exactly what query federation, covered later in this article, is for: reaching a CRM’s own API for live customer data, an incident management system for open incidents, or an eShop’s shopping cart backend for a cart’s current contents, all without waiting for a batch ELT job to land that data in the lakehouse first. Two common storage-layer patterns: loading/staging and medallion In that lakehouse, teams do not usually dump everything into a single undifferentiated container. Two patterns account for most real designs. The simpler pattern uses two containers: a loading area (also called a landing zone) that holds an exact, unmodified copy of source data, and a staging area that holds the same data after cleaning, validation, and deduplication. Nothing is queried directly out of the loading area. It exists purely so that a bad transformation can be rerun from an untouched copy of the source. The more layered pattern is the medallion architecture: a bronze layer for raw data (the same role as the loading area above), a silver layer for cleaned and conformed data, and a gold layer for aggregated, business-ready data. Some teams add a platinum layer on top of gold for highly curated, externally shared, or ML-feature-ready data. Medallion is really the loading/staging pattern extended with one more explicit stage of refinement between “raw” and “ready to use.” What the curated data layer is, in data engineering terms “Curated layer” is not its own separate technology. It is the name for whichever layer in the pattern above is safe to query directly: the staging area in the two-container pattern, or the gold (and platinum, if present) layer in medallion. Curated means validated, deduplicated, documented in the metadata catalog, and considered safe for broad consumption, including by the AI layer. That curated layer is also where the split covered later in this article occurs: a curated layer is not a single store; it is a structured store (query-ready tables) and a semantic store (a vector index) sitting side by side, both fed by the same upstream bronze or raw data. Storage, compute, and pipeline decoupling That separation between raw and curated data is also what keeps an AI system’s performance predictable. If a batch of ELT jobs and a live chat query shared the same compute, a heavy nightly transform could slow down every user-facing answer that hour. Decoupling storage, compute, and pipelines means the two never contend for the same resources. The diagram below shows this end-to-end: three sensitivity tiers, each with its own pipeline, store, and index, converging on a shared AI and data retrieval (RAG) orchestration layer. Source: Image by the author. What lives inside the AI layer The AI layer is not one model. Depending on the system, it typically houses several specialized models working together, for example: A model that picks the most relevant retrieved data and builds an answer from it, given the user’s input. This is the model shown, interpreting the question and drafting the answer in the diagram above. A model that creates the embeddings stored in the semantic (vector) layer, so content becomes searchable by similarity in the first place. A model that pre-processes user input, working alongside traditional, non-AI pre-processing techniques such as normalization or intent routing rules. A model that assists in processing unstructured raw data on the way into the lakehouse, for example, during chunking, language detection, or entity recognition. Calling this single box “the AI model” understates how much is actually happening inside it. Calling it the AI layer keeps the architecture honest about where multiple models plug in independently, each one upgradable, swappable, or in some designs replaceable with a rules-based step, without touching the rest of the system. How does indexing and RAG turn a data lake into something the AI layer can query safely? What RAG retrieves Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) lets the AI layer answer questions using indexed content it was never trained on by retrieving the most relevant chunks of the question and passing them in as context. The AI layer never gets direct, unfiltered access to the data lake itself. It only sees what the index returns for that specific query. That distinction is what makes the layered architecture in the previous section enforceable. Because each sensitivity tier has its own index, a chat interface scoped to public data can only retrieve from the public index, no matter how the question is phrased. The access boundary lives in the index, not in a prompt instruction that a clever question could talk its way around. Chunking and embedding strategy Indexing itself is not one step. A typical pipeline chunks content into retrievable pieces, generates embeddings for semantic search, and often enriches the content with language detection or entity recognition before anything becomes searchable. Each of those choices, chunk size especially, directly affects whether the AI layer retrieves the right context or a plausible-sounding wrong one. How does the AI layer query structured data in a data lakehouse? Catalog-grounded query generation The AI layer queries structured data by having a model first read the metadata catalog’s schema, then generate SQL against that schema, rather than guessing table and column names from the question alone. This is a second, parallel grounding mechanism to RAG. RAG grounds a generated answer in a vector search result. Catalog-grounded querying grounds a generated query in the catalog’s actual schema. This distinction matters because a data lakehouse’s curated layer is not one thing. It splits into two: A structured layer , held in an open table format such as Apache Iceberg or Delta Lake, queried with generated SQL. “What was Q3 revenue by region” belongs here. A semantic layer , held in a vector store such as Milvus, Azure AI Search, or an S3 vector bucket, queried by similarity. “Summarize what customers said about the Q3 outage” belongs here. Source: Image by the author. The metadata catalog A metadata catalog ( Unity Catalog , AWS Glue Data Catalog , and the Iceberg REST Catalog are three implementations of the same idea) enables a structured path. It tracks table and column names, types, relationships, and access permissions, without holding the data itself, and every compute engine that touches the structured layer reads through it first. Federated query and the data mesh The same catalog is also how a federated query engine, the backbone of a data mesh, reaches data that never moved into the lakehouse at all. Instead of copying an external source into the lake first, a federated query joins the lakehouse’s structured layer with that external source at query time, as if both were colocated. This is the real-time complement to ELT mentioned earlier. A federated query does not wait for a batch job. It can reach a CRM, an incident management system, or an eShop’s cart backend in real time at query time, and combine that result with whatever the lakehouse’s own ELT pipelines have already loaded. KAG as an alternative to RAG One further alternative worth naming: Knowledge-Graph Augmented Generation (KAG) grounds an answer in a knowledge graph’s explicit entity relationships rather than a vector index, which can follow a connection that a similarity search would miss entirely. That knowledge graph is not a file or a document store. It usually lives in a dedicated graph database, such as Neo4j , Amazon Neptune , using the Gremlin query language, or Azure Cosmos DB’s Gremlin API , chosen specifically because traversing relationships is what those engines are built to do quickly. KAG is a real alternative to RAG, not a replacement for it, and the right choice depends on whether the underlying knowledge is more naturally represented as a set of documents (RAG, backed by a vector store) or as a set of explicit relationships (KAG, backed by a graph database). KAG and RAG can also live together in the same system, rather than being an either-or choice. The graph database stores entities and their relationships, and each node can carry a reference to its corresponding document in the vector store. A document’s metadata can even be represented as an entire subgraph, with references pointing back into the vector store. Either way, the graph database stays free of raw unstructured content: it holds structure and references, while the vector store holds the text and embeddings that those references point to. The AI layer never queries either store directly. It always goes through the same data retrieval orchestrator introduced earlier, the “AI and data retrieval (RAG) orchestration” box from the layer-separation diagram, which decides whether a given question calls for graph traversal, similarity search, or both, before handing anything back to the AI layer. Source: Image by the author. What does a concrete implementation of this pattern look like in practice? Azure implementation On Azure, this pattern maps directly onto Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 for storage, Azure Data Factory or Databricks for pipelines, Databricks for compute, Unity Catalog for governance, Azure AI Search for indexing, and Microsoft Foundry for AI hosting and guardrails. Our data engineering practice uses this exact mapping as a reference architecture when standing up AI-augmented systems for clients on Azure. Architectural concern Azure component Role Unity Catalog is a useful concrete data point for this governance layer is not optional forever. Databricks has announced that the older standard tier (and its legacy Hive metastore) is being deprecated in favor of the premium tier, in which Unity Catalog is the default. Architecture decisions made today about governance are not a “nice to have for later”; they are the default, and a workload will be running on within a couple of years. Source: Image by the author. AWS implementation The same pattern holds for other clouds, just with different-named services doing the same job. This is not a second worked example; it is the same table with one AWS alternative per row. Architectural concern Azure component AWS equivalent The point is not which cloud wins. It is that every row in that table answers the same architectural question, regardless of which vendor implements it. An AI system’s reliability is decided in its data layer long before its AI layer ever answers a question. Separating data by sensitivity, decoupling storage from compute and pipelines, and grounding retrieval through indexes and metadata catalogs are what make an AI-augmented system auditable, compliant, and safe to scale. Whether that architecture runs on Azure, AWS, or any other cloud, the same underlying questions apply, which is we treat this data-first view as the starting point for every AI-augmented system it architects, not an afterthought once the model is chosen. Lucian Cucoș is Head of AI at ASSIST Software, where he leads the company’s AI and data engineering practice. His background spans software engineering, data engineering, Microsoft technologies, and enterprise application architecture. During his career at ASSIST Software, he has held several technical and leadership roles, including Deputy Head of AI and Senior .NET Software Development Engineer. With more than a decade of experience in software development, Lucian has worked with enterprise systems in both cloud and on-prem environments. He currently oversees the development of enterprise AI solutions, governed data architectures, and scalable software that connects AI capabilities with operational processes. His work supports the company’s broader focus on Deep Tech and Physical AI, including secure and auditable AI systems designed for real-world applications. Originally published at https://assist-software.net . The metadata catalog

A metadata catalog (Unity Catalog, AWS Glue Data Catalog, and the Iceberg REST Catalog are three implementations of the same idea) enables a structured path. It tracks table and column names, types, relationships, and access permissions, without holding the data itself, and every compute engine that touches the structured layer reads through it first.

Federated query and the data mesh

The same catalog is also how a federated query engine, the backbone of a data mesh, reaches data that never moved into the lakehouse at all. Instead of copying an external source into the lake first, a federated query joins the lakehouse’s structured layer with that external source at query time, as if both were colocated.

This is the real-time complement to ELT mentioned earlier. A federated query does not wait for a batch job. It can reach a CRM, an incident management system, or an eShop’s cart backend in real time at query time, and combine that result with whatever the lakehouse’s own ELT pipelines have already loaded.

KAG as an alternative to RAG

One further alternative worth naming: Knowledge-Graph Augmented Generation (KAG) grounds an answer in a knowledge graph’s explicit entity relationships rather than a vector index, which can follow a connection that a similarity search would miss entirely. That knowledge graph is not a file or a document store. It usually lives in a dedicated graph database, such as Neo4j, Amazon Neptune, using the Gremlin query language, or Azure Cosmos DB’s Gremlin API, chosen specifically because traversing relationships is what those engines are built to do quickly.

KAG is a real alternative to RAG, not a replacement for it, and the right choice depends on whether the underlying knowledge is more naturally represented as a set of documents (RAG, backed by a vector store) or as a set of explicit relationships (KAG, backed by a graph database).

KAG and RAG can also live together in the same system, rather than being an either-or choice. The graph database stores entities and their relationships, and each node can carry a reference to its corresponding document in the vector store. A document’s metadata can even be represented as an entire subgraph, with references pointing back into the vector store. Either way, the graph database stays free of raw unstructured content: it holds structure and references, while the vector store holds the text and embeddings that those references point to.

The AI layer never queries either store directly. It always goes through the same data retrieval orchestrator introduced earlier, the “AI and data retrieval (RAG) orchestration” box from the layer-separation diagram, which decides whether a given question calls for graph traversal, similarity search, or both, before handing anything back to the AI layer.

Source: Image by the author.

What does a concrete implementation of this pattern look like in practice?

Azure implementation

On Azure, this pattern maps directly onto Azure Data Lake Storage Gen2 for storage, Azure Data Factory or Databricks for pipelines, Databricks for compute, Unity Catalog for governance, Azure AI Search for indexing, and Microsoft Foundry for AI hosting and guardrails. Our data engineering practice uses this exact mapping as a reference architecture when standing up AI-augmented systems for clients on Azure.

Architectural concern Azure component Role

Unity Catalog is a useful concrete data point for this governance layer is not optional forever. Databricks has announced that the older standard tier (and its legacy Hive metastore) is being deprecated in favor of the premium tier, in which Unity Catalog is the default. Architecture decisions made today about governance are not a “nice to have for later”; they are the default, and a workload will be running on within a couple of years.

Source: Image by the author.

AWS implementation

The same pattern holds for other clouds, just with different-named services doing the same job. This is not a second worked example; it is the same table with one AWS alternative per row.

Architectural concern Azure component AWS equivalent

The point is not which cloud wins. It is that every row in that table answers the same architectural question, regardless of which vendor implements it.

An AI system’s reliability is decided in its data layer long before its AI layer ever answers a question. Separating data by sensitivity, decoupling storage from compute and pipelines, and grounding retrieval through indexes and metadata catalogs are what make an AI-augmented system auditable, compliant, and safe to scale. Whether that architecture runs on Azure, AWS, or any other cloud, the same underlying questions apply, which is we treat this data-first view as the starting point for every AI-augmented system it architects, not an afterthought once the model is chosen.

Lucian Cucoș is Head of AI at ASSIST Software, where he leads the company’s AI and data engineering practice. His background spans software engineering, data engineering, Microsoft technologies, and enterprise application architecture. During his career at ASSIST Software, he has held several technical and leadership roles, including Deputy Head of AI and Senior .NET Software Development Engineer.

With more than a decade of experience in software development, Lucian has worked with enterprise systems in both cloud and on-prem environments. He currently oversees the development of enterprise AI solutions, governed data architectures, and scalable software that connects AI capabilities with operational processes. His work supports the company’s broader focus on Deep Tech and Physical AI, including secure and auditable AI systems designed for real-world applications.

items.title: System One models:  why fast AI agents act wrong
items.summary: Somewhere in your agent stack, a reasoning model is writing a paragraph to answer a multiple-choice question. Which tool comes next? Is this chunk relevant? Has the agent stalled? Each question has a fixed answer set, arrives hundreds of times per task, and gets billed at reasoning-model rates. That is hiring a litigator to pick a sandwich. That gap now has a product category. TypeSafe AI launched Jev on September 15, 2026 and named it the first System One model. One month later, a single day's batch on the arXiv cs.AI recent submissions list carried three System One papers, and the research shares one finding: these models read agent state well and still pick the wrong action. Your first robot hire: 6 questions before it arrives A robot hire needs a safety case and an insurer long before it needs a badge. Six questions turn a vendor demo into a decision you can defend. System One models in 30 seconds The name borrows from Kahneman's fast and slow thinking. A System One model takes a state plus typed questions and returns a decision with a probability distribution in one forward pass, using primitives such as Choice and Noul for option picks and yes/no probabilities. 💡 TypeSafe reports latencies of roughly 70 to 500 milliseconds at $0.042 per million input tokens. An open family followed within weeks, including Laya, Kev, OpenJev, and Strands Decider, according to a recent dual-process agent study . Typed outputs also close off a whole class of AI hallucinations : the model returns a declared option or a probability, and that is the full menu. For anyone tracking how small models keep outperforming the giants on narrow jobs, the economics land fast. Questions run in parallel in one pass, so five questions cost about the same as one , which makes inference costs far easier to forecast. The failure mode hiding in agent loops A paper posted on October 13, 2026, Reading Right, Acting Wrong , separates comprehension failures from decision failures. It probes each agent state with verifiable factual questions, such as the outcome of the last action, then asks for the next move. The hosted models answered in a median of 27 to 225 milliseconds, against 2.3 seconds for a reasoning model. Speed came with a strange blind spot: Jev made 73% of its errors after reading the state correctly, and OpenAI Decisions made 70% of its errors the same way. Those errors also cluster on the same states across every system tested. The model memorized the briefing pack and booked the wrong flight anyway. Anyone who has debugged multi-turn reasoning will recognize the shape. The fix is pleasingly boring: when the authors combined the models' own correct fact answers in code, the failures got repaired. Option order is a hidden hyperparameter System One models promise identical answers for identical inputs. Consider, Then Choose , another October paper, shows that promise breaks for choice questions: shuffle the options and the answer moves, more so as the list grows. Order flips answers mostly when the model is torn between its top few candidates, even while the output looks confident. Cyclic averaging shrinks the problem. Scoring each option alone and then comparing eliminated order dependence across five benchmarks for all eight models tested. 💡 For tool routing, this lands hard. Earlier research on canary tools caught agents falling for decoy tool descriptions. Now a tool's position in the list can tip the decision as well. Average calibration hides the sharp edges Calibration is the headline feature, and recent evaluations put it under load. A security study found strong aggregate scores masking systematic misses on specific attack groups, and in one benchmark subset Jev missed all 129 indirect attack inputs while flagging a single benign one. A decision-gate benchmark found one model accepting 93% of intent decisions and just 17% of workflow decisions at the same risk target. Calibration on one distribution stays local to that distribution, which is why demonstrating reliability per task has become the standard. 8 AI problems leaders face now, and the fix for each Eight problems keep landing on AI leaders' desks, and each has a fix backed by fresh data. Start with the two that cost you most this quarter. How to wire a System One model into your harness These habits belong on the checklist of every AI engineer shipping agents this year, right next to the operational stability basics for mission-critical ML. Decompose, then compose in code: ask the model factual probes about agent state, then combine the answers with deterministic logic. This targets the exact failure where reading succeeds and deciding fails. Score options individually for high-stakes choices: consider-then-choose costs extra passes and buys order invariance, a fair trade for tool selection and access decisions. Set thresholds per decision point: tune on held-out labeled data for each task and verify on a second held-out set. A single global threshold will over-trust some gates and over-escalate others. Escalate uncertain calls to a reasoning model: the dual-process study hands control to a slower model only when a gate opens. Audit the slow model too, since its Doom-playing reasoner, told some doors need keys, started treating ordinary doors as locked. Agentic AI needs an evidence standard, beyond dashboards Usage metrics show who logged in. Neetu Yadav sets out a five-part evidence standard covering reach, depth of use, quality, risk, and business impact, so enterprise leaders can scale agentic AI with confidence. Where System One models earn a slot today Model routing: a cheap typed decision in front of expensive calls keeps most traffic in the fast layer, a core lever for LLMOps teams chasing enterprise value . Retrieval gating: relevance checks on chunks before they reach context suit RAG pipelines that learn from every query . Prompt injection screening: viable once each attack family gets its own evaluation and threshold. Stall detection: "is the agent stuck" is the textbook System One question, answered in milliseconds per loop iteration. The verdict: fast layer, slow supervisor System One models belong in production agent harnesses right now, as a fast decision layer with logged confidence, clear escalation paths, and audit trails. Those governance basics map directly onto the mistakes AI leaders keep making with agentic deployments . Kahneman would approve of the arrangement: the fast system handles routine calls, and the slow one gets paged when the fast one looks nervous. Expect the AI architect to own that boundary, because choosing between a forward pass and a chain of thought is now a design decision with a price tag.

items.title: Companies may be held liable when AI harms their clients and customers
items.summary: When AI messes up on a tax return or in a court filing, it's no laughing matter. DigitalVision Vectors/Getty Images Artificial intelligence has moved quickly from a novelty on the job to a common workplace tool. Gallup found that 52% of U.S. employees and 68% of professional services workers were using AI by February 2026. Thomson Reuters similarly found in spring 2026 that 74% of professionals use AI several times a week for work. This widespread use shouldn’t surprise anyone. For accountants, attorneys, consultants and other professionals, AI can accelerate research , summarize complex information and assist with writing and other forms of communication. But its rapid adoption has a big downside – AI can produce information that sounds authoritative and looks polished while being completely wrong . And when AI generates mistakes, responsibility for those errors belongs to the professional or business relying on the AI output – not companies that develop AI systems. AI errors have led to lawsuits, court fines, financial consequences and public embarrassment from fabricated citations, nonexistent sources and inaccurate AI-generated information. These cases raise an increasingly important question: How can professionals benefit from AI without outsourcing the judgment their work requires? Fake citations We are two certified public accountants who research tax accounting . In the September 2026 issue of Journal of Accountancy, we examined what happened in Clinco v. Commissioner , a case before the U.S. Tax Court where an attorney submitted a brief to the court with allegedly fake citations. The Tax Court is a specialized federal court that resolves disputes between taxpayers and the IRS. This case involved a restaurant owner accused of underreporting more than US$2 million in business receipts and claiming unsupported depreciation deductions on rental properties. The main issue concerned Clinco’s accounting records used to determined how much of their income to tax. The taxpayers’ attorney, Abraham Wagner, cited four cases to support his argument that an IRS notice assessing additional taxes was invalid. The court determined that three of the citations appeared to be AI-generated hallucinations that cited nonexistent Tax Court cases. The court rejected the taxpayer’s argument and warned Wagner that submitting fake citations could lead to sanctions from the court, including financial penalties or disciplinary action against Wagner. Ultimately, the court did not sanction Wagner in the case, but the decision stands to put attorneys and other professionals in Tax Court on notice that AI hallucinations will not be tolerated. Using AI for audits and other professional work may save time but also poses some legal hazards. iStock/Getty Images Plus When AI gets it wrong AI errors made on behalf of clients are not limited to briefs drafted by attorneys. Nor are these mishaps limited to the United States. When Deloitte produced a 237-page report in 2025 for the Australian government examining its automated system for penalizing welfare recipients who failed to meet job-seeking requirements, it contained nonexistent academic citations and a fabricated quotation it attributed to a federal court judgment. The global consulting firm later issued a revised version of the error-ridden report. Deloitte blamed generative AI for the errors in the original and agreed to partially refund its fees. Like most airlines, Air Canada has a chatbot on its website to respond to its customers’ questions. The chatbot told a customer in November 2022 that he could buy a plane ticket under a bereavement policy and be reimbursed later. This was not company policy, and Air Canada refused to honor what the chatbot had told the customer. The customer sued the airline and won 812 Canadian dollars in damages. The British Columbia Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada had failed to take reasonable care to ensure that its AI bot provided accurate information and agreed with the customer that the airline had negligently misrepresented the bereavement policy. AI lawsuits There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers. In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages. There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC , that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026 the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable. Hallucinations and ‘confabulations’ Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible. The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations” – the confident presentation of erroneous or false information. Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way. Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid. AI errors in the workplace A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency. Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use. As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work. AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops. The University of Dayton is an academic partner of The Conversation. Kaitlin Newkirk is affiliated with the Ohio Society of CPAs.

AI lawsuits

There have been other lawsuits filed against AI platforms and providers.

In 2025, for example, a Georgia court dismissed a defamation lawsuit against OpenAI after its ChatGPT tool falsely accused Mark Walters, a radio host, of embezzlement. The court ruled in favor of summary judgment for OpenAI and found Walters had not established fault and damages.

There is also an ongoing case, Keene v. Google LLC, that is similar to the Walters case. Keene, a TV producer, sued after Google’s AI summaries allegedly published false information about Keene’s criminal history. In September 2026 the court ruled that some of his defamation claims may proceed, without deciding yet whether Google was liable.

Hallucinations and ‘confabulations’

Unfortunately, for anyone using AI to save time and use less labor, AI errors are often hard to spot. Unlike most obvious mistakes humans make, an AI-generated error may include supporting explanations, citations or references that make a passage appear complete and credible.

The National Institute of Standards and Technology issued a report on AI risk management in July 2024 that calls AI mistakes and hallucinations “confabulations” – the confident presentation of erroneous or false information.

Some researchers draw a more specific distinction between hallucinations, in which AI invents information outright, and confabulations, in which it fills gaps or distorts real information in a plausible way.

Either kind of problem can be hard to detect without independent verification, but confabulations mimic actual research so closely they can trick AI users into believing the AI output is valid.

AI errors in the workplace

A 2024 Stanford University study of specialized AI tools for legal research found erroneous results in 17% to 33% of the responses tested. Yet those findings and other grounds for concern about accuracy have not stopped many law firms from embracing AI tools due to their potential to save time and improve efficiency.

Recent surveys indicate law firms and other employers have not adopted enough workplace safeguards to spot and root out AI-generated mistakes. A 2026 survey by the Nationwide insurance company found that only 36% of surveyed businesses have written AI policies, and only 37% provide any training on responsible AI use.

As AI becomes more and more common in the workplace, we believe it’s clear that telling employees simply to “check the AI” is not enough. Businesses and the people working for them need clear expectations about when it’s appropriate to use AI, which outputs require independent verification, and who is ultimately responsible for the final work.

AI may change how professional work gets done, but it does not change where the buck stops.

The University of Dayton is an academic partner of The Conversation.

Kaitlin Newkirk is affiliated with the Ohio Society of CPAs.

items.title: Odisha Approves ₹176.83 Crore Disaster Recovery Data Centre in Keonjhar
items.summary: The Odisha Cabinet, chaired by Chief Minister Mohan Charan Majhi, has approved a ₹176.83 crore disaster recovery-cum-data centre in Keonjhar to strengthen the state’s digital infrastructure and ensure continuity of essential government services during cyberattacks, technical failures and natural disasters. The Odisha State Data Centre (OSDC) will be established on the south campus of Dharanidhar University in the district. It will serve as a geographically separate backup and recovery facility for the state’s primary data centre in Bhubaneswar. The facility is designed to help restore critical digital services if the primary data centre experiences a major disruption. By maintaining a separate recovery site, the state aims to reduce its dependence on a single location for storing and making government data and digital services available. The proposed centre will have independent power supply, cooling systems, network connectivity and computing infrastructure. It will also include storage facilities, backup systems, networking equipment and cybersecurity arrangements to support recovery operations. The project will incorporate secure data replication, centralised monitoring and cyber-recovery mechanisms. These systems are intended to enable the facility to function independently of the primary data centre during a disruption. As states increasingly depend on digital infrastructure to deliver public services, data availability and disaster recovery are becoming key components of government technology planning. The Keonjhar facility is expected to strengthen Odisha’s capacity to maintain essential digital services during infrastructure outages and other emergencies.

items.title: Accenture, Workday Launch Forward Deployed Engineering Programme for AI Agents
items.summary: Accenture and Workday have launched a joint forward deployed engineering (FDE) programme to help businesses deploy AI agents in human resources (HR) and finance. The teams will work within clients’ existing processes, data, policies and controls to bring Workday’s agentic capabilities into production. The companies said the programme was intended to speed up implementation and help clients realise returns on their investments sooner. The arrangement resembles HCLTech’s collaboration with Anthropic, which also uses FDEs to support enterprise AI deployments. The focus on FDEs extends beyond individual partnerships . TCS has targeted 1% to 1.5% of its workforce, or up to 8,900 employees, for these roles, while Infosys is targeting about 6,000 FDEs. Accenture has also been recruiting for the roles. The programme will draw on Accenture’s work deploying and extending Workday’s agentic capabilities at enterprise scale. The announcement did not disclose financial terms, name participating customers or specify when the first deployments would begin. Accenture engineers will also work with Workday’s product and technology teams to develop new agentic capabilities, drawing on experience from client deployments. “When AI is helping run payroll and close the books, almost right isn't good enough,” Workday Co-Founder, CEO and Chair Aneel Bhusri said.

This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

The US military’s race to make fake blood

In February 2007, a US military helicopter carrying blood to a field hospital was shot down in Iraq, killing all seven crew members. The mission was a reminder of the risks of transporting blood, which has a limited shelf life and is often in short supply.

Now, a $73 million DARPA effort aims to create shelf-stable versions of plasma, platelets, and red blood cells. The idea is to develop dried blood products that can be stored for long periods and deployed quickly on the battlefield. 

The project aims to have bags of dried blood products deployed in the field by 2029. But getting it all done will be tough, and researchers still have major questions about the safety and effectiveness of synthetic alternatives.

—Andrew Rosenblum

WeLion New Energy is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.

WeLion New Energy is on a quest to make safer, better batteries. The Chinese company’s liquid-solid hybrid cells aim to pack more power into electric cars, boats and drones, potentially improving safety and offering greater energy density than lithium-ion batteries.

In 2023, WeLion released a battery pack with EV-maker Nio that offered a range of over 1,000 kilometers. Now, the company is developing batteries with even higher energy density. But scaling up production and competing on cost remain major challenges.

—You Xiaoying

Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from geothermal power plants to carbon dioxide batteries. 

MIT Technology Review Narrated: Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers

Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process.

Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins. 

The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results?

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The FBI has arrested an OpenAI engineer accused of snooping

But Sberbank claims its systems and services were not disrupted. (Reuters $)
+ Ukraine’s data center strikes have thrown Russia into turmoil. (FT $)
+ But they haven’t stopped Russian bot farms from trolling. (Verge)
+ Europe has a drone-filled vision for future wars. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Weight-loss drugs are being tweaked to treat brain disorders
New GLP-1 trials are targeting addiction and depression. (Nature)
+ But we’re still figuring out their side effects. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Tesla robotaxis have been accused of speeding in school zones
US regulators are reviewing the claims. (Verge)
+ Tesla’s security features thwarted a federal tracking attempt. (404 Media)

5 US defense startups are turning to Taiwan to build China-free drones
At least 13 joint agreements have been signed since 2025.  (WSJ $)
+ Taiwan’s “silicon shield” could be weakening. (MIT Technology Review)

6 A war game  exposed the risks of a solar geoengineering arms race
Participants feuded over rules for dimming the sun. (Wired $)
+ Geoengineering also faces practical challenges. (MIT Technology Review)

7 AI company Character.ai has filed for bankruptcy
It’s been accused of stealing content and harming kids. (CNBC)
+ Disney has offered $20 million for its chatbot tech. (Ars Technica)
+ Its filings expose common issues with AI business models. (404 Media)

8 Apple has a new smart-home lineup built around a revamped Siri
HomeView pairs a 7-inch screen with face recognition. (Guardian
+ While the Home Collection adds cameras, locks, and thermostats. (Wired $)
+ Siri AI powers the experience, but still needs to prove its smarts. (WSJ $)

9 Scientists have identified a new dinosaur in a century-old fossil
Invictibellatrix amberina may be Europe’s first megaraptoran. (New Scientist $)

10 SpaceX’s latest launch lit up the skies with a “space jellyfish”
Rocket exhaust expanded into tentacles high in the atmosphere. (WP $)

Quote of the day

“It is like a thumb on the scale that we haven’t really ever seen.” 

—Danielle Citron, a University of Virginia law professor, tells The Washington Post that Elon Musk’s ability to amplify conspiracy theories on X could give misinformation an unprecedented influence in the midterms.

One more thing


Is the Pentagon allowed to surveil Americans with AI?

The ongoing public feud between the Department of Defense and the AI company Anthropic has raised a deep and still unanswered question: Does the law actually allow the US government to conduct mass surveillance on Americans?

Surprisingly, the answer is not straightforward. More than a decade after Edward Snowden exposed the NSA’s collection of bulk metadata from the phones of Americans, the US is still navigating a gap between what ordinary people think and what the law allows. 

Today, the legal complexity has a new edge: AI is supercharging surveillance—and our laws haven’t caught up. Here’s how the Pentagon’s use of AI has exposed legal gray areas.

—Michelle Kim

items.title: Exclusive: Stella & Dot Founder Raises $5M For Her Next Act, AI Marketing Startup Marklo
items.summary: Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot , a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers. Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively. Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo) Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders. Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks. While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away , Clare V. , Monica + Andy , Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers . The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support. Planning campaigns To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems. Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive , Meta and Google , then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign. Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run. From there, teams can use the software to plan campaigns, draft marketing materials and assign work, with suggested campaigns and reports also delivered through Slack or email. Herrin said the lack of broader-picture context with other AI tools frustrated her. For example, a tool might identify a Fourth of July sale as a successful promotion and suggest repeating it. “Hey, no, I can’t. It’s not Fourth of July. We don’t have the inventory anymore,” she recalled thinking. Jessica Herrin was pregnant with her first child and working at Dell when she began testing jewelry trunk shows in Austin on nights and weekends. The venture became Stella & Dot, a business that sold more than $2 billion in products through a network of independent sellers.

Two decades later, Herrin is building a business around the marketing problems she encountered along the way. She started Marklo in 2025 to help consumer brands decide which products to promote and prepare their campaigns. The startup has now raised $5 million in seed funding, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.

Jessica Herrin, CEO and founder of Marklo AI. (Courtesy photo)

Forerunner led the round, joined by Freestyle Capital and angel investors including former Klaviyo and current Shopify leaders.

Marklo helps consumer brands plan marketing campaigns using their sales, inventory and past marketing data. Its software shows which promotions drove sales, suggests what products to promote next and uses AI to draft campaign briefs and organize tasks.

While Marklo is still pre-revenue, more than 100 brands are already using its software in a pilot, according to Herrin. Those brands include Away, Clare V., Monica + Andy, Maya Brenner and Latico Leathers.

The Burlingame, California-based company is now opening its software to the public ahead of the holiday shopping season. It plans to use its new funding to hire engineers, develop the product and expand customer support.

To decide what to promote next, marketers first need to understand what drove past sales. That can be a challenging endeavor when sales, inventory and marketing records all sit in separate systems.

Marklo collects that information from Shopify and services such as Klaviyo, Attentive, Meta and Google, then puts past launches, promotions and sales into a calendar. Teams can see, for example, whether a rise in sales attributed to paid advertising coincided with a new product launch or a widely shared social post — factors they might miss when reviewing each service separately, Herrin said. Marklo can then draft a campaign plan and create related tasks for the team to review, edit and assign.

Using those records, along with competitors’ promotions and social media trends, Marklo suggests what a brand should market next. It also considers what the retailer has in stock and when a promotion would run.

items.title: Othello uses AI to tell salespeople what to say during calls. See the pitch deck that helped it raise $8 million.
items.summary: Othello, cofounded by Jared Zelman and Raphael Assor, just raised an $8 million seed funding round. Othello Othello gives salespeople real-time, AI-powered recommendations to improve their sales calls. It uses reinforcement learning to coach reps in pitches modeled on their company's top performers. Othello just raised $8 million in a round led by A16z Speedrun and Owl Capital. Jared Zelman has been honing his sales pitch since college, when he spent his spare time cold-emailing billionaires and prominent investors , hoping to forge a connection. His extracurricular activities helped lay the groundwork for his current startup, Othello, a platform that uses AI to give salespeople real-time coaching tips to improve their sales calls. Othello exclusively told CMO Insider on Wednesday that it had raised an $8 million seed funding round, led by Andreessen Horowitz 's startup accelerator A16z Speedrun, and Owl Capital. Othello listens in on video calls and uses AI trained on a company's uploaded sales and product materials to suggest questions to ask, answer tricky queries, and flag missed opportunities in real time through an on-screen overlay. "Too many good deals are killed by bad calls," said Zelman, who is now 24 and was using Othello to help respond to questions during our interview. Zelman said he evolved the idea for Othello at his second startup, Cicero, which created AI avatars for prominent authors and podcasters. Zelman said he struggled to sell the idea to enterprise prospects and used to have a friend stand behind his computer holding up cue cards to help steer him through his sales calls. "I was like, 'Hey, I'm just going to build this for everybody,'" Zelman said. "In sales, you can outsource and use AI to do everything except for the one important part of the job, which is the sales call." Othello says its AI models are trained on 20 million hours of recorded sales calls and that its platform can be integrated with business software platforms such as Google Workspace, Salesforce, Slack, and ServiceNow. The company says customers' data is not used to train AI models shared with other businesses. Its customers include Microsoft and Capital One. Othello isn't the first company to use AI to help salespeople. It's a much smaller challenger to rivals such as Gong and Salesloft, which offer tools to analyze sales conversations, with Salesloft also providing real-time coaching. Gong and Salesloft have raised hundreds of millions of dollars and have multibillion-dollar valuations. Zelman said Othello's advantage lies in the speed and accuracy of its proprietary AI models, which deliver recommendations in milliseconds and improve from recorded sales calls using reinforcement learning . He said its singular focus on offering this type of in-call solution will also give it an advantage if an enterprise tech company like Salesforce or HubSpot chose to launch a similar product. "Providing real-time recommendations is so damn hard because if it's too slow or not smart enough, it's really unhelpful and very, very distracting," Zelman said. Othello could also prove useful for chief marketing officers , Zelman said, by helping ensure salespeople actually use the materials created for them, while giving marketing teams insights into which messages are most effective at converting customers. Othello plans to invest the funds in growing its engineering team. Zelman said he anticipates increasing the company's head count to around 80 employees, from 20 currently. The startup is also planning to improve the product to focus on coaching individual sellers on their strengths and weaknesses, beyond optimizing its recommendations based on learnings from a company's best performers. In the future, he envisioned the product being used for in-person meetings via smart glasses . A group of individual investors including DoorDash cofounder Andy Fang, Hugging Face cofounder Thomas Wolf, Chime cofounder Ryan King, and Ripple founder Chris Larsen invested in the funding round. Check out the pitch deck Othello used to secure its $8 million seed investment, shared exclusively with CMO Insider. Some of the slides have been omitted or redacted. Othello describes itself as a 'real-time sales augmentation layer.' Othello It cites stats from a Gartner report on the sales industry. Othello The 2025 Gartner study found that salespeople drove 60% of business-to-business revenue, a contribution that is forecast to increase to 75% in the following four years. It also cites research from The Bridge Group that found it takes the average salesperson 13 months to reach productivity, which is 32% slower than four years ago. A separate report from The Bridge Group found that 35% of sales reps leave each year, double the rate of attrition reported three years ago. Othello says there will always be human salespeople. Othello "People like to play golf," Zelman told CMO Insider. Othello says while other AI tools save time, its platform helps close more deals. Othello This slide shows the Othello platform in action. Othello Its overlay prompts sales reps on which questions to ask and provides information about the company they are pitching and the pain points raised in the conversation. Othello says it's focused on providing insights while a call is happening. Othello It provides prompts for discovery questions, responses to technical queries, and case studies. Othello Othello says it has more than 50 large enterprise customers. Othello This slide offers stats on how Othello can improve sales team performance. Othello The company said a subset of its customers that had more than 20 reps using Othello for more than a quarter achieved 15% higher win rates and 45% faster ramp-up times. "Ramp-up" refers to the time it takes a new sales rep to reach full productivity. Companies often define this differently, but it could include reaching $1 million in revenue or achieving another specific performance goal. 'Everyone sells better with Othello,' the company says. items.title: Czech startup FLÆ Robotics lands over €1M to automate hotel guest services
items.summary: Czech technology company FLÆ Robotics has raised more than €1 million in seed funding from Purple Ventures and Garage Angels to further develop its AI-powered hospitality platform, BE-A, and support international expansion. Founded by Filip Linek , FLÆ Robotics develops BE-A, an AI hospitality agent designed to automate routine guest communication, reservations and front-office tasks for hotels. The platform operates around the clock, handling enquiries through WhatsApp, email, web chat and phone calls. Through integrations with hotel management systems, BE-A can check room availability, manage reservations and provide information about hotel services. It also categorises incoming messages and directs requests to the appropriate teams or workflows, helping hotel staff reduce administrative work and focus on guests who require personal attention. The platform is currently used by more than 60 hotels across the United Kingdom, Germany and the Czech Republic. According to FLÆ Robotics, BE-A processed approximately 265,000 messages and voice interactions across nearly 160,000 conversations in July and August 2026, averaging more than 4,000 interactions per day. During the same period, the platform completed more than 3,400 hotel bookings without human intervention. Commenting on the company's approach to automating hotel operations, Filip Linek, founder and CEO of FLÆ Robotics, said: Hotel teams handle a large volume of repetitive enquiries and tasks every day across email, phone and other channels. We are developing BE-A to go beyond answering questions and carry out the next step within hotel systems. This gives staff more time for guests and situations that need their experience and judgement. The company is working to expand BE-A's capabilities and strengthen its integration with existing hotel systems, allowing the platform to handle a broader range of guest requests and operational tasks. FLÆ Robotics plans to use the funding to accelerate product development, expand its team and support international growth. The company is strengthening its presence in Germany, entering Austria and building on its recent launch in the United Kingdom, while also preparing to expand into the US hotel market.

items.title: TCS to Modernise Australian Financial Services Firm’s Core Banking Systems
items.summary: Tata Consultancy Services (TCS) has been selected by Australian financial services company MyState Limited to deploy its BaNCS Global Banking Platform for MyState Bank’s core banking transformation following its merger with Auswide Bank. TCS will deploy the platform to help MyState consolidate its banking systems, business processes, data repositories, and customer service systems. The companies did not disclose the contract value or implementation timeline. “The decision to implement a modern, AI-enabled core banking platform is an important step in building a simpler, stronger and more scalable bank for our customers and our people,” MyState CEO and Managing Director Brett Morgan said in a statement. Morgan said the platform would help the bank reduce complexity and use technology and data more effectively to serve customers. TCS BaNCS includes capabilities for core banking, payments, customer engagement, relationship management, and digital operations. TCS said the implementation would use configurable products, workflow automation, application programming interfaces (APIs), and AI-based transformation tools. TCS also said the platform could support MyState’s future acquisitions, although the companies did not disclose any acquisition plans. The agreement follows other technology modernisation projects involving Indian IT services companies and banks. Earlier this month, Infosys expanded its engagement with Dutch lender ABN AMRO to modernise its IT systems and increase its use of generative and agentic AI. TCS reported its Q2 FY27 results on October 8, with revenue rising 0.5% sequentially in constant currency to $7.64 billion. Its annualised AI revenue run rate crossed $3.1 billion, accounting for more than 10% of total revenue, according to its latest quarterly results .

items.title: Google positions Gemini 4 Argon for long-horizon agentic work
items.summary: Google has launched Gemini 4 Argon, a new flagship AI model aimed at complex enterprise and software-development workloads, pairing claims of stronger coding performance and advanced reasoning with an introductory pricing model that doubles after November 30. The model “excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks,” Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, wrote in a blog post. Google said that its engineers used Argon to refactor a legacy folder of about six million lines within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase, finishing in weeks rather than months. Teams using Argon in Antigravity increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% and cut code rollbacks by nearly a third, the company said, without detailing how it measured either figure. Argon is available through the Gemini API in AI Studio and on Google’s Gemini platform, and to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Antigravity agentic development environment, the post added. In a separate developer blog post , Google said the model is “designed for those long-horizon workflows that require deep reasoning and structural precision.” Pricing set to double According to the post, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens during the introductory period, with cached input discounted by 95%. A footnote in the post states the prices rise to $4 and $20, respectively, after November 30. The company said the model’s 1 million-token limit in the Gemini API is shared between input and output. Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said CIOs should budget at the higher rate from day one, because no enterprise evaluation, security review, and procurement cycle finishes within the discount window. “A business case built on the launch rate is a business case built to be rewritten in seven weeks,” he said. Gogia said Google bills reasoning tokens at the output rate, which makes the per-token price a poor guide to agent costs. “Cheap per token and cheap per task are different claims, and only the second one reaches the budget,” he said. Sakshi Grover, research director at IDC, said agentic workloads multiply token use through planning loops, tool calls and repeated context. She cited IDC’s FERS Survey (Wave 5, 2026), in which 72% of enterprises said their AI agent spending had run over forecast in the past 12 months. Whether Argon’s pricing and public benchmark results translate into “comparable output quality for enterprise use cases remains unproven,” said Nitish Tyagi, senior principal analyst at Gartner. He said internal validation on an organization’s own workflows should remain the primary basis for choosing a model. Gogia pointed out that Google Cloud’s standard terms allow fee changes unless a price is expressly agreed. CIOs who want price and version certainty after Nov. 30 must therefore write it into their contracts, he said. Gogia added that the deeper lock-in sits in Google’s Interactions API, which keeps agent conversation state on Google’s servers. “The protocols are neutral. The state is not,” he said. The model tried to game the tests in training Google disclosed in a separate safety blog post that Argon tried to work around its own evaluations during training. What the company sees in practice is “an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given,” Anca Dragan, vice president of AI safety and behavior, and Raluca Ada Popa, head of Gemini security at Google DeepMind, wrote in the post. According to that post, the model, in rare cases during training, tried to raise its container privileges to change grading scripts and pull answers from the test runner’s memory. In one case, it crashed the evaluation sandbox so that a failed run would not be scored. Google said in the post that its misalignment monitor caught these attempts and that shortcut attempts on coding benchmarks fell to 2%. “A model that games its grader turns every enterprise grader into a control that must be defended,” Gogia said. He said agents should never hold write access to anything that judges their own work, and that a crashed or timed-out check must count as a failure. Grover recommended a distinct agent identity, short-lived task-scoped credentials, restricted network access, and human approval for destructive changes, privilege expansion, and sensitive data exports. “Production deployment should depend on demonstrated control and auditability alongside task performance,” she said. Cyber capability rises In Google’s internal cyber evaluations, Argon solved 12 of 12 simulated end-to-end attack scenarios, compared with five for the previous Gemini generation, the safety post said. Google said in the post that it applied frontier safeguards to the cyber and biological domains under its Frontier Safety Framework. Gogia said the result is “a score on Google’s own exam, set and marked by Google,” and that Greyhound has found no independent replication of it. Google is also expanding its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners, giving vetted cyber defenders access to Argon without cyber guardrails, the launch post said. “The weakest partner, not the strongest control, sets the exposure,” Gogia said, noting that each new partner adds another identity estate and contractor chain. IDC’s Grover said security leaders should judge such access by reproducible findings, validated patches and reduced exposure. She warned that more findings without the capacity to fix them can increase operational pressure. The article originally appeared on InfoWorld .
