The model “excels at deep work in complex, real-world tasks,” Koray Kavukcuoglu, senior vice president of Google DeepMind and chief AI architect at Google, wrote in a blog post.

Google said that its engineers used Argon to refactor a legacy folder of about six million lines within Chromium’s 40 million-line codebase, finishing in weeks rather than months. Teams using Argon in Antigravity increased agentic code submissions by more than 35% and cut code rollbacks by nearly a third, the company said, without detailing how it measured either figure.

Argon is available through the Gemini API in AI Studio and on Google’s Gemini platform, and to Google AI Ultra subscribers in the Antigravity agentic development environment, the post added. In a separate developer blog post, Google said the model is “designed for those long-horizon workflows that require deep reasoning and structural precision.”

According to the post, Argon costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens during the introductory period, with cached input discounted by 95%. A footnote in the post states the prices rise to $4 and $20, respectively, after November 30. The company said the model’s 1 million-token limit in the Gemini API is shared between input and output.

Sanchit Vir Gogia, chief analyst at Greyhound Research, said CIOs should budget at the higher rate from day one, because no enterprise evaluation, security review, and procurement cycle finishes within the discount window. “A business case built on the launch rate is a business case built to be rewritten in seven weeks,” he said.

Gogia said Google bills reasoning tokens at the output rate, which makes the per-token price a poor guide to agent costs. “Cheap per token and cheap per task are different claims, and only the second one reaches the budget,” he said.

Sakshi Grover, research director at IDC, said agentic workloads multiply token use through planning loops, tool calls and repeated context. She cited IDC’s FERS Survey (Wave 5, 2026), in which 72% of enterprises said their AI agent spending had run over forecast in the past 12 months.

Whether Argon’s pricing and public benchmark results translate into “comparable output quality for enterprise use cases remains unproven,” said Nitish Tyagi, senior principal analyst at Gartner. He said internal validation on an organization’s own workflows should remain the primary basis for choosing a model.

Gogia pointed out that Google Cloud’s standard terms allow fee changes unless a price is expressly agreed. CIOs who want price and version certainty after Nov. 30 must therefore write it into their contracts, he said. Gogia added that the deeper lock-in sits in Google’s Interactions API, which keeps agent conversation state on Google’s servers.

“The protocols are neutral. The state is not,” he said.

The model tried to game the tests in training

Google disclosed in a separate safety blog post that Argon tried to work around its own evaluations during training. What the company sees in practice is “an agent trying too hard to finish the job it was given,” Anca Dragan, vice president of AI safety and behavior, and Raluca Ada Popa, head of Gemini security at Google DeepMind, wrote in the post.

According to that post, the model, in rare cases during training, tried to raise its container privileges to change grading scripts and pull answers from the test runner’s memory. In one case, it crashed the evaluation sandbox so that a failed run would not be scored. Google said in the post that its misalignment monitor caught these attempts and that shortcut attempts on coding benchmarks fell to 2%.

“A model that games its grader turns every enterprise grader into a control that must be defended,” Gogia said. He said agents should never hold write access to anything that judges their own work, and that a crashed or timed-out check must count as a failure.

Grover recommended a distinct agent identity, short-lived task-scoped credentials, restricted network access, and human approval for destructive changes, privilege expansion, and sensitive data exports. “Production deployment should depend on demonstrated control and auditability alongside task performance,” she said.

Cyber capability rises

In Google’s internal cyber evaluations, Argon solved 12 of 12 simulated end-to-end attack scenarios, compared with five for the previous Gemini generation, the safety post said. Google said in the post that it applied frontier safeguards to the cyber and biological domains under its Frontier Safety Framework.

Gogia said the result is “a score on Google’s own exam, set and marked by Google,” and that Greyhound has found no independent replication of it.

Google is also expanding its Fairwind Program to hundreds of additional partners, giving vetted cyber defenders access to Argon without cyber guardrails, the launch post said.

“The weakest partner, not the strongest control, sets the exposure,” Gogia said, noting that each new partner adds another identity estate and contractor chain.

IDC’s Grover said security leaders should judge such access by reproducible findings, validated patches and reduced exposure. She warned that more findings without the capacity to fix them can increase operational pressure.

items.title: Silicon Valley's hot new talking points: beer and cigarettes
items.summary: Jensen Huang, among other tech figures, features on the "Tech Founder Beer Matrix" as a "beer sipper" and "good hang." Bloomberg/Getty Images After Mark Zuckerberg drank a Guinness, tech bros can't stop talking about drinking beer. One X user created the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," while another ranked execs on a "beer matrix." Cigarettes are in focus, too, after Palantir's CTO said some AI researchers are taking up smoking. After Mark Zuckerberg’s cautious-looking sip of stout on Stripe cofounder John Collison’s "Cheeky Pint" podcast became a social-media talking point , a new debate has emerged: which tech leaders can actually hold their drink? Soon after Zuckerberg's much-memed appearance, ETN, a tech podcast, built what it called the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," publishing a leaderboard of guests' Guinness consumption, measured to the nearest sixth of a pint. Elon Musk , the world’s richest man, currently tops the chart after drinking three full pints during his appearance on Collison’s show. Introducing The Cheeky Pint Benchmark. We made our intern watch every episode of Cheeky Pint to bring you this breakdown of pints drank by guests to the nearest sixth. Congratulations to @elonmusk who is currently in the lead with three full pints of Guinness. pic.twitter.com/YTTP4P6BSA — etn. (@etnshow) October 13, 2026 The chart prompted characteristically competitive responses from the tech world. Antonio García Martínez, a director at Base, said the benchmark was "weak sauce in general." 1. Richest man in the world drank the most 2. This is pretty weak sauce in general, though not bad for people on a public podcast with a reputation on the line 3. Kind of curious if the Collisons match their guests https://t.co/JhqTjDztEe — Antonio García Martínez (agm.eth) (@antoniogm) October 13, 2026 Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado joked that he'd drink so much if he went on the podcast that the index would need a new scale. If they invite me, you'll need to make this log scale. https://t.co/8YaB0yWPun — martin_casado (@martin_casado) October 14, 2026 The benchmark follows a viral clip of Zuckerberg appearing to grimace after taking a sip of Guinness during a recent two-hour-plus episode with Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang . One X user came to Zuckerberg’s defense, arguing that Guinness was "performative at best" and noting that the Meta CEO had nevertheless finished two beers during the interview. Zuckerberg himself replied simply: "that’s just my face." that's just my face — Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) October 13, 2026 Wang also appeared to embrace the joke, responding to a fan-made "Tech Founder Beer Matrix" that placed founders on a spectrum from "beer sippers" to "beer tankers," and from "good hang" to "bad hang." The chart positioned Wang firmly on the beer-tanker side — despite not finishing a full pint on the podcast — alongside figures including Elon Musk, Larry Ellison, and former Apple CEO Tim Cook. you can’t possibly actually think i’m the same quality hang as tim apple https://t.co/GBwnpUe6Rt — Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) October 14, 2026 Intercom cofounder Des Traynor took issue with being placed on the "beer sippers" side of the matrix, saying he was the first "multi-pint drinker" to appear on "Cheeky Pint," and that his episode included a detailed discussion of beer. This is the most insulted I've ever been on Twitter in ~20 years, and that's saying something. Not to pull receipts, but I was the first multi-pint drinker on Cheeky Pint, and we spoke in detail about various beers on the episode itself. https://t.co/x5MlxkeqlC — Des Traynor (@destraynor) October 13, 2026 The leaderboard’s methodology is already under scrutiny. Will O'Brien, founder of autonomous aquatic vehicle firm Ulysses, argued that the figures should be adjusted for episode length, using pints per hour rather than raw totals. He also said other alcoholic drinks should count if the point is to identify who is "actually DRINKING." Totally inaccurate chart and not a proper way of measuring this metric. The pints should be normalized by time. It should be pints per hour. Elon was on for like 5 hours. Not fair vs other guests. Also some guests drank non-Guinness alcohol. They should be accounted for.… https://t.co/qn4gHoOSUW — will o’brien (@Willob) October 14, 2026 Kalshi cofounder Tarek Mansour also disputed the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," saying he had to leave his appearance before it ended. Still, he found a silver lining: he drank more than Andreessen Horowitz cofounder Marc Andreessen . This is unfair. I had to walk out mid pod. At least I beat @pmarca though https://t.co/H28i8xY4ge — Tarek Mansour (@mansourtarek_) October 13, 2026 Musk, meanwhile, basked in the glow of topping the chart, replying with beer mugs and a laughing emoji — while adding that he "hardly ever" drinks alcohol. 🍻 🤣 Funny thing is that I hardly ever drink alcohol! https://t.co/sQsfbGhocD — Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 13, 2026 The jokes come as Silicon Valley is seeing a sharper divide between those embracing vice and those seeking to optimize every aspect of their health. As Business Insider’s Henry Chandonnet reported last month, a small group of founders, engineers, and investors has embraced cigarettes in a sector previously known for its healthy obsessions. Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev also posted this week that he was "hearing more and more AI researchers are taking up smoking," adding: "superintelligence is near." Hearing more and more AI researchers are taking up smoking … superintelligence is near — Vlad Tenev (@vladtenev) October 12, 2026 That idea resurfaced after Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar described AI researchers taking up smoking to signal their confidence that artificial intelligence will cure cancer. After Sankar's comments, longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson — who is famed for his fanatical pursuit of good health — joked that he was ready to pivot to smoking, drinking, fast food, and all-nighters. ok, I'm in. pivoting to: > smoking, drinking, fast food > hard drugs, all-nighters, ragers > STIs, sun burns, deafening concerts https://t.co/2pl8bYsuE4 pic.twitter.com/Fra0WqfCi3 — Bryan Johnson (@bryan_johnson) October 13, 2026 For now, though, the emerging tech-industry trend appears to be less about optimizing for longevity than proving one is relaxed enough not to care. items.summary_html:
Jensen Huang, among other tech figures, features on the "Tech Founder Beer Matrix" as a "beer sipper" and "good hang."

Bloomberg/Getty Images

  • After Mark Zuckerberg drank a Guinness, tech bros can't stop talking about drinking beer.
  • One X user created the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," while another ranked execs on a "beer matrix."
  • Cigarettes are in focus, too, after Palantir's CTO said some AI researchers are taking up smoking.

After Mark Zuckerberg’s cautious-looking sip of stout on Stripe cofounder John Collison’s "Cheeky Pint" podcast became a social-media talking point, a new debate has emerged: which tech leaders can actually hold their drink?

Soon after Zuckerberg's much-memed appearance, ETN, a tech podcast, built what it called the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," publishing a leaderboard of guests' Guinness consumption, measured to the nearest sixth of a pint.

Elon Musk, the world’s richest man, currently tops the chart after drinking three full pints during his appearance on Collison’s show.

Introducing The Cheeky Pint Benchmark.

We made our intern watch every episode of Cheeky Pint to bring you this breakdown of pints drank by guests to the nearest sixth.

Congratulations to @elonmusk who is currently in the lead with three full pints of Guinness. pic.twitter.com/YTTP4P6BSA

— etn. (@etnshow) October 13, 2026

The chart prompted characteristically competitive responses from the tech world.

Antonio García Martínez, a director at Base, said the benchmark was "weak sauce in general."

1. Richest man in the world drank the most
2. This is pretty weak sauce in general, though not bad for people on a public podcast with a reputation on the line
3. Kind of curious if the Collisons match their guests https://t.co/JhqTjDztEe

— Antonio García Martínez (agm.eth) (@antoniogm) October 13, 2026

Andreessen Horowitz partner Martin Casado joked that he'd drink so much if he went on the podcast that the index would need a new scale.

If they invite me, you'll need to make this log scale. https://t.co/8YaB0yWPun

— martin_casado (@martin_casado) October 14, 2026

The benchmark follows a viral clip of Zuckerberg appearing to grimace after taking a sip of Guinness during a recent two-hour-plus episode with Meta’s chief AI officer, Alexandr Wang.

One X user came to Zuckerberg’s defense, arguing that Guinness was "performative at best" and noting that the Meta CEO had nevertheless finished two beers during the interview.

Zuckerberg himself replied simply: "that’s just my face."

that's just my face

— Mark Zuckerberg (@finkd) October 13, 2026

Wang also appeared to embrace the joke, responding to a fan-made "Tech Founder Beer Matrix" that placed founders on a spectrum from "beer sippers" to "beer tankers," and from "good hang" to "bad hang."

The chart positioned Wang firmly on the beer-tanker side — despite not finishing a full pint on the podcast — alongside figures including Elon Musk, Larry Ellison, and former Apple CEO Tim Cook.

you can’t possibly actually think i’m the same quality hang as tim apple https://t.co/GBwnpUe6Rt

— Alexandr Wang (@alexandr_wang) October 14, 2026

Intercom cofounder Des Traynor took issue with being placed on the "beer sippers" side of the matrix, saying he was the first "multi-pint drinker" to appear on "Cheeky Pint," and that his episode included a detailed discussion of beer.

This is the most insulted I've ever been on Twitter in ~20 years, and that's saying something.

Not to pull receipts, but I was the first multi-pint drinker on Cheeky Pint, and we spoke in detail about various beers on the episode itself. https://t.co/x5MlxkeqlC

— Des Traynor (@destraynor) October 13, 2026

The leaderboard’s methodology is already under scrutiny. Will O'Brien, founder of autonomous aquatic vehicle firm Ulysses, argued that the figures should be adjusted for episode length, using pints per hour rather than raw totals.

He also said other alcoholic drinks should count if the point is to identify who is "actually DRINKING."

Totally inaccurate chart and not a proper way of measuring this metric.

The pints should be normalized by time. It should be pints per hour.

Elon was on for like 5 hours. Not fair vs other guests.

Also some guests drank non-Guinness alcohol. They should be accounted for.… https://t.co/qn4gHoOSUW

— will o’brien (@Willob) October 14, 2026

Kalshi cofounder Tarek Mansour also disputed the "Cheeky Pint Benchmark," saying he had to leave his appearance before it ended. Still, he found a silver lining: he drank more than Andreessen Horowitz cofounder Marc Andreessen.

This is unfair. I had to walk out mid pod.

At least I beat @pmarca though https://t.co/H28i8xY4ge

— Tarek Mansour (@mansourtarek_) October 13, 2026

Musk, meanwhile, basked in the glow of topping the chart, replying with beer mugs and a laughing emoji — while adding that he "hardly ever" drinks alcohol.

🍻 🤣

Funny thing is that I hardly ever drink alcohol! https://t.co/sQsfbGhocD

— Elon Musk (@elonmusk) October 13, 2026

The jokes come as Silicon Valley is seeing a sharper divide between those embracing vice and those seeking to optimize every aspect of their health.

As Business Insider’s Henry Chandonnet reported last month, a small group of founders, engineers, and investors has embraced cigarettes in a sector previously known for its healthy obsessions.

Robinhood CEO Vlad Tenev also posted this week that he was "hearing more and more AI researchers are taking up smoking," adding: "superintelligence is near."

Hearing more and more AI researchers are taking up smoking … superintelligence is near

— Vlad Tenev (@vladtenev) October 12, 2026

That idea resurfaced after Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar described AI researchers taking up smoking to signal their confidence that artificial intelligence will cure cancer.

After Sankar's comments, longevity entrepreneur Bryan Johnson — who is famed for his fanatical pursuit of good health — joked that he was ready to pivot to smoking, drinking, fast food, and all-nighters.

ok, I'm in. pivoting to:

> smoking, drinking, fast food

> hard drugs, all-nighters, ragers

> STIs, sun burns, deafening concerts https://t.co/2pl8bYsuE4 pic.twitter.com/Fra0WqfCi3

— Bryan Johnson (@bryan_johnson) October 13, 2026

For now, though, the emerging tech-industry trend appears to be less about optimizing for longevity than proving one is relaxed enough not to care.

items.title: China clears Alibaba’s Qwen AI just in time for iPhone Duo
items.summary: In what may be a hugely significant move, China has approved the use of Alibaba AI models for Apple’s iPhone Duo and other iPhones. It’s a significant step forward for the company in China, where demand for its smartphone remains incredibly strong. China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has approved integration of AI from Alibaba in several iPhones, including all the models currently supporting Apple Intelligence. That approval extends to Apple Intelligence, as well as Alibaba’s Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen) and Tongyi Wanxiang models. This should mean Apple will be able to offer Chinese iPhone users similar image generation and AI chatbot capabilities as it provides to customers elsewhere, bar Europe. Cook’s China tour This news breaks around the same time Tim Cook, Apple’s former CEO and now executive chairman, visits China . He met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in Beijing on Monday following a weekend of stops across the country and meetings in Europe before that, including a brush with UK royalty . Cook won’t be on the move without reason, and it’s easy to speculate that the new Alibaba AI approval in China was part of his tour itinerary. If that’s the case, then it also seems possible he’s there to put the finishing touches to whatever deal the company has had to come to in order to inject Alibaba’s Qwen AI into iPhones. Countdown to Duo The company hasn’t yet discussed its plans to bring AI to the Chinese market, but the past week also saw Apple COO Sabih Khan visit the Foxconn Technology Park on October 11. The activity comes as Apple prepares to open up for iPhone Duo pre-orders across 70 nations, including China, on October 16 to ship October 23. While the Chinese approval is big news, the situation is well-known. Apple worked with Alibaba to develop AI models for use in China, and in August briefly posted and subsequently removed details explaining how Mac users in China could set up their computers to work with Qwen AI. Apple achieved regulatory clearance to offer Apple Intelligence in China in July but hasn’t yet done so. It clearly prefers to offer a wider-ranging solution, though some core features are now available in Hong Kong. We later learned that Apple has developed a proprietary AI model for China with support from Alibaba. It had to do this because US AI models are not available in China. All of this has been some time coming: Apple and Alibaba submitted co-developed AI features for approval to China’s internet regulator, the Cyberspace Administration of China, in the past year. With or without AI It may be important to point out that the lack of built-in AI in Chinese iPhones doesn’t seem to have dented enthusiasm for the product one iota. Despite recent rumor of production order cuts, JP Morgan says there’s nothing to be concerned about and that iPhone 18 Pro models are seeing higher demand in China than the iPhone 17 Pro models did last year. Counterpoint Research tells us Apple took 33% of China’s smartphone market in the week of September 14-20. Other local reports claim Apple shifted 1.3 million of the new devices in China in the first week — and that’s without the full AI experience we’re usually told matters so much to consumers. We certainly know AI matters to US AI companies, while Huawei is aggressively promoting its own AI devices in China. In China, foldables are a big attraction Interest in foldable smartphones is particularly high in China, which has already become the largest and most competitive market for these kinds of devices. China makes up more than a third of global folding smartphone sales and it is also interesting to observe that Huawei and other Chinese competitors recorded a spike in demand for their foldable devices after Apple announced iPhone Duo. With the imminent introduction of its first foldable device, it’s hard to see how any move to introduce Alibaba-supported AI support in China would hurt the company; it may even help stimulate sales in one of the few big global economies that isn’t currently on life support. And that’s got to be good for (Apple’s) business. I don’t know what time scale Apple is working on, but it typically publishes a software update just before it ships a new product, so there’s certainly time for an AI surprise for China. We don’t yet know when it will happen. We just know it’s happening. Now please subscribe to my daily, human-curated Apple-related news headline feed at The Core , or follow me on BlueSky , LinkedIn , or Mastodon .

In what may be a hugely significant move, China has approved the use of Alibaba AI models for Apple’s iPhone Duo and other iPhones. It’s a significant step forward for the company in China, where demand for its smartphone remains incredibly strong.

China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology has approved integration of AI from Alibaba in several iPhones, including all the models currently supporting Apple Intelligence. That approval extends to Apple Intelligence, as well as Alibaba’s Tongyi Qianwen (Qwen) and Tongyi Wanxiang models.

This should mean Apple will be able to offer Chinese iPhone users similar image generation and AI chatbot capabilities as it provides to customers elsewhere, bar Europe. 

Cook’s China tour

This news breaks around the same time Tim Cook, Apple’s former CEO and now executive chairman, visits China. He met with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng in Beijing on Monday following a weekend of stops across the country and meetings in Europe before that, including a brush with UK royalty. 

Cook won’t be on the move without reason, and it’s easy to speculate that the new Alibaba AI approval in China was part of his tour itinerary. If that’s the case, then it also seems possible he’s there to put the finishing touches to whatever deal the company has had to come to in order to inject Alibaba’s Qwen AI into iPhones. 

Countdown to Duo

The company hasn’t yet discussed its plans to bring AI to the Chinese market, but the past week also saw Apple COO Sabih Khan visit the Foxconn Technology Park on October 11. The activity comes as Apple prepares to open up for iPhone Duo pre-orders across 70 nations, including China, on October 16 to ship October 23. 

While the Chinese approval is big news, the situation is well-known. Apple worked with Alibaba to develop AI models for use in China, and in August briefly posted and subsequently removed details explaining how Mac users in China could set up their computers to work with Qwen AI. Apple achieved regulatory clearance to offer Apple Intelligence in China in July but hasn’t yet done so. It clearly prefers to offer a wider-ranging solution, though some core features are now available in Hong Kong.

We later learned that Apple has developed a proprietary AI model for China with support from Alibaba. It had to do this because US AI models are not available in China. All of this has been some time coming: Apple and Alibaba submitted co-developed AI features for approval to China’s internet regulator, the Cyberspace Administration of China, in the past year. 

With or without AI

It may be important to point out that the lack of built-in AI in Chinese iPhones doesn’t seem to have dented enthusiasm for the product one iota. Despite recent rumor of production order cuts, JP Morgan says there’s nothing to be concerned about and that iPhone 18 Pro models are seeing higher demand in China than the iPhone 17 Pro models did last year. Counterpoint Research tells us Apple took 33% of China’s smartphone market in the week of September 14-20. 

Other local reports claim Apple shifted 1.3 million of the new devices in China in the first week — and that’s without the full AI experience we’re usually told matters so much to consumers. We certainly know AI matters to US AI companies, while Huawei is aggressively promoting its own AI devices in China.

In China, foldables are a big attraction

Interest in foldable smartphones is particularly high in China, which has already become the largest and most competitive market for these kinds of devices. China makes up more than a third of global folding smartphone sales and it is also interesting to observe that Huawei and other Chinese competitors recorded a spike in demand for their foldable devices after Apple announced iPhone Duo. 

With the imminent introduction of its first foldable device, it’s hard to see how any move to introduce Alibaba-supported AI support in China would hurt the company; it may even help stimulate sales in one of the few big global economies that isn’t currently on life support. And that’s got to be good for (Apple’s) business. 

I don’t know what time scale Apple is working on, but it typically publishes a software update just before it ships a new product, so there’s certainly time for an AI surprise for China. We don’t yet know when it will happen. We just know it’s happening.

items.title: How I Learned That Some Startup Problems Are Too Big For A Minimum Viable Product
items.summary: By Daniel Kjellén A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary. Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause. For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on. Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda. After selling my first venture, Tink , to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing. Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours. A problem with too many heads Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another. Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget. “Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one. Why the second time is different In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder. The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you. Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it. Maximum viable product Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink. We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs. You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet. Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda , the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022. Illustration: Dom Guzman
items.summary_html:
By Daniel Kjellén

A first venture usually follows a well-worn playbook: a gap in the market, obsessive refinement of concept and pitch, eventual conviction that the solution is as bulletproof as it is revolutionary.

Then, the dreaded phase of product-market fit. Instead of building the future of an entire industry, you find yourself forced to focus on a narrow use case and spend the first invaluable years proving that your idea can make money and scale. The grand vision gets put on pause.

For most founders, this journey is the only one available. After all, investors are betting on someone who has never built a company before, so a small check and a narrow product limit what everyone stands to lose. But some ambitions need total commitment from the start, and having built a company before helps when taking them on.

Lessons from the front line Daniel Kjellén, CEO and co-founder of Freda.

After selling my first venture, Tink, to Visa for €1.8 billion (about $1.9 billion USD) in 2022, I found myself in a new position — and it wasn’t horizontal on a sun lounger. My co-founder Fredrik Hedberg and I had a real war chest of our own, and a brand-new entrepreneurial bug. For the first time in our lives, we had the experience and the resources to undertake something truly world-changing.

Compliance is a gauntlet that any founder will be painfully familiar with. Scaling Tink across Europe, to 700 people operating under a host of regulators, my team and I got used to tearing our hair out over small wording tweaks, reviews that dragged on for months, and perpetual uncertainty that stopped us from iterating fast and boldly. Products were often delayed by months, a slip that meant the world in an industry moving as fast as ours.

A problem with too many heads

Compliance was a problem that could never be solved piecemeal. Every company’s obligations depend on a million different factors, each of which sits in a different part of the business that rarely talks to one another.

Legal tracks regulations; another department oversees how they are implemented. Product teams make their own calls on features, and yet another team opens a case to check whether it was compliant. Policies, standards and regulations belong to other departments entirely, and those are usually the part of a silo a compliance startup builds for — a clear buyer and a budget.

“Solving compliance” was a mission akin to fighting the Hydra: cut off one head and two more grow back. There is no minimum viable product here. Fixing one head changes nothing. What it takes is a maximum viable product from day one.

Why the second time is different

In recent years, we’ve seen a series of inspiring examples of successful founders coming back to take on new problems. Stockholm knows this well: alumni of Spotify and Klarna have gone on to found and back a long list of new companies, using the credibility from their first successes to try something harder.

The second time around, capital and access both come easier. A successful first exit opens doors to talent, partners and investors that we simply didn’t have with Tink. It is a fantastic opportunity, and one I’m grateful for. You get to bring every lesson from what went well and what went badly, and you start with a real tailwind when people want to work with you and back you.

Money also means you can fund the full build yourself, so no investor asks you to shrink the idea before you’ve tested it.

Maximum viable product

Experience and capital used to get you only so far. Ten years ago, building something this broad would still have needed hundreds of people of various backgrounds, and many years. Language models have changed that. Our team today is 22 strong and growing, and ships at a pace I could only have dreamed of when we first built Tink.

We also feel we’ve grown thicker skin from the bruises of our first 15 years as entrepreneurs.

You know the setbacks are coming, and you know that a venture is never a one-man sprint but a team marathon. None of that guarantees success. But it’s a good place to start if you want to stand your ground and build your biggest vision yet.

Daniel Kjellén is the CEO and co-founder of Freda, the Stockholm-based AI-native compliance company that came out of stealth in September 2026. He previously co-founded the open banking platform Tink in 2012 and led it as CEO through its growth to a multimarket operation with around 700 employees before its €1.8 billion acquisition by Visa in 2022.

Illustration: Dom Guzman

items.title: OpenAI, Google pushing new AI models easily tricked into making nudes, researchers say
items.summary: Safety researchers continue to warn that a large volume of AI-generated explicit content is spreading unchecked, while regulators do little to meaningfully stop it. This non-consensual content is commonly shared in text and direct messages or stored in private clouds where it’s less likely to be detected or reported, a Google co-authored study of Internet users across the United States, Australia, and the United Kingdom found this July. That’s why the “most critical intervention point” remains at the source: the harmful AI tools used to make the fake sexual images, Google researchers concluded. Yet red-teaming in recent months suggests that as some of the leading AI image generators from Google and OpenAI become more capable, they may be getting worse at blocking explicit outputs. Read full article Comments

items.title: 38 Companies Join The Crunchbase Unicorn Board In Blockbuster September, Led By Semiconductor, Fintech And Space Tech Companies
items.summary: A total of 38 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in September, adding $71 billion in value to the board. Semiconductors, financial services and space technology led for new counts with the remainder hailing from a broad swath of industries including biotech, AI infrastructure, AI training, security and frontier labs. Twenty-one of last month’s new unicorns are U.S. headquartered. Six new unicorns joined the board from China and three from the U.K., while Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Israel, Italy, Finland, Germany and Bulgaria each added one new unicorn. Through September, 311 companies have joined the board so far this year, putting 2026 on track to be the second-highest year for new unicorn creation, following only the venture peak year of 2021, when counts topped 600. Several companies already on the board stand out for significant valuation increases via new raises last month. They include San Francisco-based Cognition , developer of AI for software engineering, which saw its value climb to $48 billion, up from $26 billion only four months earlier. Data center provider Crusoe was valued at $31 billion last month, up from $10 billion a year ago. And Paris-based frontier lab Mistral was valued at $24.4 billion in its more recent funding, up from $13.7 billion a year ago. New unicorns in September Here are September’s 38 new unicorn companies: Semiconductors Fab2 , an Austin-based semiconductor manufacturing startup, closed a $500 million Series A at a $3.7 billion valuation, led by Fundomo . The 3-year-old company builds compact chip factories and develops their manufacturing equipment internally, aiming to make semiconductor production more accessible. Celero Communications , an Irvine, California-based semiconductor company, raised a $275 million Series C, valuing it above $3 billion and bringing total funding to $415 million. Atreides Management , Valor Equity Partners and CapitalG led the round. The 2-year-old company develops digital signal processing chips for high-speed optical connectivity in AI infrastructure. Micronano Core , a Hangzhou-based AI chip developer, announced a $149 million Series C. Its IoT inference chips combine memory and computing to reduce power consumption and data movement. The 5-year-old company was valued at $1 billion. Evas Intelligence , a Beijing-based AI chip company, raised $298 million at a valuation of $2.2 billion. The 4-year-old company develops AI computing chips using the open RISC-V architecture. SiMa.ai , a San Jose, California-based developer of specialized AI chips and software, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, co-led by Fidelity and Amplify Partners , bringing total funding to $500 million. The proceeds for the 8-year-old company will support its software platform and next-generation hardware for robots, vehicles and drones. Financial services OG , a Texas-based prediction-market platform, announced a strategic partnership with Robinhood , which will take an equity stake following OG’s separation from Crypto.com . The less than 1-year-old company was valued at $5 billion. The investment amount was not disclosed; the partnership will route Robinhood event-contract trading through OG’s regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure. Saudi Arabia-based Barq , a digital payments company, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion valuation. Investors included Noon Investments , Sohar International and M20 Capital . The 3-year-old company has processed more than $117 billion in 2 years. Ridgeline , a Nevada-based financial software company, raised a $250 million Series E at a $1.43 billion valuation led by founder and chairman Dave Duffield . The 8-year-old company provides an AI-based investment management platform for asset and wealth managers. Félix , a Miami-based remittance platform for Latino immigrants operating through WhatsApp , secured $200 million in financing: an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz valued at $1.4 billion and $113 million in debt from General Catalyst ’s Customer Value Fund. The 5-year-old company plans to expand to lending and add to its Latin American reach . Space technology Munich-based space company The Exploration Co. raised a $450 million Series C, co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners , Atomico and EQT at a valuation of $2 billion. The financing for the 5-year-old company will advance its reusable Nyx spacecraft for an International Space Station mission and support development of its Storm rocket engine. Hubble Network , a Seattle-based satellite connectivity company, raised a $200 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Smith Point Capital , bringing total funding to approximately $300 million. The 5-year-old company enables standard Bluetooth devices to connect directly to satellites for tracking and sensor-data applications. Oxfordshire, U.K-based Open Cosmos , a satellite company, secured $346 million, co-led by ETF Partners and Lightrock , valued at $1 billion. The 11-year-old company manufactures satellites and provides infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation and intelligence services. Bulgaria-based EnduroSat , a satellite company, raised $205 million in a round co-led by Riot Ventures and Atreides Management , reaching a $1 billion valuation. The 11-year-old company has raised financing that will expand standardized spacecraft production, including new manufacturing capacity in the U.S. and Europe. Biotechnology and medical devices Alzheon , a Framingham, Massachusetts-based developer of treatments for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders, raised around $79 million. The 13-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. Investors were not disclosed. Shanghai-based Anew Labs , an AI drug discovery company, raised $290 million at a $1.5 billion valuation following its spinoff from ByteDance . HSG , IDG Capital , Hillhouse Capital and 5Y Capital co-led the round. Anew develops tools for biomolecular prediction and drug discovery; ByteDance retained a 56% stake. Precision Neuroscience , a New York-based brain-computer interface developer, closed a $250 million Series D, bringing total funding to $430 million and reaching a valuation of approximately $1 billion. Pershing Square and Ackman Oxman Institute led the round. The 5-year-old company is building a brain–computer interface that is minimally invasive and removable. Toronto-based Biossil , a biotechnology company, raised $153 million at a $1 billion valuation led by the OpenAI Startup Fund , with participation from Founders Fund and other investors. The 3-year-old company uses AI to identify abandoned drug candidates that could succeed under different treatment approaches. The financing will expand clinical development and support additional drug acquisitions. AI and internet infrastructure Gimlet Labs , a San Francisco-based AI cloud infrastructure company, raised a $300 million Series B at a $3 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz . The 3-year-old company distributes AI inference workloads across different types of chips to improve performance and efficiency. It announced in March that its customers include one of the leading frontier labs. Helsinki-based Verda , an AI cloud company, raised a $189 million Series B led by Emergence Capital . The financing valued the 6-year-old company above $1 billion with total funding over $450 million. The company manages physical data centers along with its cloud platform. London-based CDN77 , an internet infrastructure company supporting content delivery for large streaming, gaming and software companies, raised $570 million in its first external financing led by CVC Capital Partners . The 15-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. AI training Micro1 , a San Francisco-based AI training-data company, raised more than $100 million led by Dream Ventures at a $4 billion valuation, an eightfold increase from its valuation in September 2025. The 4-year-old company recruits and vets specialists who create training and evaluation data for AI developers. Forbes reported that participants included two frontier AI laboratories and two x.AI co-founders. AfterQuery , a San Francisco-based provider of expert-created AI training data, reached a $3.2 billion valuation in September, more than 10x its valuation five months earlier, according to Forbes . The funding amount and lead investor were not publicly disclosed. The 1-year-old company’s datasets capture professional reasoning in fields such as software engineering, law and finance. AfterQuery was part of the Winter 2025 Y Combinator batch. Robotics and autonomous driving Shanghai Zaofu Intelligent Technology , the Shanghai-based operator of Hello’s robotaxi business, raised about $100 million at a valuation close to $3 billion. Shanghai State-owned Capital Investment fund led the round. The financing to the 1-year-old company will support a 10,000-GPU computing cluster, AI model development and commercialization of Level 4 autonomous driving. Lyte AI , a Sunnyvale, California-based robotics perception company, raised a $165 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Maverick Silicon . Founded by former Apple and PrimeSense engineers, the 5-year-old company combines custom chips, sensors and spatial software to help robots perceive their surroundings. The financing will accelerate deployments across logistics, manufacturing and inspection applications. Health insurance Angle Health , a San Francisco-based health benefits company, announced a $200 million Series C at a $2.7 billion valuation. Vitruvian Partners led the financing. It also includes $400 million in secondary financing for existing investors. The 7-year-old company provides a benefits platform using AI to make healthcare more affordable for small and midsize employers. The company services 5,000 businesses. Thatch , a San Francisco-based health benefits platform, raised a $108 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included The General Partnership , Index Ventures , General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz . The 5-year-old company helps employers provide individualized health budgets for employees to select their own medical plans. It has 5,000 employers utilizing its service. Energy and EV infrastructure China-based NIO Power , a battery-swapping and charging company, agreed to a strategic transaction that gives Geely Auto a 30% stake. Geely will contribute its Yiyi battery-swapping operation and a $95 million investment. The 9-year-old company was valued around $2.4 billion. TAR , an Austin-based developer of off-grid power systems for AI data centers, raised a $120 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation, led by Spark Capital . The less than 1-year-old company builds modular systems for renewable energy and battery systems as data-center operators seek access to electricity. AI applications Brahma AI raised $150 million led by Multiples , at a valuation just over $2 billion. The 3-year-old company, headquartered in London with offices in Los Angeles and Mumbai, built an enterprise audiovisual content platform for media, advertising, sports and healthcare customers. The financing will support research, commercial expansion and a larger Silicon Valley presence. Sequen , a New York-based AI ranking and personalization company, raised a $90 million Series B at a $1.44 billion valuation, led by Prysm Capital . The 2-year-old company’s software helps enterprises respond to customer behavior in real time, improving the relevance of recommendations. Cybersecurity Rome-based Exein , a cybersecurity company protecting connected devices and autonomous machines, raised $270 million at a $1.7 billion valuation, led by Headline . The financing to the 8-year-old company will support U.S. and Asia-Pacific expansion and development of AI security models. Tel Aviv-based Guardio , a consumer cybersecurity company, raised $40 million at a $1.1 billion valuation, bringing total funding to $167 million. Wiz co-founder Assaf Rappaport joined existing investors including Ion Crossover Partners and Union Tech Ventures , among others. The 8-year-old company protects consumers against phishing, scams, malicious websites and AI-generated fraud. AI models Beijing-based Naive AI , a language-model startup, raised $120 million reaching a valuation of $1.4 billion. Investors include Tencent , IDG Capital , Matrix Partners China and HSG . The less than 1-year-old company raised $400 million across three rounds so far this year, before releasing its first public model. Arcee AI , a San Francisco-based developer of open-weight foundation models, announced a $150 million Series B led by Vista Equity Partners , Cambium Capital Partners and Emergence Capital , valuing the company above $1 billion. items.summary_html:
A total of 38 companies joined The Crunchbase Unicorn Board in September, adding $71 billion in value to the board. Semiconductors, financial services and space technology led for new counts with the remainder hailing from a broad swath of industries including biotech, AI infrastructure, AI training, security and frontier labs.

Twenty-one of last month’s new unicorns are U.S. headquartered. Six new unicorns joined the board from China and three from the U.K., while Canada, Saudi Arabia, Japan, Israel, Italy, Finland, Germany and Bulgaria each added one new unicorn.

Through September, 311 companies have joined the board so far this year, putting 2026 on track to be the second-highest year for new unicorn creation, following only the venture peak year of 2021, when counts topped 600.

Several companies already on the board stand out for significant valuation increases via new raises last month. They include San Francisco-based Cognition, developer of AI for software engineering, which saw its value climb to $48 billion, up from $26 billion only four months earlier. Data center provider Crusoe was valued at $31 billion last month, up from $10 billion a year ago. And Paris-based frontier lab Mistral was valued at $24.4 billion in its more recent funding, up from $13.7 billion a year ago.

New unicorns in September

Here are September’s 38 new unicorn companies:

Semiconductors
  • Fab2, an Austin-based semiconductor manufacturing startup, closed a $500 million Series A at a $3.7 billion valuation, led by Fundomo. The 3-year-old company builds compact chip factories and develops their manufacturing equipment internally, aiming to make semiconductor production more accessible.
  • Celero Communications, an Irvine, California-based semiconductor company, raised a $275 million Series C, valuing it above $3 billion and bringing total funding to $415 million. Atreides Management, Valor Equity Partners and CapitalG led the round. The 2-year-old company develops digital signal processing chips for high-speed optical connectivity in AI infrastructure.
  • Micronano Core, a Hangzhou-based AI chip developer, announced a $149 million Series C. Its IoT inference chips combine memory and computing to reduce power consumption and data movement. The 5-year-old company was valued at $1 billion. 
  • Evas Intelligence, a Beijing-based AI chip company, raised $298 million at a valuation of $2.2 billion. The 4-year-old company develops AI computing chips using the open RISC-V architecture. 
  • SiMa.ai, a San Jose, California-based developer of specialized AI chips and software, raised a $150 million Series C at a $1.45 billion valuation, co-led by Fidelity and Amplify Partners, bringing total funding to $500 million. The proceeds for the 8-year-old company will support its software platform and next-generation hardware for robots, vehicles and drones. 
Financial services
  • OG, a Texas-based prediction-market platform, announced a strategic partnership with Robinhood, which will take an equity stake following OG’s separation from Crypto.com. The less than 1-year-old company was valued at $5 billion. The investment amount was not disclosed; the partnership will route Robinhood event-contract trading through OG’s regulated exchange and clearing infrastructure. 
  • Saudi Arabia-based Barq, a digital payments company, raised a $329.5 million Series A at a $1.85 billion valuation. Investors included Noon Investments, Sohar International and M20 Capital. The 3-year-old company has processed more than $117 billion in 2 years.
  • Ridgeline, a Nevada-based financial software company, raised a $250 million Series E at a $1.43 billion valuation led by founder and chairman Dave Duffield. The 8-year-old company provides an AI-based investment management platform for asset and wealth managers. 
  • Félix, a Miami-based remittance platform for Latino immigrants operating through WhatsApp, secured $200 million in financing: an $87 million Series C equity round led by Andreessen Horowitz valued at $1.4 billion and $113 million in debt from General Catalyst’s Customer Value Fund. The 5-year-old company plans to expand to lending and add to its Latin American reach.
Space technology
  • Munich-based space company The Exploration Co. raised a $450 million Series C, co-led by Bessemer Venture Partners, Atomico and EQT at a valuation of $2 billion. The financing for the 5-year-old company will advance its reusable Nyx spacecraft for an International Space Station mission and support development of its Storm rocket engine. 
  • Hubble Network, a Seattle-based satellite connectivity company, raised a $200 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Smith Point Capital, bringing total funding to approximately $300 million. The 5-year-old company enables standard Bluetooth devices to connect directly to satellites for tracking and sensor-data applications.
  • Oxfordshire, U.K-based Open Cosmos, a satellite company, secured $346 million, co-led by ETF Partners and Lightrock, valued at $1 billion. The 11-year-old company manufactures satellites and provides infrastructure, connectivity, Earth observation and intelligence services.
  • Bulgaria-based EnduroSat, a satellite company, raised $205 million in a round co-led by Riot Ventures and Atreides Management, reaching a $1 billion valuation. The 11-year-old company has raised financing that will expand standardized spacecraft production, including new manufacturing capacity in the U.S. and Europe. 
Biotechnology and medical devices
  • Alzheon, a Framingham, Massachusetts-based developer of treatments for Alzheimer’s disease and other neurodegenerative disorders, raised around $79 million. The   13-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion. Investors were not disclosed.
  • Shanghai-based Anew Labs, an AI drug discovery company, raised $290 million at a $1.5 billion valuation following its spinoff from ByteDance. HSG, IDG Capital, Hillhouse Capital and 5Y Capital co-led the round. Anew develops tools for biomolecular prediction and drug discovery; ByteDance retained a 56% stake. 
  • Precision Neuroscience, a New York-based brain-computer interface developer, closed a $250 million Series D, bringing total funding to $430 million and reaching a valuation of approximately $1 billion. Pershing Square and Ackman Oxman Institute led the round. The 5-year-old company is building a brain–computer interface that is minimally invasive and removable. 
  • Toronto-based Biossil, a biotechnology company, raised $153 million at a $1 billion valuation led by the OpenAI Startup Fund, with participation from Founders Fund and other investors. The 3-year-old company uses AI to identify abandoned drug candidates that could succeed under different treatment approaches. The financing will expand clinical development and support additional drug acquisitions.

  • Gimlet Labs, a San Francisco-based AI cloud infrastructure company, raised a $300 million Series B at a $3 billion valuation, led by Andreessen Horowitz. The 3-year-old company distributes AI inference workloads across different types of chips to improve performance and efficiency. It announced in March that its customers include one of the leading frontier labs.
  • Helsinki-based Verda, an AI cloud company, raised a $189 million Series B led by Emergence Capital. The financing valued the 6-year-old company above $1 billion with total funding over $450 million. The company manages physical data centers along with its cloud platform. 
  • London-based CDN77, an internet infrastructure company supporting content delivery for large streaming, gaming and software companies, raised $570 million in its first external financing led by CVC Capital Partners. The 15-year-old company was valued at $1.9 billion.
AI training
  • Micro1, a San Francisco-based AI training-data company, raised more than $100 million led by Dream Ventures at a $4 billion valuation, an eightfold increase from its valuation in September 2025. The 4-year-old company recruits and vets specialists who create training and evaluation data for AI developers. Forbes reported that participants included two frontier AI laboratories and two x.AI co-founders.
  • AfterQuery, a San Francisco-based provider of expert-created AI training data, reached a $3.2 billion valuation in September, more than 10x its valuation five months earlier, according to Forbes. The funding amount and lead investor were not publicly disclosed. The 1-year-old company’s datasets capture professional reasoning in fields such as software engineering, law and finance. AfterQuery was part of the Winter 2025 Y Combinator batch.
Robotics and autonomous driving
  • Shanghai Zaofu Intelligent Technology, the Shanghai-based operator of Hello’s robotaxi business, raised about $100 million at a valuation close to $3 billion. Shanghai State-owned Capital Investment fund led the round. The financing to the 1-year-old company will support a 10,000-GPU computing cluster, AI model development and commercialization of Level 4 autonomous driving.
  • Lyte AI, a Sunnyvale, California-based robotics perception company, raised a $165 million Series C at a $1.6 billion valuation, led by Maverick Silicon. Founded by former Apple and PrimeSense engineers, the 5-year-old company combines custom chips, sensors and spatial software to help robots perceive their surroundings. The financing will accelerate deployments across logistics, manufacturing and inspection applications.

  • Angle Health, a San Francisco-based health benefits company, announced a $200 million Series C at a $2.7 billion valuation. Vitruvian Partners led the financing. It also includes $400 million in secondary financing for existing investors. The 7-year-old company provides a benefits platform using AI to make healthcare more affordable for small and midsize employers. The company services 5,000 businesses.
  • Thatch, a San Francisco-based health benefits platform, raised a $108 million Series C at a $1 billion valuation. Investors included The General Partnership, Index Ventures, General Catalyst and Andreessen Horowitz. The 5-year-old company helps employers provide individualized health budgets for employees to select their own medical plans. It has 5,000 employers utilizing its service.

  • China-based NIO Power, a battery-swapping and charging company, agreed to a strategic transaction that gives Geely Auto a 30% stake. Geely will contribute its Yiyi battery-swapping operation and a $95 million investment. The 9-year-old company was valued around $2.4 billion. 
  • TAR, an Austin-based developer of off-grid power systems for AI data centers, raised a $120 million Series A at a $1 billion valuation, led by Spark Capital. The less than 1-year-old company builds modular systems for renewable energy and battery systems as data-center operators seek access to electricity.

items.title: How top brands are hunting for the next breakout influencer
items.summary: Marketers at CMO Insider's "The AI Marketer: Creator and Influencer Edition" roundtable held during Advertising Week New York shared their strategies for discovering the next breakout influencer talent. Derek French A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider newsletter. Sign up for Business Insider's weekly marketing newsletter . Marketers are getting smarter about finding their next influencer partners . At a CMO Insider roundtable during Advertising Week New York, top marketers told us how they're using AI-powered platforms , social listening tools, and some surprisingly old-fashioned tactics to discover new creators and niche communities. Meredith Diehn, SVP of marketing at Goodwipes, said her company recently adopted the influencer discovery tool Modash, which has significantly reduced manual work in identifying potential partners, freeing up the team to review creators' previous content and determine whether they're a good fit. Goodwipes' searches using Modash are remarkably granular, Diehn said. "I'm going to find a creator who is a girl with IBS who lives in Nashville," she said. Diehn's team is also using a social listening tool called Nectar to uncover microcommunities already talking about the brand that might not have been obvious targets. Diehn said Goodwipes is exploring opportunities to reach communities like postpartum mothers, whose needs can make flushable wipes particularly useful. Alicia Latoya Richardson, head of community and partnerships at the creator membership community FiveTwoNine, said brands are finding success using a tool called Companion, from its parent company Billion Dollar Boy Group, to search for creators across different geographies and demographics and assess their potential value. For its client Adobe, for example, FiveTwoNine has used Companion to analyze posts created by attendees at its events and estimate the resulting earned media value . (EMV is a measure of what the same reach or engagement would have cost if bought through paid ads.) "AI has definitely elevated the way we report to clients on value," Richardson said. Mars Pet Nutrition is also using AI-powered creator-discovery tools to help it cast a wider net when searching for creators and narrow the pool to candidates most likely to deliver reach and engagement. But there are still some areas where the tech falls short, said Paolo Narag, creative excellence lead at Mars Pet Nutrition. Earlier this year, while he was working on its Sheba brand, Narag's team launched a campaign called "Ignored to Adored." The campaign played on the insight that cat owners often feel ignored by their pets, despite loving them, and leaned heavily on content creators who shot candid videos of being snubbed by their feline companions. The creator who "popped" was the American figure skater Ilia Malinin , who already had two cats and was about to adopt a third. While AI filtering helped Mars find the right influencer, the team had to dig deeper to uncover the actual storyline that ultimately worked. "We still have the human discernment to say, 'OK, let's work with their management teams,'" said Narag. "Let's talk to their creators. What are the stories that they have that we can then jump on and amplify?" Sometimes it pays to just ask Another way to discover promising creators is simply to ask different communities which influencers they trust, rather than relying solely on algorithms, said FiveTwoNine's Richardson. FiveTwoNine hosts creator events on subjects such as AI, Pinterest, and fashion. "We will ask that community that is engaged: Who are you listening to? Who are you following? Who are you paying attention to?" Richardson said. Alicia Latoya Richardson of FiveTwoNine advised marketers to poll communities they're trying to reach on the creators they are paying attention to. Derek French Authenticity is a major consideration when selecting a creator partner. A Morning Consult survey of about 2,000 US adults in September, conducted exclusively for CMO Insider, found consumers ranked creators expressing genuine opinions (33%) and demonstrating they actually use a product themselves (30%) as the top factors that make sponsored content feel authentic. Kate Ridley, chief brand officer of Stanley 1913 , said she prioritizes working with creators who genuinely appreciate its products. She added that the brand hasn't necessarily codified a tried-and-true way to identify new talent because the relevant microcommunities can change so quickly. Ridley said her approach is one of "constant listening," followed by being ready to make "quick and agile decisions" about how to tap in. "We don't have a formula, and if I'm being really candid, frequently feel lost in it," Ridley said. Read the original article on Business Insider

Marketers at CMO Insider's "The AI Marketer: Creator and Influencer Edition" roundtable held during Advertising Week New York shared their strategies for discovering the next breakout influencer talent.

Derek French

  • A version of this post appears in the CMO Insider newsletter.
  • Sign up for Business Insider's weekly marketing newsletter.

Marketers are getting smarter about finding their next influencer partners.

At a CMO Insider roundtable during Advertising Week New York, top marketers told us how they're using AI-powered platforms, social listening tools, and some surprisingly old-fashioned tactics to discover new creators and niche communities.

Meredith Diehn, SVP of marketing at Goodwipes, said her company recently adopted the influencer discovery tool Modash, which has significantly reduced manual work in identifying potential partners, freeing up the team to review creators' previous content and determine whether they're a good fit.

Goodwipes' searches using Modash are remarkably granular, Diehn said.

"I'm going to find a creator who is a girl with IBS who lives in Nashville," she said.

Diehn's team is also using a social listening tool called Nectar to uncover microcommunities already talking about the brand that might not have been obvious targets. Diehn said Goodwipes is exploring opportunities to reach communities like postpartum mothers, whose needs can make flushable wipes particularly useful.

Alicia Latoya Richardson, head of community and partnerships at the creator membership community FiveTwoNine, said brands are finding success using a tool called Companion, from its parent company Billion Dollar Boy Group, to search for creators across different geographies and demographics and assess their potential value.

For its client Adobe, for example, FiveTwoNine has used Companion to analyze posts created by attendees at its events and estimate the resulting earned media value. (EMV is a measure of what the same reach or engagement would have cost if bought through paid ads.)

"AI has definitely elevated the way we report to clients on value," Richardson said.

Mars Pet Nutrition is also using AI-powered creator-discovery tools to help it cast a wider net when searching for creators and narrow the pool to candidates most likely to deliver reach and engagement. But there are still some areas where the tech falls short, said Paolo Narag, creative excellence lead at Mars Pet Nutrition.

Earlier this year, while he was working on its Sheba brand, Narag's team launched a campaign called "Ignored to Adored." The campaign played on the insight that cat owners often feel ignored by their pets, despite loving them, and leaned heavily on content creators who shot candid videos of being snubbed by their feline companions.

The creator who "popped" was the American figure skater Ilia Malinin, who already had two cats and was about to adopt a third. While AI filtering helped Mars find the right influencer, the team had to dig deeper to uncover the actual storyline that ultimately worked.

"We still have the human discernment to say, 'OK, let's work with their management teams,'" said Narag. "Let's talk to their creators. What are the stories that they have that we can then jump on and amplify?"

Sometimes it pays to just ask

Another way to discover promising creators is simply to ask different communities which influencers they trust, rather than relying solely on algorithms, said FiveTwoNine's Richardson. FiveTwoNine hosts creator events on subjects such as AI, Pinterest, and fashion.

"We will ask that community that is engaged: Who are you listening to? Who are you following? Who are you paying attention to?" Richardson said.

Alicia Latoya Richardson of FiveTwoNine advised marketers to poll communities they're trying to reach on the creators they are paying attention to.

Derek French

Authenticity is a major consideration when selecting a creator partner. A Morning Consult survey of about 2,000 US adults in September, conducted exclusively for CMO Insider, found consumers ranked creators expressing genuine opinions (33%) and demonstrating they actually use a product themselves (30%) as the top factors that make sponsored content feel authentic.

Kate Ridley, chief brand officer of Stanley 1913, said she prioritizes working with creators who genuinely appreciate its products. She added that the brand hasn't necessarily codified a tried-and-true way to identify new talent because the relevant microcommunities can change so quickly.

Ridley said her approach is one of "constant listening," followed by being ready to make "quick and agile decisions" about how to tap in.

"We don't have a formula, and if I'm being really candid, frequently feel lost in it," Ridley said.

items.title: Microsoft knows it robbed publishers to train AI. It just doesn’t care
items.summary: Ever since OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot and its offspring Microsoft Copilot were launched, critics have pointed out that both products — and all other generative AI tools — have been built using billions of dollars of stolen intellectual property. Training AI models requires vast amounts of written material, especially books, newspapers, and magazine articles. OpenAI, Microsoft, and other Big AI firms have been stealing every piece of intellectual property (IP) they can find for training. With few exceptions, instead of paying the people and publishers who labored to create that intellectual property, Big AI steals it and call it “fair use.” But just-released evidence shows that from the start, many employees and executives at Microsoft and OpenAI warned their companies that they were committing theft — and added that doing so could put newspapers and magazines out of business. The companies ignored them and went full speed ahead. All that and more came out last month in newly unsealed court documents filed in a lawsuit by The New York Times and others against Microsoft and OpenAI for IP theft. The filing cites memos, reports, and statements by Microsoft employees and execs that show the company was well aware of the illegality of what they were doing — and the consequences. Here’s just one example. Back in 2023, at the dawn of genAI, an internal Microsoft memo warned : “Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models ‘hoovering up’ all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions.” There’s more and worse than that in the filing. Before we get to the specifics, let’s look at the details of the suit. A look at the Times suit In December 2023, The New York Times sued Microsoft and OpenAI for copyright infringement and dilution of its trademark after OpenAI used millions of Times articles to train ChatGPT without the newspaper’s permission. Microsoft was included in the suit because of its ownership stake in OpenAI and because ChatGPT is the foundation for Copilot. (ChatGPT was released to the public about a year earlier, in November 2022.) Among other complaints, the suit claims the chatbots use the paper’s reporting to allow people to read the newspaper without having to subscribe to it. It says that the paper has lost subscribers and ad revenue because of it. The suit adds that both ChatGPT and Copilot have created word-for-word copies of Times articles in response to people’s queries, and that the chatbots have created falsehoods (a.k.a. hallucinations) that they attribute to the Times . The suit also says its articles are one of the largest sources of training data for the chatbots, allowing the AI firms to train them more cheaply, and that Microsoft and OpenAI reap the profits while the Times loses revenue. There’s no specific monetary value the suit asks for, although the paper has said the value of its IP is in the billions of dollars. The Times also asks in the suit that Microsoft and OpenAI destroy the datasets that include its content. Since the suit was filed, the New York Daily News , the Center for Investigative Reporting, and seven other newspapers have joined it.
