items.summary_html:
Ever since OpenAI’s ChatGPT chatbot and its offspring Microsoft Copilot were launched, critics have pointed out that both products — and all other generative AI tools — have been built using billions of dollars of stolen intellectual property.

Training AI models requires vast amounts of written material, especially books, newspapers, and magazine articles. OpenAI, Microsoft, and other Big AI firms have been stealing every piece of intellectual property (IP) they can find for training. With few exceptions, instead of paying the people and publishers who labored to create that intellectual property, Big AI steals it and call it “fair use.”

But just-released evidence shows that from the start, many employees and executives at Microsoft and OpenAI warned their companies that they were committing theft — and added that doing so could put newspapers and magazines out of business.

The companies ignored them and went full speed ahead.

All that and more came out last month in newly unsealed court documents filed in a lawsuit by The New York Times and others against Microsoft and OpenAI for IP theft. The filing cites memos, reports, and statements by Microsoft employees and execs that show the company was well aware of the illegality of what they were doing — and the consequences.

Here’s just one example. Back in 2023, at the dawn of genAI, an internal Microsoft memo warned: “Millions of people around the world will soon consider large models ‘hoovering up’ all their work to be an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions.”

There’s more and worse than that in the filing. Before we get to the specifics, let’s look at the details of the suit.

A look at the Times suit

In December 2023, The New York Times sued Microsoft and OpenAI for copyright infringement and dilution of its trademark after OpenAI used millions of Times articles to train ChatGPT without the newspaper’s permission. Microsoft was included in the suit because of its ownership stake in OpenAI and because ChatGPT is the foundation for Copilot. (ChatGPT was released to the public about a year earlier, in November 2022.)

Among other complaints, the suit claims the chatbots use the paper’s reporting to allow people to read the newspaper without having to subscribe to it. It says that the paper has lost subscribers and ad revenue because of it.

 The suit adds that both ChatGPT and Copilot have created word-for-word copies of Times articles in response to people’s queries, and that the chatbots have created falsehoods (a.k.a. hallucinations) that they attribute to the Times. The suit also says its articles are one of the largest sources of training data for the chatbots, allowing the AI firms to train them more cheaply, and that Microsoft and OpenAI reap the profits while the Times loses revenue.

There’s no specific monetary value the suit asks for, although the paper has said the value of its IP is in the billions of dollars. The Times also asks in the suit that Microsoft and OpenAI destroy the datasets that include its content.

Since the suit was filed, the New York Daily News, the Center for Investigative Reporting, and seven other newspapers have joined it.

Microsoft and OpenAI execs admit theft

Employees of Microsoft and OpenAI, including high-level executives, have long agreed with the suit’s charges, even warning about the consequences of data theft before the suit was filed.

Most prominent among them is Brent Hecht, Microsoft’s director of applied science. The recent filing cites an internal memo he wrote in January 2023 calling the use of New York Times articles without the paper’s consent “an astonishing theft of unprecedented proportions” and “the largest theft of labor in human history.”

Note the date he wrote that memo: nearly a year before the Times filed its suit in December of 2023. That meant he had been warning Microsoft for at least a year before the suit that Microsoft and OpenAI were violating copyright laws and stealing IP.

Hecht had more to say. In a memo written after the suit was filed, he warned that because OpenAI and Copilot used information taken from the Times and other newspapers to answer users’ questions, people would no longer need to go to the newspapers’ web sites or subscribe to the print versions. He wrote that this “necessarily threatens the economic stability of those who create the content.”

He wasn’t alone. In June 2023, six months before the Times suite, Nick Turley, the OpenAI exec who headed the team developing ChatGPT, said that AI represented an “existential threat” to publishers.

Years before that, in 2020 before ChatGPT was even released, OpenAI’s policy director Jack Clark wrote a memo to OpenAI President Greg Brockman and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman warning that OpenAI’s work “is going to increasingly lead to us creating systems that substitute for the labor of the people that define the ‘culture’ of society.” He added, “OpenAI will become the symbol of how Silicon Valley is thoughtlessly stepping into other parts of life and leaving a mess on the carpet.”

The warnings from inside Microsoft and OpenAI went on and on. They were ignored for years and continue to be ignored. And while the companies were warned that what they were doing was illegal, some execs reveled in it. When an OpenAI engineer told Brockman he was working on “a hack to get around nytimes paywall” so OpenAI could get faster access to for-pay copyrighted content, Brockman replied, “ah, nice.”

Microsoft looks the other way

Microsoft is no better. When a Times reporter asked Microsoft spokesperson Alex Haurek about Hecht’s warnings, Haurek dismissed Hecht as not being a decision maker, adding that he was hired merely “to present divergent and asymmetric perspectives.” Which were then to be ignored, of course.  

As for Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella, he backs Microsoft and OpenAI to the hilt and tries to evade responsibility for both companies’ actions. In a deposition, he said that if he “had been made aware that OpenAI had scraped and trained on information that was behind a paywall,” he would have required OpenAI to retrain its models, which he says Microsoft has a right to do.

Yet for years now, he’s been aware of what OpenAI has done and how Copilot has benefited from it. Has he asked OpenAI to retrain its models on non-paywalled content?

Of course not.

Microsoft and OpenAI are flat-out wrong. The Times and the others who joined in the suit are right that their IP has been stolen. We can only hope that eventually, the courts will recognize it and finally put an end to the multi-trillion-dollar theft they’ve committed and continue to commit every day in plain sight.

items.title: Starling trains model on sovereign UK cloud, as CIO warns over concentration risk
items.summary: Starling says it will be the first UK bank to train an AI model on UK sovereign cloud. The bank, which has five million customers including 500,000 SMEs, is training a Transactional Foundation Model (TFM) on hardware running in Civo’s cloud. The TFM (a model that learns from raw financial transaction histories and payment events to create an intelligence layer for banks and fintechs) is being trained on proprietary Starling data, spanning some 15 billion anonymised transactions, it said. Starling CIO: I want to reduce concentration risk Starling’s Group CIO Harriet Rees told The Stack : “I want options that reduce concentration risk on a handful of US-providers; whether that’s more global players outside of the US that run UK operations, or players that are truly sovereign…”

items.title: Forward Deployed Engineer Job Postings in India Grew Nearly 19x in a Year: Report
items.summary: Forward Deployed Engineer (FDE) job postings in India grew nearly 19x between June 2025 and June 2026, according to the latest Indeed data. Postings rose 1,807% year-on-year in June, before moderating to nearly 16x the year-earlier level in July and more than 6x in August. The growth reflects a shift towards engineers who work directly with customers to solve business problems and deploy AI in real-world environments. Glassdoor India’s Community discussions show that professionals are still seeking clarity on FDE responsibilities, interview processes, required skills, and career prospects. “FDE may be a new title for many people, but the need behind it is easy to understand: companies want engineers who can sit with a customer, unpack a real problem and make the technology work in practice,” Sashi Kumar, Managing Director, Indeed India, said in a statement. Glassdoor India listings mention skills such as Python, Java, data engineering, machine learning , generative AI, retrieval-augmented generation, AI agents, cloud technologies, APIs, and full-stack development. Employers also seek customer communication, stakeholder management, and problem-solving skills. FDE positions appear across technology companies, consulting firms, startups, and specialist AI businesses. The roles span enterprise AI, workflow automation , customer service, infrastructure, and healthcare, with listings in Bengaluru, Hyderabad, Chennai, Delhi, Mumbai, and remote locations. Glassdoor reported an average annual base pay of approximately ₹12 lakh for FDEs in India, with a range of ₹9–16 lakh based on 28 submissions, as stated in its January 2026 update. Individual submissions show total pay of ₹22–26 lakh for FDEs with one to three years of experience in Hyderabad and ₹23–27 lakh in Bengaluru. Indeed said its FDE sample is too small to support a reliable median salary. Demand for AI-related talent is also extending to infrastructure . Indeed Hiring Lab data shows that data centre job postings have nearly doubled over two years and account for 1.3% of all Indian job postings. Software roles make up 28% of data centre postings, while demand also covers industrial engineering, project management and facility operations. Glassdoor estimated annual pay for data centre engineers and technicians at approximately ₹8–12 lakh, with senior roles reaching ₹16–19 lakh or more in Mumbai and Bengaluru.

items.title: JPMorgan: Quantifying AI benefits is "wasting time"
items.summary: JPMorgan Chase, America’s largest bank, is spending $700 million per year on AI technology, but its CFO says quantifying AI’s benefits is wasting time, and CEO Jamie Dimon is cracking down on external agents. During a Q3 earnings call on Tuesday marking a $50.2 billion revenue quarter , CFO Jeremy Barnum said he is seeking to “move away” from quantifying AI returns, despite Dimon claiming that AI investment had already “ paid for itself ” in October 2025. He said: “I am just very reluctant to spend a lot of energy quantifying it because it winds up wasting a lot of people's time inside the institution when we actually need to get them to focus on doing things… as much as important and dramatic and exciting as this theme is, it takes a long time to really do things that are visible at an institution of our size.” Barnum also said that the $2 billion annual AI investment figure previously provided by Dimon was "not exactly right" and said the actual spend was around $700 million annually. items.title: The AI Underwriting Engine Behind Recur Club’s ₹500 Cr Festive D2C Capital Push
items.summary: The festive season puts upfront operational pressures on startups and small and medium enterprises (SMEs). Businesses need upfront capital to purchase larger volumes of goods, raw materials, or finished stock before peak demand hits. As per the Confederation of All India Traders, the total festive trade in 2025 was at ₹6.05 lakh crore—of which 85% moved through traditional retail. To bridge the financing gap, Recur Club, an AI-native debt marketplace for startups and SMEs, recently announced a ₹500 crore financing initiative for direct-to-consumer (D2C) brands, targeting their working capital and expansion needs during the festive season. The Delhi-based startup saw an increased demand for debt financing across online marketplaces, quick-commerce platforms, and physical retail. Data from more than 5,000 D2C companies on its platform shows that demand for growth capital typically rises by around 35% during the festive quarter. Quick-commerce businesses recorded the highest requirement for growth capital between July and September 2026, followed by retail and consumer goods, fast-moving consumer goods (FMCG), and consumer durables. With an average ticket size of approximately ₹3 crore, the company expects the financing initiative to support around 150–170 D2C brands, depending on their individual capital requirements. Co-founder Eklavya Gupta says the company plans to deploy the capital over the next 12–15 months. “We have been financing D2C brands for the past three to four years and intend to continue growing this business. There is a seasonal surge in demand, which made this a suitable time to launch the fund,” Gupta tells AIM. AI-Led Underwriting and Credit Risk Recur Club uses AI across document collection, due diligence, underwriting and lender matching. Its platform collects financial statements, legal documents, compliance records, goods and services tax (GST) data and bank statements, then reconciles the information to assess a borrower’s financial position. The company uses existing AI models and develops small language models trained on datasets for due diligence, underwriting, and credit analysis. “Preparing and evaluating balance sheets, profit-and-loss statements and cash flows could take an analyst two days; our model can do it in around two minutes,” Gupta claims. The platform covers f inancial, legal, and compliance checks as well as background and management assessments. The system can also identify discrepancies across financial records and test scenarios, such as how a debtor default could affect a borrower’s financial position. AI handles around 70–80% of the work, according to Gupta. Human involvement remains part of the process, including conversations with business owners, meetings, and assessments that require judgement. Recur Club tracks deal-to-disbursement turnaround time and non-performing asset levels to assess its underwriting process. Gupta notes the platform’s default rate had stabilised below 0.5%, attributing the performance partly to its AI credit analyst. Recur Club plans to continue refining its models using feedback from completed transactions and lenders’ underwriting policies to improve borrower-lender matching and reduce costs. Financing Inventory and Expansion The initiative will support inventory purchases, receivables management, new sales channels, and expansion into additional cities. Recur Club has identified inventory procurement and store or capacity expansion as two key financing requirements among the D2C brands it serves. Under its inventory financing arrangement, inventory is procured on behalf of a brand, which then sells the products through its existing channels and repays the financing in installments. Recur Club says this structure is designed to help businesses manage working capital without adding the associated inventory financing to their balance sheets, subject to the terms of the arrangement. For store and capacity expansion, the five-year-old startup facilitates financing for equipment and fit-outs for new retail outlets. Brands make monthly payments until the financing is repaid, spreading expansion costs over time rather than bearing the entire expenditure upfront. Gupta said transactions typically range from ₹5 crore to ₹25 crore per company, with interest rates of around 15–17%. The applicable rate depends on the financing product and commercial arrangement. Credit risk also varies by structure. “It depends on the product and the commercial arrangement. In some structures, we take on part of the risk; in others, we do not,” the founder notes. Inventory financing carries risks if brands misjudge demand. “One challenge is forecasting inventory and sales. If expected demand does not materialise, a company can be left with inventory that is difficult to liquidate,” he adds. Recur Club said it facilitated approximately ₹275 crore for more than 100 D2C brands in the current financial year, taking its cumulative capital facilitated for the sector to ₹1,200 crore. Broader Debt Financing Recur Club says that it has facilitated more than ₹3,000 crore in capital across over 2,000 companies, working with more than 100 lending partners. The platform connects businesses with banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), venture debt funds, and other institutional lenders. The company initially focused on recurring-revenue financing for startups. It has since expanded into a multi-product debt platform serving startups, SMEs, and mid-market companies. “We initially focused on recurring-revenue financing for startups. Over time, we have evolved into a multi-debt, multi-product platform that offers several options in one place and aims to meet a company’s debt-capital needs. Startup debt financing remains one of our products, but it is now one of around 10 products we offer,” Gupta said. Gupta said transaction fees typically range from 1–3%, depending on the transaction and product. The company earns fees from businesses and investors, including for services such as credit monitoring.

Recur Club says that it has facilitated more than ₹3,000 crore in capital across over 2,000 companies, working with more than 100 lending partners. The platform connects businesses with banks, non-banking financial companies (NBFCs), venture debt funds, and other institutional lenders. 

The company initially focused on recurring-revenue financing for startups. It has since expanded into a multi-product debt platform serving startups, SMEs, and mid-market companies.

“We initially focused on recurring-revenue financing for startups. Over time, we have evolved into a multi-debt, multi-product platform that offers several options in one place and aims to meet a company’s debt-capital needs. Startup debt financing remains one of our products, but it is now one of around 10 products we offer,” Gupta said.

Gupta said transaction fees typically range from 1–3%, depending on the transaction and product. The company earns fees from businesses and investors, including for services such as credit monitoring.

items.title: WFH helped create the AI revolution. RTO could pose its biggest problem.
items.summary: Maskot/Getty Images This post originally appeared in the Business Insider Today newsletter. You can sign up for Business Insider's daily newsletter here . A baby boom, cleaner air, and AI. The work-from-home revolution might be over, but its impact is still being felt. Many of us have settled into some type of hybrid setup, balancing our days in the office with at least one spent at home. But even if you're in the cubicles every day — God bless — the WFH revolution has still affected you. Nick Bloom, a Stanford economist who's a leading expert on remote work, spoke to BI's Aki Ito about six ways the WFH era fundamentally changed things for us all . Some are a bit … personal. Remote work led to a 5% increase in fertility in the US and Northern Europe, according to Bloom's estimates. He summed it up with a line from a friend: "My wife and I discovered she can't get pregnant by email." Other effects were more widespread, such as a reduction in nitrogen dioxide in major cities thanks to the new hybrid world. But the biggest residual from the WFH era is what's dominating our current workplace convos: artificial intelligence. Bloom makes a strong case for why WFH crawled so AI could walk. Digital communications surged when we abandoned our offices, creating a treasure trove of data for models to learn on. The casual water-cooler conversation became a documented Slack thread that could be fed into an LLM. Now that most of us are in the office at least part of the time, that raises questions about how companies will source more training data. Having picked the internet to pieces, AI companies are getting desperate for training data . They've gone so far as to create virtual workplaces . Granted, people still Slack each other in the office. (I've fired off messages to colleagues sitting a few feet away. Sometimes you've got to see if you can actually make them "lol" IRL.) There's still a level of communication that goes undocumented, though. The quick coffee chat to brainstorm an idea. The impromptu deskside conversation. That's why executives were pushing us back to the office in the first place. For the organic collaboration and innovation that can only occur when rubbing elbows with colleagues. That RTO push could now pose real problems for AI's development. Companies could bug their own offices, making sure they pick up every little conversation, however benign, between workers. But that comes with plenty of legal and regulatory issues. And at a time when workers are already on edge about losing their jobs to AI, actively recording their every word to improve models won't do much to ease concerns. Still, with billions of dollars invested and the fate of the stock market depending on the tech realizing some big ROI, AI companies will have to figure something out. At least we've got some WFH babies joining the workforce in a few decades as reinforcements. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Anthropic Ditches Git In Its Monorepo, Builds In-House Version Control System
items.summary: Anthropic has migrated its main code repository from Git to an in-house version control system called Scion, after daily code merges increased more than tenfold between May and September. A team of seven engineers built Scion, an internal code review tool called Antique and related systems, completing the migration in five months, the company said in an engineering blog post published on 13 October. Anthropic described its workloads as unusual because it uses Claude to write software far more extensively than most companies. The company merged around 2,500 code changes per day in May, rising to more than 30,000 in September. Its main repository has an almost 100 GB history, while a compressed working copy exceeds 25 GB. The company performs around 25 million code checkouts daily for continuous integration (CI), excluding developer environments, agent sandboxes and research jobs. Fetching the repository naively for these workloads would generate more than 600 petabytes of Git traffic per day, according to Anthropic. “We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon,” the company said, adding that removing one bottleneck leads to further increases in code production. Git was designed around decentralised development, with each clone containing a complete repository that developers can inspect and modify offline. Anthropic said these properties were less suitable for its environment, where most clients are AI agents and automated jobs that remain connected to servers. The company had operated several hundred internal Git mirrors and used techniques such as shallow clones and sparse checkouts to manage repository traffic. These measures became harder to maintain as code merges accelerated. Scion moves commits, merges, rebases and repository history queries to the server. Clients request only the data they need, while automated jobs can retrieve repository metadata through APIs without checking out files. Anthropic said its infrastructure footprint is 200 times smaller than its previous Git mirroring setup in CPU and memory requirements. CI and research jobs now check out code in seconds rather than minutes, while CI alone has reduced CPU requirements by 25%. Anthropic is also reconsidering conventional development practices. Traditional merge queues coordinate changes and run tests before integrating code. The company said this becomes difficult when hundreds or thousands of changes can be merged while tests are still running. Instead, it has invested in post-merge and pre-deployment automated testing, allowing concurrent changes to proceed even when conflicts arise. Claude can help resolve those conflicts, according to Anthropic. The company said engineers remain responsible for architectural decisions and enforcing system constraints, as AI-generated code can introduce unnecessary complexity or inefficient implementations. Anthropic said an early internal version of Claude Mythos Preview rewrote its initial Git-to-Scion ingestion pipeline, producing an implementation that used 20 times less memory and ran four times faster while preserving the original system’s constraints. The company also uses Claude agents called ‘superfans’ to monitor infrastructure components through telemetry and logs, supplementing conventional alerts. Anthropic does not intend Scion to replace Git generally. It said the system is designed for enormous repositories used by large engineering teams or substantial numbers of coding agents. Instead, it plans to share architectural lessons that Git platforms could adopt as AI-generated code increases pressure on source control, testing and deployment infrastructure.

items.title: Sarvam AI Launches Bulbul V4 Flash for Real-Time Speech in 11 Indian Languages
items.summary: Sarvam AI has launched Bulbul V4 Flash, a text-to-speech model that generates speech in 11 languages with a time-to-first-audio latency of under 250 milliseconds. The model is priced at ₹20 per 10,000 characters, a one-third reduction from the ₹30 charged for Bulbul V3. The Bengaluru-based AI company said the new model improves pronunciation, pacing and contextual delivery while reducing the time and cost required to generate speech for real-time applications, including customer service and voice agents. “With V4 Flash, our research focused on capturing the richness and nuances of Indian languages, while making high-quality speech generation faster and more affordable,” the company said in its announcement. Bulbul V4 Flash is available through the Sarvam API, Playground and Content Studio. It offers 83 voices and 224 voice-and-style combinations for applications across banking, ecommerce, education, sales, customer support and narration. The model is up to 40% faster than Bulbul V3 under comparable workloads, according to Sarvam. The company has also optimised its inference infrastructure to handle multiple simultaneous conversations. Existing Bulbul users can migrate to V4 Flash through the existing Bulbul API. Sarvam said it expanded its proprietary speech datasets nearly sevenfold compared with V3, increasing coverage across languages, regional accents, speakers, emotional registers and conversational styles. The company pretrained V4 from scratch with a focus on Indian language representation and used a language-balanced training process to improve pronunciation and preserve the characteristics of individual languages. “Regional voices sound native, Indian English sounds Indian, and names, numbers and everyday expressions come out the way people say them,” the company said. The model also uses a contextual text normalisation layer to determine how names, dates, amounts and abbreviations should be spoken. For instance, it distinguishes between abbreviations that are pronounced as words and those spoken letter by letter. This is particularly relevant for voice agents handling customer information, where mispronouncing a name, payment amount, or booking reference can cause confusion. Sarvam said Bulbul V4 Flash draws on research involving larger language backbones, different audio representations and generative approaches, with training data scaled to more than 400 billion audio tokens. The company used the results of these experiments to develop a smaller model that retains key speech-quality improvements while meeting production requirements for latency and cost. Its streaming-first inference system prioritises audio that needs to be generated next rather than processing speech far ahead of the conversation. Sarvam said it also reduced unnecessary synchronisation and data copying to improve performance when handling concurrent requests. Sarvam also previewed Bulbul V4 Pro, another model in the V4 family that is being developed to support more expressive speech. The preview demonstrated the ability to convey emotions such as happiness, sadness, fear and anger, alongside actions such as laughing, sighing, whispering and emphasising specific words. Sarvam has not announced a release date or pricing for V4 Pro. The preview signals the company's work towards voice models that can adjust not only pronunciation and pacing but also the emotional delivery of speech, particularly for conversational AI applications.

items.title: Tool and target: US law enforcement grapple with AI-enabled terrorism and anti-tech extremism
items.summary: From the FBI to local police departments, US authorities are increasingly warning of would-be terrorists using chatbots to plan attacks and anti-AI extremist threats In May 2025, a 25-year-old man detonated a car bomb outside a Palm Springs fertility clinic, killing himself and injuring four others. For many, it was a wake up call about the threats to reproductive care facilities. For the FBI, though, it was also a sign of what the agency had feared for years: bad actors were using generative AI to plan and execute terror plots. The suspect used an unnamed generative AI tool that failed to detect his request for bomb-making instructions, law enforcement officers wrote in a previously unreported document reviewed by the Guardian. The privacy of his conversation with the AI chatbot hindered alerting police that someone was looking up how to make a bomb, according to the memo. How extremists could use AI to devise attacks and recruit new members How AI could be used to disseminate and produce everything from deepfakes to election misinformation and child sexual abuse material (CSAM) How people seeking information on how to make weaponry or bombs could use AI to circumvent police detection How to ensure that officers could take advantage of AI tools in policing, for things like social media monitoring, while managing public concern over the use of these tools Monitoring social media for opposition to AI and potential extremist attacks on datacenters

items.title: You bailed on TV. But politicians are still spending all their money there.
items.summary: Elijah Nouvelage/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Sebastián Vivallo Oñate/Agencia Makro/Getty Images; Gary Miller/Getty Images; Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images; BI Audiences have been leaving TV for the internet for a very long time. Most advertisers have figured that out some time ago. But not political advertisers: They still spend the majority of their money on TV. Political consultant Rob Flaherty explains why. If you ask pundits, 2024 was the Podcast Election (which also means it was the YouTube Election ). And maybe 2026 is the Influencer Election . One thing the chattering class won't call it is the Television Election — because everyone knows everyone has stopped watching TV. Except that's not how political campaigns are run, at all. Even in 2026, more than 60% of the estimated $11.6 billion spent in this election cycle will go to good ol' fashioned broadcast and cable TV. Another 20% will be spent on streaming TV. If you think that doesn't leave a lot of room for things where you and most people you know spend a ton of time — YouTube, Reels, TikTok, etc. — you're right. Political pros know it, too. So why isn't that changing? I asked Rob Flaherty , who has spent most of his life doing digital politics for Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and, most recently, Kamala Harris . Flaherty offered up a bunch of reasons why TV remains so dominant in political spending, even as it gets less relevant to voters. But a base reason is simply that political operatives spent money on TV because other political operatives spend money there: Flaherty even admits that in his current work — co-running an anti-AI super PAC — he has been buying some TV time just so other people in politics will take him seriously. You can hear our entire conversation about how campaigns work in the TikTok era — and how they ought to work — on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt of our chat. Peter Kafka: You said that when you were working on the Harris campaign, you spent roughly 50-50 between TV and digital — but that most campaigns still spend 70% of their budget on TV. Make the best case for why a campaign should still spend half or more of its money on TV. Rob Flaherty: Well, I would not advocate for that. But I think the steelman case that you would hear is: Digital political ad inventory is actually quite limited. There are only so many places you can spend. Social media is not a mind-changing surface; it's a base-building surface. Meanwhile, television is concentrating on a smaller number of higher-view surfaces. So you actually want to spend more money on TV because it's more expensive to buy against an NFL game than it was just to buy across from the local news and in prime time. That sounds a lot like the TV industry's own argument for years: "Yes, ratings are down, but that means the shows people are still watching are more valuable." Look, this is an industry that has a nobody-ever-got-fired-for-hiring-McKinsey problem. If you do the same thing everyone else does and you lose, then you did everything right. And if you try something different and you lose, it's you who made bad decisions. I'll even say candidly: I run Tomorrow Together , a new super PAC where we just launched a bunch of ads. We're advertising against people who don't want AI regulations . And even I — Mr. F—ing Digital — felt this pull, like I needed to have pretty significant TV spending. Because otherwise the industry won't view it as legit, because TV is legit. We still spent mostly on digital, largely because it's a super PAC and we're spending late. But I prioritized making sure we had some TV in there, because otherwise people don't think it's real. And also, the way a lot of this works is: The general consultants who are the top consultants to the candidate, very often are economically tied to the margins of TV. Spell that out. You're running a campaign. Why do you have an economic incentive to buy TV? Because you get a cut of the buy. The more TV a campaign buys, the more money you make. Basically. Usually, the general consultant hires up all the other consultants. Those consultants get a cut, either a fee or a cut of media spend. TV margins are great. They are really, really great. They are better than digital margins. For the consultant, you're making 10%, 15% on a TV buy. And by "margins," you mean the money the person buying the ads gets from the campaign? Yeah. You make more money because there's just less staff time. The other thing that's crazy is a lot of the big TV firms don't actually do the buying. They subcontract to one of three or four buying shops. So everybody's just making money all over the place. There's a rent-seeking thing: The most senior consultants who have been around for a while came up in TV. They talk to the candidates. They push them to spend more on TV.   • Audiences have been leaving TV for the internet for a very long time.
  • Most advertisers have figured that out some time ago.
  • But not political advertisers: They still spend the majority of their money on TV. Political consultant Rob Flaherty explains why.

If you ask pundits, 2024 was the Podcast Election (which also means it was the YouTube Election). And maybe 2026 is the Influencer Election.

One thing the chattering class won't call it is the Television Election — because everyone knows everyone has stopped watching TV.

Except that's not how political campaigns are run, at all.

Even in 2026, more than 60% of the estimated $11.6 billion spent in this election cycle will go to good ol' fashioned broadcast and cable TV. Another 20% will be spent on streaming TV.

If you think that doesn't leave a lot of room for things where you and most people you know spend a ton of time — YouTube, Reels, TikTok, etc. — you're right. Political pros know it, too.

So why isn't that changing? I asked Rob Flaherty, who has spent most of his life doing digital politics for Democrats, including Hillary Clinton, Joe Biden, and, most recently, Kamala Harris.

Flaherty offered up a bunch of reasons why TV remains so dominant in political spending, even as it gets less relevant to voters.

But a base reason is simply that political operatives spent money on TV because other political operatives spend money there: Flaherty even admits that in his current work — co-running an anti-AI super PAC — he has been buying some TV time just so other people in politics will take him seriously.

You can hear our entire conversation about how campaigns work in the TikTok era — and how they ought to work — on my Channels podcast. The following is an edited excerpt of our chat.

Peter Kafka: You said that when you were working on the Harris campaign, you spent roughly 50-50 between TV and digital — but that most campaigns still spend 70% of their budget on TV. Make the best case for why a campaign should still spend half or more of its money on TV.

Rob Flaherty: Well, I would not advocate for that. But I think the steelman case that you would hear is: Digital political ad inventory is actually quite limited. There are only so many places you can spend. Social media is not a mind-changing surface; it's a base-building surface.

Meanwhile, television is concentrating on a smaller number of higher-view surfaces. So you actually want to spend more money on TV because it's more expensive to buy against an NFL game than it was just to buy across from the local news and in prime time.

That sounds a lot like the TV industry's own argument for years: "Yes, ratings are down, but that means the shows people are still watching are more valuable."

Look, this is an industry that has a nobody-ever-got-fired-for-hiring-McKinsey problem. If you do the same thing everyone else does and you lose, then you did everything right. And if you try something different and you lose, it's you who made bad decisions.

I'll even say candidly: I run Tomorrow Together, a new super PAC where we just launched a bunch of ads. We're advertising against people who don't want AI regulations. And even I — Mr. F—ing Digital — felt this pull, like I needed to have pretty significant TV spending. Because otherwise the industry won't view it as legit, because TV is legit.

We still spent mostly on digital, largely because it's a super PAC and we're spending late. But I prioritized making sure we had some TV in there, because otherwise people don't think it's real.

And also, the way a lot of this works is: The general consultants who are the top consultants to the candidate, very often are economically tied to the margins of TV.

Spell that out. You're running a campaign. Why do you have an economic incentive to buy TV?

Because you get a cut of the buy.

The more TV a campaign buys, the more money you make.

Basically.

Usually, the general consultant hires up all the other consultants. Those consultants get a cut, either a fee or a cut of media spend.

TV margins are great. They are really, really great. They are better than digital margins. For the consultant, you're making 10%, 15% on a TV buy.

And by "margins," you mean the money the person buying the ads gets from the campaign?

Yeah. You make more money because there's just less staff time.

The other thing that's crazy is a lot of the big TV firms don't actually do the buying. They subcontract to one of three or four buying shops. So everybody's just making money all over the place.

There's a rent-seeking thing: The most senior consultants who have been around for a while came up in TV. They talk to the candidates. They push them to spend more on TV. And then you have campaign managers who are typically relatively more junior, particularly on Senate races, who don't want to mess up.

They don't want to do something different and radical, and they have to convince the candidate and the general consultant anyway. So you end up in this place where the easiest thing to do is just sort of the same thing.

The broader media business had the same problem: Advertisers took a long time to follow consumers to digital. They were still spending on TV when people were leaving in droves. Does politics eventually catch up?

If you talk to any politician, they would tell you digital is very important. It's the internet. And then you look at their media mix, and it's not that.

I do think presidential primaries are what drive innovation in politics. I do think you're going to see some people try a bunch of new stuff, and then that will lead to a more cogent theory of how you spend more of your campaign dollars on the places where people actually are.

I'm hopeful that change is coming. But so much of the way that media gets spent is profit-seeking and rent-seeking that you do have to break through that. It has the entrenched layer of political power on top of it, and that is one of the reasons.

items.title: I'm a CEO and a mom. I built AI agents to help run my household — and save hours every week.
items.summary: CEO Carrol Chang built AI agents to help run her family life and said they save her hours every week. Courtesy of Andela Carrol Chang, CEO of Andela, uses AI to manage her family's hectic schedules in New York City. An AI agent creates her kids' sports calendars and accounts for commuting times. Chang used to spend about five to eight hours a week on parenting admin. Now it's about two. Carrol Chang is the CEO of Andela, which helps companies implement AI by connecting them with technical talent. The wife and mother of three, who lives in New York City, built AI agents using several models to help coordinate her family's schedules and manage school emails. The following has been edited for brevity and clarity. That first year of my second child's life was joyous in so many ways, but it was also the hardest of my life. It almost broke me, and I have a wonderful husband. I was privileged to be in a stable, senior job at a supportive workplace, and it didn't matter because the weight of the calendar management , the sick pickups, being the person that the school or the day care would call, trying to organize holiday gifts for the family, and booking family travel was crushing to me. A lot of this mental load has been lifted , so I'm grateful. I now have three kids and agents for their sports and school, and for meal planning. With their sports, the games are always on different days and in different boroughs. In the past, I would have had to look them up on Google Maps and map out the commute. Is it subway? Is it bus? Is it walking? Is it taking an Uber ? I'd put that commute time on the calendar with enough of a buffer to get there before the game. Then I'd do the same thing on the way home. If there's a conflict with the kids' schedules, you have to reconcile which parent is going to go to which game. Now the agent does it for me, and it saves me so much time. The agent set up everything I'm not an engineer, so I said to AI, "Talk to me like I'm a seventh grader and teach me step-by-step what I should do in order to accomplish this task." Then I had two open browsers, and I followed the instructions. Then, it magically runs. The agent set up everything and sent me around 60 calendar invites for my kids' soccer games and back, and it was all expertly done. One says, "Uber to game, 23 minutes." I think a lot of parents are finding the time in late nights and early mornings to do this kind of admin stuff, and that's not really what we want to do. What we want is to spend time with our families. I remember calculating this, and it was about five to eight hours a week of mental labor . It was calendar management, meal planning, paying our nanny, messaging people to confirm what time to arrive for what, and ordering and unpacking groceries. Now, I probably spend two hours a week doing this stuff and checking on the agents. If you go into this thinking that AI is not going to make a mistake , you will get so frustrated that you'll give up too early. People also make mistakes, so you just have to have a system of checking the AI. It helps me stay on top of emails I also created a school agent. I instructed the agent to read the school emails, pick out information, and add calendar events as needed. First and foremost, I need it to flag school closures and add them to the calendar. I've instructed the agent to only care about events that apply to my kids. My kids go to a bilingual school, with a Spanish track and a Mandarin track. My kids are in the Spanish track, which means I want the agent to ignore the Mandarin events. The agent will look at whether an email was sent to the listserv or whether it's from an individual. If it's an individual, it has to come through to me because the teacher is emailing my husband and me directly, so we should obviously pay attention. An agent plans our dinners My husband has also taken on a lot, and we now use an agent for meal planning. There are food allergies we have to take into account. I have a note in my phone with 15 dishes that would rotate every three weeks because we found our thing, and I didn't want to spend any more time thinking about this, so we're just going to do kale sausage pasta and eggplant moussaka. Now, we don't have to do that because AI suggests new menus that meet everyone's requirements. Then it gives us instructions on what to shop for. These shopping apps have integrated AI, which makes it even easier. With the extra time I have , I sleep more, and I get higher-quality sleep. I am less stressed and more pleasant to be around. The time I spend with my kids and family each day is more enjoyable for everyone. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: IBM, MeitY Startup Hub Sign MoU to Expand Technology Access for Deep-Tech Startups
items.summary: IBM and the MeitY Startup Hub (MSH) signed a memorandum of understanding on October 13 to support Indian deep-tech startups with access to enterprise technologies, technical mentorship and commercialisation opportunities. The collaboration will focus on startups working in artificial intelligence, hybrid cloud and quantum computing, IBM said. “India’s startup ecosystem is emerging as a global engine for technology innovation. Through this collaboration with IBM, we aim to strengthen indigenous deep tech capabilities , foster technology-led entrepreneurship and create greater opportunity for innovators to build solutions that contribute to a Viksit Bharat,” said Panneerselvam Madanagopal, CEO of MSH. MSH is an initiative of the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology (MeitY), Government of India. According to IBM, the partnership will combine MSH’s nationwide startup network with IBM’s enterprise technology expertise to help startups develop, validate and scale solutions for Indian and global markets. Under the agreement, startups will be able to access IBM’s enterprise technology portfolio and innovation platforms to address business use cases. These include IBM watsonx, an AI and data platform; IBM Bob, an AI coding agent for enterprises; and IBM Sovereign Core, an AI-ready software stack for digital sovereignty. The collaboration will also cover technical orientation on hybrid cloud and quantum computing, alongside IBM’s security and automation solutions, the company said. IBM and MSH will explore initiatives to help startups develop proofs of concept for enterprise use cases across sectors including banking, finance, government and industry. The planned areas of collaboration include sovereign AI innovation, open-source ecosystem development, founder mentorship and technical skilling. The partnership will also create opportunities for startups to showcase their solutions to enterprises and investors. Identifying and supporting promising innovators in tier-2 and tier-3 cities is another stated priority, according to IBM. Sandip Patel, Managing Director of IBM India and South Asia, said the partnership aims to strengthen India’s deep-tech startup ecosystem and help founders develop technologies for domestic and international markets. “Together with MeitY Startup Hub, we aim to help founders innovate faster, scale responsibly, and build solutions that address both national and global challenges—turning promising innovation into real-world impact,” Patel said. The MoU complements IBM Ventures’ existing engagements in India. IBM said its venture arm supports enterprise technology startups through a capital-plus model that combines investment with access to IBM’s global network and technical experts.

items.summary: In an interview on October 14, 2026, Anthropic’s Head of International Startups & Digital Native, Guillaume Princen, discussed how startups and major firms are adopting Anthropic’s AI, including Claude tools, to boost employee productivity, overhaul processes, and build new products. He highlighted growing demand for frontier models like Opus 5.5, now about 40% cheaper than its predecessor, and a shift toward using different models for specific tasks across the 5.5 family. Princen emphasized Anthropic’s safety-first approach versus open-source and open-weight competitors, underscoring third-party auditing, closer cooperation with governments, and willingness to delay or limit powerful model releases—such as with Methos—if safety concerns arise, even at the expense of near-term revenue. items.title: Parallel Loop Raises $6.6 Million to Make AI Work for Enterprises
items.summary: Parallel Loop on October 14 announced its formal launch, backed by 6.6 million in seed funding, led by 3one4 Capital. The company has teams in Bengaluru, Bangkok, London, and Dubai. The company, founded in June by Prateek Jogani and Yujun Chean, is an AI operating partner for mid-market and large enterprises . They partner with more than 10 enterprises across industries and geographies, blending AI with clients’ existing technology, organisational context, and workflows. Notable companies include Licious and Havells in India and Thailand-based Tokio Marine Safety Insurance. “Intelligence has become abundant. What many organisations lack is the context, systems and capability to turn this into tangible business outcomes,” said Jogani. Although AI works rapidly, it is imperative to ensure that the basic structure of rules, decisions, and know-how is integrated into the workflow, necessitating AI to connect with systems, meetings, emails, messaging tools, and individual teams to unlock its maximum potential. This can show up as serving customers in new ways, entering new markets, and running operations faster. “Parallel Loop addresses that gap by helping our clients build capability and scale AI to transform the way they operate and achieve their most ambitious goals,” Jogani added. Its AI stack is combined with forward-deployed engineers who work alongside client teams to connect existing systems, processes and organisational knowledge, and to build AI workflows and applications. The process includes three connected capabilities. AI Enablement collaborates with the leadership team to identify valuable opportunities for AI intervention, defining roadmaps to assist in building practical capability inside the organisation. AI Stack is one secure, governed and fully modular stack shared across functions. It joins existing systems with organisational context and powers everything from instant live dashboards to end-to-end deterministic workflows. Then comes Software Factory, wherein forward-deployed engineers and AI agents work alongside the client’s team to modernise critical legacy systems and build new applications in a fraction of the usual time. The stack works with multiple model providers, including open-weight models, so clients are not locked into a single provider. It keeps an audit trail of prompts, responses, context changes and actions. Clients retain ownership of their data, organisational context, and client-specific work built for them. “Today, several hundred of our employees across the organisation use Parallel Loop as their everyday AI platform for workflows, automations, and dashboards. Work that used to sit in legacy systems and old reporting tools now starts with a simple question in chat,” Pramod Mundra, the President and CIO at Havells India Limited. “We’re excited to partner with the Parallel Loop team and lead their seed as they prepare to scale their offering across categories and geographies,” said Anurag Ramdasan, Partner, 3one4 Capital.

items.title: 9 Best AI Gateways in 2026: Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM, Kong and 5 More Ranked
items.summary: An AI gateway is a control layer between your application and model providers. It gives every service one API for many models. It also centralizes routing, retries, failover, caching, budgets and logs. This guide presents the best AI gateways for production teams in 2026. The market moved fast this year. Palo Alto Networks closed its acquisition of Portkey on May 29. Mintlify acquired Helicone , which now runs in maintenance mode. LiteLLM survived a PyPI supply chain compromise in March. Your gateway choice now carries vendor and security risk, not just feature risk. TL;DR Best overall for self-hosted performance: Bifrost. Go binary, Apache 2.0, 11 µs published overhead at 5,000 RPS. Best open-source gateway with guardrails: Portkey. MIT license, 1,600+ models, now backed by Palo Alto Networks. Widest adoption: LiteLLM. 53.8K GitHub stars, 100+ providers, Python-first. Best for API platform teams: Kong AI Gateway. LLM, MCP and A2A traffic in one stack. Best managed options: Cloudflare (edge, free core), Vercel (zero markup), OpenRouter (model access). How We Ranked These AI Gateways We weighted 6 criteria for production use: Performance evidence: published overhead, and how it was measured. Coverage: providers and models behind one OpenAI-compatible API. Governance: virtual keys, budgets, RBAC, audit logs, guardrails. Deployment: self-hosted, VPC, air-gapped, or managed only. Cost model: markup, platform fees, free tier limits. Vendor and supply chain risk: license, ownership changes, security history. Quick Comparison: 9 Best AI Gateways Rank Gateway License Deployment Coverage (vendor claim) Published overhead Entry pricing 1 Bifrost Apache 2.0 Self-hosted, VPC, air-gapped 23+ providers 11 µs at 5K RPS Free OSS; Enterprise custom 2 Portkey MIT (gateway) Self-hosted, managed, private cloud 1,600+ models Under 1 ms Free OSS; hosted from $49/mo 3 LiteLLM Open source + commercial license Self-hosted, hosted 100+ providers 8 ms P95 at 1K RPS Free OSS; Enterprise custom 4 Kong AI Gateway Open core Self-hosted, cloud, hybrid Multi-LLM via plugins Not disclosed Free trial; paid plugins 5 TrueFoundry Proprietary VPC, on-prem, air-gapped, SaaS 1,600+ models Under 3 ms internal Free 30K requests/mo 6 Cloudflare AI Gateway Proprietary Managed edge Major providers + Workers AI Not disclosed Core features free 7 Vercel AI Gateway Proprietary Managed Multi-provider, multimodal Not disclosed Zero token markup 8 OpenRouter Proprietary Managed Major labs + open models Not disclosed 5.5% fee on credits 9 Orq.ai Router Proprietary Managed 400+ models, 20+ providers Not disclosed Free tier 1. Bifrost (Maxim AI) What it is: Bifrost is an open-source AI gateway written in Go. It exposes 23+ providers through one OpenAI-compatible API. It ships under Apache 2.0 and has 8.7K GitHub stars. Why it ranks first: it has the strongest published performance numbers of any self-hosted gateway. The README reports 11 µs added latency at 5,000 RPS on a t3.xlarge. On a t3.medium, that figure is 59 µs. Maxim’s benchmark against LiteLLM reports P99 latency of 1.68 s versus 90.72 s at 500 RPS. Key features: Automatic fallbacks, weighted load balancing and semantic caching. Virtual keys with hierarchical budgets and rate limits in the open-source build. MCP gateway support, plus Code Mode for large tool sets. Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing. Drop-in endpoints for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google GenAI SDKs. Best for: high-throughput teams that must self-host inside a VPC or air-gapped network. 2. Portkey What it is: Portkey’s AI Gateway is an MIT-licensed gateway with 13K GitHub stars. It claims routing to 1,600+ models, under 1 ms latency and a 122 KB footprint. Why it ranks here: it pairs strong routing with the deepest built-in guardrail catalog. A Gateway 2.0 pre-release merges Portkey’s enterprise gateway into open source. Palo Alto Networks now owns Portkey and is folding it into Prisma AIRS. Key features: Fallbacks, retries, conditional routing, load balancing and request timeouts. Simple and semantic caching. Input and output guardrails, with bring-your-own and partner options. MCP Gateway with central auth, access control and tool-call logging. Pricing: Braintrust’s comparison lists a free tier with 10K logged requests. Paid plans start at $49 per month. Best for: teams that want guardrails and routing in one open-source gateway. 3. LiteLLM What it is: LiteLLM is the most widely adopted open-source LLM gateway. It has 53.8K GitHub stars and supports 100+ providers. It ships as a Python SDK and a proxy server. Why it ranks here: coverage and ecosystem depth are unmatched. It supports chat, embeddings, images, audio, batches, rerank, MCP and A2A endpoints. The project reports 8 ms P95 latency at 1K RPS in its own benchmarks . Key features: Virtual keys, per-team spend tracking, budgets and RPM/TPM limits. Router with retries, fallbacks and load balancing across deployments. Admin UI, guardrails and logging to Langfuse, OpenTelemetry and others. Terraform modules for AWS and GCP, plus cosign-signed Docker images. Best for: Python-first teams that need maximum provider coverage and can run the proxy. 4. Kong AI Gateway What it is: Kong AI Gateway extends Kong’s API gateway to AI traffic. It governs LLM, MCP and agent-to-agent (A2A) traffic from one platform. Why it ranks here: Kong brings mature API management to AI. Its site notes Gartner named Kong a leader in API management for the 7th year. Key features: PII sanitization, semantic prompt guards and access control. Semantic caching, routing and load balancing. User, model and time-bound token quotas, with showback and chargeback. A2A telemetry covering payloads, latency, token usage and caller identity. Best for: enterprises already standardized on Kong for API management. 5. TrueFoundry AI Gateway What it is: TrueFoundry offers an enterprise AI gateway with LLM, MCP and agent gateway features. It claims access to 1,600+ models. Why it ranks here: it leads Gartner Peer Insights for AI Gateways by volume. It holds a 4.8 rating from 210 ratings. Key features: Deployment in VPC, on-prem, air-gapped or multi-cloud environments. Latency-based routing, weighted load balancing and geo-aware routing. Serving for self-hosted models on vLLM, SGLang, KServe and Triton. SOC 2, HIPAA and GDPR compliance, with SSO, RBAC and audit logs. Pricing: free for the first 30K requests per month, with up to 3 seats. Best for: regulated enterprises that also deploy their own models. 6. Cloudflare AI Gateway What it is: Cloudflare AI Gateway is a managed gateway on Cloudflare’s edge network. Setup takes one line of code. Why it ranks here: it is the cheapest managed starting point. Core features are free on all plans, including analytics, caching and rate limiting. Key features: Request retry and model fallback. Free DLP scanning on all plans. Guardrails using Llama Guard 3 8B, billed as Workers AI inference. Unified Billing with no inference markup. Best for: teams already building on Cloudflare Workers. 7. Vercel AI Gateway What it is: Vercel AI Gateway is a managed gateway callable from any infrastructure. Your app does not need to run on Vercel. Why it ranks here: it has the cleanest pricing in the managed tier. Vercel charges no markup and no platform fee on tokens, including with BYOK. Key features: Text, image, video, speech, transcription, realtime, embeddings and reranking. Budgets per team, project, API key or team member. Provider ordering plus model fallbacks, with per-attempt request logs. AI SDK, OpenAI, Anthropic Messages and coding agent integrations. Best for: TypeScript and Next.js teams that want a managed gateway with zero markup. 8. OpenRouter What it is: OpenRouter is a hosted API that routes to models from major labs and open model providers. It uses an OpenAI-compatible interface. Why it ranks here: it is the fastest path to broad model access. It passes provider prices through with no inference markup. Key features: Automatic fallback to the next provider on errors. Routing variants: :nitro for throughput, :floor for price. Prompts and completions are not logged by default. Free models with 50 requests per day, or 1,000 after buying 10 credits. Best for: prototyping, model comparison and startups that want one bill. 9. Orq.ai Router What it is: Orq.ai Router is a managed gateway with access to 400+ models across 20+ providers. It is OpenAI-compatible. Why it ranks here: it ties routing to evaluations, monitoring and budgets in one platform. It targets EU teams with data residency and EU AI Act readiness. Key features: Smart routing, fallbacks, retries and BYOK. Budget controls and identity tracking. SOC 2 and GDPR support, with EU data residency. Best for: European teams that want gateway, evals and governance from one vendor. How to Choose the Right AI Gateway You must self-host for compliance: Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM or TrueFoundry. You already run Kong, Cloudflare or Vercel: use that platform’s gateway first. You just need many models fast: OpenRouter or Vercel. Pin gateway versions with hash checks, whatever you pick. items.summary_html:
An AI gateway is a control layer between your application and model providers. It gives every service one API for many models. It also centralizes routing, retries, failover, caching, budgets and logs. This guide presents the best AI gateways for production teams in 2026.

The market moved fast this year. Palo Alto Networks closed its acquisition of Portkey on May 29. Mintlify acquired Helicone, which now runs in maintenance mode. LiteLLM survived a PyPI supply chain compromise in March. Your gateway choice now carries vendor and security risk, not just feature risk.

TL;DR
  • Best overall for self-hosted performance: Bifrost. Go binary, Apache 2.0, 11 µs published overhead at 5,000 RPS.
  • Best open-source gateway with guardrails: Portkey. MIT license, 1,600+ models, now backed by Palo Alto Networks.
  • Widest adoption: LiteLLM. 53.8K GitHub stars, 100+ providers, Python-first.
  • Best for API platform teams: Kong AI Gateway. LLM, MCP and A2A traffic in one stack.
  • Best managed options: Cloudflare (edge, free core), Vercel (zero markup), OpenRouter (model access).
How We Ranked These AI Gateways

We weighted 6 criteria for production use:

  • Performance evidence: published overhead, and how it was measured.
  • Coverage: providers and models behind one OpenAI-compatible API.
  • Governance: virtual keys, budgets, RBAC, audit logs, guardrails.
  • Deployment: self-hosted, VPC, air-gapped, or managed only.
  • Cost model: markup, platform fees, free tier limits.
  • Vendor and supply chain risk: license, ownership changes, security history.
Quick Comparison: 9 Best AI Gateways RankGatewayLicenseDeploymentCoverage (vendor claim)Published overheadEntry pricing1BifrostApache 2.0Self-hosted, VPC, air-gapped23+ providers11 µs at 5K RPSFree OSS; Enterprise custom2PortkeyMIT (gateway)Self-hosted, managed, private cloud1,600+ modelsUnder 1 msFree OSS; hosted from $49/mo3LiteLLMOpen source + commercial licenseSelf-hosted, hosted100+ providers8 ms P95 at 1K RPSFree OSS; Enterprise custom4Kong AI GatewayOpen coreSelf-hosted, cloud, hybridMulti-LLM via pluginsNot disclosedFree trial; paid plugins5TrueFoundryProprietaryVPC, on-prem, air-gapped, SaaS1,600+ modelsUnder 3 ms internalFree 30K requests/mo6Cloudflare AI GatewayProprietaryManaged edgeMajor providers + Workers AINot disclosedCore features free7Vercel AI GatewayProprietaryManagedMulti-provider, multimodalNot disclosedZero token markup8OpenRouterProprietaryManagedMajor labs + open modelsNot disclosed5.5% fee on credits9Orq.ai RouterProprietaryManaged400+ models, 20+ providersNot disclosedFree tier 1. Bifrost (Maxim AI)

What it is: Bifrost is an open-source AI gateway written in Go. It exposes 23+ providers through one OpenAI-compatible API. It ships under Apache 2.0 and has 8.7K GitHub stars.

Why it ranks first: it has the strongest published performance numbers of any self-hosted gateway. The README reports 11 µs added latency at 5,000 RPS on a t3.xlarge. On a t3.medium, that figure is 59 µs. Maxim’s benchmark against LiteLLM reports P99 latency of 1.68 s versus 90.72 s at 500 RPS.

Key features:

  • Automatic fallbacks, weighted load balancing and semantic caching.
  • Virtual keys with hierarchical budgets and rate limits in the open-source build.
  • MCP gateway support, plus Code Mode for large tool sets.
  • Prometheus metrics and OpenTelemetry tracing.
  • Drop-in endpoints for OpenAI, Anthropic and Google GenAI SDKs.

Best for: high-throughput teams that must self-host inside a VPC or air-gapped network.

2. Portkey

What it is: Portkey’s AI Gateway is an MIT-licensed gateway with 13K GitHub stars. It claims routing to 1,600+ models, under 1 ms latency and a 122 KB footprint.

Why it ranks here: it pairs strong routing with the deepest built-in guardrail catalog. A Gateway 2.0 pre-release merges Portkey’s enterprise gateway into open source. Palo Alto Networks now owns Portkey and is folding it into Prisma AIRS.

Key features:

  • Fallbacks, retries, conditional routing, load balancing and request timeouts.
  • Simple and semantic caching.
  • Input and output guardrails, with bring-your-own and partner options.
  • MCP Gateway with central auth, access control and tool-call logging.

Pricing: Braintrust’s comparison lists a free tier with 10K logged requests. Paid plans start at $49 per month.

Best for: teams that want guardrails and routing in one open-source gateway.

3. LiteLLM

What it is: LiteLLM is the most widely adopted open-source LLM gateway. It has 53.8K GitHub stars and supports 100+ providers. It ships as a Python SDK and a proxy server.

Why it ranks here: coverage and ecosystem depth are unmatched. It supports chat, embeddings, images, audio, batches, rerank, MCP and A2A endpoints. The project reports 8 ms P95 latency at 1K RPS in its own benchmarks.

Key features:

  • Virtual keys, per-team spend tracking, budgets and RPM/TPM limits.
  • Router with retries, fallbacks and load balancing across deployments.
  • Admin UI, guardrails and logging to Langfuse, OpenTelemetry and others.
  • Terraform modules for AWS and GCP, plus cosign-signed Docker images.

Best for: Python-first teams that need maximum provider coverage and can run the proxy.

4. Kong AI Gateway

What it is: Kong AI Gateway extends Kong’s API gateway to AI traffic. It governs LLM, MCP and agent-to-agent (A2A) traffic from one platform.

Why it ranks here: Kong brings mature API management to AI. Its site notes Gartner named Kong a leader in API management for the 7th year.

Key features:

  • PII sanitization, semantic prompt guards and access control.
  • Semantic caching, routing and load balancing.
  • User, model and time-bound token quotas, with showback and chargeback.
  • A2A telemetry covering payloads, latency, token usage and caller identity.

Best for: enterprises already standardized on Kong for API management.

5. TrueFoundry AI Gateway

What it is: TrueFoundry offers an enterprise AI gateway with LLM, MCP and agent gateway features. It claims access to 1,600+ models.

Why it ranks here: it leads Gartner Peer Insights for AI Gateways by volume. It holds a 4.8 rating from 210 ratings.

Key features:

  • Deployment in VPC, on-prem, air-gapped or multi-cloud environments.
  • Latency-based routing, weighted load balancing and geo-aware routing.
  • Serving for self-hosted models on vLLM, SGLang, KServe and Triton.
  • SOC 2, HIPAA and GDPR compliance, with SSO, RBAC and audit logs.

Pricing: free for the first 30K requests per month, with up to 3 seats.

Best for: regulated enterprises that also deploy their own models.

6. Cloudflare AI Gateway

What it is: Cloudflare AI Gateway is a managed gateway on Cloudflare’s edge network. Setup takes one line of code.

Why it ranks here: it is the cheapest managed starting point. Core features are free on all plans, including analytics, caching and rate limiting.

Key features:

  • Request retry and model fallback.
  • Free DLP scanning on all plans.
  • Guardrails using Llama Guard 3 8B, billed as Workers AI inference.
  • Unified Billing with no inference markup.

Best for: teams already building on Cloudflare Workers.

7. Vercel AI Gateway

What it is: Vercel AI Gateway is a managed gateway callable from any infrastructure. Your app does not need to run on Vercel.

Why it ranks here: it has the cleanest pricing in the managed tier. Vercel charges no markup and no platform fee on tokens, including with BYOK.

Key features:

  • Text, image, video, speech, transcription, realtime, embeddings and reranking.
  • Budgets per team, project, API key or team member.
  • Provider ordering plus model fallbacks, with per-attempt request logs.
  • AI SDK, OpenAI, Anthropic Messages and coding agent integrations.

Best for: TypeScript and Next.js teams that want a managed gateway with zero markup.

8. OpenRouter

What it is: OpenRouter is a hosted API that routes to models from major labs and open model providers. It uses an OpenAI-compatible interface.

Why it ranks here: it is the fastest path to broad model access. It passes provider prices through with no inference markup.

Key features:

  • Automatic fallback to the next provider on errors.
  • Routing variants: :nitro for throughput, :floor for price.
  • Prompts and completions are not logged by default.
  • Free models with 50 requests per day, or 1,000 after buying 10 credits.

Best for: prototyping, model comparison and startups that want one bill.

9. Orq.ai Router

What it is: Orq.ai Router is a managed gateway with access to 400+ models across 20+ providers. It is OpenAI-compatible.

Why it ranks here: it ties routing to evaluations, monitoring and budgets in one platform. It targets EU teams with data residency and EU AI Act readiness.

Key features:

  • Smart routing, fallbacks, retries and BYOK.
  • Budget controls and identity tracking.
  • SOC 2 and GDPR support, with EU data residency.

Best for: European teams that want gateway, evals and governance from one vendor.

How to Choose the Right AI Gateway
  • You must self-host for compliance: Bifrost, Portkey, LiteLLM or TrueFoundry.
  • Latency at high RPS matters most: start with Bifrost, then verify on your own traffic.
  • You need guardrails and PII controls: Portkey, Kong or TrueFoundry.
  • You already run Kong, Cloudflare or Vercel: use that platform’s gateway first.
  • You just need many models fast: OpenRouter or Vercel.

Pin gateway versions with hash checks, whatever you pick. The LiteLLM incident shows why: your gateway holds every provider key you own.

Key Takeaways
  • Bifrost leads on published self-hosted performance: 11 µs overhead at 5K RPS.
  • Portkey and Helicone both changed owners in 2026. Check roadmap risk.
  • LiteLLM still has the largest ecosystem, but pin and verify releases.
  • Cloudflare and Vercel offer the cheapest managed entry points.
  • Treat every vendor benchmark as a claim. Benchmark your own workload.

Sources: Bifrost GitHub, LiteLLM GitHub, Portkey Gateway GitHub, Kong AI Gateway, TrueFoundry, Cloudflare pricing, Vercel pricing, OpenRouter FAQ, Gartner Peer Insights.

items.title: Gnani AI Launches Timbre v3.0 With AI Voices That Can Whisper, Laugh & Shout
items.summary: Gnani AI has launched Timbre v3.0, a text-to-speech model that lets businesses and content creators control how AI-generated voices deliver speech, including pauses, whispers, laughter and changes in pace. The Bengaluru-based company said that the model supports 10 languages, including Hindi, Bengali, Gujarati, Kannada, Malayalam, Marathi, Punjabi, Tamil, Telugu and Indian-accented English. It is built for applications ranging from customer service voice agents to audiobooks, podcasts, advertisements and video voiceovers. Timbre v3.0 also supports audio tags, which allow developers to specify how individual lines should be spoken. The model can generate its first audio in under 200 milliseconds, making it suitable for real-time voice conversations. “Building speech AI for India means paying attention to how people actually speak and listen,” said Bharath Shankar, Chief Product and Engineering Officer at Gnani AI. “A story needs pauses, changes in pace and expressions. With Timbre v3.0, we are bringing that clarity and control into one multilingual model, so businesses and creators can shape both what a voice says and how it says it,” he added. Timbre v3.0 allows developers to insert audio tags into text to direct how a voice delivers specific lines. These include cues for laughing, giggling, sighing, whispering and shouting, as well as instructions to pause, slow down or speak with excitement. The model can also generate non-verbal sounds such as coughs, sniffles, yawns and exhales. These features can be used in games, animation, podcasts, advertisements, social media videos and e-learning applications. For text without explicit audio tags, the model automatically adjusts its delivery based on the meaning, tone and punctuation of each sentence. The audio tags work across all supported languages. The model is built to maintain a voice’s character across languages, allowing businesses to use a consistent voice for customer interactions across different regions. It also includes text normalisation capabilities that convert written numbers, dates, currencies, symbols and abbreviations into spoken language. This is particularly relevant for banking, financial services and insurance applications, where voice agents need to clearly communicate payment amounts, account numbers, due dates and interest rates. Developers can adjust speaking speeds to give listeners more time to understand important information or move faster through routine updates. Gnani AI said Timbre currently powers more than one lakh hours of voice calls. Timbre v3.0 supports streaming playback, allowing audio to begin before the model finishes generating the full response. It also supports long-form speech synthesis for extended narration and responses. Enterprise use cases include payment reminders, collections, know-your-customer (KYC) processes, customer onboarding, insurance renewals, claims, appointment reminders and customer support across financial services, healthcare and telecom. The model can also be used for audio articles, in-app guidance and accessibility tools that read digital content aloud in a user’s preferred language.
