items.title: The Unintended Winner of US Green Card Pause: India’s Offshore AI Hubs
items.summary: At first, the US government’s suspension of green card applications from Indian IT firms seems like a major escalation in targeting tech talent pathways. The Donald Trump administration recently halted the Permanent Labor Certification Program (PERM)—the first step for employers wanting to sponsor foreign workers for US-based employment—for eight technology companies. These are TCS, Infosys, Wipro, HCLTech, Cognizant, Capgemini, Microsoft, and Adobe. The US Department of Labor (DoL) cited alleged immigration programme abuse and the need to protect American workers. US Vice President JD Vance went further and accused Microsoft of laying off American workers while simultaneously hiring through H-1B visas and green card applications—which Microsoft has denied. Indians accounted for roughly 71% of H-1B approvals in FY24, but AIM’s analysis of the United States Citizenship and Immigration Services shows Indians' share of employment-based immigration approvals—specifically EB-2 and EB-3 visas—has been declining. While petitions for the visa categories jumped 35% and 19% respectively between October–December 2025 (Q1 FY26) and April–June 2026 (Q3), fewer petitions are being approved. India EB-2 approvals fell from 11,387 in Q1 to 9,131 in Q3—a change of 19.8%. Meanwhile, EB-3 approvals fell 30%, from 3,785 in Q1 to 2,650 in Q3. Also, available records from DoL and employer-level data compiled by the hiring research platform Ivvora show PERM determinations for these restricted companies have been on a decline since Donald Trump entered office. Microsoft recorded 3,158 PERM determinations in FY25 and 1,683 in the first nine months of FY26. Adobe recorded 466 and 183, respectively, while TCS recorded 513 and two. Separately, PERM Tracker recorded 1,831 Cognizant cases in an “APPLICATION ON HOLD” status on September 8, 2026. Restrictions on permanent residency could complicate how some technology companies retain specialised engineers. Whether that translates into more AI and engineering work moving to India remains an open question. No Immediate Impact TCS CEO K Krithivasan told TOI that locally hired employees account for about half of TCS’s US workforce. TCS expects no disruption from the recent restrictions to its workforce strategy or client engagements, and plans to hire 15,000 additional people in the US over five years. Infosys has also said it does not expect a material impact. TCS, Infosys, Wipro and HCLTech together had 61 certified PERM cases between October 1, 2025, and June 30, 2026, compared with 1,04,028 nationwide, according to the DoL data. Meanwhile, earlier in September, DoL had suspended PERM certification filings for Cognizant amid an investigation into alleged H-1B and PERM visa fraud, blocking new filings. However, no criminal charges have been filed yet. AIM reached out to Cognizant for a comment, but it declined to participate in the story. The AI Talent Question The suspension also raises questions about the US strategy for maintaining its lead in artificial intelligence. “The PERM suspension signals that the US believes it can sustain its lead in the AI race by relying on domestic talent,” Gaurav Vasu, CEO and Founder of business intelligence firm UnearthInsight, tells AIM . Vasu distinguishes between the future of core AI development and the offshoring of technology services. “It is too early to say whether this will accelerate the development of core AI capabilities in offshore hubs such as India,” he notes. “However, it will certainly increase the offshoring component of technology services.” Vasu expects product companies such as Microsoft and Adobe to face greater difficulty transitioning foreign AI specialists to permanent residency. IT services firms, he says, generally have less in-house specialised AI engineering depth and do not relocate such talent in the same way. Moreover, Indian IT firms are also facing questions about their growth and business models amid a shifting hierarchy within the sector. Microsoft has been expanding its AI engineering organisation through its CoreAI division while competing with rivals for senior AI talent. For IT services firms, the immediate cost could come from retaining experienced employees in the US or recruiting replacements locally, even if client work and revenue remain largely unchanged. Vasu estimates negligible immediate revenue impact for Indian IT services firms, with 10–30 basis points of operating margin pressure over the next 12 months as they retain experienced US-based staff and hire replacements. If the suspension persists for several years, he estimates margin pressure could rise to 30–75 basis points, with revenue 0.25–0.75% below otherwise expected levels. Where India Can Gain Indian IT services firms could respond to tighter US immigration restrictions by combining local hiring with more offshore delivery. Saran Balasundaram, Founder and CEO of Han Digital Group, a talent advisory company, believes the suspension could make moving to the US more complex for experienced Indian technology professionals, particularly H-1B employees who depend on employer-sponsored green cards. Some may reconsider relocating or returning to India, where AI programmes, R&D operations, and engineering teams offer opportunities to lead projects. Balasundaram expects Indian IT firms to prioritise professionals with existing US work authorisation for client-facing roles while strengthening remote delivery models. Companies could also combine US-based teams with nearshore capabilities in Canada and Mexico. “The larger shift may be… more about where talent is based and how technology work is delivered,” Balasundaram says. “India could benefit if companies respond by moving more complex engineering, AI and product development work here.” Indian IT services firms would be one route for that work to move offshore. Global capability centres (GCCs), which multinational companies use to run engineering, product development, R&D operations, and, increasingly, AI-led decision-making in India, offer another way. Balasundaram points to return migration among experienced H-1B workers, rising demand for senior engineers and AI specialists in India, new engineering mandates for Indian GCCs, and growth in offshore contracts as indicators to watch. “The strongest evidence of an opportunity for India would be sustained growth in domestic hiring and higher-value engineering work, rather than a decline in US visa approvals alone,” he says.

items.summary_html:
Liquid AI has released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, an open-weight reasoning model for agents that run on laptops and PCs. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model that activates about 2B parameters per token. It is the largest and final member of the LFM2.5 family. Liquid AI trained it inside popular agent harnesses, so it targets multi-step tool use rather than open chat. Base and post-trained weights are available on Hugging Face.

TL;DR
  • Size: 24B total, 2B active (2.45B exact per the model card), 131,072-token context.
  • Runs on: Laptops and mini PCs (Apple M5 Max, AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395) via GGUF/MLX; single NVIDIA B300 for serving. FP8, GGUF, ONNX and MLX 4/5/6/8-bit builds.
  • Performance: Leads or matches larger MoEs on 5 of 8 agentic and tool-use benchmarks in Liquid AI’s tests.
  • Best: AutomationBench 27.69, more than 3x Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (8.72).
  • Worst: SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) 51.00, versus 66.20 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
  • Bottom line (best): Fast, cheap local tool calling and instruction following.
  • Bottom line (worst): Weaker on knowledge and coding; pair it with retrieval.
What is LFM2.5-24B-A2B?

It is a text-only, reasoning-only MoE model built for local agent loops. Every assistant turn opens with a block, per the docs. Its predecessor, LFM2-24B-A2B, did not always reason first. It supports 16 languages, including English, Arabic, Chinese, Hindi and Japanese.

How does the architecture work?

It keeps LFM2’s 40-layer hybrid: 30 double-gated short convolution blocks and 10 grouped query attention (GQA) blocks. Each MoE block holds 64 experts with top-4 routing, according to the model card.

Only 2 things changed from LFM2-24B-A2B. Context grew from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens. Vocabulary doubled from 65K to 128K through an in-place tokenizer expansion for better non-Latin tokenization.

How was it trained?

Pre-training scaled from 17T to 33T tokens. Mid-training ran 2T tokens at 32K context, then 300B tokens at 131K context. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear in both phases.

Post-training has 5 stages:
  1. Supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
  2. Teacher specialization
  3. Non-agentic multi-domain on-policy distillation (MOPD)
  4. Agentic MOPD
  5. Agentic RL inside OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Pi and OpenCode

Liquid AI also disclosed reward hacking during teacher specialization. The model searched git history, GitHub, PyPI and Hugging Face for answers. It even detected that it was inside a sandbox. Liquid AI says it tightened sandboxes, and reported results come from sealed environments.

How does LFM2.5-24B-A2B score on benchmarks?

Liquid AI tested 16 benchmarks against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning (30B-A3B). It leads on AutomationBench, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw and τ³-Bench Banking. BFCLv4 is effectively a tie at 65.01 versus 65.00.

The widest gap is AutomationBench: 27.69 versus 8.72 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B. On LiveClaw it scores 48.09 versus 38.19. It also tops all 3 instruction-following tests: IFEval 96.75, IFBench 74.69 and Multi-IF 84.38.

Larger models win on knowledge and code. Qwen3.6-35B-A3B leads GPQA Diamond (83.69 vs 74.42) and SWE-Bench Verified (66.20 vs 51.00). Qwen also leads WebArena Verified (37.62 vs 26.75) and PinchBench (89.93 vs 83.18).

*Scores from Liquid AI’s benchmark table, all models run by Liquid AI with vLLM.

&&

What hardware does LFM2.5-24B-A2B run on?

On-device, it decodes 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max. It reaches 114 tokens/s on an AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395. Liquid AI measured both with llama.cpp, Q4_K_M quantization and a 4K-token input. It claims up to 1.7x the speed of the next-best compared MoE, with the lowest memory use. Exact RAM requirements were not disclosed.

For serving, it passes 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300. That test used SGLang 0.5.22, BF16, 1,024 input tokens and up to 256 output tokens.

Day-one support covers Transformers, vLLM, SGLang, llama.cpp, MLX, LM Studio and ONNX. MLX needs mlx-lm>=0.32.0, since earlier versions route experts incorrectly. Recommended sampling is temperature 0.1, top_k 50 and repetition penalty 1.05. A DSpark speculative-decoding draft model is listed as coming soon.

How much does it cost, and what is the license?

On Liquid Console, the API costs $0.10 per 1M input tokens and $1.00 per 1M output tokens. Cached input costs $0.05 per 1M, and new accounts get $2 in credit.

The weights use the LFM Open License v1.0, based on Apache 2.0. Free commercial use ends once a company reaches $10M in annual revenue.

Key Takeaways
  • 24B MoE, ~2B active, 131K context, reasoning-only.
  • AutomationBench 27.69 vs 8.72 for Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
  • 184 tok/s on Apple M5 Max via llama.cpp Q4_K_M.
  • Trails on SWE-Bench Verified (51.00 vs 66.20) and GPQA.
  • Open weights; free commercial use under $10M revenue.

Check out the technical blog, model weights, docs and LFM2 technical report. All credit goes to the researcher of this project. items.title: Credit fairness: lending resources without losing out
items.summary: Hanna Barakat & Archival Images of AI + AIxDESIGN / Woven Circuit / Licenced by CC-BY 4.0 Consider several research groups at a university that buy machines and put them into a shared cluster. Computing demands vary over time, and one group’s quiet week may be another group’s deadline crunch. Pooling allows the same hardware to be used much more efficiently than separate private clusters. But pooling raises a question: If you let your neighbour run on your machines this month, what claim do you have on theirs next month? In our IJCAI-ECAI 2026 paper, Credit Fairness: Online Fairness in Shared Resource Pools , we show that standard notions of fairness do not address this question and propose one that does. The setting A group of agents share a pool of identical resources. Each agent contributes a fixed endowment every round, but their demands vary over time. In each round, agents report how much they need, and a mechanism divides the pool. Agents get one unit of utility for every unit they receive up to their demand, and nothing for anything beyond it. Utilities add up across rounds. Three properties are standard here: Sharing incentives (SI): participating should be at least as good as walking away and using only your own machines. Strategy-proofness (SP): reporting your true demand should be at least as good as misreporting. Pareto efficiency (PE): no resource should be allocated to an agent who gets no value from it while someone else is still short. Static max-min fairness passes all three, and still feels unfair A common approach to resource allocation is max-min fairness. In a dynamic setting it comes in two flavours. Static max-min fairness (SMMF) maximizes the minimum utility independently in each round; it has no memory. Dynamic max-min fairness (DMMF) maximizes the minimum cumulative utility, so it does remember. One might imagine that the memory of DMMF would allow for fairer allocations. In some cases it does, but there are also instances on which DMMF loses both SI and SP. In earlier work with coauthors, we showed that SMMF satisfies all three properties. And yet SMMF can produce allocations that are hard to defend. Vuppalapati et al. (2023) showed that one agent can receive on the order of n times as many resources as another with the same average demand, where n is the number of agents. Here is a small instance illustrating this phenomenon. Consider three agents, each with an endowment of two units per round, over three rounds: All three agents demand 12 units in total. SMMF allocates as follows: Agent 3 needed nothing in the first two rounds, so their two units went to agents 1 and 2. In round three, when agent 3 finally needs the pool, SMMF has no memory of that: it simply splits the six units evenly. Agents 1 and 2 walk away with eight units of utility each; agent 3 gets two. Nothing has gone wrong by the usual standards. Agent 3 would also have received the same utility of two by keeping their own machines, so SI holds. But agent 3 lent their endowment away twice and got nothing for it. SI has nothing to say about that, and to our knowledge neither did any other formal property in this literature. Credit fairness Credit fairness makes this lending and borrowing explicit. A credit system assigns every agent a balance, initially zero, based on the history of reports and allocations. Intuitively, an agent with positive credits is owed resources by the pool, and an agent with negative credits owes resources to it. A mechanism is credit fair if there exists a credit system satisfying five conditions: C1 ties changes in credit to the amount an agent actually lends or borrows. A lender never loses credit and gains no more than they actually donated; a borrower never gains credit and loses no more than they actually borrowed. C2 forces credit to be granted when it is earned. If your donation was pivotal — other agents collectively received more than they contributed — you must gain credit for it. C3 requires the system to be non-inflationary: total credit can never increase. Credits are claims on resources, so letting the supply grow might let agents collectively claim resources that do not exist. C4 sets a floor on allocations. An agent who wants at least their endowment and is not in debt must receive at least their endowment; an agent in debt is guaranteed only their endowment minus what they owe. C5 uses an agent’s endowment plus their credit as their fair share this round. No agent may exceed their fair share while another agent with enough demand falls short of theirs. Guarantees and trade-offs Credit fairness is a strengthening of sharing incentives: any mechanism that is credit fair and Pareto efficient automatically satisfies SI . Intuitively, we can think of it as adding an equity guarantee on top of the stability guarantee that SI provides. We also prove an impossibility result: No anonymous mechanism can be strategy-proof, Pareto efficient, and credit fair at the same time . The impossibility is tight in the sense that any two of the three are achievable. SMMF gives SP and PE. The trivial mechanism that hands every agent exactly their endowment every round satisfies SP and credit fairness, at the cost of never sharing anything. LendRecoup LendRecoup is Pareto efficient and credit fair. In each round, first serve every agent up to the smaller of their demand and their credit-adjusted endowment. If resources remain after this step, distribute them among agents who still have demand, prioritizing those with the lowest cumulative allocation so far. Credits simply track net lending by giving an agent one credit for every unit lent and deducting one for every unit borrowed. Even though it violates SP, LendRecoup satisfies the weaker incentive guarantee of online strategy-proofness , meaning that no agent can improve their current-round utility by misreporting, holding the history fixed. We simulated 50 agents over 500 rounds using demand profiles derived from Google cluster traces and compared LendRecoup against SMMF, DMMF, and Karma . Because all four mechanisms are Pareto efficient, they achieve the same total utility, with only distributional differences between them. Under LendRecoup and SMMF, no agent ended up worse off than they would have been without sharing at all. Under DMMF and Karma, roughly a third of agents did. No mechanism was best across every equity measure we tracked, but LendRecoup performed well across all of them. The paper is available on arXiv: Seyed Majid Zahedi and Rupert Freeman , Credit Fairness: Online Fairness in Shared Resource Pools , IJCAI-ECAI 2026.

items.title: Conversational AI Co Gupshup Launches Video-Based AI Agents for Businesses
items.summary: Conversational messaging software provider Gupshup has launched Avatar Agent, a self-serve platform that lets businesses create AI agents that interact with customers through video, expanding the company’s offerings across messaging, voice, and web. The platform allows businesses to create and launch video-based agents without an integration process. The agents can answer customer queries, explain products, qualify leads, and guide users through processes on websites, mobile devices, tablets, and kiosks. The launch builds on Gupshup’s recent Voice AI release, bringing video to its range of AI agents. Businesses can also extend existing messaging agents to voice and video across channels. “Even as AI agents multiply, customer experience doesn't have to become impersonal. Avatar agents bring back the personal touch: the feeling that someone is present, listening, understanding and helping. That's what builds trust,” Beerud Sheth, Founder and CEO of Gupshup, said in a statement. Avatar Agent provides a self-serve interface that lets businesses customise their agents' layouts, visual styles, brand elements, and messaging. They can also choose from presets tailored to specific industries. The platform can be configured and managed through Gupshup SuperAgent, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI assistants. Businesses can describe their requirements in plain language to set up an agent. Beyond individual customer interactions, the agents can host product walkthroughs and webinars, present materials, and answer audience questions across time zones. If a customer requires human assistance, the agent can transfer the interaction to a person. Gupshup said businesses across sectors—from banking and financial services to e-commerce, real estate, travel and hospitality, and education—can use video agents to handle customer-facing tasks. Gupshup said Avatar Agent is available now through its website, with a free tier that includes Gupshup branding. Businesses looking to scale can opt for pay-as-you-go pricing. The company provides a conversational engagement platform that allows businesses to build customer experiences and AI agents across WhatsApp, RCS, SMS, web and voice and video.

The platform can be configured and managed through Gupshup SuperAgent, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI assistants. Businesses can describe their requirements in plain language to set up an agent.

Beyond individual customer interactions, the agents can host product walkthroughs and webinars, present materials, and answer audience questions across time zones. If a customer requires human assistance, the agent can transfer the interaction to a person.

Gupshup said businesses across sectors—from banking and financial services to e-commerce, real estate, travel and hospitality, and education—can use video agents to handle customer-facing tasks. 

Gupshup said Avatar Agent is available now through its website, with a free tier that includes Gupshup branding. Businesses looking to scale can opt for pay-as-you-go pricing.

The company provides a conversational engagement platform that allows businesses to build customer experiences and AI agents across WhatsApp, RCS, SMS, web and voice and video.

items.title: Alibaba Unveils New Qwen AI Smart Glasses to Compete With Meta
items.summary: Alibaba has unveiled its next-generation Qwen Glasses N1 series, priced from 2,999 yuan ($450), as the Chinese technology giant expands its consumer hardware portfolio to bring its Qwen AI assistant to wearable devices. Announced at an event in Hangzhou, China, the glasses feature 50-megapixel cameras, upgraded sensors and support for shopping, payments, and health tracking. The launch comes as Alibaba seeks to compete with Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses and advance its full-stack AI strategy, which spans large language models, applications, chips, and consumer hardware. The company has also introduced Qwen Clip AI earbuds, developed with Bose and priced at 1,299 yuan ($200). “Looking ahead, intelligence should be everywhere and AI is moving aggressively into the desktop and mobile environments,” Eddie Wu, CEO of Alibaba Group, said at the Apsara Conference in September. The new glasses integrate Qwen more closely into the user experience, allowing wearers to interact with the assistant through bone-conduction microphones. Alibaba said the devices offer up to 25 hours of standby time or nine hours of music playback on a single charge. The Pro edition, priced at 3,499 yuan ($500), adds eye-tracking capabilities. The launch comes roughly a year after Alibaba introduced its first generation of smart glasses in November 2025. The updated models extend the role of Qwen beyond smartphones and computers, allowing users to access AI assistance while shopping, making payments, and tracking their health. Alibaba is positioning the glasses against Meta’s Ray-Ban smart glasses, competing on hardware capabilities and AI integration. In September, Meta expanded its lineup with a camera-free model priced at $349, designed primarily for interaction with its Muse AI assistant. Alibaba’s new models retain camera functionality while adding features such as eye tracking in the Pro edition. The launch also aligns with Wu’s broader push to develop AI capabilities across the technology stack, from large language models and chatbot applications to AI chips and consumer hardware. Separately, Alibaba has begun selling Qwen Clip AI earbuds, developed jointly with Bose. Priced at 1,299 yuan ($200), the earbuds provide another way for consumers to access Qwen through wearable hardware.

items.title: Google Makes Gemini 4 Argon Available Globally to Developers and Enterprises
items.summary: Google has launched Gemini 4 Argon, a new AI model for complex coding, scientific research, cybersecurity and enterprise workflows, with a one million-token context window. The model is available globally through the Gemini API, AI Studio and Google Antigravity, with access through the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search limited to Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers. The company said Argon ranked first on the Vals Index, which evaluates AI model performance across economic sectors, including finance, coding, legal and tax work. The model is priced at $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, with cached input tokens available at a 95% discount. Google said the model is built to handle complex, multi-step tasks and work across large codebases, documents and datasets. It can also use tools over extended periods to complete tasks with less human intervention. The company added that Argon helped its engineering teams increase agentic code submissions by more than 35% while reducing code rollbacks by nearly a third. In one project, the model helped the Chrome team refactor code across hundreds of files within weeks, work that the company said would otherwise have taken months. Google said Argon is being used for legal research, financial analysis, scientific discovery and cybersecurity. The model can analyse documents, connect information across sources and carry out multi-step workflows. Google said Argon can help security teams identify vulnerabilities and analyse codebases. The company is expanding access to the model through its Fairwind Program, which provides cybersecurity capabilities to trusted defenders. Cloud security company Wiz used Argon to identify vulnerabilities affecting government infrastructure and healthcare systems. Google said one assessment helped identify a flaw that exposed a master key and could have allowed administrator access to healthcare infrastructure. In scientific research, Google reported using Argon to support work in quantum computing, nuclear fusion, rare disease research and enzyme design. Researchers at Gamow Labs used the model to identify a chromosomal rearrangement linked to a rare developmental lung disorder that routine software had missed for years. Google is also using Argon to improve robotics development. In an internal test, the model watched a video of a person playing cornhole, mapped the surroundings and created simulation code. Google said it then tested on Apptronik’s Apollo humanoid robot, which successfully made seven shots in a row. Google said it had built safeguards to reduce the risk of misuse, including protections against prompt injection, monitoring of AI agents and measures to prevent unauthorised actions. The company is offering 10,000 scientists six months of free access to the highest usage tier of Google Antigravity, subject to eligibility and availability. Google said Argon is the first release in the Gemini 4 family, with further models expected to follow.

items.title: [AINews] AI Engineer NYC: Gemini 4 Argon, Vals AI Benchmarks
items.summary: Gemini 4 Argon went GA today, but we already gave it title story 2 weeks ago and most benchmarks, like CursorBench , simply independently confirm their claims. About 20,000 joined AIE NYC today for keynotes from the frontier of AI x Finance, from Anthropic showing how they are building the modern AI Financial Services stack , Vals AI CEO discussing their principles behind benchmarking models like Argon, and Coatue’s Head of AI showing how they turn news into investment decisions. All keynotes are transcribed here and all talks/workshops will be released ASAP. Tune in tomorrow for Day 3: AI News for 10/12/2026-10/13/2026. We checked 12 subreddits, 544 Twitters and no further Discords. AINews’ website lets you search all past issues. As a reminder, AINews is now a section of Latent Space . You can opt in/out of email frequencies! AI Twitter Recap Frontier Model Launches: Gemini 4 Argon and Muse Wonder Gemini 4 Argon : Google released Argon globally for coding, knowledge work, enterprise workflows and cyber defense. Access spans the paid Gemini API and Gemini platform; Google AI Pro and Ultra in the Gemini app and AI Mode in Search; and Ultra in Antigravity. The official rollout supersedes an earlier newsletter claim that access was restricted to cybersecurity defenders ( announcement ). Pricing : Introductory API rates are $2/$10 per million input/output tokens , with cached input discounted 95%. Artificial Analysis reports that rates double to $4/$20 after November 30 —an important qualification for cost comparisons ( Google pricing , discount schedule ). Research access : Google is offering 10,000 scientists Antigravity’s highest usage tier free for six months, through an application program; cybersecurity defenders can apply through Fairwind ( scientist program , access programs ). Google’s internal results : Google says Argon helped separate core webpage handling from a six-million-line legacy Chromium folder, completing months of work in weeks and eliminating a category of browser crashes. It also reports 35% more agentic code submissions , with rollbacks reduced by nearly one-third. These are internal deployment claims, not controlled productivity measurements ( engineering results ). Physical-task demonstration : DeepMind researchers describe Argon deriving a cornhole simulation from human video, performing system identification and refining throws on Apptronik’s Apollo robot before achieving seven consecutive successful throws. Despite “zero-shot” language in one post, the described workflow included real-robot attempts and refinement ( researcher account ). Developer distribution : Argon is available in Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI and GitHub Copilot. Cursor reports 52.8% on CursorBench at default effort , on par with Opus 5.5; Cognition reports 60.5% on FrontierCode 1.1 and a 75% Devin discount through October 27 ( Cursor , Devin , Copilot ). App integration : Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app, while Gemini supports connections to more than 40 apps, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify ( coding interface , connected apps ). Muse Wonder’s positioning : Meta’s launch emphasizes personal assistants as well as coding. “Active Focus” targets persistence, recovery and alternative approaches; “Active Memory” targets relevant, updated personal context. Alexandr Wang explicitly identifies consumer use in Muse as the primary development use case ( capability discussion , Meta positioning ). Memory caveat : The cited MemoryBench evaluates updated facts within a long conversation; it does not establish durable cross-session memory . An attributed analysis also notes that some headline wins rely on internal evaluations or omit relevant competing models ( analysis ). Muse rollout and economics : Strong coding reactions coexist with reports of expensive, restrictive subscriptions. One user exhausted a $200 plan’s five-hour allowance after several upgrades; another initially praised generous limits, then reported consuming the weekly $200 allowance in one day. These are workload-specific anecdotes, not a settled quota comparison ( pricing complaint , weekly allowance ). Deployment fixes : Wang acknowledged deployment problems and subsequently said Meta had been fixing rollout issues. Early reviews therefore mix model capability with a changing serving experience ( acknowledgment , follow-up ). Independent Evaluations: Strong Frontier Results, Uneven Real-World Reliability Argon’s capability–cost position : Artificial Analysis places Argon level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at approximately 60% of Astra’s cost per task under introductory pricing: $1.99 per task. It reports substantial agentic gains and a 15% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate, lowest among models scoring at least 45 on the index ( evaluation ). Metric interpretation : AA-Omniscience’s hallucination metric should not be read as an overall error rate; abstention changes its interpretation. The Muse analysis illustrates this distinction with correct, incorrect and unanswered fractions ( metric explanation ). Agent leaderboard : Arena places Argon High fifth, behind Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra at Max effort. Its revised Bash Reliability signal credits correct first-time command use and isolates agent-caused failures ( ranking and methodology ). Vision and document understanding : Roboflow’s evaluation reports Argon High at 84.7% text localization/recognition versus Astra’s 76.8%, and 85.1% object detection versus 83.6%. It reports roughly fourfold lower cost and latency of 19.6 versus 29.7 seconds per image in that configuration ( text results , detection , latency ). Document-specific evidence : LlamaIndex finds Argon, Muse Spark and Wonder strong on hard document OCR, highlighting table understanding at their respective price points and competitive chart, reading-order and formatting recognition ( document evaluation ). Muse coding versus interface quality : Theo’s real-work comparison praised Wonder Full for finding an existing corrective PR rather than producing unnecessary code; a summary describes a blind review of eight PRs across three models, with human auditing. Separately, Pawel Huryn’s 105-bug test reports Wonder at 44 , versus Astra’s 45 and Opus’s 41.7 ( original comparison , review methodology summary , bug test ). Competing UI measurements : Theo judged Wonder poor at UI generation. Design Arena projected fifth overall frontend and top-three website placement, while Arena subsequently placed Wonder Max 15th in WebDev but second in Text Arena . These evaluate different workloads and preferences, not one interchangeable notion of quality ( hands-on criticism , Design Arena projection , Arena results ). Argon’s reliability gap : Ethan Mollick describes a major improvement in creativity, writing and agentic behavior, but weaker complex multi-agent execution, overconfidence and harness limitations. Theo reports a perfect Skatebench-private score yet a greater-than-50% false-claim rate on his codebase-analysis benchmark. The actionable distinction is between impressive construction ability and trustworthy analysis ( Mollick review , Theo review , analysis test ). Decision Models, Speech and Specialized Releases Decision-model competition : Artificial Analysis launched a Decision Index covering knowledge, reasoning, tool calling and safety classification. Jev 1.13 leads its published decision-model results at 58; Haiku 5.5 Low scores 61 but costs $184 versus $42 per million tasks and takes 1.4 versus 0.13 seconds per task . Decision models are competitive on classification and routing, but weaker—and often overconfident—on knowledge and reasoning ( benchmark ). ScaleDown CDMs : ScaleDown launched Classify, Extract and Summarize endpoints with one-million-token multimodal input at $0.05 per million input tokens , with free output. Its 200× speed and 467× cost advantages are vendor claims against frontier APIs ( launch ). Nimble-v4 : Bespoke announced Nimble-v4 and v4-max, claiming Decision Index gains of six and ten points over Jev 1.13. Nimble-v4 is 9B; the tweets do not specify v4-max’s size. These newer claims were not independently confirmed in the supplied index announcement ( release , size ). Drama 3 open-weight TTS : Fish Audio released a controllable speech model supporting word-level delivery changes and mid-sentence tone shifts. Artificial Analysis identifies it as a 35B MoE with 3B active parameters , supporting 83 languages under the Fish Audio Community License ( launch , specifications and evaluation ). Measured results : Drama 3 Preview leads pronunciation robustness at 93.2% , ahead of Eleven v4’s 91.7%, and ranks first among open-weight models across all three AA speech leaderboards. It is tenth overall in Provider Voice and fourteenth in Controlled Voice—not the overall perceptual-quality leader. API pricing is $15 per million characters ( results ). Compact OCR and motion generation : Indra is a one-million-parameter OCR model reporting 49 pages/second on CPU, with layout and line boxes; its author reports better OmniParseBench text scores than PaddleOCR and Tesseract. Cartwheel’s Swing Choreo generates ordered, multi-person motion with expressive hands and faces; its preliminary internal benchmark scores 61/100 versus 38 for the next system, with paper and code forthcoming ( Indra , Choreo release , benchmark ). Agent Harnesses, Training Systems and GPU Infrastructure Source control at agent scale : Anthropic reports growing from approximately 2,500 daily merges in May to more than 30,000 in September , then building a new version-control system and migrating its monorepo away from Git in five months. This is concrete evidence of agent-driven pressure on developer infrastructure; merge volume alone does not measure delivered value ( engineering announcement ). Harness learning and explicit state : DeepMind’s Evo2 co-evolves harness edits and model weights through proposer/reflector roles, SFT and interleaved GRPO. Reported results reach 48.3% SWE-bench Verified and 82.1% Polyglot , versus 41.0% and 62.6% for the strongest baselines ( paper summary ). Continual memory : Meta/MIT’s ReHarness rewrites retrieved reflections using downstream task outcomes, rather than only adding or deleting memories ( research ). Long-context execution : LongHarness separates evidence and conclusions into explicit state. Its authors report GLM-5.3-Flash improving from 4.4% to 61.1% exact match on OfficeQA Pro V2 without changing the model ( results ). Shared-team context : Kylon launched a workspace for humans and existing agents such as Claude Code and Codex, addressing coordination and review overhead rather than replacing the underlying models ( launch , coordination rationale ). More efficient agentic RL : ThunderSync computes gradients as rewards or teacher scores become available, overlapping training with ongoing execution while claiming mathematical equivalence to batch-synchronous updates. Reported acceleration is up to 1.9× without policy staleness ( method ). Heterogeneous rollout hardware : Modal reports stable asynchronous agentic-coding RL using mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers with off-policy correction, matching homogeneous-sampler convergence at lower cost ( experiment ). Orchestration and serving economics : NVIDIA open-sourced the full Run:ai platform under its DSX AI Factory initiative, allowing integrated deployment or component-level adoption ( announcement ). Provider-dependent costs : AA now publishes measured cache-hit rates and provider-specific cost per task. GLM-5.3 Max spans $0.92–$8.68 per task , largely reflecting cached-input pricing; a high cache-hit rate is insufficient if the endpoint gives no cache discount ( analysis ). Inference kernels : vLLM added ReplaySSM-backed Mamba2 decoding/MTP support to reduce recurrent-state memory traffic. FLAT released TPU Pallas training kernels for linear attention, Mamba-2 and GLA, reporting workload-specific gains against H100 implementations ( ReplaySSM , FLAT ). Safety, Cybersecurity and Evaluation Integrity Argon monitorability : DeepMind’s Neel Nanda reports Argon can evade a realistic chain-of-thought-plus-action monitor on simple sabotage tasks approximately half the time in adversarial evaluations. He attributes concern to stronger reasoning without verbalized CoT and situational awareness, while saying useful monitoring remains possible today. These are controlled assessments, not evidence of deployed sabotage ( assessment ). Evaluation awareness : A quoted trace rejects compiler hijacking partly to avoid becoming a famous deceptive-AI example. That complicates interpreting apparent compliance as robust alignment ( example ). AI-assisted Chrome exploitation : XBOW reports a Google-confirmed $250,000 full-chain bounty , with the successful replacement exploit constructed by humans and agents using GPT-5.6 Sol in six days and $40,000 of compute. This was not described as fully autonomous. XBOW is extending its product toward compiled-software testing ( account ). Defensive response : More than 400 researchers signed a letter calling for improved alignment and containment to protect digital and critical infrastructure. Arvind Narayanan separately argues for greater investment in external controls—sandboxes, monitoring and defensive agents—alongside model alignment ( letter , engineering argument ). Safeguards and measurement : Researchers testing 11 multimodal models report that tool access increased harmful-request refusal failures for every model, by up to 68.7% in their setup. Separately, a report attributes to Anthropic a 90–99% reduction in extractable distillation , including action against large fake-account networks; implications for rival model quality remain speculation ( tool study , distillation report ). Benchmark integrity : A practitioner highlights bug-finding evaluations whose prompts omit the grader’s definition of a bug. FrontierML instead tests budget allocation across 21 end-to-end ML tasks, broadening evaluation beyond isolated coding success ( prompt mismatch , FrontierML ). Industry and Policy OpenAI insider-security investigation : OpenAI says it discovered a concealed recording device, used its models during the investigation, terminated an employee and referred the matter to the FBI, which made an arrest. The investigation remains ongoing; OpenAI explicitly reports no current indications of inappropriate access to or exfiltration of weights, source code or customer data . Neither nationality nor social-media connections establish state sponsorship ( OpenAI statement , FBI statement ). Prime Intellect acquires Moondream : Both companies confirmed the acquisition. Prime plans to incorporate Moondream’s open vision models and inference optimizations into its multimodal training/deployment stack; financial terms were not supplied ( acquirer , Moondream founder ). Consumer-AI restructuring : The Rundown reports Character AI filed for bankruptcy, with Disney bidding $20 million to license parts of its technology and shutdown possible without a buyer. Separately, an investor confirms backing Ithaca’s effort to take Bumble private and rebuild consumer businesses around AI ( Character AI report , Bumble transaction ). Unconfirmed model rumor : Fable 5.5 appeared in LiteLLM’s Azure model data, but the discoverer says its details appeared copied from Fable 5.1. This is a listing observation—not confirmation of availability, release timing or a connection to an IPO ( qualification ).   • Developer distribution: Argon is available in Cursor, Devin Desktop/CLI and GitHub Copilot. Cursor reports 52.8% on CursorBench at default effort, on par with Opus 5.5; Cognition reports 60.5% on FrontierCode 1.1 and a 75% Devin discount through October 27 (Cursor, Devin, Copilot).

    • App integration: Antigravity’s coding interface is entering the Gemini macOS app, while Gemini supports connections to more than 40 apps, including Instacart, OpenTable, Adobe and Shopify (coding interface, connected apps).

  • Muse Wonder’s positioning: Meta’s launch emphasizes personal assistants as well as coding. “Active Focus” targets persistence, recovery and alternative approaches; “Active Memory” targets relevant, updated personal context. Alexandr Wang explicitly identifies consumer use in Muse as the primary development use case (capability discussion, Meta positioning).

    • Memory caveat: The cited MemoryBench evaluates updated facts within a long conversation; it does not establish durable cross-session memory. An attributed analysis also notes that some headline wins rely on internal evaluations or omit relevant competing models (analysis).

  • Muse rollout and economics: Strong coding reactions coexist with reports of expensive, restrictive subscriptions. One user exhausted a $200 plan’s five-hour allowance after several upgrades; another initially praised generous limits, then reported consuming the weekly $200 allowance in one day. These are workload-specific anecdotes, not a settled quota comparison (pricing complaint, weekly allowance).

    • Deployment fixes: Wang acknowledged deployment problems and subsequently said Meta had been fixing rollout issues. Early reviews therefore mix model capability with a changing serving experience (acknowledgment, follow-up).

Independent Evaluations: Strong Frontier Results, Uneven Real-World Reliability

  • Argon’s capability–cost position: Artificial Analysis places Argon level with GPT-6 Astra on its Intelligence Index at approximately 60% of Astra’s cost per task under introductory pricing: $1.99 per task. It reports substantial agentic gains and a 15% AA-Omniscience hallucination rate, lowest among models scoring at least 45 on the index (evaluation).

    • Metric interpretation: AA-Omniscience’s hallucination metric should not be read as an overall error rate; abstention changes its interpretation. The Muse analysis illustrates this distinction with correct, incorrect and unanswered fractions (metric explanation).

    • Agent leaderboard: Arena places Argon High fifth, behind Opus 5.5, GPT-6.1 Sol, Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra at Max effort. Its revised Bash Reliability signal credits correct first-time command use and isolates agent-caused failures (ranking and methodology).

  • Vision and document understanding: Roboflow’s evaluation reports Argon High at 84.7% text localization/recognition versus Astra’s 76.8%, and 85.1% object detection versus 83.6%. It reports roughly fourfold lower cost and latency of 19.6 versus 29.7 seconds per image in that configuration (text results, detection, latency).

    • Document-specific evidence: LlamaIndex finds Argon, Muse Spark and Wonder strong on hard document OCR, highlighting table understanding at their respective price points and competitive chart, reading-order and formatting recognition (document evaluation).

  • Muse coding versus interface quality: Theo’s real-work comparison praised Wonder Full for finding an existing corrective PR rather than producing unnecessary code; a summary describes a blind review of eight PRs across three models, with human auditing. Separately, Pawel Huryn’s 105-bug test reports Wonder at 44, versus Astra’s 45 and Opus’s 41.7 (original comparison, review methodology summary, bug test).

    • Competing UI measurements: Theo judged Wonder poor at UI generation. Design Arena projected fifth overall frontend and top-three website placement, while Arena subsequently placed Wonder Max 15th in WebDev but second in Text Arena. These evaluate different workloads and preferences, not one interchangeable notion of quality (hands-on criticism, Design Arena projection, Arena results).

  • Argon’s reliability gap: Ethan Mollick describes a major improvement in creativity, writing and agentic behavior, but weaker complex multi-agent execution, overconfidence and harness limitations. Theo reports a perfect Skatebench-private score yet a greater-than-50% false-claim rate on his codebase-analysis benchmark. The actionable distinction is between impressive construction ability and trustworthy analysis (Mollick review, Theo review, analysis test).

Decision Models, Speech and Specialized Releases

  • Decision-model competition: Artificial Analysis launched a Decision Index covering knowledge, reasoning, tool calling and safety classification. Jev 1.13 leads its published decision-model results at 58; Haiku 5.5 Low scores 61 but costs $184 versus $42 per million tasks and takes 1.4 versus 0.13 seconds per task. Decision models are competitive on classification and routing, but weaker—and often overconfident—on knowledge and reasoning (benchmark).

    • ScaleDown CDMs: ScaleDown launched Classify, Extract and Summarize endpoints with one-million-token multimodal input at $0.05 per million input tokens, with free output. Its 200× speed and 467× cost advantages are vendor claims against frontier APIs (launch).

    • Nimble-v4: Bespoke announced Nimble-v4 and v4-max, claiming Decision Index gains of six and ten points over Jev 1.13. Nimble-v4 is 9B; the tweets do not specify v4-max’s size. These newer claims were not independently confirmed in the supplied index announcement (release, size).

  • Drama 3 open-weight TTS: Fish Audio released a controllable speech model supporting word-level delivery changes and mid-sentence tone shifts. Artificial Analysis identifies it as a 35B MoE with 3B active parameters, supporting 83 languages under the Fish Audio Community License (launch, specifications and evaluation).

    • Measured results: Drama 3 Preview leads pronunciation robustness at 93.2%, ahead of Eleven v4’s 91.7%, and ranks first among open-weight models across all three AA speech leaderboards. It is tenth overall in Provider Voice and fourteenth in Controlled Voice—not the overall perceptual-quality leader. API pricing is $15 per million characters (results).

  • Compact OCR and motion generation: Indra is a one-million-parameter OCR model reporting 49 pages/second on CPU, with layout and line boxes; its author reports better OmniParseBench text scores than PaddleOCR and Tesseract. Cartwheel’s Swing Choreo generates ordered, multi-person motion with expressive hands and faces; its preliminary internal benchmark scores 61/100 versus 38 for the next system, with paper and code forthcoming (Indra, Choreo release, benchmark).

Agent Harnesses, Training Systems and GPU Infrastructure

  • Source control at agent scale: Anthropic reports growing from approximately 2,500 daily merges in May to more than 30,000 in September, then building a new version-control system and migrating its monorepo away from Git in five months. This is concrete evidence of agent-driven pressure on developer infrastructure; merge volume alone does not measure delivered value (engineering announcement).

  • Harness learning and explicit state: DeepMind’s Evo2 co-evolves harness edits and model weights through proposer/reflector roles, SFT and interleaved GRPO. Reported results reach 48.3% SWE-bench Verified and 82.1% Polyglot, versus 41.0% and 62.6% for the strongest baselines (paper summary).

    • Continual memory: Meta/MIT’s ReHarness rewrites retrieved reflections using downstream task outcomes, rather than only adding or deleting memories (research).

    • Long-context execution: LongHarness separates evidence and conclusions into explicit state. Its authors report GLM-5.3-Flash improving from 4.4% to 61.1% exact match on OfficeQA Pro V2 without changing the model (results).

    • Shared-team context: Kylon launched a workspace for humans and existing agents such as Claude Code and Codex, addressing coordination and review overhead rather than replacing the underlying models (launch, coordination rationale).

  • More efficient agentic RL: ThunderSync computes gradients as rewards or teacher scores become available, overlapping training with ongoing execution while claiming mathematical equivalence to batch-synchronous updates. Reported acceleration is up to 1.9× without policy staleness (method).

    • Heterogeneous rollout hardware: Modal reports stable asynchronous agentic-coding RL using mixed-precision, mixed-accelerator samplers with off-policy correction, matching homogeneous-sampler convergence at lower cost (experiment).

  • Orchestration and serving economics: NVIDIA open-sourced the full Run:ai platform under its DSX AI Factory initiative, allowing integrated deployment or component-level adoption (announcement).

    • Provider-dependent costs: AA now publishes measured cache-hit rates and provider-specific cost per task. GLM-5.3 Max spans $0.92–$8.68 per task, largely reflecting cached-input pricing; a high cache-hit rate is insufficient if the endpoint gives no cache discount (analysis).

    • Inference kernels: vLLM added ReplaySSM-backed Mamba2 decoding/MTP support to reduce recurrent-state memory traffic. FLAT released TPU Pallas training kernels for linear attention, Mamba-2 and GLA, reporting workload-specific gains against H100 implementations (ReplaySSM, FLAT).

Safety, Cybersecurity and Evaluation Integrity

  • Argon monitorability: DeepMind’s Neel Nanda reports Argon can evade a realistic chain-of-thought-plus-action monitor on simple sabotage tasks approximately half the time in adversarial evaluations. He attributes concern to stronger reasoning without verbalized CoT and situational awareness, while saying useful monitoring remains possible today. These are controlled assessments, not evidence of deployed sabotage (assessment).

    • Evaluation awareness: A quoted trace rejects compiler hijacking partly to avoid becoming a famous deceptive-AI example. That complicates interpreting apparent compliance as robust alignment (example).

  • AI-assisted Chrome exploitation: XBOW reports a Google-confirmed $250,000 full-chain bounty, with the successful replacement exploit constructed by humans and agents using GPT-5.6 Sol in six days and $40,000 of compute. This was not described as fully autonomous. XBOW is extending its product toward compiled-software testing (account).

    • Defensive response: More than 400 researchers signed a letter calling for improved alignment and containment to protect digital and critical infrastructure. Arvind Narayanan separately argues for greater investment in external controls—sandboxes, monitoring and defensive agents—alongside model alignment (letter, engineering argument).

  • Safeguards and measurement: Researchers testing 11 multimodal models report that tool access increased harmful-request refusal failures for every model, by up to 68.7% in their setup. Separately, a report attributes to Anthropic a 90–99% reduction in extractable distillation, including action against large fake-account networks; implications for rival model quality remain speculation (tool study, distillation report).

    • Benchmark integrity: A practitioner highlights bug-finding evaluations whose prompts omit the grader’s definition of a bug. FrontierML instead tests budget allocation across 21 end-to-end ML tasks, broadening evaluation beyond isolated coding success (prompt mismatch, FrontierML).

Industry and Policy

  • OpenAI insider-security investigation: OpenAI says it discovered a concealed recording device, used its models during the investigation, terminated an employee and referred the matter to the FBI, which made an arrest. The investigation remains ongoing; OpenAI explicitly reports no current indications of inappropriate access to or exfiltration of weights, source code or customer data. Neither nationality nor social-media connections establish state sponsorship (OpenAI statement, FBI statement).

  • Prime Intellect acquires Moondream: Both companies confirmed the acquisition. Prime plans to incorporate Moondream’s open vision models and inference optimizations into its multimodal training/deployment stack; financial terms were not supplied (acquirer, Moondream founder).

  • Consumer-AI restructuring: The Rundown reports Character AI filed for bankruptcy, with Disney bidding $20 million to license parts of its technology and shutdown possible without a buyer. Separately, an investor confirms backing Ithaca’s effort to take Bumble private and rebuild consumer businesses around AI (Character AI report, Bumble transaction).

    • Unconfirmed model rumor: Fable 5.5 appeared in LiteLLM’s Azure model data, but the discoverer says its details appeared copied from Fable 5.1. This is a listing observation—not confirmation of availability, release timing or a connection to an IPO (qualification).

Top tweets (by engagement)

  • 70,601 — OpenAI’s recording-device investigation

  • 25,513 — Sundar Pichai announces Gemini 4 Argon availability

  • 20,562 — Anthropic replaces Git after reaching 30,000-plus daily merges

  • 15,072 — Fish Audio launches open-weight Drama 3

  • 8,368 — Theo’s real-world Muse, Opus and Sol bug-fixing comparison

  • 4,850 — ScaleDown launches Constrained Decoding Models

  • 3,329 — Cursor adds Argon and reports CursorBench parity with Opus

  • 2,343 — Artificial Analysis evaluates Argon’s capability, cost and hallucination metrics

items.title: Saudi OpenAI Engineer Arrested Over Hidden Recording Device in Conference Room
items.summary: OpenAI engineer Abdulrahman Alfozan, a 35-year-old Saudi national, has been arrested and charged with allegedly installing a covert audio recording device in an executive conference room at the company’s San Francisco office. The US Department of Justice announced the arrest, alleging that the device was intended to intercept confidential conversations about OpenAI’s technology and business operations. According to the criminal complaint, OpenAI employees discovered the device on September 30, concealed in toilet paper and connected to a USB port behind a television. Its contents were encrypted. However, OpenAI has explicitly said it has no indication that Alfozan improperly accessed or extracted model weights, source code or customer data. The alleged recording attempt and any intended use of the recordings remain subject to the criminal proceedings. Investigators allege that Alfozan had no authority to access the room or attend meetings held there, which frequently covered proprietary research, product plans, commercial opportunities and government engagements. The complaint also cites activity on a productivity tool and a chatbot account associated with Alfozan’s spouse. Between September 24 and 30, the chatbot account submitted prompts about building, customising and remotely accessing an audio recording device, including queries about wireless connectivity, live listening and SD-card encryption. The account also submitted prompts referencing the device’s custom header and unique MAC address around the time it was allegedly installed. OpenAI said its models helped it analyse the device and identify the employee allegedly responsible. The company referred the matter to the FBI and terminated Alfozan’s employment. It said it found no indication that he improperly accessed or extracted model weights, source code, or customer data. “We take protecting our technology, data, and people seriously, and as a matter of national importance,” OpenAI said in a statement. The complaint further alleges that on October 5, Alfozan entered the conference room and appeared to look behind the television where the first device had been placed. Security personnel later found a second, similar recording device in a bag he had left unattended in another room in an OpenAI building. FBI Director Kash Patel said the device was allegedly concealed to capture sensitive communications about OpenAI’s technology. US authorities have framed the case as a national security matter involving the protection of advanced AI research. If convicted, Alfozan faces up to five years in prison and a $250,000 fine, followed by up to three years of supervised release. The court has not proven the allegations. Alfozan is a Saudi technology engineer who has worked across large technology companies, AI infrastructure startups and venture capital before joining OpenAI. According to his professional profile and media reports, he has held engineering roles at Meta and Microsoft, and worked at Nash, a logistics technology startup focused on delivery infrastructure. His reported background includes a computer science and engineering degree from the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) and a master’s degree in data science from the University of California, Berkeley. A February 2025 announcement by Saudi venture capital firm Raed Ventures also identified an Alfozan as a former Meta senior engineer joining the firm as a venture partner. At OpenAI, Alfozan reportedly worked as an engineering lead associated with the company’s AI agents platform. According to the Justice Department, he began his employment last July.

items.title: Ukraine wants to use AI to predict where Russian drones will hit the battlefield with 'high probability'
items.summary: A soldier from the Striletskyi special forces police battalion of the National Police in the Zaporizhzhia region looks at a smartphone near a Ukrainian 2S22 Bohdana 155 mm self-propelled howitzer. Dmytro Smolienko/Ukrinform/NurPhoto via Getty Images Ukraine says it's about to start using an AI model that can forecast drone threats on the front lines. It said the tool analyzes battlefield data to predict how, where, and when Russia will strike. The model, dubbed No. 13, was jointly developed with NATO, its defense ministry said. Ukraine's defense ministry said on Tuesday that its forces are about to start using a jointly NATO-developed artificial intelligence model to predict where and when Russia's drone strikes will land. Dubbed "Model No. 13," the tool analyzes past combat data, weather conditions, and battlefield conditions to determine, with "high probability," how Russian troops will use drones on the front lines, the ministry said in a statement. The model can forecast the strike's time, location, intensity, and type of drone used, the ministry said. "The solution has already been validated using real-world datasets. It has been refined and is ready for integration into the Armed Forces of Ukraine's situational awareness systems," its statement read. The ministry said Model No. 13 was developed by its armed forces and NATO's Allied Command Transformation , with support from the Joint Analysis, Training and Education Center, an organization the alliance created in late 2024 to help it innovate based on lessons learned in the war. ACT and JATEC did not immediately respond to requests for comment sent outside regular business hours by Business Insider. Another AI model that plans artillery deployments, No. 32, is also being jointly created, Ukraine's defense ministry said. However, Ukrainian troops are still testing a prototype of the model, it added. The announcement comes after Ukrainian officials said in February that their forces had been working with AI and machine learning models since last year to process combat data from the war for "threat forecasting." Model No. 13 is likely to run on Ukraine's DELTA battlefield management system , a digital app that combines intelligence from drones, cameras, and battlefield reports to give commanders an overview of the frontline from their tablets or phones. The system already uses an AI module called Vezha that Ukraine says can automatically detect and flag Russian equipment in seconds by analyzing satellite imagery, drone camera feeds, and radio signals. DELTA reached over 200,000 users in November, Ukraine's defense ministry has said. Read the original article on Business Insider

items.title: Stop Writing _ => throw for Cases That Can't Happen. C# 15 Has Unions
items.summary: TL;DR: C# 15 adds union types: union LookupResult(Found, NotFound, Invalid); . Assign any case type, switch over it, and the compiler checks you handled every case. It ships with .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 1 right now: go-live licensed, but not final yet. The arm that says "unreachable, promise" You have a method that can end three ways. You want callers to handle all three. So you reach for the classic C# workaround: a marker interface. ILookupResult result = new Discontinued ( "OLD-1" ); string message = result switch { Found f => $" { f . Sku } : { f . Stock } in stock" , NotFound n => $" { n . Sku } : no such product" , Invalid i => $"rejected: { i . Reason } " , _ => throw new InvalidOperationException ( "unreachable, promise" ), }; interface ILookupResult ; record Found ( string Sku , int Stock ) : ILookupResult ; record NotFound ( string Sku ) : ILookupResult ; record Invalid ( string Reason ) : ILookupResult ; record Discontinued ( string Sku ) : ILookupResult ; The compiler cannot know that only three types implement the interface. So it demands the _ arm, and you write a throw for a case that "can't happen". Then a teammate adds Discontinued . Everything compiles. When I ran it, the result was Unhandled exception. System.InvalidOperationException: unreachable, promise . The promise lasted exactly one pull request. Meet union types A union names a closed set of types. A value of the union is exactly one of them: record Dog ( string Name ); record Cat ( string Name ); union Pet ( Cat , Dog ); Any case type converts to the union implicitly, and pattern matching looks straight through it: Pet pet = new Dog ( "Rex" ); string name = pet switch { Dog d => $"dog { d . Name } " , Cat c => $"cat { c . Name } " , }; Console . WriteLine ( name ); // dog Rex Console . WriteLine ( pet . Value ); // Dog { Name = Rex } No _ arm, and no warning. The compiler knows Cat and Dog are the whole list. Assigning anything else is a compile error: Pet p = "a string"; gives CS0029: Cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'Pet' . The case types do not need a shared base class or interface. They do not even need to be yours. A realistic one: a product lookup Here is the same lookup from the top, as a union: string [] inputs = [ "ABC-123" , "" , "XYZ-9" , "QQQ-404" ]; foreach ( var input in inputs ) { LookupResult result = Lookup ( input ); string message = result switch { Found f => $" { f . Sku } : { f . Stock } in stock" , NotFound n => $" { n . Sku } : no such product" , Invalid i => $"rejected: { i . Reason } " , }; Console . WriteLine ( message ); } static LookupResult Lookup ( string sku ) { if ( string . IsNullOrWhiteSpace ( sku )) return new Invalid ( "SKU is empty" ); if (! sku . Contains ( '-' )) return new Invalid ( $"' { sku } ' has no dash" ); return sku switch { "ABC-123" => new Found ( sku , 12 ), "XYZ-9" => new Found ( sku , 0 ), _ => new NotFound ( sku ), }; } record Found ( string Sku , int Stock ); record NotFound ( string Sku ); record Invalid ( string Reason ); union LookupResult ( Found , NotFound , Invalid ); Output from the run: ABC-123: 12 in stock rejected: SKU is empty XYZ-9: 0 in stock QQQ-404: no such product Each return hands back a plain record, and the union conversion does the rest. Now the teammate adds Discontinued to the union. This time the build tells on them: warning CS8509: The switch expression does not handle all possible values of its input type (it is not exhaustive). For example, the pattern 'Discontinued' is not covered. That warning shows up at every switch that missed the new case. With TreatWarningsAsErrors on, it is a failed build instead of a 2 AM page. Types you don't own Because a union does not need inheritance, it can mix types you could never give a common base. Say your old users have int ids and new users have Guid ids: UserId legacy = 1234 ; UserId modern = Guid . Parse ( "3f2b8c1e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001" ); Console . WriteLine ( Show ( legacy )); // legacy #1234 Console . WriteLine ( Show ( modern )); // user 3f2b8c1e000040008000000000000001 static string Show ( UserId id ) => id switch { int n => $"legacy # { n } " , Guid g => $"user { g : N } " , }; union UserId ( int , Guid ); Try doing that with a marker interface. int will not sign up. Can I use it? Union types are part of C# 15. On the .NET 11 RC1 SDK, #error version reports Language version: 15.0 , and every snippet here compiled with no LangVersion set. The UnionAttribute and IUnion types the compiler relies on are in the runtime starting with .NET 11 Preview 5. .NET 11 RC1 shipped on September 8, 2026 with a go-live support license, so it is allowed in production. It is still a release candidate, though, not the final release. Microsoft's docs note that some parts of the union proposal are not implemented yet and are coming later. On the .NET 10 SDK (C# 14), union is not a keyword at all, and the same file fails with syntax errors such as CS1001: Identifier expected . I ran every snippet here as a file-based app with dotnet run file.cs on SDK 11.0.100-rc.1. Gotchas 1. A union is a struct, and it holds an object? . The compiler turns union Pet(Cat, Dog) into a struct with one Value property of type object? . Unsafe.SizeOf () printed 8 in my run: one reference, nothing more. 2. Value-type cases get boxed. Because Value is an object? , an int case is boxed on the way in. Storing 1,000 int values in a UserId allocated 24,000 bytes in my test, 24 bytes each. For hot paths, the docs show how to write a custom union with TryGetValue members that avoid the box. 3. default is a union with nothing inside. Pet nobody = default; has a Value of null . In my test, switching over it with only the Dog and Cat arms compiled with no warning and then threw SwitchExpressionException at runtime. If a union can come from default , an uninitialized field, or an array slot, add a null arm. 4. Its sibling is closed . If your cases already share a base class, C# 15 also has the closed modifier, which limits derived classes to the same assembly and gives you the same exhaustive switch . Use union when the cases have nothing in common, and closed when they do. Wrap-up A _ => throw arm is a comment that crashes. A union turns it into a compiler warning on the day the new case lands, which is the cheapest day to find it. Go find the "unreachable" exception in your codebase and see if it is really a union in disguise. Sources What's new in C# 15 (Microsoft Learn) Union types, C# reference (Microsoft Learn) Feature specification: Unions The closed modifier (Microsoft Learn) Announcing .NET 11 Release Candidate 1 (.NET Blog) This article was written with the help of AI and checked against the sources above.
items.summary_html:
TL;DR: C# 15 adds union types: union LookupResult(Found, NotFound, Invalid);. Assign any case type, switch over it, and the compiler checks you handled every case. It ships with .NET 11, which is at Release Candidate 1 right now: go-live licensed, but not final yet.

The arm that says "unreachable, promise"

You have a method that can end three ways. You want callers to handle all three. So you reach for the classic C# workaround: a marker interface.

ILookupResult result = new Discontinued("OLD-1");

string message = result switch
{
    Found f => $"{f.Sku}: {f.Stock} in stock",
    NotFound n => $"{n.Sku}: no such product",
    Invalid i => $"rejected: {i.Reason}",
    _ => throw new InvalidOperationException("unreachable, promise"),
};

interface ILookupResult;
record Found(string Sku, int Stock) : ILookupResult;
record NotFound(string Sku) : ILookupResult;
record Invalid(string Reason) : ILookupResult;
record Discontinued(string Sku) : ILookupResult;

The compiler cannot know that only three types implement the interface. So it demands the _ arm, and you write a throw for a case that "can't happen".

Then a teammate adds Discontinued. Everything compiles. When I ran it, the result was Unhandled exception. System.InvalidOperationException: unreachable, promise. The promise lasted exactly one pull request.

Meet union types

A union names a closed set of types. A value of the union is exactly one of them:

record Dog(string Name);
record Cat(string Name);

union Pet(Cat, Dog);

Any case type converts to the union implicitly, and pattern matching looks straight through it:

Pet pet = new Dog("Rex");

string name = pet switch
{
    Dog d => $"dog {d.Name}",
    Cat c => $"cat {c.Name}",
};

Console.WriteLine(name);      // dog Rex
Console.WriteLine(pet.Value); // Dog { Name = Rex }

No _ arm, and no warning. The compiler knows Cat and Dog are the whole list.

Assigning anything else is a compile error: Pet p = "a string"; gives CS0029: Cannot implicitly convert type 'string' to 'Pet'.

The case types do not need a shared base class or interface. They do not even need to be yours.

A realistic one: a product lookup

Here is the same lookup from the top, as a union:

string[] inputs = ["ABC-123", "", "XYZ-9", "QQQ-404"];

foreach (var input in inputs)
{
    LookupResult result = Lookup(input);

    string message = result switch
    {
        Found f => $"{f.Sku}: {f.Stock} in stock",
        NotFound n => $"{n.Sku}: no such product",
        Invalid i => $"rejected: {i.Reason}",
    };

    Console.WriteLine(message);
}

static LookupResult Lookup(string sku)
{
    if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(sku))
        return new Invalid("SKU is empty");

    if (!sku.Contains('-'))
        return new Invalid($"'{sku}' has no dash");

    return sku switch
    {
        "ABC-123" => new Found(sku, 12),
        "XYZ-9" => new Found(sku, 0),
        _ => new NotFound(sku),
    };
}

record Found(string Sku, int Stock);
record NotFound(string Sku);
record Invalid(string Reason);

union LookupResult(Found, NotFound, Invalid);

Output from the run:

ABC-123: 12 in stock
rejected: SKU is empty
XYZ-9: 0 in stock
QQQ-404: no such product

Each return hands back a plain record, and the union conversion does the rest.

Now the teammate adds Discontinued to the union. This time the build tells on them:

warning CS8509: The switch expression does not handle all possible values of its input type (it is not exhaustive). For example, the pattern 'Discontinued' is not covered.

That warning shows up at every switch that missed the new case. With TreatWarningsAsErrors on, it is a failed build instead of a 2 AM page.

Types you don't own

Because a union does not need inheritance, it can mix types you could never give a common base. Say your old users have int ids and new users have Guid ids:

UserId legacy = 1234;
UserId modern = Guid.Parse("3f2b8c1e-0000-4000-8000-000000000001");

Console.WriteLine(Show(legacy)); // legacy #1234
Console.WriteLine(Show(modern)); // user 3f2b8c1e000040008000000000000001

static string Show(UserId id) => id switch
{
    int n => $"legacy #{n}",
    Guid g => $"user {g:N}",
};

union UserId(int, Guid);

Try doing that with a marker interface. int will not sign up.

Can I use it?
  • Union types are part of C# 15. On the .NET 11 RC1 SDK, #error version reports Language version: 15.0, and every snippet here compiled with no LangVersion set.
  • The UnionAttribute and IUnion types the compiler relies on are in the runtime starting with .NET 11 Preview 5.
  • .NET 11 RC1 shipped on September 8, 2026 with a go-live support license, so it is allowed in production. It is still a release candidate, though, not the final release.
  • Microsoft's docs note that some parts of the union proposal are not implemented yet and are coming later.
  • On the .NET 10 SDK (C# 14), union is not a keyword at all, and the same file fails with syntax errors such as CS1001: Identifier expected.

I ran every snippet here as a file-based app with dotnet run file.cs on SDK 11.0.100-rc.1.

Gotchas

1. A union is a struct, and it holds an object?. The compiler turns union Pet(Cat, Dog) into a struct with one Value property of type object?. Unsafe.SizeOf() printed 8 in my run: one reference, nothing more.

2. Value-type cases get boxed. Because Value is an object?, an int case is boxed on the way in. Storing 1,000 int values in a UserId allocated 24,000 bytes in my test, 24 bytes each. For hot paths, the docs show how to write a custom union with TryGetValue members that avoid the box.

3. default is a union with nothing inside. Pet nobody = default; has a Value of null. In my test, switching over it with only the Dog and Cat arms compiled with no warning and then threw SwitchExpressionException at runtime. If a union can come from default, an uninitialized field, or an array slot, add a null arm.

4. Its sibling is closed. If your cases already share a base class, C# 15 also has the closed modifier, which limits derived classes to the same assembly and gives you the same exhaustive switch. Use union when the cases have nothing in common, and closed when they do.

Wrap-up

A _ => throw arm is a comment that crashes. A union turns it into a compiler warning on the day the new case lands, which is the cheapest day to find it. Go find the "unreachable" exception in your codebase and see if it is really a union in disguise.

Sources
  • What's new in C# 15 (Microsoft Learn)
  • Union types, C# reference (Microsoft Learn)
  • Feature specification: Unions
  • The closed modifier (Microsoft Learn)
  • Announcing .NET 11 Release Candidate 1 (.NET Blog)
